modules.title: Starting Work
modules.purpose: Talk about yourself at work — your background, your role and what you do — clearly enough to feel confident in your first real conversations.

lessons.title: Understanding What "Professional" Means at Work
lessons.objectives_html:
• Describe in simple English what "being professional" looks like in three everyday actions.
  • Distinguish a professional response from an unprofessional one when shown two examples.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

One week before his first day, Arif gets a short call from Sadia Chowdhury in HR. She isn't calling with paperwork this time — she wants to explain, in plain terms, what "being professional" actually means at this company, before he ever walks through the door.

Key workplace lesson

"Be professional" is one of the most common pieces of advice a new employee hears — and one of the vaguest, until someone breaks it into concrete actions. At its simplest, it means three things: be on time, listen carefully, and speak to people with respect. Everything else in this course builds on that foundation.

Listen & Read
A phone call, one week before Arif's first day. Sadia Chowdhury, from HR, is calling to prepare him for what's ahead.
Sadia: Hi Arif, this is Sadia from HR — congratulations again on the offer! I just wanted to have a short chat before your first day.
Arif: Thank you so much! I'm really looking forward to it.
Sadia: Wonderful. Before you start, I just want to explain what "being professional" means here at the company — it's simple, but it matters a lot.
Arif: Of course, I'd like to know.
Sadia: Mainly three things: be on time, listen carefully when someone explains something, and always speak to people — colleagues and guests — with respect.
Arif: That makes sense. So punctuality, listening, and respect.
Sadia: Exactly. If you keep those three in mind, you'll already be seen as a professional, even on day one.
Arif: Thank you, I'll keep that in mind.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"I just wanted to..." Explaining the purpose of a call or short meeting Opening a short, purposeful conversation "I just wanted to have a short chat before your first day." Warm, not overly formal
"Being professional means..." Defining or explaining a concept in plain terms Explaining an expectation or idea clearly "Being professional here mainly means three things..." Neutral, clear, unpretentious
"That makes sense." Acknowledging that you understood an explanation Any time someone explains something to you "That makes sense. So punctuality, listening, and respect." Engaged, not just a filler word
"I'll keep that in mind." Committing to remember and follow advice Closing out advice you plan to actually use "Thank you, I'll keep that in mind." Sincere, brief
"Congratulations on the offer!" A warm opening line to someone who just got a job Starting a conversation with a new hire "Hi Arif, congratulations again on the offer!" Warm, welcoming

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0001professional adj.Doing your job the right way — on time, careful, respectfulপেশাদারपेशेवरPlease keep your tone professional when you write to a client.
V-0002punctual adj.On time, not lateসময়নিষ্ঠसमय का पाबंदBeing punctual on your first day makes a strong first impression.
V-0003respectful adj.Polite and considerate toward othersশ্রদ্ধাশীলआदरपूर्णA respectful tone helps even a difficult conversation go better.
V-0004expectation n.What people expect you to doপ্রত্যাশাअपेक्षाIt's normal to ask your supervisor to clarify their expectations.
V-0005behavior n.How someone actsআচরণव्यवहारProfessional behavior includes small things like greeting people warmly.
V-0006workplace culture n. phraseThe "personality" of a workplace — how people usually act and treat each otherকর্মক্ষেত্রের সংস্কৃতিकार्यस्थल संस्कृतिIt takes a few weeks to really understand a new workplace's culture.

Note: professional works two ways — as an adjective describing behavior ("be professional," "a professional attitude") and as a noun with an article, meaning a qualified, skilled person ("a professional," "she's a real professional"). Using one form when you mean the other is MIS-0002.

Grammar in context

Simple present tense for stating ongoing expectations and habits ("We start at 9", "Being professional means being on time"). You will see it throughout the dialogue and the practice.

Common mistake · MIS-0002
⚠️ Unclear: I want to become professional.
✅ About behavior: I want to become more professional. / I want to be more professional at work.
✅ About a person with skills or training: I want to become a professional in this field.
"I want to become professional" is not ungrammatical, but at work it is unclear. Professional is an adjective when it describes behavior (be professional, more professional) and a countable noun when it means a trained, skilled person (a professional). With the adjective, "more professional" sounds natural because professional behavior is a matter of degree; with the noun, you need the article "a". (In sport and the arts, "become / turn professional" has a third meaning: to start being paid for it.) Choose the form that matches what you mean.

Pronunciation

  • Word stress: proFESsional and resPECTful are stressed on the second syllable; PUNCtual is stressed on the first.
  • Sentence stress in the lesson's key sentence: "Be on TIME, LISten carefully, and speak with resPECT" — the three key actions carry the stress, not the connecting words.
  • Avoid a flat, list-like reading of the three actions — natural speech gives each one a small rise before the next, and a fall on the last.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Just don't be weird, and you'll be fine." (vague, and too casual for an HR orientation call)
  • ❌ Too formal/textbook: "One must consistently demonstrate exemplary conduct in accordance with organizational protocols." (technically fine, but stiff and unnatural — nobody actually talks like this)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "Being professional here mainly means three things: be on time, listen carefully, and always speak with respect." (clear, warm, and genuinely useful)

Bengali support

"Workplace culture" (V-0006) is a concept many learners over-translate word-for-word, which can make it sound distant or academic in Bengali. It's simpler than it sounds: it just means the shared, mostly unwritten habits of how people treat each other at a particular workplace — something you notice within your first few weeks, not something you need to memorize a definition for.

Hindi support

Same idea for "workplace culture" in Hindi: a literal translation can sound overly formal. It's best understood as "how things are usually done here" — through observation, not through a fixed rule list.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: Being professional here also means being well-groomed and ready before your shift starts — guests notice appearance as much as words.
  • Healthcare: Being professional here includes keeping patient information confidential, even in casual conversation with colleagues.
  • Banking: Being professional here means double-checking details out loud before confirming a transaction — precision is part of respect here.
  • IT: Being professional here often means responding to messages within a reasonable time, even a quick "got it, will check" counts.
  • Retail: Being professional here means staying polite and patient with customers even when the shop floor is busy or stressful.

Self-check

  1. Name two things that show you are being professional at work.
  2. True or false: it's fine to arrive a few minutes late as long as you apologize afterward.
  3. What's the difference between "a professional" (noun) and "professional" (adjective)?
  4. Complete: "Being professional means being on time, listening carefully, and being ___."

Spoken task: In your own words, explain what "being professional" means to you, in 2–3 sentences.

Motivation

"Professionalism isn't a rule you follow — it's a habit you build, one small choice at a time."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

A colleague asks you to help with something right when you're about to leave for lunch. Which response is most professional?

A.

Sorry, I'm going to lunch. Ask someone else.

B.

I'm just heading to lunch — could I help you right after, in about 30 minutes?

C.

(walk away without answering)

2. Fill Blank

Complete the sentence: "Being professional means being on time, listening carefully, and being ___."

3. Comprehension

Read the dialogue again (or listen to a partner or teacher read it aloud). What three things does Sadia say "being professional" mainly means?

4. Reflection

In your own words, explain what "being professional" means to you, in 2–3 sentences. Try to use at least one of this lesson's key expressions.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. The second option is respectful and honest about timing, without being dismissive — exactly the kind of everyday choice that shows professionalism.

2.

respectful — "Being professional means being on time, listening carefully, and being respectful." The blank needs an adjective after "being", parallel to the lesson's three actions (punctuality, listening, respect).

3.

Sadia names exactly three things — be on time, listen carefully, and speak with respect.

4.

Answers will vary. Sample answer: "For me, being professional means being on time and ready to work, listening carefully when someone explains something, and speaking to everyone with respect. It also means keeping my promises, even small ones." A good answer names concrete actions, not just "being good at the job".

lessons.title: Talking About Your Background and Experience
lessons.objectives_html:
• Describe your educational and work background in 2–3 clear sentences.
  • Correctly choose between past simple and present perfect when talking about experience.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

It's Arif's orientation day — an in-person induction session before his real first day at work (Module 2). At lunch, he sits next to Hasan, a front-office colleague he hasn't met yet. Hasan asks the question every new employee eventually has to answer clearly: "So, what's your background?"

Key workplace lesson

Talking about your background comes up constantly at work — in orientation, in interviews, in casual introductions, in performance conversations. The skill isn't memorizing one script; it's being able to mix a few reliable building blocks (what you studied, where you worked, how long, what you're interested in) into a short, natural answer, and knowing when to use past simple versus present perfect while doing it.

Listen & Read
Orientation day, lunch break. Arif sits down next to Hasan, a front-office colleague he hasn't met yet, in the staff canteen.
Hasan: Mind if I sit here? I don't think we've met — I'm Hasan, from the front-office team.
Arif: Not at all, please. I'm Arif — I'm starting properly on Monday.
Hasan: Nice to meet you, Arif. So, what's your background?
Arif: I studied hospitality management, and I worked at a small hotel for about a year after that.
Hasan: Oh, nice. What made you move into this kind of role?
Arif: Honestly, I've been interested in customer-facing work since college — I just wanted to try it somewhere bigger.
Hasan: That makes sense. Have you handled difficult customers before?
Arif: Yes, I've handled a few tricky situations before, mostly guests with complaints about bookings.
Hasan: Good — that'll definitely come in handy here too.
Arif: Thanks. I'm looking forward to learning how things work on this team.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"So, what's your background?" A casual, open way to ask about someone's education/work history Starting a get-to-know-you conversation "So, what's your background?" Friendly, informal
"I studied... / I worked at..." Stating a finished fact about education or past work Answering with a specific, completed fact "I studied hospitality management." Neutral, direct
"I've been interested in... since..." Describing an interest that started in the past and continues now Connecting your past to your present motivation "I've been interested in this field since college." Warm, personal
"I've handled... before" Referring to relevant past experience without a specific date Showing relevant experience briefly "I've handled customer questions before, in my last job." Confident, modest
"I'm looking forward to..." Expressing positive anticipation about upcoming work Closing an introduction on a forward-looking note "I'm looking forward to learning more here." Warm, optimistic

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0007background n.Your history — what you studied and did beforeপটভূমিपृष्ठभूमिMy background is in customer service, mostly in retail.
V-0008experience n.What you've done before and learned from doing itঅভিজ্ঞতাअनुभवI don't have direct experience in IT support, but I learn quickly.
V-0009previously adv.Before this / in the pastপূর্বেपहलेPreviously, I handled front-desk duties at a hotel.
V-0010currently adv.Right now / at the momentবর্তমানেवर्तमान मेंCurrently, I'm looking for my first full-time role.
V-0011graduate n./v.Someone who finished their studies / to finish your studiesস্নাতকस्नातकI graduated last year and this is my first job.
V-0012degree n.A university qualificationডিগ্রিडिग्रीMy degree is in tourism management, which is useful for this role.
V-0013training n.Learning how to do a job, often guided by someone elseপ্রশিক্ষণप्रशिक्षणI completed customer-service training before joining this team.

Grammar in context

GIC-0002 Past simple vs. present perfect for describing your background

  • Past simple for a finished event at a finished time, especially when you say or imply when: "I studied hospitality management." "I worked at a small hotel for a year (and then left)."
  • Present perfect connects the past to now. Use it for a situation that started in the past and continues now, usually with for or since: "I've been interested in this field since college." Also use it for experience at an unstated time that is relevant now: "I've handled difficult guests before."
  • Do not use the present perfect with a finished time expression: "I worked there in 2023", not "I have worked there in 2023".

Sentence pattern PAT-0007: "I've + past participle + for/since..." — for example, "I've worked in retail for two years."

Common mistake · MIS-0003
❌ I am working there since 2 years.
✅ I have been working there for two years.
"Since" pairs with a starting point in time (since 2024, since January), and "for" pairs with a duration (for two years). A continuing action that started in the past and still continues needs present perfect continuous ("I have been working"), not simple present ("I am working").

Pronunciation

  • Word stress: BACKground, exPERience, PREViously, CURrently, GRADuate, deGREE, TRAINing.
  • "I've" in "I've been interested" contracts naturally in speech — avoid over-enunciating it as "I have."
  • Sentence stress falls on the content words that carry new information: "I've WORKED in reTAIL for TWO YEARS," not on "have" or "in."

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Not much really, just did some stuff before this." (vague, undersells real experience)
  • ❌ Too formal/textbook: "My professional trajectory commenced with the completion of an undergraduate degree, subsequent to which I was engaged in..." (technically correct, but stiff for a lunch conversation)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "I studied hospitality management, and I've been interested in this field since college. Before this, I worked at a small hotel for about a year." (clear, specific, natural)

Bengali support

Bengali doesn't require a separate verb form for "still true now" versus "finished in the past" the way English's present perfect does, so it's easy to default to simple past or simple present for both. A quick test: if the sentence is still true or relevant right now (a skill you still have, an interest you still hold), reach for present perfect ("I've been interested in..."); if it's simply a completed fact, past simple ("I studied...") is enough.

Hindi support

Hindi's perfect forms (जैसे "कर चुका हूँ") already carry some of this same "connected to now" meaning, which can actually help — but learners often still default to simple past out of speaking habit in English. The same current-relevance test applies: still true now → present perfect; simply finished → past simple.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: "I've worked front-desk shifts for about a year, so I'm used to handling guest requests quickly."
  • Healthcare: "I studied medical administration, and I've been interested in patient care coordination since my internship."
  • Banking: "I've handled cash reconciliation before, in my previous role at a small branch."
  • IT: "I studied computer science, and I've been building small projects on my own since university."
  • Retail: "I've worked on a shop floor for two years, so I'm comfortable with busy weekend shifts."

Self-check

  1. Choose the correct sentence: "I work here since two years" / "I've worked here for two years."
  2. True or false: present perfect can describe something that started in the past and is still true now.
  3. Complete: "I've been interested in this field ___ college." (since / for)
  4. In your own words, when do you use past simple instead of present perfect?

Spoken task (role-play): With a partner (or out loud on your own), answer "So, what's your background?" in 3–4 sentences, using at least one present-perfect sentence with PAT-0007.

Motivation

"Your background isn't a script to recite — it's proof of what you can already do. Say it plainly, and let it speak for itself."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Which sentence correctly describes an experience that started in the past and still continues?

A.

I work here since two years.

B.

I've worked here for two years.

C.

I am working here two years.

2. Fill Blank

Complete the sentence: "I've been interested in this field ___ college."

3. Comprehension

Read the dialogue again. What did Arif study, and where did he work before this job?

4. Sentence Transformation

Rewrite this sentence correctly, using present perfect — "I am working in customer service since three years."

5. Role-Play

With a partner (or out loud on your own), answer "So, what's your background?" in 3–4 sentences. Use at least one present-perfect sentence built with "I've + past participle + for/since..."

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. Present perfect ("I've worked") pairs correctly with "for + duration" to describe something that started in the past and continues now.

2.

since — "I've been interested in this field since college." Since pairs with a starting point (since college); for would need a duration instead (for four years).

3.

Arif says, "I studied hospitality management, and I worked at a small hotel for about a year after that."

4.

"I have been working in customer service for three years." (Also correct: "I have worked in customer service for three years.") A duration needs for, not since, and a situation that continues up to now needs the present perfect (continuous), not the present simple.

5.

Answers will vary. Sample answer: "I studied business administration, and after that I worked in a supermarket for two years. I've been interested in customer service since then. I've handled a lot of busy weekend shifts, so I'm used to working under pressure." Check: past simple for finished facts, at least one present perfect sentence with for or since, 3–4 sentences.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself Professionally
lessons.objectives_html:
• Deliver a complete 3-part self-introduction (name, role/background, closing line) unprompted.
  • Adapt the same introduction for a peer versus a senior manager.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Later the same orientation day, Arif is taken over to meet the people he'll actually be working with. First, a few new teammates, informally. Then, briefly, the department head stops by. Same person, same basic facts about himself — but the way he says it needs to shift with the room.

Key workplace lesson

A good self-introduction always has the same three parts — Open (your name), Background (what you studied/did, and your team or department), Close (a warm, forward-looking line) — this is Communication Formula CF-0002. What changes between a peer and a manager isn't the content, it's the register: "Hi, I'm..." versus "Good morning, my name is...". Same formula, different volume of formality.

Listen & Read
Later the same orientation day. Two short, paired scenes — first an informal team meet-and-greet near the desks, then a brief visit from the department head. Same self-introduction, two registers.
Hasan: Hey everyone, this is Arif — he's joining us properly on Monday. Arif, want to introduce yourself?
Arif: Sure! Hi, I'm Arif. I studied hospitality management, and I'll be part of the front-office team.
Hasan: Nice! What did you do before this?
Arif: I worked at a small hotel for about a year. I'm really looking forward to working with you all.
Hasan: Welcome aboard, Arif!
Ms. Noor: Good morning, everyone. I'm Fatima Noor, the Front Office Department Head. Let's go around — would you like to start?
Arif: Good morning, my name is Arif. I studied hospitality management and worked at a small hotel for about a year.
Ms. Noor: Welcome, Arif. Which team will you be joining?
Arif: I'll be part of the front-office team, reporting to the front-office supervisor. I'm looking forward to contributing to the department.
Ms. Noor: Glad to have you with us.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Hi, I'm..." A casual, friendly self-introduction opener Introducing yourself to a peer or teammate "Hi, I'm Arif." Warm, informal
"Good morning, my name is..." A formal self-introduction opener Introducing yourself to a manager or senior person "Good morning, my name is Arif." Polite, formal
"I'll be part of the... team." Stating which team/department you belong to Naming your team or department "I'll be part of the front-office team." Neutral, clear
"I report to..." Naming your direct supervisor/manager Explaining the reporting line "I'll be reporting to the front-office supervisor." Neutral, informative
"I'm looking forward to..." A warm, forward-looking closing line Closing an introduction "I'm looking forward to contributing to the department." Warm, professional

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0014team n.The group of people you work withটিমटीमI'm part of the front-office team.
V-0015department n.One section of a company, like Sales or HousekeepingবিভাগविभागI'm part of the housekeeping department.
V-0016report to v. phraseTo have someone as your direct boss: you take instructions from them and give them updates...-এর অধীনে কাজ করা...को रिपोर्ट करनाI'll be reporting to the front-office supervisor.

Grammar in context

There is no new grammar in this lesson. It combines the professional language of Lesson 1.1 and the background phrasing of Lesson 1.2 (past simple / present perfect) into one introduction sequence.

Communication formula CF-0002: "The 3-Part Self-Introduction" (Open → Background → Close).

Common mistake · MIS-0004
❌ Hi, um, so my name is Arif, and, well, I studied hospitality management, and before that, actually, I was thinking about doing something else, but then I changed my mind, and I also worked at a small hotel for around a year, maybe a bit more, and there were a lot of guests, and, yeah, so that's basically it, I think.
✅ Hi, I'm Arif. I studied hospitality management and worked at a small hotel for about a year. I'm looking forward to being part of the team.
An introduction with too many extra details and hesitations loses the listener's attention. A clear 3-part structure — name, background/role, closing line (Communication Formula CF-0002) — is more professional and memorable than a long, unfocused one.

Pronunciation

  • Word stress: dePARTment, rePORT (second syllable, for both the verb and the noun).
  • "Good morning, my name is..." should be said slightly slower and more evenly than "Hi, I'm..." — formality in English is often carried by pacing, not just word choice.
  • Avoid a flat, memorized-sounding delivery — even a fixed formula should sound like it's being said to a real person, not read off a card.

Professional tone

  • ✅ Appropriate for a peer: "Hi, I'm Arif. I studied hospitality management, and I'll be part of the front-office team. I'm really looking forward to working with you all." (warm, relaxed, still complete)
  • ✅ Appropriate for a manager: "Good morning, my name is Arif. I studied hospitality management and worked at a small hotel for about a year. I'm looking forward to contributing to the department." (polite, a touch more formal, same structure)
  • ❌ Mismatched register: "Yo, I'm Arif, nice to meet ya" said to the department head — the content might be fine, but the register is wrong for the audience.

Bengali support

In Bengali, respect is shown partly through the pronoun: আপনি for a senior person, তুমি for a peer. English has only one "you", so the register shift has to come from other places: the greeting ("Good morning" rather than "Hi"), full forms ("my name is" rather than "I'm"), and a slightly slower pace. The content of the introduction stays the same.

Hindi support

Hindi marks respect with आप (formal) versus तुम (informal). English "you" is the same for everyone, so a learner cannot rely on the pronoun: the greeting, full forms and pace carry the formality instead. Do not add "sir" or "ma'am" to every sentence to make up for it; one respectful greeting is enough.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: A front-office employee introduces themselves more energetically to a fellow front-desk colleague, and more measuredly to the General Manager.
  • Healthcare: A ward assistant introduces themselves briefly and clearly to a nurse manager, keeping the "background" part focused on relevant training.
  • Banking: A teller introduces themselves to branch colleagues casually, and to the branch manager with a touch more formality and precision.
  • IT: A support associate introduces themselves to teammates informally in a stand-up, and more formally when meeting a department lead for the first time.
  • Retail: A sales associate introduces themselves warmly to shop-floor colleagues, and more formally to the store manager.

Self-check

  1. Name the three parts of Communication Formula CF-0002.
  2. True or false: the content of your introduction should change completely between a peer and a manager.
  3. Which opener is more appropriate for a manager: "Hi, I'm..." or "Good morning, my name is..."?
  4. In your own words, why does an over-long introduction lose the listener (MIS-0004)?

Spoken task (role-play): Record two versions of your own self-introduction using CF-0002 — one for a peer, one for a manager. Keep both under 30 seconds.

Motivation

"You don't get a second chance to introduce yourself — so say it like you mean it, in a way that fits the room."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Which opener is more appropriate when introducing yourself to a senior manager?

A.

Hi, I'm Arif.

B.

Good morning, my name is Arif.

C.

Yo, I'm Arif.

2. Sequencing

Put the three parts of Communication Formula CF-0002 in the correct order.

3. Comprehension

Read both scenes again. What team does Arif say he will be part of?

4. Rewriting

Rewrite this over-long introduction using CF-0002's 3-part structure: "Hi, um, so my name is Arif, and, well, I studied hospitality management, and before that, actually, I was thinking about doing something else, but then I changed my mind, and I also worked at a small hotel for around a year, maybe a bit more, and there were a lot of guests, and, yeah, so that's basically it, I think."

5. Role-Play

Record two versions of your own self-introduction using CF-0002 — one for a peer, one for a manager. Keep both under 30 seconds.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. Good morning, my name is... is the more formal opener, better suited to a first introduction to a senior manager.

2.

CF-0002 always follows Open → Background → Close, whatever the register.

3.

In both the peer and manager versions, Arif says he'll be part of the front-office team.

4.

Model answer: "Hi, I'm Arif. I studied hospitality management and worked at a small hotel for about a year. I'm looking forward to being part of the team." Keep one sentence for each part (name, background/role, closing line) and remove hesitations and side stories (MIS-0004).

5.

Answers will vary. Peer version: "Hi, I'm Nadia. I studied accounting, and I'll be part of the finance team. Really looking forward to working with you all." Manager version: "Good morning, my name is Nadia. I studied accounting and worked at an audit firm for two years. I'm looking forward to contributing to the department." Check: all three parts in each version, a clear change of register, under 30 seconds.

lessons.title: Talking About Your Job Role and Responsibilities
lessons.objectives_html:
• State your job title and main responsibility clearly.
  • Explain, in simple terms, who you report to and who you work with.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Standing at the printer during orientation, Arif runs into Nusrat, a colleague from Accounts he hasn't met yet. She asks the question every new employee eventually gets from someone outside their own team: "So what exactly do you do here?"

Key workplace lesson

Describing your role well means three things, in present tense, because they're true right now: what you're responsible for, who you report to, and who you work with. Keep it factual and current — this isn't your background story (that's past simple / present perfect, from Lesson 1.2); it's your job, today.

Listen & Read
Later during orientation, at the printer. Arif is waiting for a page to print when a colleague from another department stops to introduce herself.
Nusrat: Oh, hi! You're the new front-office trainee, right? I don't think we've officially met — I'm Nusrat, from Accounts.
Arif: Hi Nusrat, nice to meet you. Yes, I'm Arif.
Nusrat: So what exactly do you do here?
Arif: I'm responsible for greeting guests and managing check-ins and check-outs.
Nusrat: Sounds busy! Who do you report to?
Arif: I report to the front-office supervisor, and I work closely with the housekeeping team too.
Nusrat: That makes sense — you'd need to coordinate with them a lot.
Arif: Exactly. It's only my first day of orientation, but I'm already getting the hang of it.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"I'm responsible for..." Stating your main duty or task Answering "what do you do?" "I'm responsible for greeting guests and managing check-ins." Clear, confident
"I report to..." Naming your direct supervisor Explaining the reporting line "I report to the front-office supervisor." Neutral, informative
"I work with..." / "I work closely with..." Naming who you collaborate with Describing cross-team collaboration "I work closely with the housekeeping team." Neutral, collaborative
"So what exactly do you do here?" A natural, friendly way to ask about someone's role Starting a role conversation with a new colleague "So what exactly do you do here?" Curious, friendly
"It's only my first day, but..." A modest, honest way to acknowledge you're still learning Closing a role description as a newcomer "It's only my first day of orientation, but I'm already getting the hang of it." Honest, modest

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0017responsible for adj. phraseHaving the duty to do or look after something as part of your jobদায়িত্বপ্রাপ্তजिम्मेदारI'm responsible for greeting guests and managing check-ins.
V-0018colleague n.Someone you work withসহকর্মীसहकर्मीI get along well with my colleagues on the front desk.
V-0019team lead n.Someone who guides a small group of workers day-to-dayটিম লিডटीम लीडI report to the team lead before escalating anything to the manager.
V-0020manager n.The person in charge of a department or teamম্যানেজারप्रबंधकI'll flag anything serious to my manager directly.
V-0021supervisor n.The person who checks and guides your day-to-day workসুপারভাইজারपर्यवेक्षकI report to the front-office supervisor.

(This lesson also reuses V-0015 department and V-0016 report to, both introduced in Lesson 1.3.)

Note: a supervisor (V-0021) usually oversees your day-to-day work directly, while a manager (V-0020) holds broader decision-making authority over a whole team or department — in many workplaces these are two distinct roles, not interchangeable titles for "someone senior."

Grammar in context

GIC-0003 Present simple for your role now

  • Use the present simple for facts about your job that are true now and generally: "I report to the front-office supervisor." "I work closely with housekeeping."
  • Use the past simple / present perfect (Lesson 1.2) for your history: "I worked at a small hotel." "I've handled complaints before."
  • Use the present continuous only for something temporary or happening around now: "This week I'm shadowing the night manager."

Sentence pattern PAT-0008: "I'm responsible for + gerund/noun" — for example, "I'm responsible for managing check-ins."

Common mistake · MIS-0005
❌ I am responsible to manage the front desk.
✅ I am responsible for managing the front desk.
"Responsible for" is always followed by a gerund (-ing form) or a noun, never a to-infinitive — "responsible for managing," not "responsible to manage." ("Responsible to" exists separately, but it means answerable to a person, e.g. "I'm responsible to the front-office manager.")

Pronunciation

  • Word stress: COLleague, SUpervisor, MANager, TEAM lead.
  • In "responsible for", the word "for" is usually unstressed and weak (/fə/), so it sounds like "responsible-fer". This is natural, not careless.
  • Keep role descriptions evenly paced — rushing through "I'm responsible for..." can make it sound memorized rather than genuinely informative.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Vague: "I do a bit of everything, I guess." (true but unhelpful — gives the listener nothing to work with)
  • ❌ Too casual for a first work conversation: "Oh, I just kind of hang around the front desk." (undersells real responsibility)
  • ✅ Clear: "I'm responsible for greeting guests and managing check-ins. I report to the front-office supervisor, and I work closely with housekeeping." (specific, confident, complete)

Bengali support

Bengali speakers sometimes describe an ongoing role in past tense, by habit from describing their history a moment earlier (as in Lesson 1.2). The fix is simple: if it's true about your job right now, use present simple — "I'm responsible for...", not "I was responsible for..." unless the role has actually ended.

Hindi support

The same instinct can appear in Hindi speakers' English — a role that's currently true should stay in present tense in English, even though the switch from talking about background (past) to role (present) can feel abrupt at first.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: "I'm responsible for guest check-ins and check-outs. I report to the front-office supervisor."
  • Healthcare: "I'm responsible for patient records and appointment scheduling. I report to the ward manager."
  • Banking: "I'm responsible for processing daily transactions. I report to the branch manager."
  • IT: "I'm responsible for resolving level-1 support tickets. I report to the team lead."
  • Retail: "I'm responsible for restocking and customer assistance on the shop floor. I report to the store supervisor."

Self-check

  1. Complete: "I'm responsible for ___ (manage / managing) the front desk."
  2. True or false: describing your current job role uses the same tense as describing your past background.
  3. Name one difference between a "supervisor" and a "manager," as this lesson defines them.
  4. Write your own one-sentence role description using PAT-0008.

Written self-check: Complete your own role description: "I'm responsible for ___. I report to ___. I work with ___."

Spoken task (role-play): Describe your own real or target job role, using at least one sentence with PAT-0008.

Motivation

"Knowing exactly what you're responsible for isn't limiting — it's the first step to owning it fully."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Which sentence is grammatically correct?

A.

I'm responsible to manage the front desk.

B.

I'm responsible for managing the front desk.

C.

I'm responsible for manage the front desk.

2. Fill Blank

Complete the sentence using present simple: "I ___ (report) to the front-office supervisor."

3. Comprehension

Read the dialogue again. Who does Arif say he works closely with?

4. Sentence Transformation

Rewrite this sentence correctly — "I am responsible to train new staff."

5. Role-Play

Describe your own real or target job role out loud, using at least one sentence built with "I'm responsible for + gerund" (PAT-0008), and name who you report to and who you work with.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. Responsible for is always followed by a gerund or noun, never a to-infinitive.

2.

report — "I report to the front-office supervisor." Ongoing role facts use the present simple.

3.

Arif says, "I report to the front-office supervisor, and I work closely with the housekeeping team too."

4.

"I am responsible for training new staff." Responsible for takes a gerund (training), not a to-infinitive (to train).

5.

Answers will vary. Sample answer: "I'm a teller at a bank branch. I'm responsible for processing customer deposits and withdrawals. I report to the branch manager, and I work closely with the customer-service desk." Check: a "responsible for + -ing/noun" sentence, who you report to, who you work with, all in the present simple.

lessons.title: Building Basic Workplace Confidence
lessons.objectives_html:
• Deliver a single combined self-presentation (identity + background + role) fluently, without reading.
  • Self-assess your own confidence level using a simple checklist.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

At the end of orientation day, Sadia Chowdhury — the same HR colleague who called Arif before any of this began (Lesson 1.1) — gathers all the new hires for a quick "welcome round." One by one, everyone introduces themselves to the whole group at once. This is the moment everything from this module comes together.

Key workplace lesson

This lesson introduces no new language — it combines what you already have. Communication Formula CF-0002 normally follows three parts — Open → Background → Close — but this synthesis lesson extends it to four: Open → Background → Role → Close, giving your role and responsibilities (Lesson 1.4) their own step instead of folding them into Background alongside your history (Lesson 1.2). The result is one flowing turn of about a minute. The real skill here isn't new vocabulary or grammar; it's pacing — speaking at a natural, unhurried pace, with small pauses in the right places, so a combined introduction sounds confident rather than recited.

Listen & Read
The end of orientation day. Sadia Chowdhury gathers the new hires for a "welcome round" — each person introduces themselves to the whole group. This is a model monologue: one speaker, Arif, talking to the group.
Arif: Hi everyone, I'm Arif.
Arif: I studied hospitality management, and I worked at a small hotel for about a year before this.
Arif: I've been interested in hospitality since college, so this really feels like the right next step for me.
Arif: Starting Monday, I'll be part of the front-office team here.
Arif: I'm responsible for greeting guests and managing check-ins and check-outs.
Arif: I report to the front-office supervisor, and I'll be working closely with housekeeping as well.
Arif: Today was only my first day of orientation, but everyone's already been really welcoming.
Arif: I'm still learning the ropes, but I'm getting more comfortable every day.
Arif: I'm looking forward to learning from all of you.
Arif: And I'm really glad to be part of the team.
Arif: Thank you.

Key expressions

This lesson reuses the key expressions from Lessons 1.1–1.4 rather than introducing new ones. The model monologue above shows them combined into one continuous turn.

Vocabulary

There is no new vocabulary in this lesson. It brings together the background, role and reporting-line vocabulary from Lessons 1.2–1.4 (V-0007 to V-0021) in one turn.

Grammar in context

Recycled, not new: GIC-0002 (past simple vs. present perfect, for background) and GIC-0003 (present simple, for ongoing role facts) both appear in the model monologue above, combined in the same turn for the first time in this module.

Sentence patterns recycled: PAT-0007 ("I've + past participle + for/since...") and PAT-0008 ("I'm responsible for + gerund").

Communication formula CF-0002: "The 3-Part Self-Introduction" — normally three parts (Open → Background → Close); this synthesis lesson extends it to four — Open → Background → Role → Close — giving Role its own step rather than folding it into Background.

Pronunciation

  • This lesson's real focus: pacing and pausing, not new sounds or stress patterns.
  • Put a short pause after your name, another after your background, and another before your closing line — these three pauses are what separate a fluent combined introduction from a rushed one.
  • Avoid speeding up toward the end out of nervousness — the closing line ("I'm looking forward to...") deserves the same unhurried pace as the opening.

Professional tone

No new tone contrast this lesson — the focus is delivery quality (pacing, naturalness), covered under Pronunciation above, rather than a weak-vs-appropriate register comparison.

Industry overlays

This lesson's combined introduction works the same way in every industry — the industry-specific detail comes from the role and background facts you put in from your own real or target job (see the industry overlays in Lessons 1.1–1.4 for hotel, healthcare, banking, IT and retail phrasing).

Model monologue

Read Arif's combined self-introduction (the Listen & Read script above) aloud. Notice how Open → Background → Role → Close flows as one continuous turn, and where the natural pauses fall.

Self-check

  1. Which three lessons' language does this monologue combine into one turn?
  2. True or false: this lesson introduces new grammar for the first time in Module 1.
  3. Name one pause point that makes a combined introduction sound more natural.
  4. Using the confidence checklist below, rate your own practice attempt from 1 (not confident) to 5 (very confident) on: clarity, pacing, completeness (all 4 CF-0002 parts present, as extended in this lesson), and natural delivery (not sounding memorized).

Spoken task (role-play, Module 1 assessment): Record your own combined 60–90 second self-introduction — name, background, role, and a closing line — using CF-0002. This is Module 1's final speaking task.

Motivation

"Confidence isn't something you wait to feel — it's something you build, one practice attempt at a time."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Comprehension

Read the model monologue again. Which part comes first: Background or Role?

2. Labeling

Label each sentence of the model monologue as Open, Background, Role, or Close (CF-0002's parts, extended).

3. Guided Speaking

Using this scaffold, build your own combined introduction: "Hi everyone, I'm ___. I studied ___ and I worked at/have worked at ___. I'll be part of the ___ team. I'm responsible for ___. I report to ___. I'm looking forward to ___."

4. Self Assessment

After recording your own introduction, rate yourself 1 (not confident) to 5 (very confident) on each: (1) Clarity — could a stranger understand me easily? (2) Pacing — did I pause naturally, not rush? (3) Completeness — did I include all of Open, Background, Role, and Close? (4) Natural delivery — did it sound like me, not a memorized script?

5. Role-Play

Record your own combined 60–90 second self-introduction — name, background, role, and a closing line — using Communication Formula CF-0002. This is Module 1's final speaking task.

Answer Key

1.

Arif describes his background (what he studied and where he worked) before describing his current role and responsibilities.

2.

Open (name) is one line; Background (studies/past work) is two; Role (responsibilities, reporting line) is three; Close (reflection and forward-looking lines) covers the rest.

3.

Answers will vary. Sample: "Hi everyone, I'm Rina. I studied nursing and I've worked at a community clinic for two years. I'll be part of the patient-services team. I'm responsible for scheduling appointments. I report to the ward manager. I'm looking forward to working with you all."

4.

This is a personal rating, so there is no single answer. If you gave yourself 1 or 2 for any point, practice that part again: for pacing, add the three pauses from the Pronunciation section; for completeness, check that all four parts are there.

5.

Answers will vary. A strong recording: (1) includes all four parts (Open, Background, Role, Close); (2) uses the past simple for finished history and the present simple for the current role; (3) lasts 60–90 seconds with natural pauses; (4) is spoken, not read.

modules.title: First-Day Communication
modules.purpose: Follow Arif through his first day, from arrival to going home: introductions, a first tour, first tasks and first questions.

lessons.title: Arriving and Greeting on Day One
lessons.objectives_html:
• Greet a receptionist and state your name and purpose on arrival.
  • Respond naturally when welcomed by a colleague.
  • Greet a new colleague appropriately in a first, brief encounter.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

It's 8:50 on Monday morning. Arif is standing outside the hotel's staff entrance, his offer-letter email open on his phone. Today is his first day. He takes a breath, pushes the door open, and walks toward the front desk.

Key workplace lesson

Arriving on day one is really two small jobs, not one big one: (1) confirm who you are and why you're there at the front desk, and (2) greet the people you meet — briefly, warmly, professionally. You don't need a long conversation yet. Clear and friendly beats clever every time. This short arrival routine is really the start of your orientation — the process of settling into a new workplace — even before any formal training begins.

Listen & Read
The staff reception desk, 8:55 AM. Arif walks up to the desk, where Meera is on the phone. Tom, a front-office colleague, is walking past with a coffee.
Meera: (hangs up phone, smiles) Good morning! How can I help you?
Arif: Good morning. I'm Arif — I'm starting today. I'm here to see Mr. Hossain.
Meera: Oh, welcome, Arif! Let me just call him. Could you sign in here, please?
Arif: Sure, no problem.
Meera: Great. Here's your visitor badge — you'll get your proper ID card later today.
Tom: (passing by, stops) You must be the new guy! I'm Tom, I'm on the front-office team.
Arif: Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Arif.
Tom: Nice to meet you too. Welcome aboard — Mr. Hossain's expecting you upstairs.
Arif: Thanks! I'll wait here for him, then.
Meera: All set — he's on his way down now.
Tom: Good luck today! I'm sure it'll go well.
Arif: Thanks, Tom. See you around!

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"I'm here to..." Stating your purpose for being somewhere Arriving anywhere for a stated reason "I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." Neutral-professional; works in almost any first encounter
"I'm starting today" Announcing you're a brand-new employee First arrival, to reception/security/anyone who asks "I'm Arif — I'm starting today." Confident, simple; avoid over-explaining
"Nice to meet you" Standard polite response to an introduction Any first introduction, any seniority level "Nice to meet you, Tom." Genuine, brief eye-contact tone, not rushed
"Welcome aboard" Warmly welcoming a new team member Said to a new employee by an existing one "Welcome aboard — Mr. Hossain's expecting you." Friendly, informal-professional; you will hear this more often than you say it
"Sure, no problem" Agreeing readily to a small request Responding to any simple instruction/request "Could you sign in here? / Sure, no problem." Easy, unforced — avoids sounding overly eager

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0101reception n.The front desk area near the entranceরিসেপশন / অভ্যর্থনাरिसेप्शनPlease wait at reception; someone will come get you.
V-0102badge n.The card you wear or show to prove who you areব্যাজ / পরিচয়পত্রबैजVisitors must sign in and wear a visitor badge.
V-0103sign in phr. v.Write your name when you arrive, as proof you're thereসাইন ইন করাसाइन इन करनाAll visitors must sign in at reception.
V-0104orientation n.The training/introduction new employees get in their first daysওরিয়েন্টেশন / প্রাথমিক পরিচিতিओरिएंटेशनHR will run your orientation this morning.
V-0105colleague n.Someone who works at the same company as youসহকর্মীसहकर्मी / साथी कर्मचारीI met three new colleagues today.

Grammar in context

Two short patterns are all you need on arrival:

  • Present continuous for an arrangement — something already planned: "I'm starting today." (This is not about an action in progress; it states a fixed plan.)
  • "I'm here to + verb" to state your purpose: "I'm here to see Mr. Hossain."

Sentence pattern PAT-0001: "I'm here to + verb" — "I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." / "I'm here to collect my ID card."

Tip · TIP-0003
One clear "Good morning" beats a long introduction. Say your name and your purpose in one short sentence — you'll have plenty of time for conversation later.
Common mistake · MIS-0001
❌ I have come here for the joining.
✅ I'm here to see Mr. Hossain.
Bengali/Hindi speakers often translate "এসেছি.../आया हूँ..." literally as "I have come here for…" — natural spoken English simply uses "I'm here to + verb."

Pronunciation

  • Greeting intonation: "Good morning" rises slightly then falls — a flat, monotone "Good morning" reads as bored, not calm.
  • Sentence stress: "I'm STARTing toDAY"; "I'm here to SEE Mr. Hossain" — the content words carry the stress, not "I'm" or "to".
  • Connected speech: "I'm here to" often sounds like /aɪm hɪə tə/ in natural speech.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Hey, I'm the new guy." (fine with close peers weeks later; wrong for a first arrival)
  • ❌ Too formal: "Good morning. I am arriving for my initial day of employment, as per your correspondence." (technically correct, but stiff and unnatural)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "Good morning, I'm Arif. I'm starting today — I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." (clear, warm, professional, exactly as long as it needs to be)

Bengali support

"আমি ... জন্য এসেছি" translated word for word gives "I have come here for...", which sounds unnatural in English. Use "I'm here to + verb" instead: "I'm here to see Mr. Hossain."

Hindi support

Same principle: "I'm here to..." replaces the instinct to translate "मैं... के लिए आया हूँ" literally as "I have come here for..." — natural English simply says "I'm here to...".

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: Good morning — I'm starting today. Where's the staff entrance? (Arrival is often through a staff/back-of-house entrance, with a uniform check before reaching the floor.)
  • Banking: I'm here to see Mr. Islam in Operations — I believe I need to sign the register. (Sign-in is usually logged for security/compliance, sometimes with a visitor's-book or digital log rather than a badge.)
  • Retail: Hi, I'm Arif — I'm starting today, is Mr. Hossain around? (Often no formal reception at all — arrival greeting goes straight to a shift supervisor on the floor.)
  • IT: I'm here for my first day — I was told IT would set up my access badge. (Badge/access-card issuance is usually immediate and system-linked.)
  • Healthcare: I'm starting today in the admin office — I was told to check in and get my badge before going to the ward. (ID badge plus a light hygiene/protocol mention is common.)

Self-check

  1. What two things should you tell the receptionist when you arrive on your first day?
  2. What do you say when someone introduces themselves to you?
  3. True or false: "Hey, I'm the new guy" is the best way to greet a receptionist.
  4. Complete: "I'm here ___ see my supervisor."

Motivation

"A confident hello is the first sentence of a good career."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

You are arriving for your first day. Which greeting is most appropriate?

A.

Hey, I'm the new guy.

B.

Good morning, I'm Arif. I'm starting today — I'm here to see Mr. Hossain.

C.

Good morning. I am arriving for my initial day of employment as per your correspondence.

2. Fill Blank

Complete the sentence: "I'm here ___ see Mr. Hossain."

3. Comprehension

Read the dialogue again. What does Meera give Arif before he goes upstairs?

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part. Greet the receptionist, state your name and purpose, and respond to being welcomed by a colleague.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. The second option is clear, warm, and appropriately professional — not too casual, not overly formal.

2.

to — "I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." "I'm here to + verb" states your purpose simply.

3.

Meera gives Arif a visitor badge; his proper ID card comes later that day.

4.

Sample: "Good morning. I'm Arif — I'm starting today. I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." … "Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Arif." … "Thanks! See you around." Check: name and purpose in one or two short sentences, "Nice to meet you" when a colleague introduces himself, a short thank-you to close.

lessons.title: Meeting Your Supervisor and Team
lessons.objectives_html:
• Respond appropriately when a supervisor introduces you to the team as a group.
  • Respond appropriately when introduced to three or more team members in a row, without repeating the same sentence mechanically.
  • Recognize a basic marker of workplace hierarchy in how introductions are made.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Mr. Hossain, his supervisor, meets Arif at the top of the stairs. "Ready?" he asks with a smile. "Let's introduce you to the team." Arif follows him into the front-office back room, where three faces look up from their desks, one by one.

Key workplace lesson

Meeting several people quickly is common on a first day — and it's easy to sound like a robot repeating "Nice to meet you" four times in a row. This lesson teaches natural variation: the meaning stays the same, but the words shift slightly each time, exactly the way a real conversation does.

Listen & Read
The front-office back room, behind the front desk. Mr. Hossain walks Arif past three desks.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, this is the team. Everyone, this is Arif — he's joining us on the front desk.
Arif: Hi everyone, nice to meet you all.
Priyanka: Hi Arif! I'm Priyanka, I sit right next to you.
Arif: Great to meet you, Priyanka.
Tom: We actually already met downstairs!
Arif: We did — good to see you again, Tom.
Mr. Hossain: And this is Faisal, our team lead.
Faisal: Welcome, Arif. Let me know if you need anything at all.
Arif: Thank you, I really appreciate that.
Mr. Hossain: Alright — let's get you settled in at your desk.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Nice to meet you all" A single greeting to a group, not one person First moment of a group introduction "Hi everyone, nice to meet you all." Warm, brief, said once to the whole group
"Great to meet you, [name]" A varied alternative to "nice to meet you" Second/third individual introduction in a row "Great to meet you, Priyanka." Genuine — use the name, it signals attention
"Good to see you again" Acknowledging you've already met someone that day When re-meeting someone you were just introduced to elsewhere "We did — good to see you again, Tom." Friendly, slightly more relaxed than a first meeting
"Let me know if you need anything" An offer of help from a senior colleague Said by an established colleague/lead to a newcomer "Let me know if you need anything at all." Sincere, low-pressure — you will usually hear this rather than say it
"I really appreciate that" A slightly warmer alternative to "thank you" Responding to a genuine offer of help "Thank you, I really appreciate that." A notch warmer than a plain "thanks" — fits a kind offer

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0106team lead n.The person in charge of your immediate teamটিম লিডटीम लीडAsk your team lead if you're not sure who to report to.
V-0107to settle in phr. v.To get used to a new placeমানিয়ে নেওয়াसेटल होना / ढलनाTake your time settling in during your first week.
V-0108Front Office (dept.) n.The hotel team that handles check-in, check-out and guest requests at the front deskফ্রন্ট অফিস বিভাগफ्रंट ऑफिस विभागFront Office handles check-ins, check-outs and guest requests.

Grammar in context

"This is..." for introductions: "This is Arif." / "This is Faisal, our team lead." — the standard introduction pattern, contrasted briefly with self-introduction ("I'm Arif") from Module 1. Varying a fixed response is taught as a phrase-choice skill here, not a grammar point — the "grammar" of this lesson is really about avoiding unnatural repetition, a fluency skill, not a rule.

Notice This · TIP-0002
Saying "Nice to meet you" three times in a row sounds mechanical, even though it's grammatically correct every time. Real speakers vary the words — "Great to meet you," "Good to see you again" — while the meaning stays identical.

Pronunciation

  • Stress on the name, not the verb, in "Great to meet you, PRIya."
  • Falling intonation on "Good to see you again" (a settled, warm close, not a question-like rise).

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Yo, what's up." (wrong register for a first meeting with a team lead)
  • ❌ Too repetitive: "Nice to meet you." / "Nice to meet you." / "Nice to meet you." (grammatically fine, but sounds mechanical and disengaged)
  • ✅ Appropriate: Varied, genuine responses — "Great to meet you, Priyanka" / "Good to see you again, Tom" / "Thank you, I really appreciate that."

Bengali support

Bengali workplace introductions often include more formal titles by default; English first-day introductions are typically first-name and warm unless the workplace is very formal — a real cultural adjustment, not a language error.

Hindi support

The instinct to use "Sir/Madam" for every introduction is common and not wrong, but English-speaking peer-level teams often move to first names quickly — Module 7 (Foundations of Professional Tone) covers this hierarchy judgment in full; this lesson only flags it.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: This is Arif, he's joining Front Office this week. (Team introductions often happen department by department across a shift handover, not all at once.)
  • Banking: This is Arif, our new associate in Operations. (More formal address is common even at peer level initially.)
  • Retail: Guys, this is Arif — he's with us from today! (Fast, informal, often mid-shift.)
  • IT: Frequently includes a Slack/Teams-channel introduction alongside the in-person one — a light preview of Level 2's digital-messaging module.
  • Healthcare: This is Arif, he's joining the admin desk on the morning shift. (Introductions often include role/shift explicitly for safety clarity.)

Self-check

  1. Name two ways to respond to "nice to meet you" other than repeating the exact same phrase.
  2. What do you say if you're introduced to someone you already met earlier that day?
  3. True or false: it's fine to say "Nice to meet you" the exact same way every time.

Motivation

"Every name you remember is a relationship you've started."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Match each situation to the most natural response.

(1) Your supervisor introduces you to the whole team at once.________
(2) A second colleague introduces herself, right after the first.________
(3) You meet someone you already met downstairs this morning.________

Responses: (a) "Good to see you again." (b) "Hi everyone, nice to meet you all." (c) "Great to meet you, Priyanka."

2. Error Correction

Arif meets four colleagues and says 'Nice to meet you' all four times. Suggest two better alternatives for the 2nd and 3rd introduction.

3. Comprehension

Who is the team lead?

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part through the whole team-introduction sequence, varying your responses naturally.

Answer Key

1.

(1) → (b) "Hi everyone, nice to meet you all." (2) → (c) "Great to meet you, Priyanka." (3) → (a) "Good to see you again."

2.

Sample: 2nd introduction — "Great to meet you, Priyanka." 3rd introduction — "Good to meet you, Faisal. Thanks for the welcome." Any natural variation is correct, as long as it is not the same sentence repeated and it uses the person's name.

3.

Mr. Hossain introduces Faisal as "our team lead."

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses at least 2 different phrasings across the 3 individual responses (does not repeat "Nice to meet you" verbatim more than once); each response is directed at the correct person/situation from the dialogue.

lessons.title: Receiving Instructions and Understanding Routines
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify the key action and deadline in a spoken instruction.
  • Restate a multi-part instruction accurately in your own words.
  • Ask one simple clarification question when part of an instruction is unclear.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

At the back-office computer, Arif's login screen is still loading when Mr. Hossain leans over. "Let me walk you through how mornings usually work here," he says, "and I've got a couple of small things for you to do before lunch."

Key workplace lesson

Supervisors rarely give instructions slowly or perfectly — they talk at a normal, natural pace, sometimes give more than one thing at once, and expect you to catch the important parts. This lesson is about catching what matters — the action, the object, and the deadline — even inside natural, imperfect speech.

Listen & Read
Arif's new desk. Mr. Hossain speaks at a natural, unhurried but real pace — not artificially slow.
Mr. Hossain: So, mornings here — we usually check email first, then there's a quick team huddle at 9:30. Nothing formal, just five minutes.
Arif: Got it — check email, then a short huddle at 9:30.
Mr. Hossain: Exactly. Now, for today — could you set up your email signature, and then Priyanka's going to send you the client list to look through before lunch?
Arif: Okay, so email signature first, and then I'll go through the client list Priyanka sends — before lunch.
Mr. Hossain: Perfect. Oh, and one more thing — if anything on the list looks off, just flag it, don't try to fix it yourself yet.
Arif: Sorry, just to check — when you say "flag it," do you mean tell you, or note it somewhere?
Mr. Hossain: Good question — just message me directly if you spot anything.
Arif: Got it, I'll message you directly if I see anything unusual.
Mr. Hossain: Perfect, you've got it.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Got it" Confirming you understood After receiving an instruction "Got it — check email, then a short huddle at 9:30." Quick, natural — the single most useful confirmation phrase in English workplaces
"So, [restated instruction]" Restating an instruction in your own words Confirming a multi-part instruction "So, email signature first, and then the client list before lunch." Neutral, careful — signals you're actively processing, not just agreeing
"Just to check..." Introducing a targeted clarifying question When one specific detail is unclear "Just to check — do you mean tell you, or note it somewhere?" Polite, confident — not apologetic
"Good question" A supervisor's typical response to a clarifying question You will usually hear this, not say it "Good question — just message me directly." Signals the question was welcome, not a bother
"I'll [action] if [condition]" Confirming understanding of a conditional instruction Closing the loop on an instruction with a condition attached "I'll message you directly if I see anything unusual." Clear, confirms both the action and the trigger

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0109huddle n.A quick, casual team check-inসংক্ষিপ্ত মিটিং / দলগত আলোচনাसंक्षिप्त बैठक / हडलDon't be late for the morning huddle.
V-0110email signature n.Your name and title that appears at the end of your emailsইমেইল সিগনেচারईमेल हस्ताक्षरHR will show you the signature format to use.
V-0111to flag (something) v.To tell someone about a problem so they knowচিহ্নিত করা / জানানোनिशान लगाना / बतानाIf a number looks wrong, flag it — don't fix it yourself.
V-0112client list n.The list of people or companies the business works withক্লায়েন্ট তালিকাक्लाइंट सूचीReview the client list before your first call.

Grammar in context

GIC-0001 Sequencing and simple conditions in instructions

  • Sequence words put steps in order: first … then … and then … before lunch. "Check email first, then there's a quick huddle at 9:30."
  • "If" + present simple gives a condition: "If anything looks off, just flag it." Use the present simple after if, even though it is about the future: "If I see anything, I'll message you" (not "if I will see").

Sentence patterns: PAT-0002 "So, [first step] first, and then [second step] — [deadline]." PAT-0003 "I'll + action + if + condition (present simple)."

Communication formula CF-0001: Listen → Restate → Clarify. Catch the action and deadline, say them back, and ask about the one part that is unclear.

Tip · TIP-0001
If you're unsure about an instruction, confirm what you understood before starting the task — restating it out loud (LISTEN → REPEAT) catches most misunderstandings before they become mistakes.

Pronunciation

  • Connected speech in fast instructions: "set up your email signature" often runs together as /ˈsetʌpjər/ in natural speech.
  • Stress on key content words in Mr. Hossain's first line: "check EMAIL first, then a quick HUDDLE at nine-THIRTY."

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Okay." (technically a response, but gives the supervisor no confidence the instruction landed)
  • ❌ Too apologetic: "Sorry, I'm really not sure I understood any of that, sorry, could you say it all again?" (over-apologizes and asks for a full repeat instead of a targeted question)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "So, email signature first, and then I'll go through the client list Priyanka sends — before lunch." (restates confidently, confirms understanding)

Bengali support

The conditional pattern "if... just...": Bengali learners sometimes translate this too literally into a formal "যদি...তাহলে" structure, which sounds overly formal for this casual instruction context — the natural English is much lighter.

Hindi support

Avoid over-formalizing "अगर...तो" into "If... then..." in speech here; natural spoken English often drops "then" entirely in casual instructions ("If anything looks off, just flag it").

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: We do a five-minute handover with the night shift before the doors open. (Morning routine often centers on a shift handover briefing rather than a "huddle.")
  • Banking: If a client's documents look incomplete, flag it to your supervisor — don't process it. (Instructions often reference compliance/verification steps explicitly.)
  • Retail: Check the stock room first, then we do a quick team check-in before opening. (Routine centers on opening/stock checks.)
  • IT: "Huddle" is near-universal terminology already (daily stand-up) — this industry needs almost no translation of the concept, only confirmation.
  • Healthcare: If anything in a patient file looks incomplete, flag it immediately — don't guess. (Instructions often carry a safety-first framing.)

Self-check

  1. What are the two things you should listen for in any instruction?
  2. Complete: "___ to check — do you mean tell you, or note it somewhere?"
  3. True or false: it's better to ask "can you repeat everything?" than a specific clarifying question.

Motivation

"Understanding first, performing second — that's how good work begins."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Comprehension

Read Mr. Hossain's instruction again. What are the two tasks, and what is the deadline?

2. Matching

Put the steps of the morning routine in the correct order: (a) the team huddle at 9:30 (b) checking email

First:________
Then:________
3. Multiple Choice

Something in an instruction is unclear. What's the best response?

A.

Okay.

B.

Sorry, I didn't understand anything, can you repeat all of that?

C.

Just to check — do you mean tell you, or note it somewhere?

4. Role-Play

A partner reads you this instruction: "Can you print the client list, and then pop a copy in the tray for the night team before you go?" Restate it, then ask one clarifying question about the unclear part.

5. Fill Blank

Complete using the pattern: "I'll ___ you directly if I ___ anything unusual." (use 'message' and 'see')

Answer Key

1.

Tasks: (1) set up his email signature, (2) go through the client list Priyanka sends. Deadline: before lunch.

2.

First: (b) check email. Then: (a) the team huddle at 9:30.

3.

Correct: C. A targeted clarifying question is more useful than a vague request to repeat everything.

4.

Sample: "So, print the client list first, and then put a copy in the tray for the night team before I go. Just to check — which tray do you mean? The one at the front desk, or the one in the back office?"

5.

"I'll message you directly if I see anything unusual." Use the present simple after if (PAT-0003).

lessons.title: Finding Your Way and Asking Where Things Are
lessons.objectives_html:
• Politely ask where something is located.
  • Understand and follow simple spoken directions inside a building.
  • Thank the person who helped, closing the exchange naturally.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

An hour in, Arif realizes he has no idea where the washroom is — or the printer, for that matter. Priyanka is nearby, typing.

Key workplace lesson

Not knowing your way around on day one is completely normal — the skill isn't avoiding the question, it's asking it well and actually following the answer. This lesson pairs a short polite-question pattern with real listening practice for directions.

Listen & Read
The back office, near Priyanka's desk.
Arif: Priyanka, sorry to bother you — could you tell me where the washroom is?
Priyanka: Of course! Go straight down this hallway, and it's on your left, just past the printer.
Arif: Down the hallway, past the printer, on the left — got it. And where's the printer, exactly?
Priyanka: Right before the washroom — you can't miss it, it's the big grey one.
Arif: Perfect, thank you so much.
Priyanka: No problem at all!

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Sorry to bother you, but..." A polite opener before asking a small favor Interrupting someone who's working "Sorry to bother you — could you tell me where the washroom is?" Genuinely polite, not overly apologetic — one "sorry" is enough
"Could you tell me where... is?" The standard polite location question Asking where anything is located "Could you tell me where the printer is?" Neutral-polite, works with anyone
"You can't miss it" Reassurance that a location is easy to find Given by the person answering, as encouragement "It's the big grey one — you can't miss it." Friendly, received more than produced here
"Thank you so much" A slightly warmer thank-you After someone gives real, useful help "Perfect, thank you so much." A notch warmer than plain "thanks," fits a helpful favor

Vocabulary

IDWordMeaningBengaliHindiExample
V-0113hallway n.The passage/corridor between roomsকরিডোরगलियारा / कॉरिडोरFollow the hallway to reach the break room.
V-0114washroom n.The toilet/bathroom at workওয়াশরুমवॉशरूमAsk a colleague if you can't find the washroom.
V-0115break room n.The room where employees relax during breaksব্রেক রুমब्रेक रूमCoffee and tea are free in the break room.

Grammar in context

Polite embedded questions: "Could you tell me where the washroom is?" — not "Where is the washroom?" directly, though both are understood; the embedded form is the more natural workplace default. Prepositions of place: down the hallway, on your left, just past the printer, right before — shown in the dialogue and in the directions list below.

Sentence patterns: PAT-0004 "Could you tell me where + [place] + is?" (statement word order after "where": "where the washroom is", not "where is the washroom"). PAT-0005 "Go straight down…, and it's on your left/right, (just) past/before…"

Pronunciation

  • Question intonation: rising slightly at the end of "...could you tell me where the washroom is?" (not a sharp, demanding rise).
  • Stress on location words in directions: "down this HALLway, on your LEFT, just past the PRINTer."

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: "Where's the washroom." (no softener, reads as a demand)
  • ❌ Too apologetic: "I'm so sorry, I know this is a silly question, but I really don't know where anything is, sorry..." (undermines the speaker unnecessarily)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "Priyanka, sorry to bother you — could you tell me where the washroom is?" (one light softener, clear question, done)

Bengali/Hindi support

Bengali and Hindi keep the normal question order inside a longer question, so learners often say "Could you tell me where is the washroom?" In English, the inner question uses statement order: "Could you tell me where the washroom is?" (বাংলা: "ওয়াশরুম কোথায়?" → English: "where the washroom is"; हिंदी: "वॉशरूम कहाँ है?" → "where the washroom is".)

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: Is the staff washroom the same as the guest one, or is there a separate one? (Distinguishing guest areas from staff-only areas matters here.)
  • Banking: Could you show me where the archive room is? I think I need someone to let me in. (Secure areas may require an escort.)
  • Healthcare: Could you tell me how to get to the admin wing from here? (Wayfinding often includes wards/units.)
  • Retail: No significant variation — general pattern applies directly.
  • IT: No significant variation — general pattern applies directly.

Directions from Arif's desk

  1. Front desk — go back through the door behind you, and it's straight ahead.
  2. Mr. Hossain's office — go down the hallway, and it's the first door on your right.
  3. Printer — go straight down the hallway, and it's on your left, just before the washroom.
  4. Washroom — go straight down the hallway, and it's on your left, just past the printer.
  5. Break room — go straight down the hallway, and it's on your right, past the printer.

Self-check

  1. What phrase softens a direct question like "Where's the washroom?"
  2. What do you say after someone gives you directions?
  3. True or false: you should avoid asking where things are on your first day.

Motivation

"It's okay not to know where everything is yet — that's what day one is for."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Read Priyanka's directions in the dialogue again. Where is the washroom?

A.

Straight down the hallway, on the right, before the printer

B.

Straight down the hallway, on the left, past the printer

C.

Next to reception

2. Fill Blank

Complete: "Sorry to bother you, but could you tell me ___ the printer is?"

3. Reading Directions

Use the "Directions from Arif's desk" list. Which place is described? (a) "Go down the hallway, and it's the first door on your right." (b) "Go straight down the hallway, and it's on your right, past the printer."

4. Role-Play

Ask a colleague for directions to two different places and respond appropriately to their answers.

5. Role-Play

A new colleague asks you where the break room is. Give directions from Arif's desk using the pattern: "Go straight down..., and it's on your..., past..."

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. Priyanka says: go straight down the hallway, and it's on your left, just past the printer.

2.

where — "Sorry to bother you, but could you tell me where the printer is?" (Statement order: "where the printer is".)

3.

(a) Mr. Hossain's office. (b) The break room.

4.

Sample: "Sorry to bother you — could you tell me where the break room is?" … "Down the hallway, on the right, past the printer — got it. Thank you so much." Check: one softener, the embedded question in statement order, the directions repeated back, a thank-you.

5.

"Go straight down the hallway, and it's on your right, past the printer."

lessons.title: Ending Your First Day Professionally
lessons.objectives_html:
• Give a brief, positive end-of-day comment to a supervisor.
  • Say goodbye to colleagues appropriately.
  • Confirm the next day's start time where relevant.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

It's 5:30. Arif's screen is still open, but the back office is starting to quiet down. Mr. Hossain stops by his desk on his way out.

Key workplace lesson

How you leave matters almost as much as how you arrive. A short, positive close — not a long story, not a silent slip out the door — leaves the right impression and closes the day the way it started: clearly and warmly.

Listen & Read
Arif's desk, end of day.
Mr. Hossain: Heading out? How was your first day?
Arif: Really good, thank you — a lot to take in, but I enjoyed it.
Mr. Hossain: Glad to hear it. Same time tomorrow, 9 o'clock?
Arif: Perfect, I'll see you at 9.
Mr. Hossain: Great. Have a good evening, Arif.
Arif: Thanks, you too. See you tomorrow!
Priyanka: Bye, Arif! Good first day.
Arif: Thanks, Priyanka — see you tomorrow.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"A lot to take in, but..." Honestly acknowledging a busy day, framed positively Answering "how was your day" honestly but positively "A lot to take in, but I enjoyed it." Genuine, not falsely enthusiastic — this is the model, not "everything was perfect!"
"Same time tomorrow?" Confirming next-day timing Closing a shift/day, confirming logistics "Same time tomorrow, 9 o'clock?" Brief, practical — often supervisor-initiated
"I'll see you at [time]" Confirming you've understood and agreed to a time Responding to a next-day time check "Perfect, I'll see you at 9." Clear, confirms both understanding and agreement
"Have a good evening" A standard end-of-day farewell Leaving work, said to anyone "Have a good evening, Arif." Warm-neutral, works at any seniority level
"See you tomorrow" A casual, forward-looking goodbye Leaving, when you'll see the person again soon "Thanks, you too. See you tomorrow!" Mirrors the arrival greeting from Lesson 2.1

Vocabulary

There is no new vocabulary in this lesson: it brings together the language of Module 2.

Grammar in context

"Have a good [time period]" as a fixed farewell pattern (evening, weekend, etc.). Future confirmation with "I'll...": "I'll see you at 9" — light, functional future-tense use, not a tense lecture.

Sentence pattern PAT-0006: "Have a good + [evening / weekend / day off]."

Tone ladder TL-0001: Leaving at the end of the day

  • ❌ Too casual: (leaving without a word) / "Bye."
  • Basic: "See you."
  • Better: "See you tomorrow!"
  • ✅ Professional (taught rung): "Thanks — have a good evening. See you tomorrow at 9."
  • ❌ Too formal: "I shall now take my leave. I wish you a pleasant evening."

Pronunciation

  • Falling intonation for genuine closure: "See you tomorrow" should fall at the end — a rising "See you tomorrow?" sounds like a question, not a warm goodbye.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual: (leaving without a word, or a flat "Bye.") — technically not wrong, but misses an easy chance to leave a good impression.
