  • ❌ Overenthusiastic: "Today was literally the best day of my entire life, I can't believe how amazing everyone is!" (insincere-sounding, disproportionate for a first day)
  • ✅ Appropriate: "Really good, thank you — a lot to take in, but I enjoyed it." (honest, warm, proportionate)

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: I'm heading out — I've let the evening shift know where I left off. (Shift-based industries: a handover variant is the relevant overlay, not a plain goodbye.)
  • Retail: I'm heading out — I've let the evening shift know where I left off. (Same handover variant.)
  • Healthcare: I'm heading out — I've let the evening shift know where I left off. (Same handover variant.)
  • Banking: The model dialogue applies directly with no significant variation.
  • IT: The model dialogue applies directly with no significant variation.

Self-check

  1. Give one honest, positive way to answer "How was your day?" after a busy first day.
  2. What confirms you understood a next-day timing check?
  3. True or false: leaving without saying goodbye is the safest option on a busy day.

Motivation

"One good day is the start of a good habit."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Your supervisor asks how your first day was. What's the best response?

A.

Fine.

B.

Really good, thank you — a lot to take in, but I enjoyed it.

C.

Today was literally the best day of my entire life!

2. Comprehension

What time will Arif start tomorrow?

3. Fill Blank

Complete: "Great. Have a good ___, Arif."

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part through the full end-of-day sequence with your supervisor and a colleague.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. The second option is honest, warm, and proportionate — the model this lesson teaches.

2.

At 9 o'clock (9 AM) — "Same time tomorrow, 9 o'clock?" "Perfect, I'll see you at 9."

3.

evening — "Great. Have a good evening, Arif."

4.

Sample: "Really good, thank you — a lot to take in, but I enjoyed it." … "Perfect, I'll see you at 9." … "Thanks, you too. See you tomorrow!" … "Thanks, Priyanka — see you tomorrow." Check: an honest, positive comment; the next-day time confirmed; a goodbye to each person.

modules.title: Greetings & Small Talk
modules.purpose: Move from basic greetings to comfortable small talk: choosing formal or informal language, starting a conversation, keeping to safe topics and ending politely.

lessons.title: Formal and Informal Greetings
lessons.objectives_html:
• Choose an appropriately formal or informal greeting based on who you're speaking to.
  • Recognize when a greeting you've heard is too formal or too casual for the context shown.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

It's a Monday morning, a few weeks into the job, and greetings have stopped feeling like a performance for Arif — except he's about to greet three completely different people inside two minutes: the security guard at the gate, a peer arriving at the same time, and Mr. Kabir, the Head of Finance, waiting for the lift in the lobby.

Key workplace lesson

Module 2 taught you how to greet. This lesson teaches you to choose — the same "hello" does not fit every person you'll meet in a single morning. Getting this right isn't about memorizing a rule for each job title; it's about reading two things fast: how well you know this person, and how senior they are relative to you. This lesson gives you three real snapshots of the same morning, back to back, so the contrast does the teaching.

Listen & Read
A
Front gate, 8:50 AM. Arif walks in past the security guard, Nasir, whom he now sees every morning.
Arif: Morning!
Nasir: Morning, sir! Nice day today.
Arif: It really is. See you later, Nasir.
Nasir: See you, sir.
B
A minute later, at the entrance. Priyanka, a front-office colleague who joined a couple of weeks before Arif, arrives at the same moment.
Arif: Morning! Good weekend?
Priyanka: Morning! Yeah, pretty quiet. Yours?
Arif: Same — mostly just resting up for this week.
Priyanka: Smart move. See you at the desk!
C
The lobby, by the lift. Mr. Kabir, the Head of Finance, is waiting — Arif has only met him once before, briefly, since starting the job.
Arif: Good morning, sir.
Mr. Kabir: Good morning. Arif, isn't it? Settling in well?
Arif: Yes, sir, thank you — very well so far.
Mr. Kabir: Glad to hear it.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note Register
"Morning!" A quick, informal greeting Peers, people you already know a little "Morning! Good weekend?" Relaxed, warm, brief Informal
"Good morning" The safe, neutral-professional default Almost anyone you don't know well, or aren't sure about "Good morning." Calm, pleasant, works nearly everywhere Neutral-professional
"Good morning, sir" / "Good morning, ma'am" A formal, respectful greeting Someone clearly senior, or in a formal first encounter "Good morning, sir." Respectful, unhurried — but not the default for everyone Formal

Vocabulary

  • V-0116 sir / ma'am — formal address terms for someone whose name you may not know, or whose seniority calls for extra formality. Recycled from Module 2: all of Arif's Day One greeting phrases ("Good morning", "Nice to meet you", "Welcome aboard").

Grammar in context

There's no new grammar structure here — the skill is register selection, not sentence construction. All three greetings below are grammatically simple; what changes is which one fits which person.

Career English Upgrade Ladder — TL-0002: Greeting someone whose status you're unsure of

  • ❌ Too casual: "Hey!" / "Yo!" — fine for a close peer, risky for anyone else
  • Basic: "Morning!"
  • Better / neutral-safe default: "Good morning."
  • Formal: "Good morning, sir." / "Good morning, ma'am."
  • Taught rung for this lesson: "Good morning" is the safe default when you're unsure — it is never wrong to start neutral and let the other person's response tell you how relaxed they want the conversation to be.

Common mistake MIS-0006: greeting a senior director with "Morning!" the same way you'd greet a peer — not offensive, but reads as not-yet-attuned to the room. The fix isn't over-correcting into stiff formality either (see the ❌ Too formal example below).

Pronunciation

  • "Good morning" carries level, even stress across both words — rushing it ("g'morning") reads as informal even when the words are formal.
  • "Sir" and "ma'am" are said clearly and briefly, never stretched out — an over-long "siiir" can sound sarcastic rather than respectful.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual (with the director): "Yo, morning!" — fine with Hasan at lunch, wrong for someone several levels senior you barely know.
  • ❌ Too formal (with a peer): "Good morning, sir." said to a fellow new hire your own age — technically polite, but creates unnecessary distance with someone you'll be working beside daily.
  • ✅ Appropriate, three ways:
  • To the security guard (know him a little, informal role): "Morning!"
  • To a peer arriving at the same time: "Morning! Good weekend?"
  • To Mr. Kabir, the Head of Finance, waiting for the lift: "Good morning, sir."

Bengali support

Bengali workplace culture often defaults to an honorific ("স্যার" / "ম্যাডাম") far more broadly than English does — used with almost anyone senior, and often even with peers as a mark of general respect. In English, "sir"/"ma'am" is reserved for genuinely formal moments; using it with every colleague can sound distant rather than respectful. The skill isn't dropping respect — it's learning that English signals respect differently with peers (warmth, first names) than with clear seniority (sir/ma'am, "Good morning").

Hindi support

The same pattern applies to "साहब" / "मैडम" — a habit of addressing almost anyone respectfully senior this way doesn't map directly onto English's narrower use of "sir"/"ma'am". Save it for clear seniority or a first formal encounter; use first names and "Good morning" with peers.

Industry overlays

  • Hospitality: The guest/colleague line matters here more than seniority alone — guests typically get a slightly more formal greeting by default ("Good morning, welcome") regardless of their actual seniority, while colleagues get the register described above.
  • Banking: Customers at the counter are greeted formally and consistently ("Good morning, how can I help you today?"), while co-workers follow the peer/senior distinction in this lesson.

Self-check

  1. Which greeting is the safest default when you're not sure how formal to be?
  2. True or false: it's always safest to use "sir" or "ma'am" with everyone, just in case.
  3. Your co-worker (someone your own level, whom you already know a little) walks in at the same time as you. Which greeting fits best — "Morning!", "Good morning", or "Good morning, sir"?
  4. A senior director you've never spoken to is waiting for the lift. Which greeting fits best?

Motivation

"The right word at the right moment is worth more than a long, careful sentence."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Match each greeting to the person it fits best: (a) a senior director you barely know; (b) a peer you already know a little; (c) someone you don't know well, or aren't sure about.

Morning!

________

Good morning.

________

Good morning, sir.

________
2. Multiple Choice

In Scene C, why does Arif greet Mr. Kabir differently from how he greets Priyanka?

A.

Because Mr. Kabir is a stranger he must be suspicious of

B.

Because Mr. Kabir is clearly senior and Arif doesn't know him well yet

C.

Because the lobby is a more formal room than the entrance

3. Controlled Practice

For each situation, write the greeting you would use. (1) Your flatmate, who also works at your company, walking in beside you. (2) The CEO, whom you have never met, in the lift. (3) A colleague from another department you've spoken to twice before.

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part across all three scenes — the security guard, the peer, and the director — adjusting your greeting each time.

Answer Key

1.

Morning! → A peer you already know a little; Good morning. → Someone you don't know well, or aren't sure about; Good morning, sir. → A senior director you barely know. Familiarity and seniority both push the register up or down — "Good morning" is the safe middle choice when unsure.

2.

Correct: B. The choice tracks the person — seniority and how well Arif knows them — not the location.

3.

Suggested answer: 1) Morning! / 2) Good morning, sir. / Good morning, ma'am. / 3) Good morning. (or "Morning!" once you know them a little better)

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses a distinctly different rung of TL-0002 for each of the three people (informal for the guard/peer, formal "Good morning, sir" for the director); does not use the same exact greeting for all three.

lessons.title: Starting a Conversation
lessons.objectives_html:
• Open a short small-talk exchange using a safe, natural opener.
  • Ask one natural follow-up question to keep a conversation going for 2–3 turns.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

The coffee machine has become the unofficial meeting point of the whole floor. Two or three minutes here, before the workday properly starts, might be the most social part of Arif's whole morning — if he knows how to use them.

Key workplace lesson

Small talk isn't wasted time — it's how colleagues become comfortable working with each other. But it only works if it goes somewhere. An opener alone ("Busy morning?") can die in one word ("Yeah.") unless you're ready to follow it with a real question. This lesson is about the pair: opener + follow-up, not just the opener on its own.

Listen & Read
Coffee machine corner, 8:52 AM. Arif and Priyanka, both a few weeks into their jobs, arrive at the same moment.
Priyanka: Morning! Busy morning so far?
Arif: Not too bad, actually. You?
Priyanka: Pretty quiet too, for once. Good weekend?
Arif: Yeah, really good, thanks — just relaxed at home mostly. Yours?
Priyanka: Same, honestly. How was your commute today, by the way? The traffic looked bad.
Arif: A bit slow, but okay. How about yours?
Priyanka: Not too bad — I left a little earlier than usual.
Arif: Smart move. Right, I'd better grab this coffee and get to my desk!

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Busy morning?" A light opener about workload Passing a colleague who looks occupied or relaxed "Busy morning?" Casual, low-pressure — either answer works
"How's your day going?" A general, safe opener Mid-morning, any colleague "How's your day going so far?" Warm, slightly more open-ended than "Busy morning?"
"Yeah, [detail] — how about you?" Answering + returning the question Keeping a conversation balanced, not one-sided "Pretty quiet so far — how about you?" Shows genuine interest, not just politeness

Vocabulary

  • V-0117 busy — having a lot to do; the most common workload descriptor in small talk.
  • V-0118 quiet — (of a workday) not busy; the natural opposite of "busy" in this context.
  • V-0119 weekend — Saturday and Sunday (or a learner's actual days off); one of the safest small-talk topics.
  • V-0120 commute — the journey to and from work; a common, safe follow-up topic ("How was your commute?").

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0009 — Opener + Follow-up: [Opener question]? → [short answer], + how about you? / what about your [topic]?

This two-step shape is the real skill of this lesson. A follow-up doesn't need to be clever — returning the same question, or asking about one extra detail, is enough to keep the exchange natural and two-sided.

Dialogue walkthrough

Two peers, Arif and Priyanka, meet at the coffee machine. Priyanka opens with a workload question; Arif answers and returns it; the exchange naturally extends into the weekend and the commute before both head to their desks. Notice that neither line is long — small talk works in short exchanges, not speeches.

Pronunciation

  • Question intonation rises gently at the end of "Busy morning?" — a flat, falling tone can sound more like a statement than a genuine question.
  • "How about you?" is said as one smooth phrase, not word-by-word — rushing slightly here sounds more natural, not less polite.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Opener with no follow-up readiness: "Busy morning?"... (silence after the answer) — technically fine, but the conversation stalls awkwardly.
  • ✅ Opener + follow-up: "Busy morning?" → "Not too bad, actually. You?" → "Pretty quiet too — good weekend?"

Bengali support

কথোপকথন শুরু করা মানেই দীর্ঘ কথা বলা নয় — সংক্ষিপ্ত প্রশ্ন-উত্তর বিনিময়ই যথেষ্ট, যতক্ষণ না দুজনেই কথা বলার সুযোগ পাচ্ছেন। প্রশ্নটি ফিরিয়ে দেওয়া ("You?") ভদ্রতা দেখানোর সবচেয়ে সহজ উপায়।

Industry overlays

  • Hospitality/retail: The same opener + follow-up shape works with colleagues during a quiet moment on shift, but with customers this becomes a service-toned version, previewed lightly here and taught properly in Level 2's customer-service units.
  • Office: Small talk with a senior manager tends to stay closer to the safe defaults (weather, weekend) rather than personal detail, even when the shape of the exchange is identical.

Self-check

  1. What are two safe topics to build a follow-up question around?
  2. True or false: a good opener is enough on its own, without a follow-up.
  3. Your colleague says "Pretty busy, actually." What's a natural way to keep the conversation going?

Motivation

"Conversation is a skill, not a talent."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Comprehension

In the dialogue, what opener does Priyanka use first?

2. Fill Blank

Complete the follow-up: "Pretty quiet, actually. ___ you?"

3. Guided Practice

Build your own opener + follow-up pair for a colleague you're meeting at the start of a shift. Write both lines.

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part in the coffee-machine exchange, then continue it for two more turns of your own once the dialogue ends.

Answer Key

1.

"Busy morning so far?" — a question about workload. She then moves on to the weekend and the commute.

2.

How about (or What about) — "Pretty quiet, actually. How about you?" This is the simplest, most natural way to return a question.

3.

Suggested answer: Opener: "Morning! Quiet start today?" Follow-up: "Yeah, not bad — how was your weekend?"

4.

What to listen/look for: Answers each opener and returns at least one question of their own in each of the two extended turns, rather than only answering.

lessons.title: Safe and Unsafe Small-Talk Topics
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify at least 5 workplace-safe small-talk topics and 5 topics to avoid.
  • Politely redirect a conversation that has drifted into an unsafe topic.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Small talk has been going well for Arif — until today, when a colleague asks him something a little too personal while they're both waiting for a meeting room to free up.

Key workplace lesson

Not every topic that feels like "just talking" is workplace-safe. Salary, politics, religion, relationship status, and health details can all make a conversation uncomfortable — even when nobody meant harm. This lesson isn't about memorizing a fixed list forever; it's about building judgment: could this topic make either person uncomfortable, or reveal something they haven't chosen to share? If yes, it's worth steering elsewhere — warmly, not awkwardly.

Listen & Read
Outside a meeting room, waiting for it to free up. Arif and a colleague, Farid, have a few minutes to spare.
Farid: So, how are you finding the job so far? Good salary bump from your last place?
Arif: (pauses briefly) That's a fair question — I'd rather not get into the exact numbers, but honestly, I've been really happy with the role so far.
Farid: Fair enough! I get it.
Arif: What about you — how long have you been on this team?
Farid: About two years now. Time's gone fast.
Arif: That's great to hear. Looks like the room's free now, by the way.
Farid: Ah, good timing. Let's head in.
Arif: After you.

Safe vs. unsafe: the working list

Usually safe Usually unsafe / needs care
Weather Salary / how much someone earns
Weekend plans Politics
Commute Religion
Local food / restaurants Relationship status / personal relationships
General hobbies or sports Health details or medical history
Company news (public, non-sensitive) Someone's age

V-0124 sensitive topic — a subject that could make someone uncomfortable or reveal private information; the general category behind everything in the right-hand column above.

Vocabulary

  • V-0121 appropriate — suitable for the situation; fitting the workplace context.
  • V-0122 inappropriate — not suitable for the situation; the opposite of appropriate.
  • V-0123 personal — relating to someone's private life rather than their work.
  • V-0124 sensitive topic — see above.
  • V-0125 redirect — to guide a conversation toward a different, safer topic without shutting the other person down.

The Polite Redirect Formula — CF-0003

ACKNOWLEDGE → DECLINE SOFTLY → REDIRECT

  1. Acknowledge the question was asked (don't ignore it — that reads as rude).
  2. Decline softly — a brief, warm reason not to answer, without over-explaining.
  3. Redirect — offer a related, safer angle, or hand it elsewhere (e.g., HR).

Example: "That's a fair question [acknowledge] — I'd rather not get into the exact number [decline softly], but honestly, I've been really happy with the role so far [redirect]."

Common mistake MIS-0007

Answering bluntly ("That's none of your business" or "Why do you want to know?") shuts the conversation down and can feel hostile, even when the original question genuinely was too personal. The fix is the formula above: acknowledge, decline gently, then redirect — staying warm while still not answering.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too blunt: "That's private. Why would you ask that?"
  • ❌ Over-sharing to avoid awkwardness: giving the full personal detail just because it was asked — this teaches colleagues that any question is fair game.
  • ✅ Warm redirect: "That's a good question for HR, actually — I'm honestly not sure myself." / "I'd rather not get into that, but thanks for asking."

Bengali support

কোন বিষয়টি "ব্যক্তিগত" তা সংস্কৃতিভেদে ভিন্ন হতে পারে — যা এক কর্মক্ষেত্রে স্বাভাবিক প্রশ্ন, অন্য কর্মক্ষেত্রে তা অতিরিক্ত ব্যক্তিগত মনে হতে পারে। এখানে লক্ষ্য কোনো কঠোর নিয়ম মুখস্থ করা নয়, বরং সচেতনতা তৈরি করা — প্রশ্নটি অন্য কাউকে অস্বস্তিতে ফেলতে পারে কিনা তা বোঝা।

Industry overlays

This is one of the few genuinely industry-independent lessons in Level 1 — the safe/unsafe judgment and the redirect skill apply almost identically in an office, a hotel, a bank, or a clinic.

Self-check

  1. Name two topics that are usually safe for workplace small talk.
  2. Name two topics that usually need care.
  3. A colleague asks how much you earn. Using the Polite Redirect Formula, write a short response.

Motivation

"Professionalism protects relationships."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Sorting

Sort each topic into Safe, Unsafe, or Depends: weather, salary, weekend plans, religion, local restaurants, relationship status, company news, someone's age.

2. Multiple Choice

In the dialogue, which step of the Polite Redirect Formula does Arif's line "That's a fair question" represent?

A.

Acknowledge

B.

Decline softly

C.

Redirect

3. Situational Response

A colleague asks: "Are you married? Any kids?" Using the Polite Redirect Formula (Acknowledge → Decline softly → Redirect), write your response.

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part. A colleague asks about your salary, then about your relationship status. Redirect both questions politely.

Answer Key

1.

Safe: weather, weekend plans, local restaurants. Unsafe / needs care: salary, religion, relationship status, someone's age. Depends: company news — safe when it is public and non-sensitive (a new restaurant opening in the hotel), not when it is about people's jobs, pay or rumours. The key question is whether the topic could make someone uncomfortable or reveal something private.

2.

Correct: A. "That's a fair question" acknowledges Farid's question before Arif declines and redirects in the rest of the same line.

3.

Suggested answer: Ha, that's kind of you to ask — I tend to keep that side of things private, but I'm settling into the job well, thanks!

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses all three steps of the Polite Redirect Formula (acknowledge, decline softly, redirect) for both questions, without bluntly refusing to answer.

lessons.title: Ending a Conversation Politely
lessons.objectives_html:
• End a small-talk conversation politely without seeming abrupt or rude.
  • Transition smoothly back to work.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Break time is nearly over, and Arif is mid-conversation with a colleague. Cutting it off badly could feel rude; letting it run on could make him late back to his desk. This lesson is the last piece of the small-talk skill set: knowing when, and how, to stop.

Key workplace lesson

A conversation that ends well leaves both people feeling good about it — just like Module 2 taught you that how you leave at the end of the day matters as much as how you arrive. The same idea applies here, on a much smaller scale: a short, warm closing line, plus a light reason for leaving, closes the exchange cleanly.

Listen & Read
Break room, break time almost over. Arif and Priyanka have been chatting for a few minutes.
Priyanka: Anyway, that's my weekend! Pretty uneventful compared to yours.
Arif: Ha, sounds relaxing though. Listen, it was nice talking to you — I'd better get back to it.
Priyanka: Yeah, me too, actually. Catch up later?
Arif: Definitely. See you at lunch!
Priyanka: See you then. Have a good one!
Arif: You too!

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"Well, I'd better get back to it." A light, standard way to end and return to work Ending small talk to resume a task "Well, I'd better get back to it — catch up later!" Casual but clear, never abrupt
"It was nice talking to you — let's catch up later." A warm, complete closing Ending a longer or particularly pleasant exchange "It was nice talking to you — let's catch up later." Warm, forward-looking
"Catch up (with someone)" To talk again and share news, later Signaling the conversation will continue another time "Let's catch up at lunch." Informal but very common at work

Vocabulary

  • V-0126 catch up (phrasal verb) — to talk again later and share news; a natural way to promise a future conversation without committing to details.
  • V-0127 get back to it — to return to work or a task; the standard way to signal you're ending small talk, not the person.

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0010 — Closing + Transition: [Closing comment], + [transition back to work] e.g. "It was nice talking to you — I'd better get back to it." The two halves work together: the first half is warm (protects the relationship), the second half is practical (signals the real reason you're leaving isn't the other person).

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too abrupt: (walking away mid-sentence, no closing line at all) — reads as rude, even if unintentional.
  • ❌ Overexplaining: giving a long list of reasons why you have to go — unnecessary and can feel like an excuse.
  • ✅ Clean close: "It was nice talking to you — I'd better get back to it. Catch up later!"

Bengali support

কথোপকথন শেষ করা মানেই সম্পর্ক শেষ করা নয় — একটি সংক্ষিপ্ত, উষ্ণ সমাপ্তি বাক্য এবং কাজে ফেরার হালকা কারণ যথেষ্ট। দীর্ঘ ব্যাখ্যার প্রয়োজন নেই।

Industry overlays

Universal — no industry-specific variation needed. The same closing shape works identically in every workplace setting covered so far.

Self-check

  1. What are the two parts of a good conversation-closing?
  2. True or false: it's polite to explain in detail exactly why you need to leave.
  3. Write a closing line for ending small talk and heading back to your desk.

Motivation

"Knowing when to stop is also a communication skill."

Module 3 final task

Exercise 4 is the final task for Module 3: a short, unscripted small-talk role-play that uses all four lessons — choosing the right register (Lesson 3.1), opening and following up (Lesson 3.2), staying on safe topics or redirecting when needed (Lesson 3.3), and closing cleanly (Lesson 3.4).
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Which line in the dialogue signals that Arif is ending the conversation?

A.

"Ha, sounds relaxing though."

B.

"It was nice talking to you — I'd better get back to it."

C.

"See you then. Have a good one!"

2. Fill Blank

Complete the phrase: "Well, I'd better ___ ___ to it."

3. Guided Practice

Write your own closing line that combines a warm comment with a transition back to work, for a conversation with a colleague at the printer.

4. Role-Play Assessment

Module 3 final task. Play a short, unscripted small-talk exchange with a colleague from start to finish: choose an appropriate greeting for who you're speaking to, open with a safe small-talk topic and a follow-up, stay on safe ground (redirecting politely if the conversation drifts), and close the conversation cleanly to get back to work.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. This line combines the warm closing comment with the practical transition back to work — exactly the two-part pattern this lesson teaches.

2.

get back — "Well, I'd better get back to it." This is the standard phrase for returning to work after small talk.

3.

Suggested answer: It was good chatting — I should get this printing done before my next call. Catch up soon!

4.

Scoring: give one point for each of the four Module 3 skills shown in one continuous exchange — register choice at the greeting, an opener with at least one follow-up question, a polite redirect if the partner introduces a sensitive topic, and a two-part closing line (warm comment + transition back to work). 4 points = task complete; 3 = complete with one weak area to practice; 2 or fewer = repeat the lesson whose skill was missing.

modules.title: Understanding Instructions
modules.purpose: Understand instructions completely: listen for the key details, confirm what you heard, organize multi-step tasks, and say clearly when something is unclear.

lessons.title: Listening for Key Information
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify the core action, object, and deadline in a spoken instruction.
  • Take a brief mental or written note of a 2-part instruction without losing the second part.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Supervisors rarely give instructions slowly or perfectly — they talk at a normal pace, sometimes pack two things into one sentence, and expect you to catch what matters. This lesson trains one specific skill: catching the action, the object, and the deadline inside instructions that are never repeated for you.

Key workplace lesson

Every instruction, however casually phrased, usually has three parts hiding inside it: what to do (the action), what it's done to (the object), and when it's needed by (the deadline). Missing the deadline is the single most common way new employees accidentally look unreliable — not because they didn't do the task, but because nobody registered when it was due. Training your ear to grab all three parts, every time, turns a spoken instruction into one clear action item you can act on with confidence — that's this lesson's whole job.

The three parts

Part Question it answers Example
Action What do I need to do? "restock", "file", "update"
Object What am I doing it to? "the shelf", "the folder", "the chart"
Deadline By when? "before your shift ends", "by 2 PM", "before the client call"

Vocabulary

  • V-0128 key information — the specific facts that actually matter in what someone said (as opposed to filler or small talk).
  • V-0129 note down — to briefly write something so you don't forget it.
  • V-0130 task — a piece of work you've been asked to do.
  • V-0131 action item — a specific task that came out of an instruction or a meeting.

Grammar in context

GIC-0004 — Instruction forms: imperative vs. "Can you...?" Workplace instructions arrive in two common shapes:

  • Imperative: "Restock the top shelf before your shift ends." — direct, common from a busy supervisor; not rude, just efficient.
  • "Can you...?" (softened request): "Can you restock the top shelf before your shift ends?" — same instruction, softer delivery. Both mean the same thing: you're being asked to do it. Don't wait for a "please" to treat an imperative as a real instruction.

Three graded listening clips

(Audio for these clips is not available yet. Read each one quickly, as if it were spoken at a natural speed, or ask a partner or teacher to read them aloud to you, getting faster each time.)

Clip A (retail, easier pace): "Can you restock the top shelf before your shift ends?" → Action: restock · Object: the top shelf · Deadline: before shift ends

Clip B (office, natural pace, two parts): "File these invoices, and make sure the totals match the report before you send it up." → Action: file (+ check totals match) · Object: invoices / the report · Deadline: before sending it up

Clip C (IT, fastest, two actions): "Update the dashboard with this week's numbers and flag anything that looks off to me by end of day." → Action 1: update (the dashboard) · Action 2: flag anything unusual · Deadline: end of day

Pronunciation

  • Real workplace speech runs words together ("wanna," "gonna," "shift ends" as almost one sound) — train your ear for the whole phrase, not each word separately.
  • The deadline is often tucked at the very end of the sentence, sometimes almost an afterthought in tone — don't relax your attention once the action and object are clear.

Professional tone

This lesson has no weak-vs-strong tone contrast — the skill here is pure listening accuracy, not speaking register.

Bengali support

নির্দেশনা শোনার সময় তিনটি জিনিস ধরার চেষ্টা করুন: কী করতে হবে (action), কীসের উপর করতে হবে (object), এবং কোন সময়ের মধ্যে করতে হবে (deadline)। deadline প্রায়ই বাক্যের একদম শেষে, হালকা স্বরে বলা হয় — মনোযোগ শিথিল করবেন না বাক্য শেষ হওয়া পর্যন্ত।

Industry overlays

The three clips above already model this lesson's industry range on purpose: retail (restocking), office (filing/reporting), and IT (dashboards) — the skill of catching action/object/deadline is identical in every case; only the vocabulary changes.

Self-check

  1. What are the three parts to listen for in any instruction?
  2. True or false: an imperative sentence ("File this.") is less of a real instruction than "Can you file this?"
  3. In Clip B above, what's the deadline?

Motivation

"Listening well is a professional skill, not a passive act."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Comprehension

Clip A: "Can you restock the top shelf before your shift ends?" What is the deadline?

2. Comprehension

Clip B has two actions packed into one instruction. What is the second one?

3. Note Taking

Read Clip C (or have a partner read it aloud) and note down the action(s), object, and deadline in three short phrases.

4. Quiz

For each of the three clips, write the action, object, and deadline you identified. This is the lesson's full listening quiz across all three graded clips.

Answer Key

1.

"Before your shift ends." Note that the deadline comes at the very end of the sentence.

2.

Make sure the totals match the report (before sending it up). The second action is easy to lose if you stop listening after "file".

3.

Suggested answer: Action 1: update dashboard. Action 2: flag anything unusual. Deadline: end of day.

4.

Suggested answer: Clip A — Action: restock; Object: the top shelf; Deadline: before shift ends. / Clip B — Action: file (+ check totals match); Object: invoices / the report; Deadline: before sending it up. / Clip C — Action: update (+ flag anything unusual); Object: the dashboard; Deadline: end of day.

lessons.title: Confirming and Repeating Instructions
lessons.objectives_html:
• Confirm an instruction by repeating it back accurately.
  • Use at least 3 different natural confirmation phrases, not just "okay."
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif caught every part of Mr. Hossain's instruction — action, object, deadline. Now comes the part that actually shows it: saying it back, out loud, in his own words.

Key workplace lesson

"Okay" tells your supervisor you heard something. It doesn't tell them you understood the right thing. Repeating an instruction back — briefly, in your own words — does two jobs at once: it proves you understood, and it gives your supervisor one last chance to correct you before you've already started the wrong task.

Listen & Read
An office desk, mid-morning. Mr. Hossain, Arif's supervisor, stops by with two instructions during the same short visit.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, can you email the client the updated quote before lunch?
Arif: So you'd like me to email the client the updated quote before lunch? Got it.
Mr. Hossain: Perfect. Oh, and one more thing — could you also file yesterday's receipts, and then send me a short summary once that's done?
Arif: Just to confirm, I should file yesterday's receipts first, and then send you a summary once that's finished?
Mr. Hossain: Exactly right.
Arif: Got it — I'll get the quote out first, then take care of the receipts and summary after.
Mr. Hossain: Sounds good. Thanks, Arif.
Arif: No problem.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"So you'd like me to..." Restating the instruction as you understood it Right after receiving a clear instruction "So you'd like me to email the client before lunch?" Neutral, careful
"Just to confirm, I should..." A slightly more formal restatement Multi-part or important instructions "Just to confirm, I should file these first, then send the summary." Careful, thorough
"Got it — I'll..." A quick, confident confirmation Simple, single-part instructions "Got it — I'll have it ready by 2." Brisk, confident

Vocabulary

  • V-0132 confirm — to state something back to make sure it's correct.
  • V-0133 restate — to say something again, in your own words, to show you understood it.
  • V-0134 to make sure — to check or confirm something is correct.

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0011 — Confirmation Restatement: So you'd like me to + [verb]...? / Just to confirm, I should + [verb]... / Got it — I'll + [verb]... All three forms do the same job — restate the instruction in your own words — but at different levels of formality/thoroughness. Using only one of them, every time, starts to sound robotic; this lesson's whole point is having at least three ready to alternate between.

Common mistake

Saying only "Okay" or "Okay, okay" after every instruction gives your supervisor zero information about whether you actually understood — it sounds compliant, not competent. A brief restatement takes one extra second, lets you both make sure you agree on the task, and prevents far more expensive mistakes later.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too thin: "Okay." (said after every instruction, with no restatement) — technically polite, but proves nothing.
  • ❌ Too repetitive: "Got it. Got it. Got it." (the same phrase three times in one conversation) — sounds mechanical rather than genuinely engaged.
  • ✅ Confirmed and varied: "So you'd like me to email the client before lunch? Got it." → later: "Just to confirm, I should file these first, then send the summary."

Bengali support

শুধু "ঠিক আছে" বলাটা আপনি শুনেছেন তা বোঝায়, কিন্তু আপনি সঠিকভাবে বুঝেছেন তা প্রমাণ করে না। নির্দেশনাটি নিজের ভাষায় সংক্ষেপে ফিরিয়ে বলাই সবচেয়ে নিরাপদ অভ্যাস — এতে ভুল বোঝাবুঝি সাথে সাথেই ধরা পড়ে।

Industry overlays

This confirmation habit is identical across every industry — a hotel front-desk instruction, a retail restocking instruction, and an office filing instruction are all confirmed the same way; only the task content changes.

Self-check

  1. Why is repeating an instruction back better than just saying "okay"?
  2. Name two of the three confirmation phrases from this lesson.
  3. Your supervisor says: "Can you print 20 copies of this before the 3 o'clock meeting?" Write your confirmation, using one of this lesson's phrases.

Motivation

"Confirming shows respect, not weakness."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Transformation

Transform this instruction into a confirmation using "So you'd like me to...?": "Can you print 20 copies of this before the 3 o'clock meeting?"

2. Multiple Choice

In the dialogue, which confirmation phrase does Arif use for the second, two-part instruction?

A.

Got it — I'll...

B.

Just to confirm, I should...

C.

Okay, okay.

3. Guided Practice

Your supervisor gives you three instructions in a row. Confirm all three, using a different one of the three confirmation phrases each time.

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part in the dialogue, confirming both instructions from Mr. Hossain using two different confirmation phrases (not "okay" both times).

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: So you'd like me to print 20 copies of this before the 3 o'clock meeting?

2.

Correct: B. Arif uses "Just to confirm, I should..." for the more detailed, multi-part instruction — matching the lesson's guidance to use the more thorough form for complex instructions.

3.

Suggested answer: 1) "So you'd like me to...?" 2) "Just to confirm, I should..." 3) "Got it — I'll..."

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses at least 2 different confirmation phrases from PAT-0011 across the two instructions, and each restatement accurately reflects the instruction given (not a vague "okay").

lessons.title: Understanding Priorities, Sequence and Deadlines
lessons.objectives_html:
• Correctly order 3 tasks given out of sequence in a spoken instruction.
  • Identify which of several tasks is most urgent.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Mr. Hossain has three things for Arif today — but he doesn't give them in the order they should be done, and he doesn't announce which one matters most. Arif has to work that out from how the instruction is phrased.

Key workplace lesson

Real instructions rarely arrive as a neat numbered list. A supervisor might mention the most urgent task last, almost as an afterthought, or list tasks in the order they came to mind rather than the order they should be done. Priority isn't a personality trait some people are naturally good at — it's a listening skill: catching the urgency words and re-sorting the tasks yourself before you start.

Listen & Read
Office floor, mid-morning. Mr. Hossain gives Arif three tasks in one go, out of the order they should actually be done, with one clearly urgent.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, can you set up the meeting room for this afternoon, and file yesterday's receipts whenever you get a chance? Oh, and actually — the client's been waiting on a reply, that one's urgent, could you get to that first?
Arif: Got it. So the client reply is urgent — I'll do that first. Then I'll set up the meeting room for this afternoon, and file the receipts whenever I get a chance after that.
Mr. Hossain: Exactly right. Thanks, Arif.
Arif: No problem — I'll message you once the client's been taken care of.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example
"First... then... after that..." Sequencing multiple tasks Restating tasks in the order to do them "First I'll reply to the client, then update the file, and after that prep the room."
"Urgent" / "as soon as possible" Marking the highest-priority task Identifying what needs doing first "That one's urgent — I'll do it first."
"By end of day (EOD)" A same-day deadline Tasks due before the workday ends "The report's needed by end of day."
"Whenever you get a chance" A low-priority, flexible deadline Tasks with no real time pressure "The filing's fine whenever you get a chance."

Vocabulary

  • V-0135 priority — the task that should be done first, or that matters most right now.
  • V-0136 urgent — needing action very soon; higher priority than other tasks.
  • V-0137 by end of day (EOD) — workplace shorthand for "before the workday finishes today."
  • V-0138 whenever you get a chance — a low-pressure deadline; no fixed time, do it when you have a free moment.

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0012 — Sequencing + Priority Restatement: First, I'll + [verb]... Then... After that... The urgent one is + [task], so I'll do that first. This pattern does two jobs at once: it puts the tasks in the right order, and it explicitly names which one is most urgent — even if the original instruction buried that detail in the middle.

Bengali/Hindi support

"EOD" (by end of day) এবং "ASAP" (as soon as possible)-এর মতো সংক্ষিপ্ত রূপ সরাসরি বাংলায় অনুবাদ করা যায় না — এগুলো ইংরেজি কর্মক্ষেত্রের নিজস্ব সংক্ষিপ্ত ভাষা, যা মুখস্থ করে নেওয়াই ভালো: EOD মানে আজকের কর্মদিবস শেষ হওয়ার আগে, ASAP মানে যত দ্রুত সম্ভব।

Common pitfall

  • ❌ Missed priority: doing the three tasks in the exact order they were mentioned, without noticing that the urgent one was actually mentioned last.
  • ✅ Correctly reordered: "So the client reply is urgent — I'll do that first, then set up the room for this afternoon, and file the receipts whenever I get a chance after that."

Professional tone

  • ❌ Uncommitted: "Umm, I guess I'll just do them in whatever order?" — technically responsive, but gives no sign you actually registered which task was urgent.
  • ✅ Confident and clear: "Since the client reply is urgent, I'll handle that first, then move on to the room setup and the filing." — shows you understood the priority and are acting on it, not just agreeing to agree.

Industry overlays

Multi-tasking under priority is universal across every industry — a hotel front desk, a retail floor, and an office all face the same "three things at once, one of them urgent" pattern; only the specific tasks change.

Self-check

  1. What are two words that signal a task is high priority?
  2. What does "EOD" mean?
  3. Your supervisor says: "Reply to the client whenever you get a chance, but the invoice needs to go out by end of day — oh, and can you also restock the samples, that's urgent." Put these three tasks in the correct order.

Motivation

"Priority is a skill you can learn, not a personality trait."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Sequencing

Based on the dialogue, put these three tasks in the correct order to do them: (a) file yesterday's receipts; (b) set up the meeting room; (c) reply to the client.

2. Multiple Choice

Which word in the dialogue signals the highest-priority task?

A.

Whenever

B.

Urgent

C.

Afternoon

3. Guided Practice

Restate this instruction in priority order using PAT-0012: "Reply to the client whenever you get a chance, but the invoice needs to go out by end of day — oh, and can you also restock the samples, that's urgent."

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part. Your supervisor gives you three tasks out of order, with one marked urgent. Restate all three in the correct priority order.

Answer Key

1.

1. Reply to the client (marked urgent, although it was mentioned last). 2. Set up the meeting room (needed this afternoon). 3. File yesterday's receipts ("whenever you get a chance").

2.

Correct: B. "That one's urgent" is the clearest priority signal in the instruction.

3.

Suggested answer: The samples are urgent, so I'll restock those first. Then I'll send the invoice, since that's needed by end of day. I'll reply to the client whenever I get a chance after that.

4.

What to listen/look for: Correctly identifies the urgent task and places it first regardless of the order it was mentioned in, and uses sequence connectors (first, then, after that) to restate all three tasks clearly.

lessons.title: Saying When Something Is Unclear
lessons.objectives_html:
• Say clearly and politely that part of an instruction is unclear.
  • Avoid pretending to understand when you don't.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Mr. Hossain's instruction was almost entirely clear — except for one term Arif has never heard before. He has a choice: nod and guess, or say something.

Key workplace lesson

This is the fallback skill for everything Module 4 has taught so far — and it's deliberately the last lesson in the module, because it only works well once you already know how to listen for key information (Lesson 4.1), confirm accurately (Lesson 4.2), and sort priority (Lesson 4.3). This lesson is a light preview of a skill Module 5 covers in full: for now, the goal is simply learning to name the specific unclear part, instead of either guessing silently or repeating a flat, unhelpful "I don't understand."

Listen & Read
Office desk, afternoon. Mr. Hossain gives Arif an instruction that includes one term Arif hasn't heard before.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, once you've gone through the client list, if anything looks off, just escalate it — don't try to fix it yourself yet.
Arif: Got it on going through the list — but I'm not sure I understood the last part. When you say "escalate it," could you clarify what exactly you mean?
Mr. Hossain: Good question — just message me directly if you spot anything unusual, don't change anything in the file.
Arif: Got it — message you directly, don't edit the file myself. Thanks for clarifying.
Mr. Hossain: No problem at all — better to ask than guess.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example Tone note
"I'm not sure I understood the last part." Flagging confusion about one specific part When most of an instruction was clear except one piece "I'm not sure I understood the last part — could you say that again?" Calm, specific, not apologetic
"Could you clarify what you mean by...?" Asking about one specific unclear term When a single word or phrase was the problem "Could you clarify what you mean by 'escalate it'?" Confident, targeted
"I don't understand." A vague, general statement of confusion Avoid as your only tool — it doesn't say what's unclear "I don't understand." (said flatly, with no explanation of which part) Too vague on its own

Vocabulary

  • V-0139 clarify — to make something clearer or easier to understand.
  • V-0140 the last part — a way of pointing to the specific piece of an instruction that wasn't clear, rather than the whole thing.
  • V-0141 what exactly — used to ask for a precise detail ("What exactly do you mean by...?").

Common mistake MIS-0008

Relying only on a flat "I don't understand" tells your supervisor almost nothing useful — they now have to guess which part confused you and re-explain the whole thing from scratch. Naming the specific part ("the last part," "what you mean by 'escalate it'") gets you a faster, more targeted answer and shows you were actually following along.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too vague: "I don't understand." (with no indication of what part)
  • ❌ Pretending to understand: nodding and saying "okay" while genuinely unsure — the most costly option, since the mistake only surfaces later.
  • ✅ Specific and confident: "I'm not sure I understood the last part — when you say 'escalate it,' do you mean tell you directly, or note it somewhere?"

Bengali support

"আমি বুঝিনি" শুধু বললে আপনার সুপারভাইজারকে পুরো নির্দেশনাটা আবার প্রথম থেকে ব্যাখ্যা করতে হয়। কোন নির্দিষ্ট অংশটা অস্পষ্ট তা বলে দিলে (যেমন, "শেষ অংশটা", বা "'escalate it' বলতে ঠিক কী বোঝাচ্ছেন") দ্রুত এবং সঠিক উত্তর পাওয়া যায়।

Industry overlays

Light — this fallback skill applies identically across industries; only the specific unclear term changes (a hotel-specific term, a software term, a banking term).

Self-check

  1. Why is naming the specific unclear part better than saying "I don't understand"?
  2. True or false: pretending to understand is a safe option if you're fairly confident you can figure it out later.
  3. Rewrite "I don't understand" as two better, more specific alternatives.

Motivation

"Asking is not weakness — guessing wrong is the real risk."

Module 4 final task

Exercise 4 is the final task for Module 4. It combines all four lessons: catching the key information (Lesson 4.1), confirming it accurately (Lesson 4.2), sorting priority when there is more than one task (Lesson 4.3), and flagging the one part that is genuinely unclear (Lesson 4.4).
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

In the dialogue, which part of the instruction does Arif flag as unclear?

A.

Going through the client list

B.

What "escalate it" means

C.

When the task is due

2. Rewriting

Rewrite "I don't understand" as two better, more specific alternatives.

3. Guided Practice

Your supervisor says: "Once you're done, just loop in the front desk." You don't know what "loop in" means. Write what you would say.

4. Role-Play Assessment

Module 4 final task. A partner reads you this instruction: "Can you print the rooming list for the Haque group and leave it at the front desk before 2? Oh, and reconcile the deposit sheet by end of day." Confirm the parts you understood, flag the unfamiliar term, and once your partner explains it ("check that the deposits on the sheet match the payments in the system"), restate both tasks in order.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. Arif confirms the first part (going through the list) but specifically names "escalate it" as the unclear term.

2.

Suggested answer: I'm not sure I understood the last part — could you say that again? / Could you clarify what exactly you mean by "escalate it"?

3.

Suggested answer: I'm not sure I understood that last part — could you clarify what you mean by "loop in"?

4.

Sample: "Got it — print the rooming list for the Haque group and leave it at the front desk before 2. I'm not sure I understood the last part, though — what exactly do you mean by 'reconcile the deposit sheet'?" … "So, first the rooming list by 2, then I'll check the deposit sheet against the system by end of day." Scoring (1 point each): confirms the first task accurately; names the unclear term ("reconcile") instead of saying "I don't understand"; restates both tasks with their deadlines; keeps the order (2 PM before end of day). 4 = task complete; 3 = complete with one area to practice; 2 or fewer = review the lesson for the missed skill.

modules.title: Asking for Help & Clarification
modules.purpose: Ask for help with confidence: ask someone to repeat or explain, ask a precise clarifying question, and choose the right person and tone.

lessons.title: Asking Someone to Repeat or Explain
lessons.objectives_html:
• Politely ask someone to repeat something without apologizing excessively.
  • Politely ask someone to explain something in a different way.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Mr. Hossain passes Arif's desk on his way to a meeting and gives him an instruction over his shoulder, fast, without stopping. Arif catches most of it — but not all of it. Module 4 taught Arif to notice and flag that something is unclear. This lesson teaches the exact next move: asking for it back, cleanly, in one sentence, without turning a two-second gap into a confession.

Key workplace lesson

Missing part of what someone said is completely normal — it happens to fluent speakers in their own language too, in a noisy office or a fast conversation. The real mistake most learners make isn't missing it. It's over-apologizing for missing it: "I'm so sorry, I'm really sorry, could you..." turns an ordinary two-second request into something that sounds like a mistake was made. One clear, brief request — with at most one short "sorry" — reads as confident. Repeating the apology, or stretching it out, reads as anxious, and it also just wastes both people's time.

Listen & Read
A corridor outside the office, mid-morning. Mr. Hossain is on his way to a meeting and gives Arif an instruction without slowing down.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, before you send the quote, check with Priyanka about the discount code, and make sure it's applied before it goes to the printer — I'll explain the code when I'm back.
Arif: Sorry, could you say that again? I caught the discount code part, but I missed what happens after.
Mr. Hossain: Check the discount code with Priyanka, apply it to the quote, and don't send the quote to the printer until the code's confirmed.
Arif: Got it, thank you.
Mr. Hossain: One more thing — the client wants "priority processing." I know that sounds vague.
Arif: Could you explain that a different way? I'm not sure what "priority processing" actually means for this order.
Mr. Hossain: It just means their order jumps to the front of today's queue — nothing more technical than that.
Arif: That makes sense. I'll take care of both.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example
"Sorry, could you say that again?" Asking someone to repeat their exact words You missed the words themselves "Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catch the last part."
"Could you explain that a different way?" Asking someone to rephrase, not just repeat You heard the words but the meaning didn't land "Could you explain that a different way? I'm not sure I followed."
"One more time?" A short, informal repeat request With a peer, or in a fast, informal moment "One more time? Sorry, missed that."

Vocabulary

  • V-0142 repeat — to say something again, in the same words.
  • V-0143 explain differently — to describe the same idea using different words, not just saying it louder or slower.
  • V-0144 one more time — a short, informal way of asking for a repeat.

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0013 — Repeat/Rephrase Request: Sorry, could you + say/repeat + that again? / Could you explain that + in a different way / another way? Both forms attach politely to almost anything that was just said, and both fit into one calm sentence — no apology paragraph required. The choice between them depends on what was missing: use the repeat version when you didn't catch the words, and the rephrase version when you heard the words clearly but the meaning didn't land.

Common mistake

MIS-0009 — Over-apologizing: "I'm so sorry, I'm really sorry, could you say that again?" The extra apologies don't make the request more polite — they make a completely normal moment sound like a mistake was made. One short "sorry" (or none, with a peer) is enough; the confidence is in moving straight to the actual request.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Over-apologetic: "Oh no, I'm so sorry, I'm really sorry about this, could you maybe say that one more time?" — three apologies for a two-second request.
  • ❌ Too abrupt: "What?" — technically gets the repeat, but sounds impatient or rude, especially with a supervisor.
  • ✅ Confident and brief: "Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catch the last part." — one short acknowledgment, then straight to the request.

Bengali/Hindi support

একবার "sorry" বলাই যথেষ্ট — বারবার ক্ষমা চাওয়ার দরকার নেই। এটি ভুল স্বীকার করা নয়, শুধু কিছু মিস করা — এটা খুবই স্বাভাবিক ঘটনা। एक बार "sorry" कहना काफी है — बार-बार माफी माँगने की ज़रूरत नहीं। कुछ सुनाई न देना कोई गलती नहीं है, यह हर किसी के साथ होता है।

Industry overlays

Universal across every industry — a nurse asking a doctor to repeat an instruction, a bank clerk asking a manager to explain a procedure again, and a hotel employee asking a supervisor to clarify a task all use exactly this language; only the specific instruction content changes.

Self-check

  1. What's the difference between asking someone to repeat something and asking them to explain it differently?
  2. Why is saying "sorry" three times not actually more polite than saying it once?
  3. Your supervisor gives you an instruction very quickly and you miss the last part entirely. What exactly do you say?

Motivation

"Clarity is a gift to both people in the conversation."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

In the dialogue, why does Arif use two different request phrases with Mr. Hossain?

A.

The first time he missed the words; the second time he heard the words but not the meaning

B.

He was just being extra polite the second time

C.

He wanted to sound less repetitive

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this over-apologetic request into one confident sentence: "Oh no, I'm so sorry, I'm really sorry about this, could you maybe say that one more time?"

3. Guided Practice

A colleague explains a process to you, but you only understood the words — not what they mean in practice. What exactly do you say?

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part in the dialogue — ask Mr. Hossain to repeat the first instruction and to explain the second one differently, using the two different request types correctly.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: A. Arif's first request ("could you say that again?") is for missed words; his second ("could you explain that a different way?") is for an unclear meaning — the two phrases are not interchangeable.

2.

Suggested answer: Sorry, could you say that again? / Could you say that one more time?

3.

Suggested answer: Could you explain that a different way? I heard you, but I'm not sure I followed.

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses the repeat-request form for missed words and the rephrase-request form for an unclear meaning (not the same phrase for both), and does not over-apologize (MIS-0009) — at most one short "sorry" per request.

lessons.title: Asking the Right Clarifying Question
lessons.objectives_html:
• Ask a specific clarifying question targeted at the actual point of confusion, not a vague "what do you mean?"
  • Choose between a yes/no confirming question and an open clarifying question depending on the situation.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif understood almost all of Priyanka's request for the updated numbers — except one detail: which meeting she means. He could ask "What do you mean?" and hope the answer covers it. Or he could ask exactly the question that's actually bothering him. This lesson is about the second option.

Key workplace lesson

"What do you mean?" is not wrong, but it puts all the work back on the other person — they have to guess which part confused you and re-explain the whole thing. A targeted question does the opposite: it shows exactly what you already understood and names the one piece that's still unclear. That's faster for both people, and it also makes you look like someone who was actually listening, not someone who tuned out.

Listen & Read
Vague version
Priyanka's desk, late afternoon. She's asked Arif for something, but he's not sure which of two things she means.
Priyanka: Arif, can you send me the updated numbers before the meeting?
Arif: Sorry, what do you mean?
Priyanka: The numbers... for the meeting. The ones we talked about.
Arif: Oh — okay, I'll figure it out.
Targeted version
The same moment, replayed — this time Arif asks a targeted question instead.
Priyanka: Arif, can you send me the updated numbers before the meeting?
Arif: Just to check — do you mean the team meeting at 11, or the client meeting at 4 PM?
Priyanka: The 4 PM one, sorry — I should have said that.
Arif: No problem, I'll have them ready by 3:30.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example
"Just to check — do you mean X or Y?" A yes/no-style confirming question between two specific options You have a good guess and just need it confirmed "Just to check — do you mean the report for this week or last week?"
"Could you tell me specifically what...?" An open clarifying question about one exact detail You don't have a guess, but you know exactly which detail is missing "Could you tell me specifically what format they want it in?"
"Do you mean...?" A direct way to name your best guess and check it You have one clear guess "Do you mean the version with the March numbers?"

Vocabulary

  • V-0145 specifically — exactly, in particular (used to narrow a question to one detail).
  • V-0146 do you mean — a phrase for naming your guess and checking it against what the other person meant.
  • V-0147 just to check — a soft opener for a confirming question.

Grammar in context

Pattern PAT-0014 — Targeted Clarifying Question: Just to check — do you mean + [option A] + or + [option B]? / Could you tell me specifically + what/when/which + [the missing detail]? The first half of the pattern (yes/no confirming) works when you can narrow the confusion down to two real options. The second half (open clarifying) works when you genuinely don't know the answer yet, but you do know exactly which detail is missing. Naming the detail — not just saying "I'm confused" — is what makes both versions targeted instead of vague.

Before/after, worked example:

  • ❌ Vague: "Sorry, what do you mean?"
  • ✅ Targeted: "Just to check — do you mean the report for this week or last week?"

Common mistake

MIS-0010 — Asking a vague clarifying question: "What do you mean?" or "Can you explain?" after an instruction that was mostly clear, except for one detail. It forces the other person to re-explain everything instead of just answering the one real gap, and it can also make it look like you weren't following at all — when really, you understood 90% of it.

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too vague: "Sorry, what do you mean?" — after Priyanka's request, this makes it sound like Arif understood nothing.
  • ❌ Guessing silently and getting it wrong: submitting last week's report without checking, because asking felt like extra effort.
  • ✅ Targeted and confident: "Just to check — do you mean the report for this week or last week?" — shows exactly what was understood and names the one real gap.

Bengali/Hindi support

"কী বলতে চাইছেন?" (or "आपका क्या मतलब है?") অনেক সময় বাংলা/হিন্দিতে স্বাভাবিক শোনালেও, ইংরেজিতে এর সরাসরি অনুবাদ ("What do you mean?") প্রায়ই খুব অস্পষ্ট শোনায়। নির্দিষ্ট বিকল্প বা বিস্তারিত উল্লেখ করে প্রশ্ন করা অনেক বেশি পেশাদার শোনায়। "आपका क्या मतलब है?" का सीधा अनुवाद अंग्रेज़ी में अक्सर बहुत अस्पष्ट लगता है — किसी खास विकल्प या विवरण का नाम लेकर पूछना कहीं ज़्यादा पेशेवर लगता है।

Industry overlays

The same skill applies everywhere the exact same words can carry two different real meanings — "the report" (this week or last week), "the room" (which floor, which number), "the client" (which one, of several). The example content changes by industry; the targeting skill doesn't.

Self-check

  1. What's the problem with asking "What do you mean?" when you actually understood most of an instruction?
  2. When should you use a yes/no confirming question instead of an open clarifying question?
  3. Priyanka says: "Can you send me the updated numbers before the meeting?" You're not sure which meeting she means — there are two today. Write a targeted clarifying question.

Motivation

"A good question saves everyone time."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

In Scene A (the vague version), what problem does Arif's question create?

A.

It's rude to Priyanka

B.

It doesn't tell Priyanka which specific detail Arif is unsure about, so she can't answer it properly

C.

It takes too long to say

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this vague question as a targeted one: You're told "Can you book the room for tomorrow?" but there are two meeting rooms on your floor. Write a targeted clarifying question.

3. Guided Practice

A colleague says, "Can you follow up with the client?" You work with two clients this week. Ask a targeted clarifying question.

4. Role-Play

Play Arif's part in both versions of the scene — first the vague question, then the targeted one — so the contrast is clear in your own voice.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. "What do you mean?" gives Priyanka nothing to work with — she doesn't know Arif is confused about which numbers, so her reply ("the numbers... for the meeting") doesn't actually fix anything.

2.

Suggested answer: Just to check — do you mean the small meeting room or the main conference room?

3.

Suggested answer: Just to check — do you mean the client from Tuesday's call, or the new one?

4.

What to listen/look for: Scene B's question names the two specific real options (the 11 o'clock team meeting vs. the 4 PM client meeting) rather than repeating Scene A's vague "what do you mean?" (MIS-0010).

lessons.title: Asking Colleagues vs. Asking Supervisors
lessons.objectives_html:
• Judge whether a question is better directed to a colleague or a supervisor.
  • Adjust the phrasing of the same question for each audience.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif has a genuine question about a task. Before he even opens his mouth, there are two decisions to make: who should he ask, and how should he phrase it for that person? Module 3 taught Arif to choose the right greeting for the right person. This lesson applies the same judgment to asking for help.

Key workplace lesson

Not every question needs a supervisor, and not every question can be answered by a peer. Day-to-day, practical questions ("Where's the stapler?", "Do you know if the client called back?") usually go to a colleague — asking a supervisor wastes their time and can make a small question look bigger than it is. Questions about a decision, a deadline change, or something that could affect the client or the business usually need a supervisor, even if a colleague happens to know the answer too. Getting this judgment right is itself a professional skill — separate from the language used to ask.

Listen & Read
Asking a colleague (low-stakes)
The shared printer area, mid-morning.
Arif: Hey, quick question — do you know if the printer on this floor is working? Mine's stuck on an error.
Priyanka: Yeah, it's fine — I printed something ten minutes ago. Try turning it off and on.
Arif: Will do, thanks.
Asking a supervisor (higher-stakes)
Outside Mr. Hossain's office, early afternoon. Arif isn't sure whether today's deadline has changed.
Arif: Do you have a moment? I wanted to check something about today's deadline.
Mr. Hossain: Of course — what's on your mind?
Arif: I heard the client meeting might move to tomorrow. Should I still finish the report by today, or does that change things?
Mr. Hossain: Good catch — it has moved. You can take until tomorrow morning now.
Arif: That's helpful to know, thank you.

Key expressions

Expression Meaning When to use Example
"Hey, quick question..." A casual opener for a low-stakes question With a peer or colleague you know "Hey, quick question — do you know where the stapler is?"
"Do you have a moment? I wanted to check something." A more formal opener that asks permission first With a supervisor, or anyone senior "Do you have a moment? I wanted to check something about the client's order."

Vocabulary

  • V-0148 quick question — a casual way to signal that what follows is short and low-effort to answer.
  • V-0149 do you have a moment — a polite way of checking someone's availability before asking something, especially with someone senior.

Grammar in context

There is no new sentence pattern in this lesson — both openers above are fixed, idiomatic phrases rather than fill-in-the-blank frames. The actual skill here is judgment (who to ask) and register-matching (which fixed opener fits), directly recycling Module 3's register-choice skill (TL-0002) and Module 1's peer/manager introduction distinction into a new situation: asking, not greeting or introducing.

Worked example, same underlying question, two audiences:

  • To a peer (Priyanka): "Hey, quick question — do you know if the printer on this floor is working?"
  • To a supervisor (Mr. Hossain): "Do you have a moment? I wanted to check something about today's deadline."

Professional tone

  • ❌ Too casual with a supervisor: "Hey, quick question, is the deadline still today?" — the same phrasing that works fine with Priyanka can sound underprepared when used with Mr. Hossain for something that actually matters (a deadline).
  • ❌ Too formal with a peer: "Do you have a moment? I wanted to check something." said to Priyanka about where the stapler is — technically fine, but unnecessarily heavy for a two-second question.
  • ✅ Matched to the audience: casual opener + low-stakes question with a peer; formal opener + a question that matters with a supervisor.

Bengali/Hindi support

সহকর্মী ও ঊর্ধ্বতন কর্মকর্তা — উভয়ের কাছে প্রশ্ন করার ধরন একই হওয়া উচিত নয়। ছোট, দৈনন্দিন প্রশ্ন সহকর্মীকে সরাসরি জিজ্ঞাসা করা যায়, কিন্তু গুরুত্বপূর্ণ বা সিদ্ধান্ত-সম্পর্কিত প্রশ্নের জন্য ঊর্ধ্বতন কর্মকর্তার কাছে যাওয়াই ভালো, এমনকি সহকর্মী উত্তরটি জানলেও। सहकर्मी और वरिष्ठ अधिकारी — दोनों से पूछने का तरीका एक जैसा नहीं होना चाहिए। छोटे, रोज़मर्रा के सवाल सीधे सहकर्मी से पूछे जा सकते हैं, लेकिन महत्वपूर्ण या निर्णय से जुड़े सवालों के लिए वरिष्ठ अधिकारी से पूछना बेहतर है, भले ही सहकर्मी को भी जवाब पता हो।

Industry overlays

Hierarchy steepness varies by industry — a hospital's chain of command is often stricter than a small retail team's, so the same question (say, about a schedule change) may need to go up a level in a hospital where it could go directly to a peer in a smaller, flatter team. The judgment skill is the same everywhere; where exactly the line sits shifts by workplace.

Self-check

  1. Give one example of a question that's fine to ask a colleague, and one that should go to a supervisor instead.
  2. Why might asking a supervisor a very small, routine question sometimes be a mistake — even if they technically know the answer?
  3. You need to know whether a client meeting has been moved. Who would you ask, and what exactly would you say?

Motivation

"Knowing who to ask is part of professional judgment."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Situational Judgment

For each question below, decide whether it's better asked to a colleague or a supervisor. (1) "Where's the stapler?" (2) "Has the client's contract been approved yet?" (3) "Is the printer working?" (4) "Can we move the project deadline?"

2. Guided Practice

Say the same question two ways: (a) to a peer, casually, and (b) to a supervisor, more formally. Question: "Do you know if today's meeting is still happening?"

3. Controlled Practice

Write down one question you would ask a colleague this week, and one you would ask a supervisor instead — and say briefly why each belongs with that person.

4. Role-Play Assessment

Module 5 assessment. You are told: "Your supervisor just gave you three instructions quickly — you're unsure about one detail in the second instruction, and separately, a colleague nearby might know a quick, unrelated answer." (1) Decide which question goes to the colleague and which goes to the supervisor. (2) Role-play both: the casual version to the colleague, and the appropriately formal, targeted clarifying version to the supervisor.

Answer Key

1.

(1) Colleague. (2) Supervisor. (3) Colleague. (4) Supervisor. Small, routine questions (the stapler, the printer) go to a colleague; anything involving an approval, a decision or a deadline change goes to a supervisor, even if a colleague happens to know the answer.

2.

Suggested answer: (a) Hey, quick question — is today's meeting still happening? / (b) Do you have a moment? I wanted to check whether today's meeting is still happening.

3.

Suggested answer: Colleague: "Do you know where the extra forms are kept?" — routine, low-stakes. / Supervisor: "Can I take next Friday off?" — needs an actual decision.

4.

What to listen/look for: Correctly separates the low-stakes question (colleague, casual opener) from the instruction-related clarifying question (supervisor, formal opener + a targeted question per PAT-0014, not a vague one per MIS-0010); uses a clearly different register for each.

modules.title: Basic Workplace Vocabulary
modules.purpose: Review and extend the workplace vocabulary you have already met — places, people, tasks, tools and task status — so you can use it accurately.

lessons.title: People, Roles and Departments
lessons.objectives_html:
• Correctly name 12–15 common workplace roles and departments.
  • Use at least 5 of them in a spoken sentence about your own or a target workplace.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif already knows some of the map of his workplace — Mr. Hossain, Priyanka, his own team. This lesson fills in the rest of it: the departments and roles he hasn't had a reason to name yet, so that when someone mentions "Accounts" or "the new intern," he knows exactly who and what that means.

Key workplace lesson

You've already been using role and department words since Module 1 — "supervisor," "colleague," "team lead," "department" all appeared in real dialogue before this lesson ever named them as vocabulary. This lesson isn't your first encounter with workplace roles; it's the moment those words get organized into a proper map, with the gaps filled in. Knowing who's who — and which department handles what — is often the difference between solving a problem in one conversation and bouncing between three people who all say "that's not my area."

Listen & Read
The office break room, mid-morning. Arif and Priyanka are catching up between tasks.
Priyanka: Have you met the new intern yet? She's shadowing someone in Sales this week.
Arif: Not yet. Is she working with the receptionist too, or just Sales?
Priyanka: Just Sales for now. If your laptop acts up again, by the way, IT support is on the third floor.
Arif: Good to know — I was about to ask HR, but that's clearly the wrong department.
Priyanka: Different problem, different department — you'll get the hang of who's who soon enough.

Recycled from earlier modules (cross-reference, not re-taught)

Word First introduced ID
manager Module 1 V-0020
supervisor Module 1 V-0021
colleague Module 1 / Module 2 V-0018 / V-0105
team lead Module 1 / Module 2 V-0019 / V-0106
department Module 1 V-0015

New vocabulary

ID Word Meaning Bengali Hindi
V-0150 HR (Human Resources) The department that handles hiring, pay, leave, and workplace policy মানবসম্পদ বিভাগ (এইচআর) मानव संसाधन विभाग (एचआर)
V-0151 front desk The staffed counter where visitors or guests are first greeted ফ্রন্ট ডেস্ক (অভ্যর্থনা কাউন্টার) फ्रंट डेस्क (स्वागत काउंटर)
V-0152 housekeeping The department responsible for cleaning and maintaining a building's rooms/areas হাউসকিপিং বিভাগ हाउसकीपिंग विभाग
V-0153 Accounts (dept.) The department that handles money, invoices, and payments অ্যাকাউন্টস বিভাগ लेखा (अकाउंट्स) विभाग
V-0154 Sales (dept.) The department responsible for selling products or services বিক্রয় বিভাগ बिक्री (सेल्स) विभाग
V-0155 IT support The team that fixes computer, network, and technical problems আইটি সাপোর্ট आईटी सपोर्ट
V-0156 customer service The team or role that helps and responds to customers directly গ্রাহক সেবা ग्राहक सेवा
V-0157 receptionist The person who staffs the front desk/reception area রিসেপশনিস্ট रिसेप्शनिस्ट
V-0158 intern A student or new person doing temporary, often unpaid or short-term, work to gain experience ইন্টার্ন (শিক্ষানবিশ) इंटर्न (प्रशिक्षु)
V-0159 trainee A person who is currently being trained for a role, usually paid and longer-term than an intern ট্রেইনি (প্রশিক্ষণার্থী) ट्रेनी (प्रशिक्षणार्थी)

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure here — this lesson recycles two patterns you already know from Module 1 directly: "X works in..." (department) and "X is responsible for..." (role/function). Priyanka works on the front desk. · Housekeeping is responsible for the guest floors.

Common mistake

MIS-0011 — Confusing "front desk" and "reception": these overlap but aren't identical. Reception (V-0101) is the general area/function near the entrance; front desk is the specific staffed counter itself. Both are correct, but they behave differently: reception is normally used without "the" after at ("Please wait at reception"), while front desk always takes "the" ("Leave it at the front desk"). "Leave it at the reception" is the mistake to avoid. In hotels, front desk is the usual name for the counter and for the team that works there.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: front desk, housekeeping, food & beverage, concierge, reservations.
  • Bank: teller, loan officer, branch manager, compliance.
  • Hospital/clinic: ward assistant, nursing staff, admissions, billing.
  • IT company: developer, QA, IT support, project coordinator.
  • Retail: sales associate, store manager, stock/inventory team.

Self-check

  1. Name three departments in a typical office, and one thing each is responsible for.
  2. What's the difference between an intern and a trainee?
  3. A new colleague asks, "Who do I talk to about a payment that hasn't come through?" Which department do you send them to?

Motivation

"Learning the map of your workplace is learning the map of your success."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Match each role/department to what it's responsible for: (a) money, invoices and payments; (b) cleaning and maintaining rooms and areas; (c) hiring, pay, leave and workplace policy; (d) fixing computer and network problems.

HR

________

IT support

________

Accounts

________

Housekeeping

________
2. Categorization

Sort these into two groups: a PERSON/role, or a DEPARTMENT. receptionist, Sales, intern, Accounts, trainee, HR

3. Guided Practice

Describe your own (or a target) workplace using at least 5 of this lesson's words — name at least 2 departments and 2 roles.

4. Rewriting

A colleague says: "Ask the reception if you need help with that." Correct the sentence in two ways: once with "reception" and once with "front desk".

Answer Key

1.

HR → Hiring, pay, leave, and workplace policy; IT support → Fixing computer and network problems; Accounts → Money, invoices, and payments; Housekeeping → Cleaning and maintaining rooms/areas. Each department maps to one core function — knowing this map means knowing exactly who to ask when something comes up.

2.

Suggested answer: Person/role: receptionist, intern, trainee / Department: Sales, Accounts, HR

3.

Suggested answer: In my hotel, the front desk and housekeeping work closely together. The front desk manager reports issues, and housekeeping handles the rooms. We also have an intern helping in reservations this month.

4.

"Ask at reception if you need help with that." (no "the") / "Ask the front desk if you need help with that."

lessons.title: Places, Tools and Documents at Work
lessons.objectives_html:
