• Name the common physical places, tools, and documents found in a typical workplace.
  • Describe what an object is used for using a simple functional sentence.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif can already find the washroom and the break room. This lesson rounds out the rest of the physical world he works in — the rooms, tools, and paperwork he needs the right words for, so he can ask for them, find them, or explain what he needs without pointing and guessing.

Key workplace lesson

Physical vocabulary is some of the most immediately useful language you'll learn — you need it within your first hour on any job, and it varies more by industry than almost any other word category in this course. This lesson gives you the general-office core; the industry overlays below show how the same categories (places, tools, documents) map onto very different real objects depending on where you work.

Listen & Read
The office corridor, just before a 3 PM meeting.
Arif: Do you know where the meeting room is for the 3 PM?
Priyanka: Second floor, next to the storeroom. Bring your ID card — the door needs a swipe.
Arif: Got it. I also need to print this form before I go — is the printer on this floor working?
Priyanka: Should be. If not, check the notice board — IT usually posts an update there.

Recycled from earlier modules (cross-reference, not re-taught)

Word First introduced ID
reception Module 2 V-0101
break room Module 2 V-0115
washroom Module 2 V-0114
hallway Module 2 V-0113

New vocabulary

ID Word Meaning Bengali Hindi
V-0160 meeting room A room set aside for meetings/discussions মিটিং রুম (সভা কক্ষ) मीटिंग रूम (बैठक कक्ष)
V-0161 storeroom / warehouse A room or building for storing supplies, stock, or equipment স্টোররুম / গুদাম स्टोररूम / गोदाम
V-0162 ID card A card that identifies who you are and often what you're allowed to access আইডি কার্ড (পরিচয়পত্র) आईडी कार्ड (पहचान पत्र)
V-0163 computer / laptop The device used for most office/desk work কম্পিউটার / ল্যাপটপ कंप्यूटर / लैपटॉप
V-0164 printer The machine used to print documents on paper প্রিন্টার प्रिंटर
V-0165 form A document with blank spaces to fill in information ফর্ম फॉर्म
V-0166 file (noun) A folder or document that holds related papers or records ফাইল फ़ाइल
V-0167 email A written message sent electronically ইমেইল ईमेल
V-0168 memo A short, official written note sent within a company মেমো (স্মারকলিপি) मेमो (ज्ञापन)
V-0169 notice board A board where announcements or notices are posted for staff নোটিশ বোর্ড नोटिस बोर्ड
V-0170 register / log A written record kept of events, entries, or activity over time রেজিস্টার / লগ रजिस्टर / लॉग

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure — this lesson recycles two functional patterns: "This is used for..." and "I need a... to...". A printer is used for printing documents. · I need a form to request leave.

Industry overlays

  • Hotel: PMS terminal (property management system), housekeeping trolley, key card (a specific type of "ID card"), guest registration form.
  • Bank: deposit slip (a specific "form"), teller counter, vault/storeroom, transaction log.
  • Hospital/clinic: patient file (a specific "file"), ward, medication log/register.
  • IT company: server room (a specific "storeroom"), ticketing system (a digital "log").

Self-check

  1. Name three documents you might use or fill out in an average office week.
  2. What's the difference between a "form" and a "memo"?
  3. You need somewhere to hold today's meeting. Which word do you use?

Motivation

"The right tools, the right words."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Categorization

Sort these into three groups: PLACE, TOOL, or DOCUMENT. meeting room, printer, form, storeroom, computer, memo, notice board, file

2. Multiple Choice

Which document is best described as "a short, official written note sent within a company"?

A.

Form

B.

Memo

C.

Register

3. Guided Practice

Describe what 3 objects from this lesson are used for, using "This is used for..."

4. Labeling

Label a simple floor plan of your own (or a target) workplace with at least 5 words from this lesson.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Place: meeting room, storeroom, notice board / Tool: printer, computer / Document: form, memo, file

2.

Correct: B. A memo is a short internal note; a form has blank spaces to fill in, and a register/log is an ongoing record of entries.

3.

Suggested answer: A printer is used for printing documents. / A notice board is used for posting announcements. / An ID card is used for identifying yourself and accessing certain areas.

4.

Answers will vary. Check that the plan labels at least five places or objects with words from this lesson (for example: meeting room, storeroom, printer, notice board, front desk) and that each label is spelled correctly.

lessons.title: Time, Schedules and Deadlines
lessons.objectives_html:
• Name common workplace time/schedule vocabulary and use it to describe a schedule.
  • Understand a short spoken schedule announcement.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Module 4 taught Arif to catch a deadline inside a fast instruction. This lesson gives him the full vocabulary set around time at work — the words for describing his own schedule, not just reacting to someone else's.

Key workplace lesson

You've seen "urgent" and "by end of day" before — Module 4 taught you to recognize them inside someone else's instruction. This lesson turns the same vocabulary around: now you're the one describing your shift, asking about a deadline, or explaining that you're taking a day off. Time vocabulary also splits sharply by industry — a shift-based job (hotel, retail, healthcare) runs on a completely different rhythm from a fixed-hours office job, and this lesson's overlays make that difference explicit.

Listen & Read
Near the exit, end of the workday. Mr. Hossain catches Arif on his way out.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, check the roster before you head out — your shift starts an hour earlier tomorrow.
Arif: Understood. Is that overtime, or is my normal shift just moving?
Mr. Hossain: Just moving — no overtime. And don't forget, the client report deadline is tomorrow by end of day.
Arif: Noted. I'll make sure I'm on time either way.

Recycled from earlier modules (cross-reference, not re-taught)

Word First introduced ID
by end of day (EOD) Module 4 V-0137
urgent Module 4 V-0136
punctual Module 1 V-0002

New vocabulary

ID Word Meaning Bengali Hindi
V-0171 shift A scheduled block of working time (e.g., morning shift, night shift) শিফট (কর্মঘণ্টা) शिफ्ट (कार्य-अवधि)
V-0172 roster The published schedule showing who works which shift and when রোস্টার (ডিউটি তালিকা) रोस्टर (ड्यूटी सूची)
V-0173 on time At the planned time; not late সময়মতো समय पर
V-0174 late Arriving or finishing after the expected time দেরি হওয়া देर होना
V-0175 overtime Extra time worked beyond your normal scheduled hours ওভারটাইম (অতিরিক্ত সময়) ओवरटाइम (अतिरिक्त समय)
V-0176 deadline The latest time or date by which something must be finished সময়সীমা (ডেডলাইন) समय सीमा (डेडलाइन)
V-0177 leave Approved time away from work (e.g., sick leave, annual leave) ছুটি छुट्टी
V-0178 day off A single day scheduled without work ছুটির দিন अवकाश का दिन

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure — this lesson recycles time prepositions (at, by, before, on) already seen in earlier modules. My shift starts at 9. · The deadline is by Friday. · I'm on leave on Tuesday.

Common mistake

MIS-0012 — Confusing "on time" and "in time": "on time" means exactly at the expected moment ("The meeting started on time, at 10 sharp"). "in time" means before a deadline, with some room to spare ("I finished the report in time for the 3 PM meeting" — could have been 2:45 or 2:59). Using "in time" when you mean "on time" can accidentally suggest something was almost late when it wasn't.

Industry overlays

  • Shift-based (hotel, retail, healthcare): shift, roster, shift handover, overtime are daily vocabulary.
  • Fixed-hours office: "shift" is rarely used; "working hours," "leave," and "deadline" do most of the work instead.

Self-check

  1. What's the difference between "leave" and "a day off"?
  2. Correct the mistake: "I finished the form on time for the 3 PM meeting" (meaning: with 15 minutes to spare).
  3. Your roster shows a shift starting an hour earlier tomorrow, with no extra pay mentioned. Is that overtime? How do you know?

Motivation

"Respecting time is respecting people."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Categorization

Sort these into two groups: about SCHEDULE, or about A DEADLINE/TIMING RESULT. shift, roster, on time, late, deadline, overtime

2. Rewriting

Fix the mistake: "I finished the form on time for the 3 PM meeting" (meaning: with 15 minutes to spare, not exactly at the deadline).

3. Guided Practice

Describe your own (or a target) work schedule using at least 4 words from this lesson.

4. Comprehension

Read this schedule announcement (or have someone read it aloud) and answer: "Tomorrow's morning shift now starts at 8, not 9. Anyone on leave should confirm with their team lead by end of day." (1) What time does the shift start now? (2) What should someone on leave do, and by when?

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Schedule: shift, roster, overtime / Timing result: on time, late, deadline

2.

Suggested answer: I finished the form in time for the 3 PM meeting.

3.

Suggested answer: My shift starts at 8 and I check the roster every Sunday. I try never to be late, and I take my day off on Wednesdays.

4.

Suggested answer: 1) 8 AM. 2) Confirm with their team lead, by end of day.

lessons.title: Tasks, Responsibility and Priority
lessons.objectives_html:
• Name common vocabulary for describing task status and responsibility.
  • Describe the status of 3 tasks using this lesson's vocabulary.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif already knows how to confirm a task and put three tasks in priority order. This lesson gives him the vocabulary to describe where a task stands at any moment — useful the next time someone asks, "How's that going?"

Key workplace lesson

"How's that going?" is one of the most common questions in any workplace, and a vague answer ("it's fine," "still working on it") doesn't actually tell anyone anything useful. This lesson's words — pending, in progress, complete — give you a precise, three-word vocabulary for exactly where any task stands. This is also a preview of a skill Level 2 will teach in full ("Daily Work Updates") — here, it's introduced just enough to recognize and use simply, not mastered in depth.

Listen & Read
Mr. Hossain's office doorway, mid-afternoon.
Mr. Hossain: How's the client report coming along?
Arif: It's in progress — I'm about halfway. The invoice part is still pending; I'm waiting on numbers from Accounts.
Mr. Hossain: Can you follow up with them today? I'd like the whole thing complete by tomorrow.
Arif: Will do. Should I delegate the printing part to someone, given my backlog this week?
Mr. Hossain: Good idea — go ahead.

Recycled from earlier modules (cross-reference, not re-taught)

Word First introduced ID
responsible for Module 1 V-0017
task Module 4 V-0130
priority Module 4 V-0135

New vocabulary

ID Word Meaning Bengali Hindi
V-0179 assignment A specific piece of work given to someone to complete দায়িত্ব / অ্যাসাইনমেন্ট असाइनमेंट (सौंपा गया कार्य)
V-0180 complete (task status) Fully finished, with nothing left to do সম্পন্ন / সম্পূর্ণ पूर्ण / पूरा
V-0181 in progress Started, but not yet finished চলমান (কাজ চলছে) प्रगति पर (काम जारी है)
V-0182 pending Not yet started, often because it's waiting on something or someone else অমীমাংসিত / মুলতুবি लंबित (शुरू नहीं हुआ)
V-0183 delegate (verb) To officially give a task to someone else to do দায়িত্ব অর্পণ করা कार्य सौंपना (डेलिगेट करना)
V-0184 follow up To check on something again after some time has passed ফলো আপ করা (পুনরায় খোঁজ নেওয়া) फॉलो अप करना (दोबारा जानकारी लेना)
V-0185 backlog A build-up of unfinished tasks waiting to be done ব্যাকলগ (জমে থাকা কাজ) बैकलॉग (लंबित कार्यों का ढेर)

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure — this lesson recycles the "responsible for" pattern (Module 1) and introduces simple task-status phrasing: "This is + [pending/in progress/complete]." The invoice is pending. · The report is in progress. · That task is complete.

Common mistake

MIS-0013 — Confusing "pending" and "in progress": pending means the task hasn't started yet, usually because it's waiting on something (approval, information, another person). in progress means work has already begun. Saying a task is "pending" when it's actually "in progress" can make it sound like nothing has happened yet, when really you're partway through.

Industry overlays

Task-status vocabulary is close to universal — a hotel housekeeping checklist, a bank's loan application, and an IT support ticket all move through the same pending → in progress → complete stages; only the specific task content changes.

Self-check

  1. What's the difference between "pending" and "in progress"?
  2. When might you choose to delegate a task rather than do it yourself?
  3. You have three tasks: one waiting on a colleague's reply, one you're halfway through, and one fully done. Describe all three using this lesson's vocabulary.

Motivation

"Small, consistent progress builds trust."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice

Which word describes a task that hasn't started yet because it's waiting on someone else?

A.

In progress

B.

Pending

C.

Complete

2. Rewriting

A colleague says a task is "pending" but they've actually already started it and are halfway through. What's the correct word, and write the corrected sentence.

3. Guided Practice

Describe the status of 3 real or imagined tasks using this lesson's vocabulary (pending, in progress, complete).

4. Controlled Practice

Write a short, 2-line status update for your supervisor about a task, using at least 2 words from this lesson.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. "Pending" specifically implies the task hasn't started and is waiting on something; "in progress" means work has already begun.

2.

Suggested answer: The task is in progress, not pending. ("The report is in progress — I'm about halfway.")

3.

Suggested answer: The client email is complete and sent. The report is in progress. The invoice approval is pending — I'm waiting on Accounts.

4.

Suggested answer: The client report is in progress and should be complete by tomorrow. The invoice part is still pending — I'm following up with Accounts today.

lessons.title: Core Workplace Verbs and Professional Phrases
lessons.objectives_html:
• Recognize and use a core set of high-value workplace phrases already met across Modules 1–5.
  • Use at least 5 new core workplace verbs at a basic recognition level.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif has said most of the phrases in this lesson before — across five modules, in five different situations. This lesson gathers the best of them into one place, and adds a small set of new verbs he'll need soon, ready to recognize even before he needs to produce them fluently.

Key workplace lesson

This is the module's capstone lesson, and it works differently from the other four: instead of introducing a new topic, it collects the highest-value phrases you've already used in real dialogue and turns them into a proper phrase bank — reusable across almost any workplace situation, not tied to one topic. It also hands you a small set of new verbs (submit, update, review, escalate, notify, coordinate) that Level 2 and Level 3 will build on — you only need to recognize them for now, not use them with full confidence yet.

Listen & Read
Mr. Hossain's office, late afternoon. A wrap-up conversation before the end of the day.
Mr. Hossain: Have you submitted the report yet?
Arif: Not yet — I wanted you to review it first. I'll update you once it's sent.
Mr. Hossain: Sounds good. If Accounts still hasn't replied by tomorrow, escalate it to their team lead, and notify me either way.
Arif: Got it. I'll coordinate with Priyanka so nothing falls through the cracks.
Mr. Hossain: Sorry, could you say that again? Missed the last part.
Arif: Just to confirm — I'll coordinate with Priyanka, submit the report once you've reviewed it, and escalate to their team lead if Accounts still hasn't replied tomorrow.
Mr. Hossain: Perfect. Thanks for letting me know where things stand.
Arif: I'll take care of it.

Phrase bank — consolidated from Modules 1–5

ID Phrase First used Function
P-0025 "Could you please...?" Module 2 ("Could you sign in here, please?") Softened request
P-0026 "I'll take care of it." Module 5 (Lesson 5.1: "I'll take care of both") Confirming ownership of a task
P-0027 "Let me check and get back to you." New in this lesson Buying time honestly instead of guessing
P-0028 "Thanks for letting me know." Module 6 (this lesson's dialogue) Acknowledging information
P-0029 "Got it." Module 2 (Lesson 2.3) Quick, confident confirmation
P-0030 "Just to confirm..." Module 4 Formal restatement/confirmation opener
P-0031 "Sorry, could you say that again?" Module 5 Polite repeat request

These are short, fixed phrases: learn each one as a whole, rather than translating it word by word.

New core verbs (recognition level)

ID Word Meaning Bengali Hindi
V-0186 submit To formally hand in or send something for review/approval জমা দেওয়া जमा करना (सबमिट करना)
V-0187 update (verb) To add the latest information to something, or to inform someone of the latest status হালনাগাদ করা (আপডেট করা) अपडेट करना
V-0188 review To look over something carefully, usually to check it before it's finalized পর্যালোচনা করা (রিভিউ করা) समीक्षा करना (रिव्यू करना)
V-0189 escalate To pass a problem up to someone more senior when it can't be solved at your level ঊর্ধ্বতন কর্তৃপক্ষের কাছে পাঠানো (এসকেলেট করা) उच्च अधिकारी तक पहुँचाना (एस्कलेट करना)
V-0190 notify To formally inform someone about something অবহিত করা (জানানো) सूचित करना
V-0191 coordinate To organize people or tasks so they work together smoothly সমন্বয় করা समन्वय करना (कोऑर्डिनेट करना)

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure — this lesson is pure consolidation. The phrases above attach to situations you already know how to build sentences around; the new verbs slot into the same simple-present/imperative patterns used since Module 1 ("I'll submit it," "Please review this," "Notify me if anything changes").

Industry overlays

Light — these phrases and verbs are close to universal across every industry this course covers; example sentences vary (a hotel escalates a guest complaint, a bank escalates a compliance issue), but the language itself doesn't change.

Self-check

  1. Which phrase would you use to confirm you understood an instruction, formally?
  2. What's the difference between "review" and "submit"?
  3. When would you "escalate" something rather than just handling it yourself?

Motivation

"A strong vocabulary is a strong voice."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Match each phrase to the situation it fits best: (a) politely asking for a repeat; (b) being honest that you don't know the answer yet; (c) formally restating an instruction before acting on it; (d) confirming you own a task, without over-explaining.

"Just to confirm..."

________

"I'll take care of it."

________

"Let me check and get back to you."

________

"Sorry, could you say that again?"

________
2. Multiple Choice

What's the difference between "review" and "submit"?

A.

They mean exactly the same thing

B.

"Review" is checking something before it's finalized; "submit" is formally sending it in

C.

"Review" is only for documents; "submit" is only for forms

3. Guided Practice

Use 5 phrases or words from this lesson in original sentences about your own (or a target) workplace.

4. Guided Practice Assessment

Module 6 assessment. Describe your own (or a target) workplace's people, places, schedule, and a current task, using at least 5 target words from across this whole module (not just this lesson) in real sentences about your own situation.

Answer Key

1.

"Just to confirm..." → Formally restating an instruction before acting on it; "I'll take care of it." → Confirming you own a task, without over-explaining; "Let me check and get back to you." → Being honest that you don't know the answer yet; "Sorry, could you say that again?" → Politely asking for a repeat. Each phrase does a specific job — matching the phrase to the function, not just memorizing the words, is what makes the phrase bank actually useful.

2.

Correct: B. Review usually happens before submit — you check something over, then you formally hand it in.

3.

Suggested answer: I'll submit the form once my supervisor has reviewed it. If there's a problem, I'll escalate it and notify the team lead. I'll coordinate with my colleague so we don't submit it twice.

4.

What to listen/look for: Uses at least 5 distinct words/phrases from Module 6 (any lesson) accurately and in a real sentence about the learner's own or a target workplace, not just a list of isolated words.

modules.title: Foundations of Professional Tone
modules.purpose: Learn why tone is part of the message: the PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → MESSAGE → TONE → ACTION framework, polite requests, professional replies and respect for hierarchy.

lessons.title: Why Tone Matters: Same Message, Different Sound
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify whether a spoken message sounds rude, casual, passive, or professional.
  • Explain in simple terms why the same words can sound different depending on tone.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif needs a report from Priyanka before a client call. He could ask for it in a dozen different ways, using almost the same words each time — and every one of those ways would land completely differently. This lesson is about that gap: the space between what you say and how it sounds when it arrives.

Key workplace lesson

Every module so far has quietly used tone without naming it — Module 3 taught you to choose a greeting based on who you're talking to; Module 5 taught you to ask for help without over-apologizing. This lesson finally puts a name on the skill underneath all of that: tone — the attitude your words carry, separate from their literal meaning. The same five words, said five different ways, can sound like an order, a favor, a plea, or a professional request. Getting this right is not about finding one "magic phrase." It's about learning to hear — and then control — the difference.

Listen & Read
Version 1 — Rude
Arif, at Priyanka's desk, mid-afternoon.
Arif: Send me the report. Now.
Version 2 — Casual
Arif, at Priyanka's desk, mid-afternoon.
Arif: Hey, can you send me the report?
Version 3 — Passive
Arif, at Priyanka's desk, mid-afternoon.
Arif: Um... maybe, if it's not too much trouble, could you possibly send the report sometime?
Version 4 — Professional (neutral-safe default)
Arif, at Priyanka's desk, mid-afternoon.
Arif: Could you send me the report, please?
Version 5 — Confident and respectful
Arif, at Priyanka's desk, mid-afternoon.
Arif: Could you send me the report by 3 PM? I need it for the client call.
Paired example A — the rude version, and Priyanka's real reaction
Immediately after Version 1, showing the actual effect rather than just the line itself.
Arif: Send me the report. Now.
Priyanka: (pausing, surprised) ...Sure. Give me a minute.
Priyanka (thinking, not said aloud): That came out of nowhere. Did something go wrong that he isn't telling me?
Paired example B — the confident-and-respectful version, and Priyanka's real reaction
Immediately after Version 5, showing the actual effect rather than just the line itself.
Arif: Could you send me the report by 3 PM? I need it for the client call.
Priyanka: Got it — I'll have it to you by 2:30, just to be safe.
Priyanka (thinking, not said aloud): Good, now I know exactly why and when. I can plan around this.

Vocabulary

  • V-0192 tone — the attitude or feeling behind words, separate from their literal meaning. বাচনভঙ্গি / স্বর (শব্দের আক্ষরিক অর্থের বাইরে যে মনোভাব প্রকাশ পায়) · लहजा / भाव (शब्दों के शाब्दिक अर्थ से अलग, उनके पीछे का रवैया)
  • V-0193 rude — disrespectful; ignoring how the other person will feel. রূঢ় / অভদ্র · असभ्य / रूखा
  • V-0194 casual — relaxed and informal; fine with people you know well, risky with people you don't. নৈমিত্তিক / সহজ-সরল (অনানুষ্ঠানিক) · अनौपचारिक / सहज
  • V-0195 passive (tone sense) — unclear, hesitant, or avoiding directness, often out of a wish to seem polite. Not the same as "polite" — passive tone can actually create more confusion, not less. দ্বিধাগ্রস্ত / অস্পষ্ট (ইতস্তত ভাব) · अनिश्चित / झिझकभरा
  • V-0196 confident (tone sense) — clear and self-assured, without being aggressive. স্পষ্ট ও আত্মবিশ্বাসী (আক্রমণাত্মক না হয়ে) · आत्मविश्वासी / स्पष्ट (आक्रामक हुए बिना)
  • V-0197 respectful — showing consideration for the other person's time, position, or feelings. শ্রদ্ধাশীল / সম্মানজনক · सम्मानजनक

The framework: PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → MESSAGE → TONE → ACTION

From this lesson onward, this five-step question set sits behind almost everything you say or write at work. Before speaking, ask yourself:

Step Question
Purpose What do I actually need to happen?
Audience Who am I talking to, and what's my relationship to them?
Message What information do they actually need?
Tone What tone fits this purpose, this audience, and this moment?
Action What should happen next, and is that clear?

Bengali note: এই পাঁচটি প্রশ্ন (উদ্দেশ্য → শ্রোতা → বার্তা → স্বর → পরবর্তী পদক্ষেপ) মনে মনে জিজ্ঞাসা করাটা প্রথমে কৃত্রিম মনে হতে পারে, কিন্তু কয়েক সপ্তাহ অভ্যাসের পর এটি স্বতঃস্ফূর্ত হয়ে যায় — একজন অভিজ্ঞ পেশাদারও কথা বলার আগে এই ফিল্টারটি নিজের অজান্তেই ব্যবহার করেন।

Hindi note: ये पाँच सवाल (उद्देश्य → श्रोता → संदेश → लहजा → अगला कदम) शुरुआत में सायास लग सकते हैं, लेकिन कुछ हफ्तों के अभ्यास के बाद यह अपने आप दिमाग में आने लगता है — एक अनुभवी पेशेवर भी बोलने से पहले इसी फ़िल्टर का इस्तेमाल करता है, भले ही वह इसे नाम न दे।

Same message, five tones

Here is one purpose — Arif needs the report from Priyanka — said five different ways.

# Version Tone What it does to the relationship
1 "Send me the report. Now." Rude Sounds like an order from someone with authority Arif doesn't have over Priyanka. Damages the relationship.
2 "Hey, can you send me the report?" Casual Fine between close peers who talk this way every day; risky if Priyanka is senior, new, or more formal by habit.
3 "Um... maybe, if it's not too much trouble, could you possibly send the report sometime?" Passive So hedged that Priyanka isn't sure how urgent it is, or whether Arif is even sure what he needs.
4 "Could you send me the report, please?" Professional (neutral-safe default) Clear, polite, works in almost any relationship.
5 "Could you send me the report by 3 PM? I need it for the client call." Confident and respectful Everything #4 has, plus the why and the when — Priyanka can prioritize it correctly.

Notice that #1 and #3 fail in opposite directions — #1 is too hard, #3 is too soft — while #4 and #5 both work. This module's whole job is teaching you to land consistently in the #4–#5 range without over-thinking every sentence.

Common mistake

MIS-0014 — Assuming "please" alone fixes tone: "Send me the report, please." still reads as a command with one polite word stapled on, not a genuinely polite request. Tone lives in the whole sentence structure (see the request patterns in Lesson 7.2), not in a single magic word.

Tips & tricks

TIP-0004 — The 3-second tone check: Before you speak or send a message, silently run Purpose → Audience → Tone in under 3 seconds. It doesn't need to be a long process — even a half-second pause before a request ("Wait — who am I asking, and how urgent is this really?") catches most tone mistakes before they happen.

Practice

  1. Recognition: Read each of the five versions above aloud. Label each one: rude, casual, passive, professional, or confident-and-respectful.
  2. Discussion: Why does version 3 (passive) fail even though it sounds "extra polite"?
  3. Framework walkthrough: Pick a real request you need to make this week. Answer all five framework questions for it, out loud or in writing.

Self-check

  1. In your own words, what is "tone"?
  2. Why doesn't adding "please" always make a sentence sound polite?
  3. Which of the five versions of "send me the report" would you actually use with your own supervisor? Why?

Motivation

"How you say it is part of what you say."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Read each of the five versions of "send me the report." Match each one to its tone label: rude, casual, passive, professional, or confident and respectful.

"Send me the report. Now."

________

"Hey, can you send me the report?"

________

"Um... maybe, if it's not too much trouble, could you possibly send the report sometime?"

________

"Could you send me the report, please?"

________

"Could you send me the report by 3 PM? I need it for the client call."

________
2. Short Answer

Version 3 ("Um... maybe, if it's not too much trouble...") uses lots of soft, polite- sounding words. Why does it still fail as a request?

3. Guided Practice

Pick a real request you need to make this week (to a colleague, a supervisor, or a friend). Answer all five framework questions for it — Purpose, Audience, Message, Tone, Action — out loud or in writing.

4. Multiple Choice Assessment

A new employee says, "Can you send me the report, please?" in a flat, hurried voice while walking away without waiting for an answer. Even though the words are polite, how is this likely to land?

A.

As clearly professional, because the words include "please"

B.

As somewhat rude or dismissive, because tone lives in more than just word choice — delivery and body language carry it too

C.

As passive, because "please" is a soft word

Answer Key

1.

"Send me the report. Now." → Rude; "Hey, can you send me the report?" → Casual; "Um... maybe, if it's not too much trouble, could you possibly send the report sometime?" → Passive; "Could you send me the report, please?" → Professional; "Could you send me the report by 3 PM? I need it for the client call." → Confident and respectful. All five versions ask for the exact same thing. Only the tone changes — and the tone is what decides how Priyanka feels about helping.

2.

Suggested answer: It's so hedged and unclear that Priyanka can't tell how urgent it really is, or whether Arif even knows what he needs. Being extra soft isn't the same as being clear.

3.

Suggested answer: Purpose: I need my supervisor to approve my leave request before Friday. Audience: my supervisor, someone senior I respect but know reasonably well. Message: which dates, and why I need an answer by Friday. Tone: professional and respectful, not overly formal since we talk daily. Action: a clear yes/no by Thursday so I can book my ticket.

4.

Correct: B. Polite words said in a rushed, dismissive way can still land badly — tone is carried by delivery as much as by vocabulary. This is why MIS-0014 warns that "please" alone doesn't fix tone.

lessons.title: Making Polite and Confident Requests
lessons.objectives_html:
• Rewrite a blunt request into a polite, confident one.
  • Make an original polite request appropriate to a given workplace situation.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Now that Arif can hear the difference between tones, the next step is producing them on purpose. This lesson is about the single most common thing anyone does at work: asking for something — information, a document, help, time. Getting the request itself right, in the moment, is a specific skill.

Key workplace lesson

A request has two jobs at once: it has to be clear (the other person knows exactly what you need) and respectful (the other person doesn't feel ordered around). Softening a request doesn't mean being vague — Lesson 7.1's "passive" version proved that too much softening actually makes things less clear. The skill here is a specific set of modal-based openers that stay both clear and polite at the same time.

Listen & Read
Pair 1 — Asking for the invoice
Open-plan office, mid-morning.
Arif (❌ blunt): Send me the invoice.
Priyanka: (a short pause) ...Okay. Which one, exactly?
Arif (✅ polite and confident, same request): Could you send me the invoice for the Haque account, please?
Priyanka: Sure, sending it over now.
Pair 2 — Asking Hasan to check something before a meeting
Near the printer, early afternoon.
Arif (❌ blunt): Fix this today.
Hasan: (surprised) Fix... what, exactly? Is something wrong with it?
Arif (✅ polite and confident, same request): Would you mind looking at this today? It's for tomorrow's meeting, so any errors would be good to catch now.
Hasan: Got it — I'll look at it this afternoon.
Pair 3 — Asking Mr. Hossain to double-check numbers, no urgency
Mr. Hossain's office doorway, late afternoon.
Arif (❌ blunt): Check the numbers.
Mr. Hossain: (looking up) Which numbers? And by when?
Arif (✅ polite and confident, same request): When you get a chance, could you double-check the numbers on page 2? No rush — end of the week is fine.
Mr. Hossain: That works. I'll take a look tomorrow.

Key expressions

Pattern PAT-0015 — the softened-request family: "Could you...?" / "Would you mind + verb-ing?" / "When you get a chance, could you...?" — three openers that keep a request both clear and polite, at three slightly different levels of formality.

Expression Function Example Register
"Could you...?" The everyday, safe default request opener "Could you send me the file?" Neutral-polite
"Would you mind + verb-ing?" A slightly softer, more formal request opener "Would you mind sending me the file?" Polite-formal
"When you get a chance, could you...?" Adds "no rush" without being vague about what you need "When you get a chance, could you check this for me?" Polite, relaxed on timing

Vocabulary

  • V-0198 would you mind — a polite, slightly more formal way to ask someone to do something; always followed by a verb-ing form. আরেকটু আনুষ্ঠানিক ও ভদ্র অনুরোধ করার ধরন (এর পরে verb-ing বসে) · अधिक विनम्र और थोड़ा औपचारिक अनुरोध का तरीका (इसके बाद verb-ing आता है)
  • V-0199 when you get a chance — a phrase that removes urgency from a request without making it unclear what you need. যখন সময় পাবেন / সুযোগ হলে (তাড়াহুড়ো নেই এমন অনুরোধে ব্যবহৃত হয়) · जब मौका मिले (बिना जल्दबाज़ी वाले अनुरोध में)

Grammar in context

GIC-0005 — Modals for softened requests: "Could you...?" vs. "Would you mind...?" vs. "Can you...?"

  • "Can you...?" — the most casual of the three; fine with close colleagues, a little too casual for someone senior or someone you don't know well.
  • "Could you...?" — the safe, neutral-polite default; works almost everywhere. The past form "could" doesn't refer to the past here — it's simply softer-sounding than "can."
  • "Would you mind + verb-ing?" — the most formal of the three; useful when the request is a bigger ask, or the relationship is more formal.
  • Common mistake: using "must" or "have to" when asking a colleague for something ("You must send this today") — these words state an obligation, not a request, and sound like an order even between equals. Save "must"/"have to" for describing rules or genuine deadlines set by someone else, not for your own requests.

❌ / ✅ Contrastive examples

❌ Blunt ✅ Polite and confident
"Send me the invoice." "Could you send me the invoice, please?"
"Fix this today." "Would you mind looking at this today? It's for tomorrow's meeting."
"Check the numbers." "When you get a chance, could you double-check the numbers on page 2?"

Common mistake

MIS-0015 — Softening the opener but not the rest of the sentence: "Could you send this now?" still sounds like a disguised order — the modal opener is polite, but the bare word "now" undoes it. The fix isn't to remove urgency altogether; it's to explain it: "Could you send this by 2 PM? I need it before the client call." (This is the same fix Lesson 7.1's Version 5 used — reason and timeframe instead of a bare urgency word.)

A real formal register, for contrast

Real job postings and official notices use an even more formal request register than everyday office speech — for example, a university employment notice inviting applications typically reads along the lines of "applications are invited from eligible candidates" rather than anything resembling a spoken request. You won't need this register for asking a colleague for a file, but recognizing it helps you calibrate: everyday workplace requests sit comfortably between this very formal, written register and the too-casual "hey, can you..." — most of what you say out loud belongs in the middle, at "Could you...?" or "Would you mind...?"

Pronunciation

"Could you" is often said quickly as one connected sound ("Could-jə") in natural speech — this is normal and not sloppy, but the meaning and politeness stay exactly the same either way.

Practice

  1. Rewriting: Turn each ❌ blunt request above into a ✅ polite one, without copying the example — use your own wording.
  2. Controlled: Complete: "___ you send me the schedule?" / "Would you mind ___ (check) this for me?"
  3. Guided: Build an original request for a real situation this week, using one of the three openers.
  4. Role-play: Ask a partner (or imagine asking a colleague) for something you genuinely need, using "Could you...?" and then again using "Would you mind...?" Notice how the second one feels slightly more formal.

Self-check

  1. Which of the three request openers is the safest default when you're unsure how formal to be?
  2. Why does "Could you send this now?" still sound like an order, even with "could you"?
  3. Rewrite this into a polite, confident request: "Give me the numbers by lunch."

Motivation

"Politeness is strength, not weakness."

lessons.title: Responding Professionally
lessons.objectives_html:
• Agree to a request professionally.
  • Decline a request professionally without sounding rude or overly apologetic.
  • Acknowledge information professionally.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Arif spends most of his day on the receiving end of requests, not just making them. In one afternoon he might need to agree to something, turn something down, and simply acknowledge news — three very different jobs that a new employee often runs together by instinct, using the wrong tone for each.

Key workplace lesson

Three response types, three different needs:

  • Agreeing needs to sound willing, not grudging.
  • Declining needs to sound honest and helpful, not rude and not over-apologetic.
  • Acknowledging needs to sound engaged, not silent or dismissive.

Getting these three mixed up is one of the fastest ways to seem harder to work with than you actually are — a perfectly reasonable "no" can sound rude if it's too blunt, or unconfident if it's buried under five apologies.

Listen & Read
Pair 1 — Agreeing to help Priyanka
Open-plan office, morning.
Priyanka: Arif, could you cover the front desk for ten minutes while I make a call?
Arif (❌ weak agreement): Umm... okay, I guess so.
Priyanka: (hesitating) Are you sure that's okay? I can ask someone else.
Arif (✅ professional agreement, replayed): Sure, I can do that. Go ahead.
Priyanka: Thanks, back in ten minutes.
Pair 2 — Declining a same-day request from Mr. Hossain
Mr. Hossain's office, mid-afternoon.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, can you finish the full report today?
Arif (❌ blunt decline): No, I can't.
Mr. Hossain: (pausing) Alright... when, then?
Arif (❌ over-apologetic decline, alternative wrong version): Oh no, I'm so sorry, I really can't, I'm really really sorry about this, I feel terrible.
Arif (✅ professional decline, replayed): I'm not able to finish it today, but I can have it to you by tomorrow morning.
Mr. Hossain: That works. Tomorrow morning is fine.
Pair 3 — Acknowledging a schedule change
Hallway, near the meeting room.
Mr. Hossain: Just so you know, the client meeting has moved to 10 AM.
Arif (❌ disengaged acknowledgment): (no response, walks on)
Mr. Hossain: (calling after him) Arif — did you catch that?
Arif (✅ professional acknowledgment, replayed): Thanks for letting me know — 10 AM, got it.

Vocabulary

  • V-0200 I'm not able to — a clear, professional way to say "no" without bluntness or over-apologizing; always followed by naming what you can do instead. আমি এখন পারব না (একই সাথে কী করতে পারবেন তা জানানো হয়) · मैं अभी नहीं कर पाऊँगा/पाऊँगी (साथ में यह भी बताया जाता है कि आप क्या कर सकते हैं)

Three response types

1. Agreeing

  • ❌ Weak: "Umm... okay, I guess so." — sounds reluctant, plants doubt.
  • ✅ P-0032 "Sure, I can do that." — clear, willing, no hedging.

2. Declining

  • ❌ Blunt: "No, I can't." — technically honest, sounds cold with no path forward.
  • ❌ Over-apologetic: "Oh no, I'm so sorry, I really can't, I'm really really sorry about this, I feel terrible." — the apology becomes the message instead of useful information.
  • ✅ PAT-0016 — "I'm not able to [X] right now, but I can [Y] by [time]." e.g. "I'm not able to finish this today, but I can have it to you by tomorrow morning."

3. Acknowledging

  • ❌ Silent / no response, or "k" — reads as disengaged, leaves the sender unsure it was received.
  • ✅ "Thanks for letting me know." (recycled P-0028, Module 6 Lesson 5) — short, warm, confirms receipt.

Grammar in context

No new grammar structure — Pattern PAT-0016's "I'm not able to [X], but I can [Y] by [time]" uses grammar you already know (present simple + "but" + "by" for a deadline); the skill is combining them into one balanced sentence that says no and yes at the same time.

Common mistake

MIS-0016 — Over-apologizing when declining: Piling on multiple "sorry"s ("I'm so sorry, I'm really sorry, sorry about this") doesn't make a decline more polite — past a certain point, it signals anxiety rather than professionalism, and can even make the other person feel they need to comfort you. One honest acknowledgment plus a clear alternative (Pattern PAT-0016) is more professional than five apologies.

Practice

  1. Recognition: Label each example above as agree / decline / acknowledge, and as ❌ or ✅.
  2. Rewriting: Turn each ❌ example into its ✅ version, in your own words.
  3. Guided speaking: Respond to three prompts in a row — one you'll agree to, one you'll decline, one you'll simply acknowledge — using the right response type for each.
  4. Role-play: A partner (or imagined colleague) makes three different requests/statements to you in sequence. Respond to all three appropriately, in real time.

Self-check

  1. What's wrong with declining a request using five "sorry"s in a row?
  2. Complete Pattern PAT-0016: "I'm not able to review this today, but I can ___."
  3. Your supervisor tells you the client meeting has moved to 10 AM. What's a professional way to acknowledge this?

Motivation

"How you say no matters as much as how you say yes."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Matching

Label each response as agree, decline, or acknowledge, and as ❌ (weak/wrong) or ✅ (professional).

"Umm... okay, I guess so."

________

"Sure, I can do that."

________

"No, I can't."

________

"I'm not able to finish it today, but I can have it to you by tomorrow morning."

________

"Thanks for letting me know."

________
2. Rewriting

Rewrite this over-apologetic decline into a professional one using Pattern PAT-0016: "Oh no, I'm so sorry, I really can't review this today, I feel terrible, I'm really sorry."

3. Guided Practice

Respond to three prompts in a row, using the correct response type each time — (1) A colleague asks you to help with a quick task you can do. (2) Your supervisor asks you to finish something today that you genuinely can't finish until tomorrow. (3) A colleague tells you the meeting room has changed.

4. Role-Play

A partner (or imagined colleague) makes three different requests/statements to you in sequence — one you'll agree to, one you'll decline, one you'll simply acknowledge. Respond to all three appropriately, in real time.

Answer Key

1.

"Umm... okay, I guess so." → Agree — ❌ weak; "Sure, I can do that." → Agree — ✅ professional; "No, I can't." → Decline — ❌ blunt; "I'm not able to finish it today, but I can have it to you by tomorrow morning." → Decline — ✅ professional; "Thanks for letting me know." → Acknowledge — ✅ professional. Each response type has its own failure mode — agreeing can sound reluctant, declining can sound cold or overwrought, and acknowledging can sound disengaged. The fix is the same each time — clarity plus warmth, without excess.

2.

Suggested answer: I'm not able to review this today, but I can look at it first thing tomorrow.

3.

Suggested answer: (1) Sure, I can do that. (2) I'm not able to finish it today, but I can have it to you by tomorrow morning. (3) Thanks for letting me know — I'll head to the new room.

4.

Sample: (agree) "Sure, I can do that." (decline) "I'm not able to do it this afternoon, but I can do it first thing tomorrow." (acknowledge) "Thanks for letting me know." Check: the speaker correctly identifies which response type each prompt calls for and responds using the matching pattern (agree, PAT-0016 for decline, acknowledge), without mixing tones (e.g. over-apologizing on the agree, or sounding blunt on the decline).

lessons.title: Tone, Hierarchy and Respect at Work
lessons.objectives_html:
• Adjust tone appropriately when speaking to someone more senior vs. a peer.
  • Identify at least 2 common tone mistakes new employees make with senior colleagues.
  • Combine tone, register, and content into one coherent interaction.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson opening

Everything Module 7 has taught separately — reading tone, making requests, responding well — now has to work together, in real time, with someone senior. This lesson is a rehearsal: a single connected interaction with Mr. Hossain that pulls together greeting, requesting, responding to an instruction, and closing, all under one hierarchy-aware tone.

Key workplace lesson

Hierarchy doesn't mean fear or stiffness — it means calibration. The same request that works perfectly with Priyanka (a peer) needs a slightly different shape with Mr. Hossain (a supervisor): usually a touch more formal, a touch more explanatory, but never distant or robotic. New employees tend to fail in one of two directions with someone senior — treating them exactly like a peer (over-familiarity), or over-correcting into stiff, distant formality (over-stiffness). Both miss the same target: natural respect.

Listen & Read
Common-mistakes mini-scenario — same request, two ways
Two different new employees, same supervisor, same situation — needing to leave 15 minutes early to catch a delayed bus.
Employee A (❌ over-familiar): Hey, I'm heading out a bit early, that cool?
Supervisor: (pausing, unsure how to read this) ...Sure, I suppose. Is everything okay?
Employee B (❌ over-stiff): Respected Sir, I am writing to humbly request your kind permission to depart the premises fifteen minutes prior to the standard time.
Supervisor: (a little taken aback) ...You can just ask me normally, you know. But yes, that's fine.
Full connected rehearsal — Arif and Mr. Hossain
Mr. Hossain's office doorway, late afternoon.
Arif: Good afternoon — do you have a minute?
Mr. Hossain: Of course, come in.
Arif: I wanted to check if it would be alright to leave a little early today — I've finished the priority items, and I can pick up the rest first thing tomorrow.
Mr. Hossain: That's fine. Before you go, can you send Priyanka the updated file?
Arif: Sure, I can do that. Should I copy you on it as well?
Mr. Hossain: Yes, please — and let her know it still needs her sign-off.
Arif: Got it, I'll send it now and mention the sign-off.
Mr. Hossain: Perfect, thanks, Arif.
Arif: Thank you — have a good evening.

Common mistakes

MIS-0017 — Over-familiarity with someone senior: treating a supervisor exactly like a peer too soon — first-name-only casualness, joking before the relationship has earned it, or using Lesson 7.2's most casual opener ("Can you...?") with someone clearly senior. Not offensive, but reads as not-yet-attuned to the relationship (echoes MIS-0006 from Module 3).

MIS-0018 — Over-stiffness with someone senior: over-correcting into distant, robotic formality — heavily formal phrasing, avoiding any warmth at all, treating every interaction like a formal letter even in ordinary spoken conversation. This can read as cold or even anxious, rather than respectful.

Common-mistakes mini-scenario

Two new employees, same situation: both need to ask their supervisor if they can leave 15 minutes early to catch a delayed bus.

  • Employee A (over-familiar): "Hey, I'm heading out a bit early, that cool?" — too casual for a supervisor they've known only a few weeks; sounds like they're informing, not asking.
  • Employee B (over-stiff): "Respected Sir, I am writing to humbly request your kind permission to depart the premises fifteen minutes prior to the standard time." — technically polite, but so formal for a spoken, in-person request that it sounds unnatural and distant.
  • What actually works (see the Tone Ladder below): calibrated between the two — clear, respectful, and natural.

Career English Upgrade Ladder — TL-0003: Asking your manager for something, while respecting hierarchy

Situation: asking to leave 15 minutes early to catch a delayed bus.

  • ❌ Too casual: "Hey, I'm heading out a bit early, that cool?"
  • Basic: "I need to leave a bit early today."
  • Better: "Is it okay if I leave a little early today?"
  • Professional (taught rung): "Would it be alright if I left a little early today? I can finish the rest of this tomorrow morning."
  • Advanced: "I wanted to check if it would be alright to leave a little early today — I've finished the priority items, and I can pick up the rest first thing tomorrow."
  • ❌ Too formal: "Respected Sir, I am writing to humbly request your kind permission to depart the premises fifteen minutes prior to the standard time."
  • Why Professional is the taught rung here (not Advanced): Professional already includes both the request and a plan for the unfinished work — enough to satisfy a supervisor who knows Arif reasonably well. Advanced would suit a first, more formal ask with someone Arif barely knows; the skill is choosing the rung that matches the actual relationship, not to always reach for the most elaborate version.

Full connected interaction — a rehearsal

Look again at the full conversation between Arif and Mr. Hossain in the Listen & Read section. Notice how it uses almost nothing new: the greeting (Module 3), the request (Lesson 7.2), the agreement and instruction-response (Lesson 7.3), all held together by one consistent, respectful, senior-appropriate tone.

Practice

  1. Recognition: In the mini-scenario, name what's wrong with Employee A's and Employee B's versions, in your own words.
  2. Guided: Using the Tone Ladder, write your own "professional" rung for a different hierarchy-aware request (e.g., asking to work from home one day, or asking for a clearer deadline).
  3. Full role-play: Perform the complete connected interaction above with a partner, or record yourself doing both roles.

Self-check

  1. What are the two opposite tone mistakes new employees make with someone senior?
  2. In the Tone Ladder above, why is "Professional" the taught rung rather than "Advanced"?
  3. In the full interaction, which line shows Arif both agreeing to a task and checking one detail — combining two Module 7 skills in a single sentence?

Career upgrade

By the end of Level 1, you're no longer just producing correct English — you're choosing the right register for the room, in real time. That's the skill this whole module has been building toward, and it's exactly what the Level 1 capstone will ask you to do.

Module assessment

Before/after rewriting task — 3 short workplace messages, each with a tone problem (too blunt, too casual for the audience, or over-apologetic). Rewrite each into a version that fits Module 7's standards. This activity directly feeds into the Level 1 capstone.

Motivation

"Respect is communicated, not assumed."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Short Answer

In the mini-scenario, what's wrong with Employee A's request? What's wrong with Employee B's request? Name one issue for each.

2. Guided Practice

Using the Tone Ladder (TL-0003) as a model, write your own "professional" rung for a different hierarchy-aware request — for example, asking to work from home one day, or asking your supervisor for a clearer deadline.

3. Role-Play

Perform the full connected interaction with Mr. Hossain (greeting, request, agreeing to a task, checking a detail, closing) with a partner, or record yourself doing both roles.

4. Rewriting Assessment

Module 7 assessment. Rewrite each of these 3 workplace messages so it fits a professional, appropriately calibrated tone: (1) To your supervisor: "Give me the file." (2) To your supervisor: "Yo boss, can't make it in early tmrw, that ok?" (3) To a colleague: "I'm so so sorry but I can't finish this today, I feel terrible, sorry, sorry."

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Employee A sounds too casual for a supervisor they don't know well yet — it reads more like announcing a decision than asking permission. Employee B is so formal and elaborate for a spoken, in-person request that it sounds unnatural and distant rather than respectful.

2.

Suggested answer: Would it be alright if I worked from home tomorrow? I have everything I need to finish the report, and I'll be reachable all day. / Could you clarify the deadline for this? I want to make sure I'm prioritizing it correctly against my other tasks.

3.

Use the Listen & Read dialogue as the model. Check that all four stages are there (greeting, request, agreeing to the task with a clarifying check, closing) and that the tone stays consistent and senior-appropriate throughout — neither over-familiar nor over-stiff.

4.

Suggested answer: (1) Could you send me the file, please? (2) Good morning — would it be alright if I came in a little later tomorrow? I'll make up the time in the afternoon. (3) I'm not able to finish this today, but I can have it ready by tomorrow morning. What to listen/look for: Each rewrite removes the original tone problem (bluntness, mismatched casualness for a supervisor, or over-apologizing) while keeping the message clear, and applies a pattern taught in Module 7 (a softened request opener, hierarchy-aware calibration, or PAT-0016's decline-with-alternative structure).

assessment.title: Level 1 Assessment
assessment.objectives_html:
• Demonstrate the core communication skill from each of Level 1's 7 modules, tested one at a time.
  • Produce short spoken and written responses under exam conditions, without a rehearsed script.
assessment.body_html:
About this assessment

Every module ended with its own small assessment. This is different: one sitting, three parts, drawing on all seven modules at once — but unlike the capstone that follows it, each item here stands alone. This assessment checks whether a specific skill was learned; the capstone checks whether all of them can work together in one real day. Sit this first, then move on to the capstone.

Part A — Reading: choose the best response (items 1–7)

Read each short workplace situation and choose the most appropriate response. There is one item per module, in order. (Audio is not available yet, so this part is read, not heard.)

Part B — Speaking (items 8–14)

Respond aloud to each prompt, and record yourself if you can. There is no single correct wording: each response is scored with the criteria below, and a sample answer is given in the key so you can compare.

Part C — Writing (items 15–18)

Write a short response to each scenario. Most combine two modules' language, the same way real situations rarely stay inside one lesson.

Scoring

Part A: 1 point for each correct answer (7 points).

Parts B and C: score each item from 0 to 3 — one point for each criterion it meets. Only criteria that apply to that kind of task are used:

Criterion (1 point)Part B — speakingPart C — writing
TaskDoes exactly what the prompt asks (for example, names both options, states the purpose, restates the deadline).Same.
LanguageUses the module's workplace phrases and vocabulary accurately.Same, with correct grammar and spelling.
Tone and deliveryRegister fits the listener; clear and easy to understand, without long hesitation or repeated apologies.Register fits the reader; polite, clear and appropriately brief.

Maximum: Part A 7 + Part B 21 + Part C 12 = 40 points.

Passing this assessment

"One test, seven modules, no surprises — you've already done every one of these before."

Pass mark: 28 of 40 (70%), with at least 4 of 7 in Part A. For any item where you scored 0 or 1, review the module named in the item before moving on to the capstone.

Nothing in Parts A–C is new. Every scenario echoes a lesson you've already worked through. If a particular item feels hard, that module is worth a quick review before moving on to the capstone — but there's no need to prepare anything new to sit this assessment.
assessment.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 1 — A new colleague asks, "So what's your background?" What's the best response?

A.

I don't really want to talk about that.

B.

I studied business and worked in retail for two years before this.

C.

Why do you want to know?

2. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 2 — It's your first day. The receptionist says, "Good morning, how can I help you?" What do you say?

A.

Yeah, I'm here for the job.

B.

Good morning, I'm Nadia — I'm starting today, I have a 9 AM meeting with HR.

C.

Is this the right building?

3. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 3 — A colleague you don't know well asks, "How's your weekend going?" during a coffee break. What's an appropriate reply?

A.

It's fine, actually I had a huge fight with my landlord about rent.

B.

Pretty relaxing, thanks — how about yours?

C.

Why are you asking me that?

4. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 4 — Your supervisor says, "Send the invoice to the client before 5 PM." What should you say to confirm?

A.

Okay.

B.

Got it — send the invoice to the client before 5.

C.

What invoice?

5. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 5 — Your manager says, "Update the file," but there are two files on your desk. What should you ask?

A.

What do you mean?

B.

Which file do you mean — the sales report or the client list?

C.

(Update both files, just in case.)

6. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 6 — Your supervisor asks how a task is going. Which response uses the clearest workplace vocabulary?

A.

It's, you know, mostly done I think.

B.

I've submitted the draft; it's pending your review now.

C.

I did the thing.

7. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 7 — You need a colleague to send you a file today. Which request is best calibrated — polite but clear?

A.

Send me the file.

B.

Could you send me the file by 4 PM today? I need it for a client call.

C.

I am writing to humbly request that you kindly forward the file at your earliest convenience.

8. Role-Play Assessment

Module 1 — Introduce yourself the way you would to a new colleague: include your name, your role or background, and one welcoming or open line.

9. Role-Play Assessment

Module 2 — It's your first day. Greet the receptionist and explain why you're there.

10. Role-Play Assessment

Module 3 — A peer asks, "Busy day?" during a break. Respond naturally, then ask a follow-up question of your own.

11. Role-Play Assessment

Module 4 — Your supervisor says, "Before you leave, email the vendor the updated order and copy me on it." Confirm the instruction back in your own words.

12. Role-Play Assessment

Module 5 — Your supervisor says, "Fix the numbers before the meeting" without saying which numbers. Ask a specific clarifying question.

13. Role-Play Assessment

Module 6 — Give a one-sentence status update on a task, using at least one workplace status verb (submitted, pending, in progress, reviewed, and so on).

14. Role-Play Assessment

Module 7 — Make a polite request to a colleague for something you need before the end of the day.

15. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 3 + 7 — A colleague misreads a casual comment you made as rude. Write what you'd say to clarify, keeping it warm but clear.

16. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 4 + 5 — You receive an instruction with a deadline that seems unrealistic. Write a response that confirms what you understood and asks one clarifying question.

17. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 1 + 2 — Write a short self-introduction you'd give when meeting your whole team for the first time, not one-on-one.

18. Writing Assessment

Modules 6 + 7 — Write a short, professional message to your supervisor requesting one extra day to finish a task, using at least one workplace status verb.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. A short, concrete 2–3 sentence background is exactly what Module 1 trains — neither evasive nor defensive.

2.

Correct: B. The correct option greets, identifies the speaker, and states the purpose — the complete first-day arrival pattern from Module 2.

3.

Correct: B. Brief, safe, and reciprocal — financial or personal-conflict details are an unsafe small-talk topic per Module 3.

4.

Correct: B. Restating the action, object, and deadline is Module 4's confirmation-restatement skill; "Okay" confirms nothing specific.

5.

Correct: B. A targeted clarifying question that names both possibilities beats a vague question or a guess — Module 5's core skill.

6.

Correct: B. "Submitted" and "pending" are the precise status verbs Module 6 introduces, in place of vague filler.

7.

Correct: B. A softened opener plus a specific deadline and reason — clear and polite without over-formality between peers, per Module 7.

8.

Sample: "Hi, I'm Nadia. I studied business, and I've worked in retail for two years. I'll be on the front-office team — really looking forward to working with you." Task point: name, background or role, and a welcoming close. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

9.

Sample: "Good morning. I'm Nadia — I'm starting today. I'm here to see Mr. Hossain." Task point: greeting, name, and purpose (PAT-0001). Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

10.

Sample: "Pretty busy, actually — it's been non-stop since nine. How about you?" Task point: a short answer plus a returned question. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

11.

Sample: "So, before I leave, I'll email the vendor the updated order and copy you on it." Task point: the action, the object, the person to copy and the deadline ("before I leave") are all restated. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

12.

Sample: "Just to check — do you mean the numbers in this week's sales report, or the figures in the client invoice?" Task point: names the specific options instead of "What do you mean?" (MIS-0010). Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

13.

Sample: "The client report is in progress — the invoice section is still pending, and I'll submit it by Thursday." Task point: at least one status word used correctly. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

14.

Sample: "Could you send me the updated rota before 5 today? I need it to plan tomorrow's shifts." Task point: a softened request with a time and a reason. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

15.

Sample: "I think my comment this morning came out wrong — I didn't mean it as a criticism at all. I only meant the queue was long. Thanks for telling me." Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Task point: acknowledges the misunderstanding, corrects it plainly, and keeps a warm, non-defensive tone — without over-apologizing.

16.

Sample: "Just to confirm — you'd like the full inventory report by 3 PM today? Could you tell me which section is most urgent, so I can finish that first?" Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Task point: restates the instruction accurately before asking a targeted (not vague) clarifying question about the deadline.

17.

Sample: "Hi everyone, nice to meet you all. I'm Nadia — I studied business and I've worked in retail for two years. I'll be on the front desk with you, and I'm really looking forward to working with you all." Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Task point: adapts the three-part self-introduction to a group setting — name, role or background, and an open, welcoming close.

18.

Sample: "Hi Mr. Hossain, the monthly report is in progress — I've finished the sales section, but the expense figures are still pending from Accounts. Would it be possible to have one extra day, until Thursday, to finish it? Thanks, Nadia." Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Task point: uses a softened request pattern, states the reason briefly, and includes a precise status verb (in progress, pending, and so on) rather than a vague description.

capstone.title: Your First Weeks at Work
capstone.objectives_html:
• Carry one realistic workplace day, in English, from arrival to close, without a script.
  • Draw on greetings, self-introduction, instructions, clarifying questions, workplace vocabulary, polite requests, small talk, and tone-repair — switching between them as the situation demands, not one at a time.
  • Self-assess a spoken or role-played performance against a real workplace communication rubric.
capstone.body_html:
About this capstone

Every lesson since Module 1 has taught one piece of workplace communication at a time. Real workdays don't come in pieces. A single ordinary Wednesday might ask you to greet someone, follow an instruction, ask a question, report progress, make a request, chat for thirty seconds, fix a misunderstanding, and close out the day — all before lunch is really over, and all without stopping to think "which module is this?"

This capstone is not a new lesson and not a quiz. It's one continuous simulation — a single workday, told in nine connected steps — built entirely from language you already know. Nothing below is new. The only new thing is doing it all in one sequence, the way a real day actually works.

How it's used: read or perform the nine steps in order, then self-assess using the rubric that follows, then do the same nine steps again yourself — as a full role-play, alone or with a partner. The goal isn't to recognize the right answer. It's to produce your own version of each step, in your own words, under the same conditions your first weeks in a job give you: no script, and no time to plan every sentence in advance.

The simulation: an ordinary Wednesday

It's a normal Wednesday, several weeks into the job. Nothing about today is special — and that's exactly the point. This is the day every lesson so far has been quietly preparing you for.

Step 1 — Arrive and greet (Module 2)

Arif arrives at 8:50, the same as always. Nothing here is new; it's the easy, automatic part of the day — which is exactly why it comes first.

Listen & Read
Front gate, 8:50 AM.
Arif: Morning, Nasir!
Nasir: Morning, sir! Another sunny one today.
Arif: It really is. Have a good one.

Step 2 — Introduce yourself to the team (Module 1)

Priyanka is showing a new hire, Meghla, around the floor. Arif gets to be on the other side of a first-day introduction for once.

Listen & Read
The back office, a few minutes later. Priyanka is showing a new hire, Meghla, around.
Priyanka: Meghla, this is Arif — he's on the front desk with me.
Arif: Hi Meghla, nice to meet you. I'm Arif — I joined the front-office team a few weeks ago, so I still remember how confusing the first days are. Let me know if you ever need help finding your way around.
Meghla: Thanks, Arif — I appreciate that.

Notice the shape: name, a short line of background, then something useful for the other person — the same three-part self-introduction from Module 1, just delivered from more experience.

Step 3 — Receive instructions from your supervisor (Module 4)

Mr. Hossain stops by Arif's desk with a two-part instruction — an action and object, plus a deadline tucked at the end, exactly the shape Module 4 trained Arif's ear to catch.

Listen & Read
Mr. Hossain stops by Arif's desk mid-morning.
Mr. Hossain: Arif, can you pull last week's client feedback forms and send Priyanka a summary? She needs it before the 3 PM review.
Arif: Got it — pull last week's feedback forms, summary to Priyanka before 3.

Step 4 — Ask a clarifying question (Module 5)

One detail in the instruction is genuinely ambiguous — today is Wednesday, so "last week" could mean two different things. Arif doesn't guess, and doesn't ask a vague "what do you mean?" either.

Listen & Read
A moment later, at his desk. Today is Wednesday.
Arif: Just to check — by "last week," do you mean the calendar week that ended Sunday, or the last seven days?
Mr. Hossain: Calendar week — Monday to Sunday.

Step 5 — Complete the task and give a status update (Module 6)

An hour later, Mr. Hossain checks in. Arif reports progress using the plain, confident workplace verbs Module 6 introduced — pulled, reviewing, submitted — not a long explanation.

Listen & Read
An hour later. Mr. Hossain checks in briefly on his way past.
Mr. Hossain: How's the summary coming along?
Arif: I've pulled the forms and I'm reviewing them now — I'll have the summary submitted to Priyanka well before 3.

Step 6 — Make a polite request (Module 7)

Partway through, Arif hits a column he isn't sure how to read and needs thirty seconds of Priyanka's time. This is Module 7's softened-request family in its natural habitat — a small, low-stakes ask between peers.

Listen & Read
Twenty minutes later. Arif isn't sure how to read one column in the forms.
Arif: Priyanka, would you mind taking a quick look at this column before I finalize the summary? I want to make sure I'm reading these ratings correctly.
Priyanka: Sure, give me a second... yes, that's the satisfaction score, not the response time.
Arif: Perfect, thank you — that saves me from getting it wrong.

Step 7 — Small talk on a break (Module 3)

Lunch. A short, safe exchange with Hasan — an opener, a follow-up, nothing more. Small talk doesn't need to be clever; it needs to be brief and comfortable.

Listen & Read
Lunch break, staff room.
Hasan: Busy morning?
Arif: Yeah, pretty full — client feedback summary due by 3. You?
Hasan: Same old. You still coming Friday?
Arif: Wouldn't miss it.

Step 8 — Handle a small misunderstanding (Modules 4, 5 and 7 together)

Back at his desk, Arif sends the summary — and Priyanka comes back confused about which week it actually covers. This step is the capstone's real test: clarifying what went wrong (Module 5), correcting it plainly (Module 4), and doing both without over-apologizing or sounding defensive (Module 7).

Listen & Read
Back at his desk, just after sending the summary. A message from Priyanka.
Priyanka (message): Wait, I thought you said the summary covers this week, not last week?
Arif (message): Sorry for the confusion — I meant the calendar week that just ended (Mon-Sun), not this current week. Let me know if you'd like this week's numbers added as well.
Priyanka (message): Got it, that makes sense — this is exactly what I needed. Thanks for clearing that up.

Step 9 — End-of-day update and a professional close (Modules 2 and 6)

5:40 PM. One last check-in with Mr. Hossain before heading out — a short status update and a clean, professional close to the day, the same combination Module 2 first introduced back on Arif's actual first day.

Listen & Read
5:40 PM, Mr. Hossain's office doorway.
Arif: Before I head out — the client feedback summary is submitted, and Priyanka confirmed she had what she needed for the 3 PM review. Tomorrow I'll follow up on the two forms that came in incomplete.
Mr. Hossain: Sounds good. Thanks for staying on top of that.
Arif: Have a good evening.
Mr. Hossain: You too, Arif.

Why this counts as "Level 1 complete"

Look back at what just happened: nine situations, five different people, three registers (peer, new colleague, supervisor), one genuine mistake, and not a single moment where Arif had to stop and think about grammar. That's the actual target of Level 1 — not perfect English, but functioning English: understanding what's said, responding appropriately, and keeping a workday moving. Every phrase Arif used above was taught somewhere between Module 1 and Module 7; today was simply the day they all had to work together.

Self-assessment rubric

Use this rubric to score a recording of yourself performing the nine steps (Practice, below), or to score a partner's performance if you're practicing together. Every row applies here, because the capstone is one continuous spoken role-play.

Score area Weight What "good" looks like
Clarity 15% The message is understandable without excessive repetition or hesitation.
Appropriateness 15% Register matches the audience — peer, new colleague, or supervisor.
Confidence 10% Delivered without excessive hedging or apologizing.
Listening / response accuracy 20% Responds to what was actually said, not a generic memorized line.
Vocabulary 10% Uses workplace vocabulary and expressions accurately in context.
Tone 15% Neither too casual nor too formal for the situation.
Pronunciation 10% Intelligible; stress and intonation roughly match the taught patterns.
Professional behavior 5% Basic courtesy markers present — thanks, an appropriate close, no dropped threads.

How to score it: give each row a mark from 0 to 4 (0 = not shown, 1 = rarely, 2 = sometimes, 3 = mostly, 4 = consistently). Multiply by the row's weight and divide by 4 — for example, 3 for Clarity gives 15 × 3 ÷ 4 ≈ 11 points. Add the rows for a total out of 100. 70 or more: Level 1 complete. Below 70: repeat the steps that use the modules behind your lowest rows, then perform the whole day again.

Score the whole performance, not each step separately. Watch or read back the whole nine-step performance once, then score each row for the performance as a whole. Someone who handles Step 8's misunderstanding well but stumbles on a word in Step 3 is doing better, overall, than one who never makes a mistake but sounds stiff and over-apologetic throughout — because Step 8 is closer to what a real workday actually demands.

Practice

  1. Full role-play (the actual capstone task): Perform all nine steps in one continuous sequence, either with a partner taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded separately and then played back in order. Don't read from this page while performing — glance at the setting line for each step, then produce the conversation yourself, in your own words.
  2. Self-score: Immediately afterward, score your own performance against the rubric above. Be honest rather than generous — the rubric exists to show you where to focus next, not to make you feel good.
  3. Written reflection: In 3–4 sentences, describe the one step you found hardest, and why. Was it a language problem (not knowing the right phrase) or a confidence problem (knowing the phrase but hesitating to use it)? The fix is different for each.
  4. Repeat once: Perform the full nine steps a second time, focusing only on whichever rubric row scored lowest the first time.

Self-check

  1. Which step required combining more than one module's language at the same time, rather than using one skill in isolation?
  2. In Step 4, why does Arif ask a specific clarifying question instead of just guessing which week was meant?
  3. In Step 8, what does Arif do instead of simply saying "sorry" several times?
  4. Pick any one step above and rewrite Arif's line in your own words, keeping the same meaning and the same register.

You've completed Level 1

"You didn't memorize a script today. You had a workday."

That's the real marker of finishing Level 1: not that every sentence was perfect, but that a full, ordinary, occasionally-messy workday — greetings, instructions, a genuine misunderstanding, a polite request, small talk, and a professional close — happened entirely in English, and it held together. Level 2 builds on exactly this foundation: the same kind of real workday, with more responsibility, more writing, and more of the workplace's formal side.
capstone.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Role-Play Assessment

Level 1 capstone task. Perform all nine steps of "Your First Weeks at Work" in one continuous sequence — with a partner taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded and played back in order. Do not read from the page; produce each line yourself from the setting description alone.

2. Short Answer

Look back at Step 8. Name the two things Arif does in his reply that keep the misunderstanding from becoming a bigger problem.

3. Guided Practice

Write your own Step 10 — one more short situation that could realistically happen later the same day (for example, a colleague asks Arif for help, or Arif has to explain a small delay). Say which earlier module's language it would use, the same way each step above is labeled.

Answer Key

1.

Score with the self-assessment rubric above. A strong performance completes all nine steps in order, adjusting register correctly for each audience (peer, new colleague, supervisor), asks a genuinely targeted clarifying question in Step 4, makes a softened request in Step 6, and resolves Step 8's misunderstanding by correcting the mistake plainly without over-apologizing.

2.

Suggested answer: He corrects the actual mistake plainly and specifically (which week the summary covers) instead of just apologizing, and he offers a concrete next step (adding this week's numbers too) instead of leaving the conversation on the apology.

3.

Suggested answer: Example: Priyanka asks Arif to double-check one more form before she leaves for the day. Arif: "Sure, send it over — I can look at it in the next ten minutes." (Module 7 — agreeing to a request willingly, not grudgingly.)

modules.title: Daily Work Updates
modules.purpose: Give clear daily updates — in person, under pressure and in writing — and match the amount of detail to the person asking.

lessons.title: Giving a Clear Status Update
lessons.objectives_html:
• Structure a spoken update as done / in progress / blocked.
  • Deliver a full update in under 30 seconds without filler.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

It's been a few weeks since Arif's first day, and the front desk routine no longer feels new. This morning, Ms. Fatima Noor stops by the counter between check-ins. "Arif, where are we on the room-inventory recount?" she asks. It's a simple question, but Arif notices he has a choice: ramble through everything he did this week, or answer in one clean pass. He picks the second one.

Key Workplace Lesson

A status update has exactly three parts, and almost every rambling, confusing update is really just these three parts said out of order, with extra padding around them:

  • Done — what's finished.
  • Doing — what's currently in progress.
  • Blocked — what's stuck, and on what.

Said in that order, in one or two sentences each, an update takes under thirty seconds and tells the listener everything they need. Said out of order — starting with a story about why something took so long, or burying the blocked item in the middle of a long account of the doing part — the same information takes three minutes and leaves the listener unsure what actually matters.

The habit worth building is simple: before answering "where are we on this," silently sort what you know into done / doing / blocked, then say it in that order.

Listen & Read
The front desk, mid-morning. Ms. Fatima Noor stops by between check-ins.
Ms. Noor: Arif, where are we on the room-inventory recount?
