Arif: I've wrapped up the morning checklist and submitted the maintenance request for the ice machine. I'm about halfway through the recount now — that part's on track. It's held up a little on the storage-room key, which housekeeping still has.
Ms. Noor: Good — I'll get you that key myself. Thanks, Arif, that's exactly what I needed to know.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
I've finished... / I've wrapped up... Reporting a completed item Neutral
I'm working on... /...is on track Reporting an in-progress item Neutral
...is held up on... / I'm blocked on... Reporting a stuck item Neutral

Vocabulary

  • wrapped up (V-0250) — finished, completed. "I've wrapped up the morning checklist."
  • on track (V-0251) — progressing as planned, no concerns. "The recount is on track for today."
  • held up (V-0252) — stuck, delayed by something specific. "The linen order is held up at the supplier."
  • submitted (V-0253) — sent in and waiting on someone else. "I've submitted the maintenance request."
  • Recycled: pending (V-0182), in progress (V-0181) — both from Level 1 Module 6's task-status vocabulary, now put to direct daily use.

Grammar in Context: Done / Doing / Blocked Structure (PAT-0025)

Structure: [Done: present perfect] + [Doing: present continuous] + [Blocked: what, and on what]

"I've finished the morning checklist. I'm working on the room-inventory recount now — about halfway through. It's held up a little on the storage-room key, which housekeeping still has."

Present perfect ("I've finished") signals a completed action with present relevance — exactly what "done" needs. Present continuous ("I'm working on") signals something happening right now — exactly what "doing" needs. Bengali and Hindi speakers often use a simple past form where English prefers the present perfect, so they say "I finished the checklist" when "I've finished the checklist" fits a status update better: the finished task still matters to what happens next, which is exactly what the present perfect signals. ("I just finished…" is also common, especially in American English.)

Common Mistake (MIS-0040)

Mistake: Giving an update as a long, unsorted account of everything that happened, instead of sorting it into done / doing / blocked first.

❌ "So this morning I started on the recount, and then Priyanka needed something so I helped with that, and then I got back to it, and housekeeping had the storage key so I couldn't finish, but I did get the checklist done earlier..."

✅ "I've finished the morning checklist. I'm about halfway through the recount. It's held up on the storage-room key, which housekeeping has."

Why it matters: The first version makes the listener do the sorting work themselves, while guessing whether they've heard everything. The second version does the sorting for them.

Professional Tone

An update doesn't need to be more formal to be more useful — it needs to be more ordered. The done/doing/blocked structure works in the same plain, direct register whether the listener is a peer or a supervisor; Lesson 3 will show how the amount of detail changes by audience, without changing this underlying shape.

Industry Overlays

  • IT: "I've closed two tickets. I'm working on the login bug now. It's blocked on a reply from the vendor."
  • Retail: "I've finished the morning restock. I'm working on the window display. It's held up — we're still waiting on the new signage."

Self-Check

  1. What are the three parts of a status update, in order?
  2. Why does "I've finished" fit a done item better than "I finished" in a spoken update?
  3. Sort this into done/doing/blocked: "I emailed the supplier this morning, I'm still waiting to hear back, and I already restocked the shelves."

Motivation

"A good update takes thirty seconds and saves everyone an hour."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

Label each part of Arif's update as Done, Doing, or Blocked: "I've wrapped up the morning checklist. I'm about halfway through the recount. It's held up on the storage-room key."

2. Guided Practice

Build a status update from these 3 facts: (1) you finished cleaning the pool area, (2) you are currently restocking towels, (3) you are waiting on a delivery of new pool chairs.

3. Role-Play

Give a 30-second status update on a real or invented task of your own, using the done/doing/blocked structure.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Done: wrapped up the checklist. Doing: halfway through the recount. Blocked: storage-room key.

2.

Suggested answer: I've finished cleaning the pool area. I'm restocking towels now. I'm blocked on the new pool chairs — still waiting on that delivery.

3.

What to listen/look for: All three parts (done, doing, blocked) are present, in that order, using present perfect for done and present continuous for doing, under 30 seconds, avoiding MIS-0040's unsorted rambling account.

lessons.title: Reporting Problems and Delays
lessons.objectives_html:
• Report a delay with a reason and a next step, not just an apology.
  • Avoid excuse-first framing when something has gone wrong.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

The linen delivery Arif was counting on for this afternoon's turnover isn't going to arrive on time. He could wait for someone to ask and then explain — or he could tell Ms. Noor now, before it becomes her problem too. He picks up the phone at the front desk and calls her office line.

Key Workplace Lesson

A delay reported early, with a reason and a plan, reads as competence. The same delay discovered late, or explained only with an apology and no plan, reads as a problem the listener now has to solve themselves. The difference isn't the bad news — it's what comes with it.

The reliable shape is: what happened → why (briefly) → what you're doing about it → when it will actually be ready. Notice that "why" comes briefly, second, not first and at length. Once a reason turns into a long explanation, it starts sounding like an excuse, even when it's completely true.

Listen & Read
A
Arif calls Ms. Noor about the delayed linen delivery — excuse-first framing (❌).
Arif: Hi, Ms. Noor — I'm really sorry about this, the thing is the supplier's truck broke down this morning, and I tried calling them a few times but couldn't get through, and it's just been one of those mornings...
Ms. Noor: Okay — but will we have linen for this afternoon's turnover or not?
B
Arif calls again with the same situation — problem-then-plan (✅).
Arif: Hi, Ms. Noor — the linen delivery is going to be late. I ran into a hold-up with the supplier's truck. I've already called our backup supplier, and I'll have enough linen here by 2 PM.
Ms. Noor: Good thinking — thanks for catching that early, Arif.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
I ran into a hold-up with... Naming the problem briefly Neutral
...because / due to / since... Giving a brief cause Neutral
Here's what I'm doing about it... Showing ownership of the fix Confident
I'll have it by... Giving a revised, concrete timeline Confident

Vocabulary

  • ran into (V-0254) — encountered unexpectedly. "I ran into a hold-up with the linen delivery."
  • a hold-up (V-0255) — a delay-causing obstacle. "There's a hold-up at the supplier's end."
  • revised timeline (V-0256) — an updated, more realistic schedule. "Here's the revised timeline for the delivery."
  • I'll have it by (V-0257) — commits to a specific, concrete new time. "I'll have the rooms turned over by 3 PM instead."
  • Recycled: ASAP / EOD (from Level 1 Module 4's urgency vocabulary).

Grammar in Context: Cause-and-Next-Step Structure (PAT-0026)

Structure: [What happened] + [because/due to] + [what you're doing about it] + [I'll have it by]

"The linen delivery is going to be late — I ran into a hold-up because the supplier's truck broke down. I've already called the backup supplier, and I'll have enough linen here by 2 PM."

Keeping the "because" clause short (one phrase, not a paragraph) is what keeps this sounding like a report rather than an excuse. The listener needs to know that there's a reason, not relive the whole story of it.

Common Mistake (MIS-0041)

Mistake: Leading with the reason and apology, and only mentioning a plan at the end, if at all — excuse-first framing.

❌ "I'm really sorry, the thing is the supplier's truck broke down and then I couldn't reach anyone for an hour, and honestly it's been a really busy morning too, so..."

✅ "The linen delivery is going to be late — I ran into a hold-up with the supplier. I've already called a backup, and I'll have enough here by 2 PM."

Why it matters: Excuse-first framing makes the listener wait through the justification before finding out whether there's actually a plan. Leading with the situation and the fix respects their time and reads as ownership rather than defensiveness.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Excuse-first (❌) "I'm sorry, the thing is..." Sounds defensive; buries the plan
Problem-then-plan (✅) "Here's what's happening, and here's what I'm doing about it." Sounds ownership-driven and calm

Industry Overlays

  • Office: "The report's going to be a day late — I ran into a hold-up with the data from Accounts. I've flagged it with them and I'll have it by tomorrow noon."
  • IT: "The rollout's delayed — we ran into a hold-up with a server issue. We're already patching it and I'll have an update by EOD."

Self-Check

  1. What are the four parts of a good delay report, in order?
  2. Why does keeping the "because" part brief matter?
  3. Rewrite this excuse-first report: "Sorry, I know this is late, but honestly the printer's been broken all week and nobody fixed it."

Motivation

"A problem reported early is a problem half-solved."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this excuse-first report using PAT-0026: "Sorry, I know this is late, but honestly the printer's been broken all week and nobody fixed it."

2. Guided Practice

Report an invented delay of your own using the cause + next-step structure (PAT-0026).

3. Role-Play

Practice reporting a delay proactively, before being asked, using PAT-0026.

Answer Key

1.

A strong answer states the problem, gives a brief cause, shows a concrete fix in progress, and ends with a specific revised time — avoiding MIS-0041's excuse-first framing. Suggested answer: The report's going to be late — I ran into a hold-up because the printer's been down. I've sent it to be printed at the front desk instead, and I'll have copies by 3 PM.

2.

Sample: "The pool towels won't be ready by noon — the laundry machine broke down this morning. I've arranged extra towels from the spa, and I'll have the pool area stocked by 1 PM." Check: what happened → brief cause → what you are doing → a specific new time.

3.

What to listen/look for: The report includes a brief cause (not a long justification), a concrete next step already in motion, and a specific revised time — avoiding MIS-0041's excuse-first framing.

lessons.title: Matching Update Detail to Your Audience
lessons.objectives_html:
• Give a shorter, casual update to a peer and a fuller, structured one to a manager for the same task.
  • Explicitly apply PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → MESSAGE → TONE → ACTION to a status-update situation.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif finishes the room-inventory recount just before lunch. Hasan, passing by the desk, asks casually how it went. Twenty minutes later, Ms. Noor asks the same question — but she needs the answer to decide whether to release rooms for a same-day booking. Same finished task, same person answering. The right answer isn't the same both times.

Key Workplace Lesson

Level 1 Module 7 introduced the framework every professional message should pass through before you speak: Purpose → Audience → Message → Tone → Action. A status update is one of the clearest places to see this framework actually change what you say, not just how you say it.

  • Purpose: why is this person asking? A curious peer wants to know you're fine; a manager who needs the answer for a decision wants the specific number that decision depends on.
  • Audience: what does this listener actually need, not what would be nice to tell them?
  • Message: the same underlying facts, but shaped by what the audience needs from them.

A peer update can stay short and casual because nothing is riding on it. A manager update needs the structure from Lessons 1–2 (done/doing/blocked, or problem/cause/plan) because a decision depends on getting it right. Giving a peer a full formal report is wasted effort; giving a manager a peer-level casual answer risks leaving out exactly the detail they needed.

Listen & Read
A
Hasan asks Arif casually how the recount went (peer, low-stakes).
Hasan: Hey, did you finish that room recount yet?
Arif: Yeah, all done, no issues!
Hasan: Nice, that was fast.
B
Ms. Noor asks Arif the same question, but she needs the answer to release rooms for a same-day booking (manager, decision-relevant).
Ms. Noor: Arif, how did the room recount go? I need to know before I can confirm the same-day booking.
Arif: The recount's finished — all forty-two rooms accounted for, ready to release for booking.
Ms. Noor: Perfect, that's exactly what I needed. I'll confirm the booking now.

Key Expressions

Expression Audience Register
All done, no issues! Peer, low-stakes Casual
The recount's finished — all rooms accounted for, ready to release for booking. Manager, decision-relevant Structured

Grammar in Context

No new grammar in this lesson — it reapplies Level 1 Module 7's PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → MESSAGE → TONE → ACTION framework directly to the done/doing/blocked structure from Lessons 1–2, showing that the same underlying facts can be compressed or expanded depending on who's asking and why.

Common Mistake (MIS-0042)

Mistake: Giving every audience the same amount of detail, regardless of what they actually need it for.

❌ (To a peer just making conversation) "So I finished the recount, all forty-two rooms are accounted for, I cross-checked with housekeeping's log, found two discrepancies which I resolved by..."

✅ (To the same peer) "All done, no issues!"

Why it matters: A peer who wasn't going to use the detail anyway now has to wait through it out of politeness. The opposite mistake — a too-casual answer to a manager who needed the specifics — is just as real, and often more costly, since a decision may now rest on incomplete information.

Professional Tone

Register Example When to use
Casual/peer "All done, no issues!" Low-stakes, curiosity-driven questions
Structured/manager "The recount's finished — all rooms accounted for, ready to release for booking." Decision-relevant questions

Self-Check

  1. What question should you silently ask yourself before deciding how much detail to give?
  2. Why might a fuller, structured answer actually be less helpful to a peer than a short one?
  3. The same finished task ("fixed the printer") needs to go to a peer and to your manager, who needs to know because a client's documents were stuck in it. Give both versions.

Motivation

"The same news, told well, fits any audience."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Which version fits which audience — "All done, no issues!" or "The recount's finished — all rooms accounted for, ready to release for booking"? Match each to Hasan (peer, curious) or Ms. Noor (manager, needs the fact for a decision).

2. Guided Practice

You've just fixed a printer that was blocking a client's documents. Write a peer version and a manager version of this same update.

3. Role-Play

Give both versions of one real update of yours — a short casual version for a peer, and a fuller structured version for a manager who needs it for a decision.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: "All done, no issues!" fits Hasan. "The recount's finished — all rooms accounted for, ready to release for booking" fits Ms. Noor.

2.

Suggested answer: Peer: "Fixed it, all good now!" Manager: "The printer's fixed — the client's documents went through, so there's no delay on their end."

3.

What to listen/look for: The peer version stays short and casual; the manager version includes the specific fact the decision depends on, using done/doing/blocked or problem/cause/plan structure — avoiding MIS-0042's one-size-fits-all detail level.

lessons.title: The Standup Habit
lessons.objectives_html:
• Give a spoken update in a multi-person round without losing the done/doing/blocked structure under time pressure.
  • Write the same update as a short 2–3 line chat message.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Every morning before the shift starts, the Front Office team gathers for a five-minute standup. Ms. Noor runs the round, and Hasan, Priyanka and Arif each get thirty seconds to say what's done, what's in progress, and what's blocked. Then, because the evening-shift staff weren't there, Arif types the same update into the team chat so they don't miss it.

Key Workplace Lesson

A standup round is Lessons 1–3's structure under a new pressure: time. With four people and five minutes, nobody gets long to speak, and rambling costs the whole team, not just the listener. The done/doing/blocked shape from Lesson 1 becomes even more valuable here — it lets you speak fast without sounding rushed, because the order is already decided before you open your mouth.

Writing the same update afterward is a different skill, not just a shorter one. Speech can carry tone in a pause or a smile; a chat message can't, so it has to say everything in fewer words without sounding cold. Some things speech includes are simply dropped in chat — "I have wrapped up the checklist" can become "Checklist done" without losing meaning. This kind of compression is normal and expected in team chat messages, though it would sound wrong in a formal email or to a customer. (You'll see the full range of when this compression is and isn't appropriate in Module 4.)

Listen & Read
The morning Front Office standup — four people, thirty seconds each.
Ms. Noor: Okay, quick round — done, doing, blocked, keep it short. Hasan, you first.
Hasan: Done — checked in the early arrivals. Doing — restocking the welcome desk. No blockers.
Priyanka: Done — confirmed today's group booking. Doing — the seating chart. Blocked on the final guest count from the client.
Arif: Done — wrapped up the morning checklist. Doing — the room recount. Blocked on the storage-room key.
Ms. Noor: Good, all clear. I'll chase down that guest count, Priyanka. Let's get moving.

Key Expressions

Expression Where it's used
Done:... / Doing:... / Blocked:... Fast spoken or written shorthand for the full structure
Quick update: Common chat-message opener before a compressed status

Grammar in Context

No new grammar in this lesson — it consolidates the status-verb set from Lessons 1–2 (present perfect for done, present continuous for doing) and shows, for the first time, that the same structure can compress into short labels ("Done:", "Doing:", "Blocked:") when speed matters, in speech or in writing.

Common Mistake

This lesson recycles Lesson 1's MIS-0040 (unsorted rambling) under time pressure: in a standup round, rambling doesn't just waste your own thirty seconds — it eats into everyone else's turn. The fix is the same fix: done, then doing, then blocked, in that order, every time.

Professional Tone

Context Example Why
Spoken standup "Done: wrapped up the checklist. Doing: the recount. Blocked: the storage key." Fast, ordered, easy to follow live
Written chat message "Quick update: checklist done, recount in progress, blocked on the storage key." Compressed but still clear without the speaker present

Industry Overlays

  • Retail: A shift-change standup: "Done: restocked the front shelves. Doing: the register count. Blocked: waiting on the delivery to log."
  • IT: A daily team standup: "Done: fixed the login bug. Doing: testing the patch. Blocked: need QA sign-off."

Self-Check

  1. Why does the done/doing/blocked structure matter even more in a standup round than in a one-on-one update?
  2. Give one example of something a spoken update includes that a chat-message version can safely drop.
  3. Module 1 Assessment: Give a spoken 3-part update (done/doing/blocked) on a real or invented task, then write the same update as a 2-line chat message for someone who missed the standup.

Motivation

"Said well out loud, and said well in writing — that's what a team actually runs on."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

In the standup round, Priyanka says: "Done — confirmed today's group booking. Doing — the seating chart. Blocked on the final guest count from the client." Identify the three parts.

2. Guided Practice

Compress this spoken update into a 2-line chat message: "I have finished cleaning the pool area. I am currently restocking the towels. I am blocked on the new pool chairs — still waiting on that delivery."

3. Role-Play

Module 1 Assessment: Give a spoken 3-part update (done/doing/blocked) on a real or invented task, under 30 seconds. Then write the same update as a 2-line chat message for someone who missed the standup.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Done: confirmed the group booking. Doing: the seating chart. Blocked: the final guest count from the client.

2.

Suggested answer: Quick update: pool area done, restocking towels now, blocked on the pool chair delivery.

3.

What to listen/look for: The spoken version keeps all three parts in order, under 30 seconds, using present perfect for done and present continuous for doing. The written version compresses the same content into 2 lines without losing the done/doing/blocked information, avoiding MIS-0040's unsorted rambling.

modules.title: Making & Responding to Requests
modules.purpose: Make and answer requests: add conditions and trade-offs, decline without damaging the relationship, suggest alternatives, pass requests on accurately and write them briefly.

lessons.title: Requests with Conditions and Trade-offs
lessons.objectives_html:
• Make a request that includes a condition using if/as long as/provided that.
  • Offer something in return to make a request feel like a fair exchange, not a demand.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif needs Hasan to cover the front desk for twenty minutes so he can run a guest's luggage up to the fourth floor personally. He could just ask — but the shift is busy, and a request that accounts for that, and offers something back, is more likely to get a genuine yes instead of a reluctant one.

Key Workplace Lesson

Level 1 Module 7 taught the basic softened request: "Could you...?" / "Would you mind...?" This lesson adds two things a simple request often leaves out: a condition that respects the other person's own constraints, and a trade-off that makes clear you're not asking for something for nothing.

A conditional request has two useful shapes:

  • An open condition: "Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, if you get a chance?" — leaves room for a genuine no.
  • A specific condition: "As long as it doesn't clash with your break, could you cover the desk for twenty minutes?" — shows you've already thought about their situation.

Adding a trade-off — "I'll cover your break tomorrow in return" — turns the request into an exchange rather than a one-way ask, which is often what makes a busy colleague say yes.

Listen & Read
Arif asks Hasan to cover the front desk so he can deliver a guest's luggage personally.
Arif: Hasan, could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, if you get a chance? I want to take this guest's luggage up myself — it's the anniversary couple in 412.
Hasan: Sure, as long as it doesn't get busy in the next few minutes.
Arif: Thanks — I'll cover your break tomorrow in return.
Hasan: Deal. Go on, I've got it.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
if you get a chance Softens a request, leaves room for a genuine no Polite
as long as Introduces a condition on the listener's side Neutral
in return Introduces a trade-off Neutral
I can cover for you Offers a concrete trade-off Confident

Vocabulary

  • if you get a chance (V-0258) — softens a request as optional, not urgent. "Could you check the storeroom, if you get a chance?"
  • as long as (V-0259) — introduces a condition. "As long as it's not too busy, could you help me at the desk?"
  • in return (V-0260) — signals a trade-off is being offered. "I'll take the late shift on Friday in return."
  • I can cover for you (V-0261) — a concrete, specific trade-off offer. "If you cover the desk now, I can cover for you during your break tomorrow."
  • Recycled: Could you...? / Would you mind...? (Level 1 Module 7, Lesson 2).

Grammar in Context: Conditional Request Structure (PAT-0027)

Structure: [Could you / Would you mind] + [request], + [if/as long as/provided that] + [condition] (+ [I'll... in return])

"Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, if you get a chance? I'll cover your break tomorrow in return."

"As long as it doesn't clash with your break, would you mind taking this delivery to Room 412?"

Notice the condition can come before or after the request — both are natural. What matters is that the request accounts for the other person's situation, not just your own need.

Common Mistake (MIS-0043)

Mistake: Stating the condition but forgetting the trade-off, so a reasonable request still sounds one-sided.

❌ "Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, as long as it's not too busy for you?" (sounds fine, but nothing is offered back)

✅ "Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, as long as it's not too busy for you? I'll cover your break tomorrow in return."

Why it matters: A condition alone shows awareness of the other person's situation; a trade-off shows the exchange is fair. Together, they make a request easy to say yes to.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Bare request "Can you cover the desk?" Fine for something small; can feel presumptuous for a real favor
Conditional + trade-off "Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, if you get a chance? I'll cover your break tomorrow in return." Reads as fair and considerate

Industry Overlays

  • Retail: "As long as the queue's manageable, could you take my till for ten minutes? I'll restock your section after."
  • IT: "Could you review this ticket today, provided that it doesn't push back your sprint work? I can take the next one off your list."

Self-Check

  1. Name the two places a condition can go in a request.
  2. Why does adding a trade-off often make a request more likely to get a genuine yes?
  3. Turn this bare request into a conditional request with a trade-off: "Can you help me carry these boxes?"

Motivation

"A well-built request respects the other person's time as much as your own."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

In "Could you cover the desk for twenty minutes, if you get a chance? I'll cover your break tomorrow in return," identify the request, the condition, and the trade-off.

2. Guided Practice

Turn this bare request into a conditional request with a trade-off, using PAT-0027: "Can you help me carry these boxes?"

3. Role-Play

Make a real or invented request of your own that includes a condition and a trade-off, using PAT-0027.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Request: cover the desk for twenty minutes. Condition: if you get a chance. Trade-off: I'll cover your break tomorrow.

2.

Suggested answer: Could you help me carry these boxes, as long as you're not in the middle of something? I can help you with your closing checklist after.

3.

What to listen/look for: The request includes a clear condition (if/as long as/provided that) and a specific trade-off offered in return — avoiding MIS-0043's one-sided phrasing.

lessons.title: Turning Down a Request Without Damaging the Relationship
lessons.objectives_html:
• Decline a request clearly, without a blunt refusal or a vague non-answer.
  • Offer a specific alternative when turning down a request.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Priyanka asks Arif to swap shifts on Saturday. Arif already has plans he can't move. He could say a flat "no," he could avoid answering and hope she forgets, or he could turn her down clearly and still leave her with something useful to work with.

Key Workplace Lesson

There are three common ways to respond to a request you can't fulfill, and only one of them actually works:

  • Blunt refusal: "No, I can't." — technically clear, but offers nothing and can feel dismissive.
  • Vague non-answer: "Maybe, I'll see." — avoids the discomfort of saying no, but leaves the other person unable to make other plans, which is often worse than a clear no.
  • Real decline with alternative: states clearly that you can't, then offers something you genuinely can do instead.

Level 1 Module 7 introduced the basic decline structure: "I'm not able to [X] right now, but I can [Y] by [time]." This lesson extends it with a specific alternative and a check-in question — "Would that work?" — that hands the decision back to the other person instead of assuming your alternative is good enough.

Listen & Read
Blunt refusal (❌)
Priyanka: Arif, could you swap shifts with me on Saturday? Something's come up.
Arif: No, I can't.
Priyanka: Oh. Okay.
Vague non-answer (❌)
Priyanka: Arif, could you swap shifts with me on Saturday? Something's come up.
Arif: Um, maybe — let me see how it goes, I'll let you know.
Priyanka: Okay... when will you know? I need to sort this out soon.
Real decline with alternative (✅)
Priyanka: Arif, could you swap shifts with me on Saturday? Something's come up.
Arif: I'm tied up on Saturday — I already have plans I can't move. What I can do instead is take your Tuesday shift. Would that work?
Priyanka: Actually, yes — that works even better. Thanks, Arif.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
I'm tied up until... States clearly why you can't, with a specific time Neutral
What I can do instead is... Introduces a genuine alternative Confident
Would that work? Checks whether the alternative actually helps Polite

Vocabulary

  • I'm tied up until (V-0262) — states a specific commitment that prevents you from helping now. "I'm tied up until 3 PM."
  • what I can do instead is (V-0263) — introduces a genuine alternative. "What I can do instead is help you after my shift."
  • would that work (V-0264) — checks whether the alternative is actually useful to the other person. "Would that work for you?"
  • Recycled: I'm not able to (Level 1 Module 7, Lesson 3).

Grammar in Context: Decline-with-Alternative Structure (PAT-0028)

Structure: [I'm not able to / I'm tied up until] + [reason/time] + [What I can do instead is] + [alternative] + [Would that work?]

"I'm tied up until Sunday — I already have plans I can't move. What I can do instead is take your Tuesday shift. Would that work?"

Ending with "Would that work?" is what separates a genuine offer from an assumption. It respects that your alternative might not actually solve their problem, and invites them to say so.

Common Mistake (MIS-0044)

Mistake: Giving a vague non-answer instead of a clear decline, leaving the other person unable to make other plans.

❌ "Um, maybe — let me see how Saturday goes, I'll let you know." (Priyanka can't plan around this — she doesn't know if she has a swap or not.)

✅ "I'm tied up on Saturday — I already have plans I can't move. What I can do instead is take your Tuesday shift. Would that work?"

Why it matters: A clear decline, even with disappointing news, lets the other person move on and make other arrangements. A vague non-answer just delays the same disappointment — often to a worse moment.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Blunt refusal (❌) "No, I can't." Clear but offers nothing; can feel dismissive
Vague non-answer (❌) "Maybe, I'll see." Avoids discomfort but leaves the other person stuck
Decline with alternative (✅) "I'm tied up until Sunday. What I can do instead is take your Tuesday shift. Would that work?" Clear, respectful, and still useful

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "I'm tied up with a client until 4 PM. What I can do instead is have my colleague assist you now, or I can call you back at 4. Would that work?"
  • Education: "I'm not able to take an extra class this week — I'm already covering two. What I can do instead is recommend Ms. Rahman, who has space. Would that work?"

Self-Check

  1. Why is a vague non-answer often worse than a clear "no"?
  2. What question turns an assumed alternative into a genuine offer?
  3. Priyanka asks you to swap Saturday's shift. Decline clearly and offer a specific alternative.

Motivation

"Saying no well is a professional skill, not a personal failure."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Label each response to "Could you swap shifts with me on Saturday?" as blunt refusal, vague non-answer, or real decline-with-alternative: (1) "No, I can't." (2) "Maybe, I'll see." (3) "I'm tied up on Saturday. What I can do instead is take your Tuesday shift. Would that work?"

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this vague non-answer as a real decline with alternative, using PAT-0028: "I don't know, maybe, I'll try."

3. Role-Play

A colleague asks you for a favor you genuinely can't do right now. Decline clearly and offer a specific alternative, using PAT-0028.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: (1) Blunt refusal. (2) Vague non-answer. (3) Real decline with alternative.

2.

Suggested answer: I'm tied up until Friday — I've got another commitment. What I can do instead is help you first thing Monday. Would that work?

3.

What to listen/look for: The decline is clear (not blunt, not vague), includes a specific alternative, and ends by checking whether that alternative would work — avoiding MIS-0044's vague non-answer.

lessons.title: Negotiating Timing and Scope
lessons.objectives_html:
• Respond to an unrealistic deadline or scope with a specific counter-proposal, not a vague objection.
  • Offer a phased approach when the full request can't be done at once.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Noor asks Arif to have the full storeroom inventory finished by the end of his shift today — on top of his usual desk duties. It's not possible as asked. Arif could just say "that's too much," or he could come back with something specific she can actually say yes to.

Key Workplace Lesson

"That's too much" or "I can't do all that" are objections — true, but not useful on their own, because they leave the other person to solve the problem themselves. A counter-proposal does the opposite: it acknowledges the request, states realistically what's achievable, and offers a specific alternative — often by splitting the work into phases.

A good counter-proposal answers the question the other person actually needs answered: not "can you do this?" but "what can you actually get done, and by when?"

Listen & Read
Ms. Noor asks Arif to finish the full storeroom inventory by end of shift, on top of his desk duties.
Ms. Noor: Arif, can you get the full storeroom inventory done by the end of your shift today?
Arif: I can definitely get started on it. Realistically, though, what's achievable today is the ground floor, given my desk duties this afternoon.
Ms. Noor: Okay — what about the rest?
Arif: Could we split it into two days — ground floor today, upper floors tomorrow morning? A phased approach means it's still fully done by tomorrow lunchtime.
Ms. Noor: That works. Thanks for being upfront about it.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Realistically, Introduces an honest assessment Neutral
what's achievable is States a concrete, doable scope Confident
split it into Proposes breaking work into stages Neutral
a phased approach Names the overall strategy Professional

Vocabulary

  • realistically (V-0265) — honestly, given the actual constraints. "Realistically, I can't finish the full inventory today."
  • what's achievable is (V-0266) — states a concrete, doable alternative. "What's achievable is the ground floor by end of shift."
  • split it into (V-0267) — proposes breaking a large task into stages. "Could we split it into two days?"
  • a phased approach (V-0268) — names the overall strategy of doing work in stages. "I'd suggest a phased approach — ground floor today, upper floors tomorrow."
  • Recycled: priority / urgent / EOD (Level 1 Module 4).

Grammar in Context: Counter-Proposal Structure (PAT-0029)

Structure: [Acknowledge the request] + [Realistically, what's achievable is] + [specific alternative scope or timing] (+ [a phased approach, if splitting the work])

"I can definitely get started on the inventory. Realistically, though, what's achievable today is the ground floor, given my desk duties. Could we split it into two days — ground floor today, upper floors tomorrow?"

The counter-proposal doesn't say no to the task — it says yes to a version of it that's actually achievable, which is usually exactly what the other person needs to hear.

Common Mistake (MIS-0045)

Mistake: Responding to an unrealistic deadline or scope with a vague objection instead of a specific counter-proposal.

❌ "That's way too much for today, honestly." (True, but Ms. Noor still doesn't know what she can actually expect by end of shift.)

✅ "Realistically, what's achievable today is the ground floor. Could we split it into two days?"

Why it matters: A vague objection leaves the deadline problem unsolved and hands it back to the other person. A specific counter-proposal solves it on the spot.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Vague objection (❌) "That's too much for today." True but unhelpful — leaves the problem unsolved
Specific counter-proposal (✅) "Realistically, what's achievable today is the ground floor. Could we split it into two days?" Solves the timing problem on the spot

Industry Overlays

  • IT: "Realistically, what's achievable by Friday is the login fix. The reporting feature would need a phased approach — could we split it into this sprint and next?"
  • Sales: "Realistically, I can call the top twenty leads today. What's achievable is finishing the rest by Wednesday — a phased approach across three days."

Self-Check

  1. Why is "that's too much" not enough on its own, even when it's true?
  2. What are the three parts of a good counter-proposal?
  3. Your manager asks for a report by tomorrow morning that realistically needs three days. Give a counter-proposal.

Motivation

"A specific counter-proposal is more persuasive than a general objection."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Is this a vague objection or a specific counter-proposal? "Realistically, what's achievable today is the ground floor. Could we split it into two days?"

2. Guided Practice

Your manager asks for a full report by tomorrow morning that realistically needs three days. Write a counter-proposal using PAT-0029.

3. Role-Play

Someone gives you a deadline or scope that isn't realistic. Respond with a specific counter-proposal using PAT-0029, including a phased approach if the task needs splitting.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: A specific counter-proposal — it names a concrete achievable scope and a specific alternative timing.

2.

Suggested answer: I can definitely start on it today. Realistically, what's achievable by tomorrow morning is the first two sections. Could we split it into a phased approach — the rest by Thursday?

3.

What to listen/look for: The response names a concrete achievable scope or timing rather than a vague objection, and offers a specific alternative — avoiding MIS-0045's unhelpful "that's too much" framing.

lessons.title: Relaying a Request Between People
lessons.objectives_html:
• Relay a request or message accurately from one person to another, adjusting tense and pronouns.
  • Use basic reported speech to pass on what someone asked, wants to know, or said they'd do.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A guest at the front desk asks Arif if housekeeping can send extra towels. Arif isn't housekeeping — he has to pass the request on to Rupa, a colleague in housekeeping, and then pass her answer back to the guest. Getting the details right at each handoff is the whole job.

Key Workplace Lesson

Relaying a message means you're speaking about what someone said, not repeating their exact words. This requires a small but important shift: reported speech. "Can you send extra towels?" becomes "She's asking if you can send extra towels." "I'll check and get back to you" becomes "She said she'd get back to you."

The shift is mostly about tense and pronouns, not meaning. If you relay the exact words without adjusting them, the listener has to work out who "I" and "you" now refer to — and the message gets confusing fast.

Listen & Read
A guest asks Arif for extra towels; Arif relays the request to Rupa in housekeeping, then relays her answer back to the guest.
Guest: Excuse me — could we get some extra towels sent up to Room 308?
Arif: Of course, I'll pass that on right away.
Arif: Rupa, a guest in 308 is asking if you can send up some extra towels.
Rupa: Sure — tell them I'll have someone bring those up within fifteen minutes.
Arif: She said she'd have someone bring extra towels up to your room within fifteen minutes.
Guest: Wonderful, thank you.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
...asked me to pass on... Introduces a relayed request Neutral
...wants to know if... Introduces a relayed question Neutral
...said she'd get back to you Reports a promised future action Neutral

Vocabulary

  • asked me to pass on (V-0269) — introduces a message relayed from someone else. "The guest asked me to pass on that they'd like extra towels."
  • wants to know if (V-0270) — introduces a relayed question. "Ms. Noor wants to know if the linen delivery has arrived."
  • said she'd get back to you (V-0271) — reports a promise to follow up. "She said she'd get back to you by 3 PM."

Grammar in Context: Reported Speech — Tense Shifts When Relaying a Message (GIC-0006)

Whether the tense changes depends on two things:

  • The reporting verb. With a present reporting verb (is asking, wants to know, says), the tense does not change: "He wants to know if you're free this afternoon."
  • Whether it is still true. With a past reporting verb (said, asked), the tense usually moves back one step ("She said she could help"). But if the information is still true or still in the future when you relay it, keeping the original tense is also correct and very common in speech: "Rupa said she'll send the towels up in fifteen minutes."
Original Relayed
"I can help." She said she could help. (past reporting verb: tense moves back)
"Are you free this afternoon?" He wants to know if you're free this afternoon. (present reporting verb: no change)
"I'll get back to you." She said she'd get back to you. / She said she'll get back to you. (both correct: the promise is still in the future)

Pronouns also shift to match who's speaking now: "I" often becomes "she/he," and "you" may need to become the actual person being discussed.

Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi often relay a message by directly quoting the original speaker's words, sometimes without shifting tense or pronouns, and letting context and tone carry the meaning. In English, the pronoun shift (and, after a past reporting verb, often a tense shift) is what tells the listener this is now your description of the exchange, not a direct quote. Learning to make that shift deliberately, rather than skipping it, is what makes a relayed message sound natural in English.

Common Mistake (MIS-0046)

Mistake: Relaying a message word-for-word from the original speaker, without shifting tense or pronouns, leaving the listener unsure who "I" and "you" now refer to.

❌ (To the guest, relaying Rupa's words exactly) "She said: 'I'll check and get back to you.'" (Get back to whom — Rupa, Arif, or the guest?)

✅ "She said she'd get back to you by 3 PM."

Why it matters: A direct quote can leave the listener doing the work of figuring out who's who. A properly shifted reported-speech sentence does that work for them.

Professional Tone

Register Example When to use
Direct quote (rarely needed) "She said, 'I'll get back to you.'" Only when the exact wording genuinely matters
Reported speech (usual choice) "She said she'd get back to you." Everyday relaying of a message or request

Industry Overlays

  • Healthcare admin: "The doctor wants to know if you've taken your morning medication."
  • Banking: "The manager asked me to pass on that your loan application has been approved."

Self-Check

  1. What two things usually shift when you relay someone's exact words as reported speech?
  2. Rewrite as reported speech: Rupa said, "I'll check the storeroom."
  3. A guest asks: "Can I get a late checkout?" Relay this question to your supervisor using reported speech.

Motivation

"An accurately relayed message is a small act of trustworthiness."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite as reported speech, using GIC-0006: Rupa said, "I'll check the storeroom."

2. Guided Practice

A guest asks: "Can I get a late checkout?" Relay this question to your supervisor using reported speech.

3. Role-Play

Practice a full three-part relay — receive a request, pass it to a colleague using reported speech, then relay their answer back, adjusting tense and pronouns each time.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: She said she'd check the storeroom.

2.

Sample: "The guest in Room 215 is asking if she can get a late checkout." (Also correct: "…asked if she could get a late checkout.")

3.

What to listen/look for: Both relayed messages use reported speech with correctly shifted tense and pronouns, not a direct word-for-word quote — avoiding MIS-0046's confusing literal relay.

lessons.title: Written Requests: Short and Clear
lessons.objectives_html:
• Write a short request that states the ask clearly in the first line or two.
  • Apply the module's conditional, decline, and counter-proposal language in writing.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif needs to email the maintenance team about a jammed door lock on the third floor. He could write everything he's thinking as it comes to him — or he could put the actual request in the first line, the way a busy reader needs it.

Key Workplace Lesson

Spoken requests can build up to the ask gradually, because the listener can ask questions along the way. A written request doesn't have that safety net — if the actual ask is buried in the third paragraph, a busy reader may skim past it entirely.

The fix is simple: state the request in the first line or two, then add only the detail the reader actually needs to act on it. Everything from this module — conditions, trade-offs, declines, counter-proposals — still applies in writing; it just needs to arrive faster.

This lesson works through three written requests of increasing complexity: (1) a simple request with the ask in the first line, (2) a request with a condition and trade-off (Lesson 2.1), and (3) a written decline with an alternative (Lesson 2.2).

Worked Example 1 (Simple Request)

Subject: Jammed lock — Room 312

Hi Maintenance team,

Could someone take a look at the door lock in Room 312 today? It's jamming and a guest is currently unable to lock their door.

Thanks,
Arif

The ask is in the first line. Everything after it supports that one request.

Worked Example 2 (Request with a Condition)

Subject: Extra towels for tomorrow's group check-in

Hi Rupa,

Could you set aside an extra stock of towels for tomorrow's group check-in, as long as it doesn't clash with the Friday linen count? I can help sort them in return if that's useful.

Thanks,
Arif

The condition and trade-off from Lesson 1 both fit naturally into two sentences.

Worked Example 3 (Decline with Alternative, Written)

Subject: Re: Covering the desk Saturday morning

Hi Hasan,

I'm tied up Saturday morning — I already have a commitment I can't move. What I can do instead is cover your Sunday afternoon shift. Would that work?

Thanks,
Arif

The decline structure from Lesson 2 works the same way in an email as it does out loud — clear ask, clear reason, clear alternative.

Common Mistake (MIS-0047)

Mistake: Burying the actual request somewhere in the middle of a longer message, so the reader has to search for what's actually being asked.

❌ "Hi, hope you're doing well. Things have been busy this week, especially with the group check-in coming up, and I noticed the towel stock is getting low, so I was wondering, would it be possible to maybe set some aside?"

✅ "Could you set aside an extra stock of towels for tomorrow's group check-in?"

Why it matters: A reader with thirty seconds needs the ask up front. Context can follow — it shouldn't come first.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Buried request (❌) Ask appears in paragraph three Reader may miss it entirely
Request-first (✅) Ask appears in line one or two Reader can act immediately

Self-Check

  1. Where should the actual ask appear in a written request?
  2. Look at Worked Example 2 — which words carry the condition, and which carry the trade-off?
  3. Module 2 Assessment: (a) Role-play a spoken negotiation: someone gives you an unrealistic deadline, and you respond with a specific counter-proposal (Lesson 3). (b) Write a short request (3–4 sentences) to a colleague that includes a condition and a trade-off (Lesson 1).

Motivation

"A clear written request respects the reader who has thirty seconds, not thirty minutes."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this buried request so the ask appears in the first line: "Hi, hope you're doing well. Things have been busy this week, especially with the group check-in coming up, and I noticed the towel stock is getting low, so I was wondering, would it be possible to maybe set some aside?"

2. Role-Play

Module 2 Assessment (Part A — Spoken): Someone gives you an unrealistic deadline or scope. Respond with a specific counter-proposal, using PAT-0029.

3. Guided Practice

Module 2 Assessment (Part B — Written): Write a short request (3–4 sentences) to a colleague that includes a condition and a trade-off, with the ask in the first line or two.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Could you set aside an extra stock of towels for tomorrow's group check-in? Things have been busy this week and I noticed stock is getting low.

2.

What to listen/look for: The response states a concrete achievable scope or timing and offers a specific alternative, avoiding a vague objection (MIS-0045).

3.

Sample: "Hi Rupa, could you set aside twenty extra pillows for the conference group arriving on Friday, as long as it doesn't clash with your weekend stock count? I can help carry them up to the fifth floor in return. Thanks, Arif" Score 0–3: (1) the request is in the first line; (2) there is a clear condition (as long as / if you get a chance); (3) there is a specific trade-off.

modules.title: Telephone English Basics
modules.purpose: Use the telephone with confidence: answer and identify yourself, take a message, cope with a bad line, put callers on hold or transfer them, and handle difficult calls.

lessons.title: Answering and Identifying Yourself
lessons.objectives_html:
• Answer a work phone call with a greeting, your name or department, and an offer to help.
  • Adjust the greeting slightly for an internal call versus an external call.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

The front desk phone rings. Arif doesn't know yet whether it's a guest calling from their room, another department calling internally, or an outside caller booking a room. The first thing he says has to work for all three.

Key Workplace Lesson

A phone call has no face, no body language, and no second chance at a first impression — the caller judges the whole interaction by how the first ten seconds sound. A complete phone greeting does three things in one breath: greets the caller, identifies who's answering, and offers help.

The exact wording shifts slightly by context:

  • External call: "Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"
  • Internal call: "Hi, this is Arif — how can I help?" (shorter, since a colleague already knows the department).
Listen & Read
A
An external caller phones the front desk to ask about room availability.
Arif: Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?
Caller: Hi, I'd like to ask about room availability for this weekend.
Arif: Of course — may I ask who's calling, please, so I can pull up your details if you're already a guest?
B
Rupa calls the front desk internally from housekeeping.
Arif: Hi, this is Arif — how can I help?
Rupa: Hey Arif, it's Rupa — room 405 is ready for check-in whenever you need it.
Arif: Perfect, thanks for the update.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
...this is [Name] speaking Identifies who's answering Neutral/formal
May I ask who's calling? Asks for the caller's identity, politely Polite
How can I help you today? Offers help, opens the conversation Professional

Vocabulary

  • speaking (V-0272) — used after your name to confirm you're the one talking. "This is Arif speaking."
  • may I ask who's calling (V-0273) — politely asks for the caller's name. "May I ask who's calling, please?"
  • how can I help you today (V-0274) — opens the conversation by offering help. "How can I help you today?"
  • Recycled: basic greetings (Level 1 Module 2, Lesson 1).

Grammar in Context: Phone Greeting-and-ID Formula (PAT-0030)

Structure: [Greeting] + [Company/Department, if external] + [This is Name speaking] + [How can I help you today?]

"Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"

For an internal call, the department name is usually dropped since the caller already knows where they're calling:

"Hi, this is Arif — how can I help?"

Common Mistake (MIS-0048)

Mistake: Answering a work phone the same way you'd answer a personal call — with just "Hello?" — leaving the caller unsure who or what they've reached.

❌ "Hello?"

✅ "Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"

Why it matters: A bare "Hello?" forces the caller to ask where they've reached and who they're speaking to, which wastes time and can feel unprofessional, especially for an external caller.

Professional Tone

Register Example When to use
Bare answer (❌ for work lines) "Hello?" Personal calls only
Full phone greeting (✅) "Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?" Any work phone line, external calls especially
Shortened internal version "Hi, this is Arif — how can I help?" Internal calls, where department is already known

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "Good afternoon, City Bank customer service, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"
  • IT support: "IT Helpdesk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"

Self-Check

  1. What three things does a complete phone greeting include?
  2. Why might the greeting be shorter for an internal call than an external one?
  3. Answer an incoming external call at your own workplace with a complete greeting.

Motivation

"The first ten seconds of a call are the whole call's first impression."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

Identify the three parts of this phone greeting: "Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?"

2. Guided Practice

Answer an incoming external call at your own workplace with a complete greeting, using PAT-0030.

3. Role-Play

Practice answering both an external call and an internal call, adjusting your greeting appropriately for each.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Greeting + department: Good morning, Front Desk. Identification: this is Arif speaking. Offer to help: How can I help you today?

2.

Sample: "Good morning, Riverside Clinic reception, this is Nadia speaking. How can I help you today?" Check: greeting + organization or department + "this is … speaking" + an offer to help.

3.

What to listen/look for: The external-call greeting includes all three parts (greeting, ID, offer to help); the internal-call greeting is appropriately shortened — avoiding MIS-0048's bare "Hello?" answer in either case.

lessons.title: Taking a Message Accurately
lessons.objectives_html:
• Ask the right questions to take a complete phone message.
  • Confirm and restate the message's key details before ending the call.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Noor is in a meeting when a supplier calls asking for her. Arif has to take a message — and whatever he writes down is the only version of this call Ms. Noor will ever see. If a detail is wrong or missing, it stays wrong.

Key Workplace Lesson

A complete phone message needs four things: who called, a callback number, what it's regarding, and what happens next. Getting the first three means asking, not guessing; the fourth means telling the caller what you'll actually do with the message — and then restating everything back to them so any mistake gets caught immediately, not after they've hung up.

Level 1 Module 4 introduced "Just to confirm..." as a general confirmation opener. On the phone, where there's no way to check a written note together, that restatement step becomes essential rather than optional.

Listen & Read
A supplier calls asking for Ms. Noor, who is in a meeting; Arif takes a complete message.
Caller: Hi, could I speak with Ms. Noor, please?
Arif: I'm sorry, she's in a meeting right now. Would you like me to take a message?
Caller: Yes, please. This is Mr. Siddique from Delta Linens, and it's regarding tomorrow's delivery — it might be delayed by a few hours.
Arif: Could I get a callback number, in case she has questions?
Caller: Sure, it's 01711-582403.
Arif: Just to confirm, that's Mr. Siddique, 01711-582403, regarding tomorrow's delivery being delayed by a few hours — I'll pass that along as soon as she's out of her meeting.
Caller: That's perfect, thank you.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Would you like me to take a message? Offers to take a message Polite
...regarding... Introduces the topic of the message Neutral
She'll get back to you Tells the caller what happens next Professional
I'll pass that along Confirms the message will reach the right person Professional

Vocabulary

  • take a message (V-0275) — offer to record a message for someone unavailable. "Would you like me to take a message?"
  • regarding (V-0276) — introduces the topic of a call or message. "He's calling regarding tomorrow's delivery."
  • get back to you (V-0277) — states that someone will respond later. "She'll get back to you this afternoon."
  • I'll pass that along (V-0278) — confirms the message will reach its recipient. "I'll pass that along as soon as she's out of her meeting."
  • Recycled: Just to confirm... (Level 1 Module 4, Lesson 2).

Grammar in Context: Message-Taking Question Set + Confirmation-Restatement (PAT-0031)

Structure: [Ask: name? number? regarding what?] + [Just to confirm, that's [name], [number], regarding [topic]] + [Next step: I'll pass that along]

"Could I get your name and a callback number?... And what's this regarding?... Just to confirm, that's Mr. Siddique, 01711-582403, regarding tomorrow's linen delivery — I'll pass that along as soon as she's free."

Asking the first three questions gets the raw information; stating the next step and restating everything back is what catches a misheard name or number before it becomes a lost message, and tells the caller exactly what happens now.

Common Mistake (MIS-0049)

Mistake: Taking a message without confirming or restating the key details, so an error — a misheard name, a wrong digit in the number — goes unnoticed until it's too late to fix.

❌ (Writes down the message and ends the call without restating anything) "Okay, got it, I'll tell her."

✅ "Just to confirm, that's Mr. Siddique, 01711-582403, regarding tomorrow's linen delivery — I'll pass that along."

Why it matters: The caller is the only person who can catch a mistake in the message, and they can only do that if you say the details back to them before hanging up.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
No confirmation (❌) "Okay, got it, I'll tell her." Any mistake goes unnoticed until too late
Confirmed and restated (✅) "Just to confirm, that's Mr. Siddique, 01711-582403, regarding tomorrow's delivery." Errors get caught immediately

Industry Overlays

  • Healthcare admin: "Just to confirm, that's Mrs. Islam, calling regarding her appointment on Thursday — I'll pass that along to Dr. Rahim."
  • Banking: "Just to confirm, that's Mr. Chowdhury, 01819-306274, regarding a delayed transfer — I'll pass that along to the accounts team."

Self-Check

  1. What four pieces of information does a complete phone message need?
  2. Why does restating the details matter more on the phone than in person?
  3. Practice: Take a message from an invented caller, then confirm all the details back to them.

Motivation

"A message is only useful if every detail survives the handoff."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Guided Practice

Fill in a message note from this call: "This is Mr. Siddique from Delta Linens, calling regarding tomorrow's delivery — it might be delayed. My number is 01711-582403." Include: name, number, regarding, and next step.

2. Guided Practice

Using the filled-in message note from Exercise 1, confirm and restate the details back to the caller using PAT-0031.

3. Role-Play

Take a message from an invented caller for someone who's unavailable, asking all four key questions and confirming the details before ending the call.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Name: Mr. Siddique (Delta Linens). Number: 01711-582403. Regarding: tomorrow's delivery may be delayed. Next step: pass along to Ms. Noor when free.

2.

Suggested answer: Just to confirm, that's Mr. Siddique, 01711-582403, regarding tomorrow's delivery being delayed — I'll pass that along.

3.

What to listen/look for: All four details (name, number, regarding, next step) are collected and restated back to the caller before the call ends — avoiding MIS-0049's unconfirmed message.

lessons.title: Asking Someone to Repeat or Slow Down
lessons.objectives_html:
• Ask a caller to repeat, slow down, or spell something out, using phone-specific language.
  • Recognize that asking again is more professional than guessing on a bad connection.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A caller gives Arif a callback number, but the line crackles right through the last four digits. Arif could guess, write down something close, and hope — or he could say something, right away, before the caller moves on.

Key Workplace Lesson

Level 1 Module 5 taught the general clarification request, "Sorry, could you say that again?" Phone calls add problems speech alone doesn't have: a bad connection, a caller speaking too fast, or a name that could be spelled several ways. Each has its own natural phone-specific phrase, and using the right one gets you a useful answer faster than a generic "what?"

Listen & Read
A caller's connection breaks up while giving Arif a callback number and an unfamiliar surname.
Caller: Hi, it's [connection crackles] — calling about my reservation, my number's oh one seven [crackle] — three two —
Arif: I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little — could you say that number again, one digit at a time?
Caller: Sure — zero, one, seven, one, four, four, one, two, two, three, three.
Arif: Thank you. And could you spell your surname for me, please, just so I get it exactly right?
Caller: It's C-H-O-W-D-H-U-R-Y.
Arif: Let me just repeat that back to make sure I've got it — 01714-412233, Chowdhury. Is that correct?
Caller: That's exactly right, thank you.

Key Expressions

Expression When to use Register
I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little. Bad connection Neutral
Could you spell that for me, please? An unclear or unfamiliar name Polite
Let me just repeat that back to make sure I've got it. Confirming after a difficult section Professional
Could you slow down just a little, please? Fast speech Polite

Vocabulary

  • the line's breaking up (V-0279) — the connection is unclear or cutting out. "I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little — could you say that again?"
  • could you spell that (V-0280) — asks for a name or word letter by letter. "Could you spell that for me, please?"
  • let me just repeat that back (V-0281) — signals you're about to confirm what you heard. "Let me just repeat that back to make sure I've got it right."
  • Recycled: Sorry, could you say that again? (Level 1 Module 5, Lesson 1).

Grammar in Context

No new grammar structure in this lesson — it extends Level 1 Module 5's general clarification request (PAT-0013) with phone-specific triggers: a bad connection ("the line's breaking up"), an unclear name ("could you spell that?"), and fast speech ("could you slow down?").

Common Mistake (MIS-0050)

Mistake: Pretending to understand on a bad connection or with an unclear name, rather than asking for clarification — and writing down a guess instead of the actual information.

❌ (Line crackles through the callback number; writes down a guess) "Okay, got it, thanks."

✅ "I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little — could you say that number again, one digit at a time?"

Why it matters: A guessed detail can look just as confident as a correct one on paper, but it sends the wrong callback number, the wrong name, or the wrong room to whoever reads the message next.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Pretending to understand (❌) "Okay, got it, thanks." Risks recording wrong information
Asking for clarification (✅) "I'm sorry, the line's breaking up — could you repeat that, one digit at a time?" Gets the actual, correct information

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "Could you spell your surname for me, please? I want to make sure I pull up the right account."
  • IT support: "Sorry, the line's breaking up — could you repeat the error code you're seeing?"

Self-Check

  1. Name three phone-specific reasons you might need to ask someone to repeat something.
  2. Why is guessing worse than asking again, even though asking again takes a few extra seconds?
  3. A caller gives you a name that sounds unclear over a bad connection. What do you say?

Motivation

"Asking again is not weakness — getting it wrong is."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Which phrase fits which situation — "the line's breaking up," "could you spell that for me," or "could you slow down"? (1) A bad connection. (2) An unfamiliar surname. (3) A caller speaking very quickly.

2. Guided Practice

A caller gives you a callback number, but the connection breaks up right through it. Respond appropriately.

3. Role-Play

Practice a call where you need to ask for repetition, spelling, and confirm what you heard, all in one exchange.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: (1) The line's breaking up. (2) Could you spell that for me? (3) Could you slow down?

2.

Suggested answer: I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little — could you say that number again, one digit at a time?

3.

What to listen/look for: The learner asks for clarification using a phone-specific phrase rather than guessing, and confirms the corrected information before ending the exchange — avoiding MIS-0050's guessed detail.

lessons.title: Putting Someone on Hold and Transferring
lessons.objectives_html:
• Ask permission before putting a caller on hold, and thank them when you return.
  • Transfer a call clearly, telling the caller who they're being connected to.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A guest on the phone needs to speak with housekeeping, not the front desk. Arif can't answer the question himself — but he can make sure the guest never feels dropped, ignored, or confused about what's happening next.

Key Workplace Lesson

Being put on hold or transferred without warning is one of the most frustrating parts of any phone call — the caller can't see what's happening, so silence can feel like being cut off. Two small habits fix this: ask before you put someone on hold, and say who you're connecting them to before you transfer.

Listen & Read
A guest calls the front desk asking a housekeeping question; Arif puts them on hold briefly and transfers them.
Guest: Hi, could I ask about getting my room serviced earlier today?
Arif: Of course — could you hold the line for a moment while I check with housekeeping?
Guest: Sure, no problem.
Arif: Thanks for waiting. I'll put you through to Rupa in housekeeping now — she can arrange the earlier service directly.
Guest: Perfect, thank you.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Could you hold the line for a moment? Asks permission before holding Polite
Thanks for waiting. Acknowledges the caller's patience on return Professional
I'll put you through to... Announces a transfer Neutral
I'll connect you with... Alternative way to announce a transfer Neutral

Vocabulary

  • hold the line (V-0282) — wait on the phone without hanging up. "Could you hold the line for a moment?"
  • put you through (V-0283) — transfer the call to another person or department. "I'll put you through to housekeeping."
  • thanks for waiting (V-0284) — acknowledges the caller's patience after a hold. "Thanks for waiting — I have an answer for you now."
  • I'll connect you with (V-0285) — names who the caller is about to speak with. "I'll connect you with Rupa in housekeeping."

Grammar in Context: Hold-and-Transfer Formula (PAT-0032)

Structure: [Could you hold the line for a moment?]... [Thanks for waiting] + [I'll put you through to / connect you with [name/department]]

"Could you hold the line for a moment while I check?... Thanks for waiting — I'll put you through to Rupa in housekeeping, who can help with that directly."

Naming the person or department before transferring means the caller isn't left guessing who they'll be speaking to next.

Common Mistake (MIS-0051)

Mistake: Putting a caller on hold or transferring them without asking first or explaining what's happening, leaving them confused about whether they've been cut off.

❌ (Puts the caller on hold immediately, without a word)

✅ "Could you hold the line for a moment while I check?... Thanks for waiting — I'll put you through to housekeeping now."

Why it matters: Silence on the other end of a phone call is ambiguous — it could mean "please wait" or "the call dropped." A short spoken heads-up removes that doubt entirely.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Silent hold/transfer (❌) (no explanation) Caller unsure if they've been disconnected
Announced hold/transfer (✅) "Could you hold the line for a moment?... Thanks for waiting — I'll put you through to housekeeping." Caller knows exactly what's happening

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "Could you hold the line while I check with our loans department?... Thanks for waiting — I'll connect you with Mr. Islam now."
  • IT support: "I'll need to put you through to Level 2 support for this — could you hold the line for a moment?"

Self-Check

  1. What should you do before putting a caller on hold?
  2. What should you say when you come back from a hold?
  3. A caller needs to speak with a different department. Ask them to hold, then announce the transfer.

Motivation

"A clean transfer means the caller never feels lost."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this silent transfer using PAT-0032: (Arif puts the caller on hold without a word, then transfers them without explanation.)

2. Guided Practice

A caller needs to speak with a different department. Ask permission to hold, then announce the transfer, using PAT-0032.

3. Role-Play

Practice a full hold-and-transfer exchange from start to finish.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Could you hold the line for a moment while I check with housekeeping?... Thanks for waiting — I'll put you through to Rupa now, who can help directly.

2.

Sample: "Could you hold the line for a moment while I check with Accounts? … Thanks for waiting — I'll put you through to Mr. Islam in Accounts now; he can help with your invoice." Check: permission to hold, thanks on return, the person or department named before the transfer.

3.

What to listen/look for: The learner asks permission before holding, thanks the caller for waiting, and names who they're being connected to before transferring — avoiding MIS-0051's silent hold or transfer.

lessons.title: Handling a Difficult or Unclear Caller & Ending the Call
lessons.objectives_html:
• Apply the module's greeting, message-taking, and clarification skills together under a difficult or unclear call.
  • Close a call clearly, checking for anything else needed before saying goodbye.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A caller phones the front desk sounding frustrated — their reservation confirmation email never arrived, and they're anxious to reach the hotel before they lose their room. Arif has to greet them, calm the frustration, get every detail right on a bad connection, and finish the call in a way that leaves them reassured, not more anxious.

Key Workplace Lesson

A difficult call doesn't call for new language — it calls for everything from this module, applied calmly, in the right order: a proper greeting, patient clarification if the connection or the caller's speech is unclear, an accurate restated message if one is needed, and a hold or transfer only when it's actually explained. Staying calm through all of it, rather than rushing to end an uncomfortable call, is what actually resolves it.

Ending well matters just as much as starting well. A rushed goodbye right after fixing the problem can leave a caller unsure whether everything's actually settled.

Listen & Read
A frustrated caller phones about a missing reservation confirmation email, on a connection that briefly breaks up.
Arif: Good afternoon, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?
Caller: I'm calling because I booked a room last week and never got any confirmation email! I'm worried I'm going to show up and have nothing.
Arif: I completely understand — let's sort this out right now. Could I get your name and booking reference, please?
Caller: It's [connection crackles] — Hoque, and the reference is — [crackle]
Arif: I'm sorry, the line's breaking up a little — could you spell your surname and repeat the reference number for me?
Caller: H-O-Q-U-E. Reference is 4-4-7-7-2-1.
Arif: Let me just repeat that back — Mr. Hoque, reference 447721. One moment while I check. ... Thanks for waiting — your reservation is showing correctly on our end. I'll resend the confirmation email right now.
Caller: Oh, that's a huge relief, thank you.
Arif: Of course. Is there anything else I can help you with today?
Caller: No, that's everything.
Arif: Thank you for calling — have a great day.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
I completely understand — let's sort this out. Acknowledges frustration calmly Professional
Is there anything else I can help you with today? Checks for remaining needs before closing Professional
Thank you for calling — have a great day. Closes the call warmly Professional

Vocabulary

This lesson uses no new vocabulary — it consolidates Lessons 1–4's language (phone greeting, message-taking, clarification requests, hold-and-transfer) under a single, more difficult call.

Grammar in Context: The Call-Closing Formula (CF-0005)

Structure: [Summarize what's been resolved] + [Is there anything else I can help you with today?] + [Thank you for calling] + [warm closing line]

"So to confirm, your reservation is showing correctly on our end, and I've sent the confirmation email again just now. Is there anything else I can help you with today?... Thank you for calling — have a great day."

Checking for anything else before saying goodbye is what turns a resolved problem into a genuinely finished call.

Common Mistake (MIS-0052)

Mistake: Ending a call abruptly right after resolving the immediate issue, without checking whether anything else is needed or thanking the caller.

❌ "Okay, that's sorted then. Bye." (click)

✅ "So that's all sorted — your reservation is confirmed and the email's on its way. Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for calling, and have a great day."

Why it matters: An abrupt ending can make a caller feel rushed off the phone, even if their actual problem was solved — undoing some of the trust built during the call.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Abrupt close (❌) "Okay, that's sorted. Bye." Feels rushed, undermines the resolution
Full closing formula (✅) "Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for calling, have a great day." Leaves the caller reassured and valued

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "So your transfer is confirmed and should arrive by tomorrow. Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for calling City Bank."
  • IT support: "So the ticket's logged and someone will call you back within the hour. Is there anything else I can help you with today?"

Self-Check

  1. What should you check for before ending any call, even after the main issue is resolved?
  2. Why can rushing to end a call undo some of the trust built during it?
  3. Module 3 Assessment: Handle a full simulated difficult call — greet the caller, stay calm through a frustrated or unclear moment, take or confirm a message accurately if needed, and close the call using the full call-closing formula. Scoring is in the answer key for Exercise 3.

Motivation

"How you end a hard call is what the caller remembers."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

In the dialogue, identify each of the four module skills Arif uses — greeting, clarification, message/detail confirmation, and closing.

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this abrupt call ending using CF-0005: "Okay, that's sorted then. Bye."

3. Role-Play

Module 3 Assessment: Handle a full simulated difficult call from start to finish — greet the caller, stay calm through a frustrated or unclear moment, confirm any message details accurately, and close using the full call-closing formula (CF-0005).

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Greeting: 'Good afternoon, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking.' Clarification: 'the line's breaking up — could you spell your surname...' Confirmation: 'Let me just repeat that back...' Closing: 'Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for calling.'

2.

Suggested answer: So that's all sorted — your reservation is confirmed. Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for calling, and have a great day.

3.

Scoring (1 point each, 4 = task complete, 3 = complete with one area to practice, 2 or fewer = review Lessons 3.1–3.5): (1) complete greeting; (2) calm clarification instead of guessing; (3) every detail restated correctly; (4) the full closing formula. What a strong call shows: the call opens with a complete greeting, handles the difficulty calmly using clarification language rather than guessing, confirms any details restated, and closes with the full formula (check for anything else + thank you + warm close) — avoiding MIS-0052's abrupt ending.

modules.title: Digital Messaging (WhatsApp/Teams/Slack)
modules.purpose: Write clear team-chat messages: choose the right register, keep to one idea per message, mark urgency honestly, read the room in group chats and choose chat, call or a conversation.

lessons.title: Chat Register: How Chat Differs from Email and Speech
lessons.objectives_html:
• Name "register" as the level of formality a message uses, and place chat on the spectrum between speech and email.
  • Recognize when a message is too formal or too informal for team chat.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening
