Why it matters: If the customer has to guess at what an answer meant, the interaction hasn't actually been resolved — it's only been postponed until the confusion resurfaces later.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Jargon-heavy (❌) "Your rate is BB, so F&B is bundled in." Accurate but unclear to the customer
Plain and checked (✅) "Breakfast's already included — does that answer your question?" Clear, and confirms understanding

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "In other words, there's no monthly fee as long as you keep the minimum balance. Does that answer your question?"
  • IT support: "To put it simply, the update runs automatically overnight — you don't need to do anything. Does that answer your question?"
  • Hotel: "Your rate includes breakfast — in other words, it's not billed separately. Does that answer your question?"

Self-Check

  1. Why is a technically correct answer not always a clear answer?
  2. What does "does that answer your question?" accomplish that simply finishing an explanation doesn't?
  3. Rewrite a piece of workplace jargon from your own field in plain language, using "in other words" or "to put it simply."

Motivation

"If the customer has to ask what you meant, you haven't answered yet."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this jargon-heavy answer in plain language and add an understanding-check: "Your reservation is on an OTA rate, so modifications have to go through the booking platform, not us directly."

2. Guided Practice

A customer in your own field asks a question that would normally get a jargon-heavy answer. Write a plain-language response using PAT-0040.

3. Recognition

A colleague says, "I always give the technically correct answer, so I've done my job." What's missing from that view, based on MIS-0067?

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: To put it simply, since you booked through a travel website, any changes need to be made there rather than with us directly. Does that answer your question?

2.

Sample (a bank): "Your account has a minimum balance requirement — in other words, as long as you keep at least 5,000 taka in the account, there's no monthly fee. Does that answer your question?" Check: no unexplained internal terms, a plain restatement, an understanding check.

3.

Suggested answer: Technically correct isn't the same as understood — if the customer doesn't grasp the answer, the question hasn't really been resolved, even though the words were accurate.

lessons.title: "I Don't Know" — But I'll Find Out
lessons.objectives_html:
• Admit uncertainty honestly instead of guessing or deflecting.
  • Pair an admission of not knowing with a concrete next step.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A guest asks Arif whether the hotel's pool is heated in winter. Arif genuinely doesn't know — he hasn't yet worked a winter at this hotel. He has two choices: guess an answer that sounds confident, or say he doesn't know and find out.

Key Workplace Lesson

Not knowing something isn't the problem — pretending to know is. A confident-sounding guess that turns out to be wrong damages trust far more than an honest "I don't know" ever could, as long as the honest answer comes with a next step: checking, confirming, or finding out and following up.

Listen & Read
A
Guessed, risky (contrastive pair, part 1). A guest asks about the pool.
Guest: Is the pool heated in winter?
Arif: Oh yeah, I think it's heated — probably.
Guest: You think?
Arif: ...I'm actually not totally sure.
B
Honest + next step (contrastive pair, part 2). The same question, handled properly.
Guest: Is the pool heated in winter?
Arif: That's a good question — I'm not sure. Let me check on that and get back to you before you check out.
Guest: Sure, thanks.
Arif: (Later) I confirmed it — the pool is heated year-round, so you're all set.

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"Let me check on that." Signaling you'll verify before answering
"I'll find out and get back to you." Honest uncertainty + a promise to follow up
"Let me confirm that for you." Verifying a detail you're not fully sure of
"I'll take care of it." (recycled, Level 1 Module 6, Lesson 5) Once you've found the answer, this closes the loop

Vocabulary

  • let me check on that (V-0324) — a natural way to pause before giving an uncertain answer. "Let me check on that for you."
  • I'll find out and get back to you (V-0325) — an honest admission of not knowing, paired with a commitment to follow up. "I'm not sure off the top of my head — I'll find out and get back to you."
  • let me confirm that for you (V-0326) — used when you have a likely answer but want to verify it before committing to it. "Let me confirm that for you before I give you a final answer."
  • Recycled: I'll take care of it (Level 1 Module 6, Lesson 5).

Grammar in Context: Honest-Uncertainty-Plus-Next-Step Structure (PAT-0041)

Structure: [Honest admission — I'm not sure / let me check] + [Concrete next step — I'll find out and get back to you / let me confirm that for you]

"That's a good question — I'm not actually sure. Let me check on that and get back to you before you check out."

Common Mistake (MIS-0068)

Mistake: Guessing at an answer to sound confident, or deflecting the question entirely instead of admitting uncertainty.

❌ "Oh yeah, I think the pool's heated — probably."

✅ "That's a good question — I'm not sure. Let me check on that and get back to you."

Why it matters: A wrong confident guess is far more damaging than an honest "I don't know," because it can send the customer away with information they'll later find out was false.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Guessed (❌) "I think it's heated — probably." Sounds confident but risks being wrong
Deflected (❌) "You'd have to ask someone else." Passes the problem without helping
Honest + next step (✅) "I'm not sure — let me check on that and get back to you." Trustworthy and still helpful

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "I'm not certain of today's exact exchange rate — let me confirm that for you."
  • IT support: "I'm not sure what's causing that error yet — I'll find out and get back to you."
  • Hotel: "Let me check on that and get back to you before you check out."

Self-Check

  1. Why is an honest "I don't know, but I'll find out" more trustworthy than a confident guess?
  2. What makes "let me check on that" different from simply saying "I don't know" and stopping there?
  3. Think of a question in your own field you genuinely wouldn't know the answer to. Write how you'd respond using PAT-0041.

Motivation

"'I don't know, but I'll find out' is more trustworthy than a confident guess."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

A colleague guesses an answer rather than admitting uncertainty. Which mistake does this match, and why is it risky?

2. Guided Practice

A customer asks you something in your own field that you genuinely would not know. Respond using PAT-0041 (honest admission + concrete next step).

3. Role-Play

Role-play: a customer asks a question you don't know the answer to. Admit it honestly and give a concrete next step, then close the loop once you've found out.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: MIS-0068 — a confident wrong guess can send the customer away with false information, which is more damaging than honestly admitting uncertainty.

2.

Sample (IT support): "That's a good question — I'm not sure whether the new software works on older laptops. Let me check with the vendor and get back to you by tomorrow morning." Check: an honest admission, no guess, a concrete next step with a time.

3.

Suggested answer: I'm not sure — let me check on that and get back to you. (Later) I confirmed it — here's the answer. What to listen/look for: Admits uncertainty honestly rather than guessing; Gives a concrete next step (checking, confirming, following up); Closes the loop once the answer is found.

lessons.title: Handling a Simple Complaint (Non-Escalated)
lessons.objectives_html:
• Respond to a mild, non-escalated complaint by listening, acknowledging, and offering help.
  • Recognize that this lesson covers ordinary complaints only — a full angry-customer de-escalation toolkit comes later, in Level 3.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A guest mentions, in an ordinary tone, that their room wasn't cleaned before check-in. It's not an angry confrontation — just a real problem, calmly raised. This is the everyday version of a complaint, and it's the one Arif will meet most often.

Key Workplace Lesson

Most complaints you'll actually handle aren't dramatic — they're a guest mentioning, calmly, that something didn't go as expected. The instinct to jump straight to explaining or defending skips the part the customer actually needs first: to feel heard. A light, three-part shape covers most of these ordinary moments: listen without interrupting, acknowledge the concern in your own words, and offer something concrete. (Truly angry or difficult customers need a more advanced toolkit — that's covered later, in Level 3.)

Listen & Read
A
Explains first, sounds like an excuse (contrastive pair, part 1). A guest mentions their room wasn't ready.
Guest: My room wasn't cleaned when I got here this afternoon.
Arif: Yeah, housekeeping's been really short-staffed today, so things got a bit behind.
Guest: Okay... but is someone going to clean it?
B
Listen, acknowledge, offer (contrastive pair, part 2). The same complaint, handled properly.
Guest: My room wasn't cleaned when I got here this afternoon.
Arif: I understand your concern — your room should have been ready when you arrived. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention.
Guest: Thanks, I just want to be able to settle in.
Arif: Of course. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted right away.

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"I understand your concern." Acknowledging the complaint before offering anything
"Let me see what I can do." Signaling you'll try to help, without over-promising
"I appreciate you bringing this to my attention." Thanking the customer for raising the issue

Vocabulary

  • I understand your concern (V-0327) — an acknowledgment that shows you've actually heard the complaint. "I understand your concern — that shouldn't have happened."
  • let me see what I can do (V-0328) — an honest offer to help, without promising a specific outcome yet. "Let me see what I can do to fix that for you."
  • I appreciate you bringing this to my attention (V-0329) — a way of thanking the customer for raising the issue rather than staying silent. "I appreciate you bringing this to my attention."

Grammar in Context: Listen-Acknowledge-Offer Structure (PAT-0042)

Structure: [Listen without interrupting] + [I understand your concern / acknowledgment] + [Let me see what I can do / concrete offer]

"I understand your concern — your room should have been ready when you arrived. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted right away."

Common Mistake (MIS-0069)

Mistake: Jumping straight to explaining or defending what happened, before acknowledging the customer's concern.

❌ "Well, housekeeping's been really short-staffed today, so..."

✅ "I understand your concern — your room should have been ready. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted right away."

Why it matters: An explanation that comes before an acknowledgment sounds like an excuse, even when it's true. Acknowledging first shows the customer their concern registered before anything else is said.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Explains first (❌) "Housekeeping's short-staffed today, so..." Sounds like an excuse
Acknowledges first (✅) "I understand your concern — let me see what I can do." Sounds like the concern was heard

Industry Overlays

  • Retail: "I understand your concern — I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me see what I can do about a replacement."
  • Banking: "I understand your concern about the delay. Let me see what I can do to look into it right away."
  • Hotel: "I understand your concern — your room should have been ready. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted."

Self-Check

  1. Why does explaining before acknowledging tend to sound like an excuse?
  2. What's the difference between this lesson's light complaint-handling shape and full de-escalation for an angry customer (which this lesson does not cover)?
  3. Write a listen-acknowledge-offer response to a mild complaint in your own field.

Motivation

"Being heard is often the first thing an unhappy customer actually needs."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this explanation-first response as a listen-acknowledge-offer response, using PAT-0042: "Yeah, the kitchen's been backed up all night, so orders are running late."

2. Guided Practice

A customer in your own field raises a mild, ordinary complaint. Write a listen-acknowledge-offer response using PAT-0042.

3. Recognition

This lesson deliberately does not cover handling an angry or difficult customer. Why might that skill need its own separate lesson later, rather than being folded into this one?

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: I understand your concern — your order is taking longer than it should. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me see what I can do to speed that up for you.

2.

Sample (a restaurant): "I understand your concern — your soup should have arrived hot. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me get you a fresh bowl right away." Check: no explanation or excuse before the acknowledgment; a concrete offer.

3.

Suggested answer: An angry customer needs active de-escalation — calming the emotion, not just acknowledging a concern — which is a more advanced skill than this lesson's light listen-acknowledge-offer shape covers.

lessons.title: Closing a Customer Interaction Well
lessons.objectives_html:
• Close a customer interaction in a way that confirms resolution and leaves a positive final impression.
  • Combine greeting, answering, and complaint-handling into one connected customer interaction.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

The room is fixed, the question is answered, the guest is smiling again — and then Arif just... walks away. Nothing was technically wrong with the help he gave. But the interaction ended without a proper close, and the guest is left unsure whether it's really over.

Key Workplace Lesson

How an interaction ends shapes what the customer remembers about the whole thing — more than any single moment in the middle. A good closing confirms that the customer's need was actually met, thanks them, and leaves the door open if anything else comes up. This lesson doesn't introduce new vocabulary; it brings together everything from this module — the channel-adapted greeting, the plain-language answer, the honest "I'll find out," and the listen-acknowledge-offer complaint response — into one connected interaction, closed properly at the end.

Listen & Read
A guest approaches the front desk. Arif greets, answers a question, checks on something he's unsure of, handles a mild complaint, and closes the interaction properly.
Guest: Hi there.
Arif: Welcome! Thanks for stopping by — how can I help you today?
Guest: Does my rate include breakfast?
Arif: Yes, it does — in other words, breakfast is already part of what you paid. Does that answer your question?
Guest: Perfect. Also, is the pool heated right now?
Arif: That's a good question — I'm not sure. Let me check on that and get back to you.
Guest: Sure. One more thing — my room wasn't cleaned when I checked in earlier.
Arif: I understand your concern — your room should have been ready. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted right away.
Guest: I'd appreciate that, thanks.
Arif: (A short while later) I confirmed the pool is heated year-round, and housekeeping is heading up to your room now. I'm glad we could sort that out. Is there anything else I can help you with?
Guest: No, that's everything — thank you.
Arif: Thanks for your patience — have a great stay!

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"Is there anything else I can help you with?" Checking for any remaining needs before closing
"I'm glad we could sort that out." Confirming resolution in a warm, natural way
"Thanks for your patience / for stopping by / for calling." A channel-adapted thank-you to close on
"Have a great stay / day!" A warm final line

Grammar in Context: The Customer-Interaction Closing Formula (CF-0008)

Structure: [Confirm the need is met] + [Is there anything else I can help you with?] + [Channel-adapted thanks] + [Warm final line]

"I'm glad we could sort that out for you. Is there anything else I can help you with? Thanks for your patience — have a great stay!"

Common Mistake (MIS-0070)

Mistake: Ending the interaction as soon as the immediate problem is resolved, without checking for anything else or thanking the customer.

❌ (Room issue just fixed) "Okay, that's sorted." (walks away)

✅ "I'm glad we could sort that out. Is there anything else I can help you with? Thanks for your patience — have a great stay!"

Why it matters: An abrupt ending can undo the goodwill built up during the rest of the interaction — the customer is left unsure whether everything is really settled, and the positive final impression is lost.

Full Connected Interaction

In the dialogue, Arif handles one guest from greeting to close:

  1. Greet (Lesson 1): "Welcome! How can I help you today?"
  2. Answer clearly (Lesson 2): explains the rate in plain language, checks understanding.
  3. Admit uncertainty honestly (Lesson 3): "Let me check on that and get back to you," then follows up.
  4. Handle a mild complaint (Lesson 4): listens, acknowledges, offers help.
  5. Close well (this lesson): confirms resolution, checks for anything else, thanks the guest warmly.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Abrupt (❌) "Okay, that's sorted." (walks away) Undoes earlier goodwill
Warm close (✅) "I'm glad we could sort that out. Anything else I can help with? Have a great stay!" Leaves a positive final impression

Industry Overlays

  • Retail: "Glad we could get that sorted. Anything else I can help you find today? Thanks for stopping by!"
  • Banking: "I'm glad we could resolve that. Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thanks for your patience."
  • Phone/chat support: "Glad that's fixed now. Anything else I can help with? Thanks for calling/reaching out — have a great day!"

Self-Check

  1. Why does an interaction's ending carry so much weight in how the whole thing is remembered?
  2. What are the four parts of CF-0008, and why does each one matter?
  3. Write a full connected interaction in your own field: greet, answer or handle an issue, and close well.

Motivation

"How an interaction ends is what a customer carries out the door."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

Rewrite this abrupt ending as a proper close, using CF-0008: "Okay, that's sorted." (walks away)

2. Role-Play

Module 7 Assessment: Role-play a full simple customer interaction from start to finish — greet the customer on any channel, answer a question clearly, admit honest uncertainty about something and follow up, respond to a mild complaint, and close the interaction well.

3. Recognition

Why does this lesson introduce no new vocabulary or pattern of its own?

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: I'm glad we could sort that out for you. Is there anything else I can help you with? Thanks for your patience — have a great day!

2.

Use the Listen & Read dialogue as the model. Score 0–5, one point for each step shown: Greets appropriately for the chosen channel (PAT-0039); Answers at least one question in plain language with an understanding-check (PAT-0040); Admits uncertainty honestly rather than guessing, with a concrete next step (PAT-0041); Responds to a mild complaint with listen-acknowledge-offer (PAT-0042); Closes the interaction using CF-0008 (confirm, check for anything else, thank, warm line). 5 = task complete; 4 = complete, practice the missed step; 3 or fewer = review the lessons for the missed steps.

3.

Suggested answer: It's a synthesis lesson — its purpose is to combine everything already learned in Module 7 (greeting, plain-language answers, honest uncertainty, complaint handling) into one connected interaction, closed properly with CF-0008.

modules.title: Workplace Etiquette
modules.purpose: Workplace etiquette: punctuality and lateness messages, digital etiquette and confidentiality, addressing people at every level, and a full simulated workday.

lessons.title: Punctuality and Time Norms at Work
lessons.objectives_html:
• Notify others proactively when you're running late, instead of staying silent.
  • Use natural language for arrival timing across in-person, phone, and chat situations.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif's bus is stuck in traffic, and the morning stand-up starts in five minutes. He's not going to make it on time — but there's a real difference between arriving late and arriving late with no warning at all.

Key Workplace Lesson

Being exactly on time isn't always possible — traffic, transit delays, and unexpected obstacles happen to everyone. What separates a professional response from an unprofessional one isn't the lateness itself; it's whether you say something about it, and how soon. A short, proactive message sent as soon as you know you'll be late does almost all the work of actually being on time.

Listen & Read
A
Silent, no warning (contrastive pair, part 1). Arif is running late for the morning stand-up.
Priyanka: Where's Arif? Stand-up started six minutes ago.
Hasan: No idea, he hasn't said anything.
Arif (arriving): Sorry, sorry — traffic.
B
Proactive heads-up (contrastive pair, part 2). The same morning, handled properly.
Arif (message): Sorry, I'm running a few minutes behind — my bus is stuck in traffic. I'll be there shortly, around 9:10.
Priyanka (message): No worries, we'll start without you and catch you up.
Arif (message): On my way, thanks!

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"I'm running a few minutes behind." A simple, honest heads-up about lateness
"I'll be there shortly." Reassuring the other person you're still coming, soon
"On my way." A short update once you've actually started heading there

Vocabulary

  • running a few minutes behind (V-0330) — a natural, non-alarming way to say you'll be slightly late. "Sorry, I'm running a few minutes behind — traffic."
  • I'll be there shortly (V-0331) — reassures the other person that you're still coming and it won't be long. "I'll be there shortly, please start without me."
  • on my way (V-0332) — a short, common update once you've actually left. "On my way, be there in ten."
  • Recycled: punctuality concept (Level 1 Module 6, Lesson 3).

Grammar in Context: Lateness Notification Formula (PAT-0043)

Structure: [Brief apology] + [I'm running a few minutes behind / on my way] + [I'll be there shortly, or a specific time if you know it]

"Sorry, I'm running a few minutes behind — my bus is stuck in traffic. I'll be there shortly, around 9:10."

Common Mistake (MIS-0071)

Mistake: Staying silent about running late instead of sending a short, proactive heads-up.

❌ (No message sent; arrives 12 minutes late with no explanation)

✅ "Sorry, I'm running a few minutes behind — I'll be there shortly, around 9:10."

Why it matters: A proactive heads-up lets colleagues adjust — start without you, reschedule a few minutes, or simply not worry. Silence leaves them guessing whether you're coming at all.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Silent (❌) (no message, just arrives late) Leaves colleagues uncertain and possibly worried
Proactive (✅) "Running a few minutes behind — I'll be there shortly." Respects everyone else's time and planning

Industry Overlays

  • Office: "Sorry, running a few minutes behind on my commute — I'll be there shortly."
  • Client meeting: "I'm running a few minutes behind due to traffic — I'll be there shortly, around 2:10."
  • Retail/hospitality shift: "On my way, running about five minutes behind — I'll be there shortly."

Self-Check

  1. Why does sending a short heads-up matter more than the lateness itself?
  2. What's the difference between "I'll be there shortly" and "on my way," and when would you use each?
  3. Write a lateness notification for your own workplace using PAT-0043.

Motivation

"Saying you'll be late is itself being on time."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Rewriting

You realize you'll be about ten minutes late to a client meeting. Write a short proactive heads-up message using PAT-0043.

2. Guided Practice

Think of a time you were running late for something at work or school. Write what you actually said (or should have said) using PAT-0043.

3. Recognition

Why does MIS-0071 (staying silent about being late) damage trust more than the lateness itself?

Answer Key

1.

Sample: "Sorry, I'm running about ten minutes behind — the traffic is heavy. I'll be there around 2:10. Thanks for your patience."

2.

Sample: "Sorry, I'm running about fifteen minutes behind — my train is delayed. I'll be there around 9:15; please start without me." Check: a brief apology, the reason in a few words, a specific time if you know it.

3.

Suggested answer: It leaves colleagues uncertain whether you're coming at all, unable to plan around it — while a short heads-up lets them adjust and shows you respect their time.

lessons.title: Digital Etiquette and Confidentiality Basics
lessons.objectives_html:
• Recognize and mark confidential information appropriately in digital communication.
  • Avoid forwarding or sharing information without checking permission first.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Noor shares a draft staffing schedule in the team chat, with a quick note: some names on it aren't finalized yet. Arif almost forwards it to a colleague who asked about their shift — then stops. Is this something he's actually free to share?

Key Workplace Lesson

Digital tools make sharing effortless — a forward, a screenshot, or a copy-paste takes seconds. That ease is exactly why digital etiquette matters: information that would never casually leave a private conversation can spread instantly online, unless everyone pauses to check what's actually shareable and what isn't.

Listen & Read
Ms. Noor shares a draft staffing schedule in the team chat.
Ms. Noor (chat): Sharing the draft schedule for next month — some names aren't finalized yet. This is confidential for now, please don't forward it without permission.
Arif (chat, to a colleague who asks about it): I've seen a draft, but it's confidential for now — let me check with Ms. Noor before I share any details.
Arif is in a group chat discussing an unannounced organizational change. A friend outside the chat asks what's going on.
Friend (message): Hey, I heard something's changing at the hotel — what's going on?
Arif (message): I can't really say yet — it's on a need-to-know basis until it's officially announced. I'll let you know once it's public!
Arif receives a screenshot of a private message from a colleague, with no context on whether it's okay to share further.
Colleague (chat): Here's that screenshot you asked about.
Arif (chat): Thanks — I'll keep this between us for now, since I'm not sure if it's okay to share further.

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"This is confidential." Marking information as not for general sharing
"Please don't forward this without permission." Setting an explicit boundary on sharing
"Keep this between us for now." A softer, informal way to ask for discretion
"This is on a need-to-know basis." Explaining that only certain people should have this information

Vocabulary

  • confidential (V-0333) — information that should not be shared beyond the people it was given to. "This draft schedule is confidential for now."
  • forward without permission (V-0334) — sharing a message or document with someone else without first checking if that's allowed. "Please don't forward this without permission."
  • keep this between us (V-0335) — an informal request for discretion. "Keep this between us until it's officially announced."
  • need-to-know basis (V-0336) — describes information limited to only the people who genuinely require it. "This is on a need-to-know basis for now."
  • Recycled: thread / DM / reply-all (Level 2 Module 4, Lesson 4) — the same channel concepts now applied to who should and shouldn't see a message.

Grammar in Context: Confidentiality Reminder Structure (PAT-0044)

Structure: [This is confidential / keep this between us] + [reason or scope, if useful] + [please don't forward without permission]

"This draft schedule is confidential for now — some names aren't finalized. Please don't forward it without permission."

Common Mistake (MIS-0072)

Mistake: Forwarding or sharing a message, document, or screenshot without checking whether it's actually permitted first.

❌ (Forwards a confidential draft schedule to a colleague who asked, without checking)

✅ "I have a draft, but it's confidential for now — let me check if I can share it before I send it over."

Why it matters: Once something is forwarded, it can't be un-shared — checking first costs a few seconds, while an accidental leak can cost real trust.

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Careless (❌) (Forwards without asking) Risks a real confidentiality breach
Careful (✅) "This is confidential — let me check before I share it." Protects trust and shows good judgment

Scenario Cards

  1. A colleague asks you to forward a client's private contact details "just this once." What do you say?
  2. You're added to a group chat discussing an unannounced organizational change. A friend outside the chat asks what's going on. What do you say?
  3. You receive a screenshot of a private message from a colleague, with no context on whether it's okay to share further. What's the safest response?

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "This account information is on a need-to-know basis — please don't forward it."
  • Healthcare admin: "This is confidential patient information — keep this between us and the care team."
  • Office/HR: "This draft org chart is confidential for now — please don't forward it without permission."

Self-Check

  1. Why does digital ease of sharing make confidentiality more important, not less?
  2. What's the difference between "keep this between us" and "this is on a need-to-know basis"?
  3. Write a confidentiality reminder for a real or invented piece of workplace information, using PAT-0044.

Motivation

"Digital etiquette is really just respect, typed instead of spoken."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

For each scenario card in the lesson, decide: is this information confidential, need-to-know, or safe to share freely?

A.

confidential

B.

need-to-know

C.

safe to share

2. Guided Practice

Write a confidentiality reminder for a real or invented piece of workplace information, using PAT-0044.

3. Role-Play

Role-play: a colleague asks you to forward a confidential document "just this once." Decline appropriately without being unfriendly.

Answer Key

1.

(1) A client's private contact details — confidential: don't forward them, even "just this once". (2) An unannounced organizational change — need-to-know until it is officially announced. (3) A screenshot of a private message — treat it as need-to-know and don't share it until the person who wrote it confirms you can.

2.

Sample: "This guest list for the minister's visit is confidential — the visit hasn't been announced. Please don't forward it without permission." Check: marks it as confidential, gives the reason or scope briefly, sets the sharing boundary.

3.

Suggested answer: I'd love to help, but this one's confidential for now — let me check if I can share it before I send it over. What to listen/look for: Declines to forward without permission (avoids MIS-0072); Explains briefly why (confidential / need-to-know basis); Stays warm and collegial rather than sounding suspicious or cold.

lessons.title: Hierarchy, Titles, and Respectful Address
lessons.objectives_html:
• Address colleagues at different levels of seniority appropriately, across in-person, phone, and chat.
  • CC a senior colleague into an email thread appropriately, when it's genuinely useful rather than just visible.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif calls a peer by their first name without a second thought. Minutes later, the hotel's General Manager stops by the front desk — and Arif catches himself before defaulting to the same casual tone. The underlying respect doesn't change; the specific words do.

Key Workplace Lesson

Level 1 Module 7 introduced noticing hierarchy in person — a title, a tone shift, a moment of extra formality. That same awareness has to travel across every channel: a phone call, a chat message, and an email thread all carry the same respect, expressed in slightly different ways. Titles and CC'ing are two of the clearest tools for showing it.

Listen & Read
Arif messages Hasan, a peer, on chat.
Arif (chat): Hey Hasan, can you cover the desk for five minutes? Be right back.
Hasan (chat): Sure thing, go ahead.
Arif calls Ms. Noor, his supervisor, with a question.
Arif: Good afternoon, Ms. Noor, this is Arif — could I ask you something when you have a moment?
Ms. Noor: Of course, go ahead.
Arif emails Dr. Rahman, the General Manager, about a guest concern, CC'ing Ms. Noor.
Arif (email): Dear Dr. Rahman, I hope this finds you well. I wanted to flag a guest concern from this morning — I've copied in Ms. Noor so she's kept in the loop. Happy to discuss further at your convenience.
Dr. Rahman (email): Thanks for flagging this, Arif — I'll follow up with Ms. Noor directly.

Key Expressions

Expression Use
"Mr. / Ms. / Dr. + surname" The standard respectful address for someone senior or less familiar, until invited to use first names
"I'll CC [senior colleague] so they're kept in the loop." Explaining why you're including someone senior on a thread

Vocabulary

  • Mr. / Ms. / Dr. + surname conventions (V-0337) — the standard pattern for addressing someone senior or unfamiliar respectfully. "Good morning, Dr. Rahman."
  • CC'ing a senior colleague appropriately (V-0338) — including a senior colleague on a thread specifically because they need visibility, not just to be safe. "I'll CC Ms. Noor so she's kept in the loop on this."

Grammar in Context: Hierarchy-Adapted Address Structure (PAT-0045)

Structure: [Title + surname, if senior or unfamiliar] + [channel-appropriate greeting] + [first name once invited, or with a clearly familiar peer]

Peer (chat): "Hey Hasan, quick question — "
Supervisor (phone): "Good morning, Ms. Noor, this is Arif — "
Senior executive (email): "Dear Dr. Rahman, I hope this finds you well — "

Common Mistake (MIS-0073)

Mistake: Using first names with senior colleagues by default, regardless of the relationship, or CC'ing a senior colleague on every thread "just to be safe" rather than when it's genuinely useful.

❌ "Hey Rahman, quick thing — " (to the General Manager, unprompted)

✅ "Good morning, Dr. Rahman, quick question when you have a moment — "

Why it matters: Defaulting to first names with someone senior can read as overly familiar before that familiarity has been established; over-CC'ing senior colleagues on everything can read as covering yourself rather than genuinely keeping them informed.

Three Parallel Exchanges

  • Peer (chat): "Hey Hasan, can you cover the desk for five minutes?"
  • Supervisor (phone): "Good afternoon, Ms. Noor, this is Arif — could I ask you something when you have a moment?"
  • Senior executive (email): "Dear Dr. Rahman, I hope this finds you well. I wanted to flag a guest concern — I've copied in Ms. Noor so she's kept in the loop."

Professional Tone

Register Example Effect
Too casual (❌) "Hey Rahman" to the General Manager Reads as overly familiar
Appropriately formal (✅) "Good morning, Dr. Rahman" Reads as respectful without being stiff

Bengali/Hindi Note

In Bengali and Hindi, honorifics and respectful forms of address (such as "Sir/Madam," "Apu," "Bhaiya," or a title before a name) are woven into the grammar and everyday speech far more consistently than in English, where respect is shown mainly through title-plus-surname and tone rather than through the language's own structure. English learners sometimes under-signal respect in English for exactly this reason — not because they intend to be casual, but because English simply doesn't offer as many automatic honorific markers, so the respect has to be built deliberately into word choice and phrasing instead.

Self-Check

  1. Why might defaulting to first names with a senior colleague feel more natural in English than it would in Bengali or Hindi — and why can that still come across as too casual?
  2. When is CC'ing a senior colleague genuinely useful, versus just "covering yourself"?
  3. Write three versions of the same message to a peer, a supervisor, and a senior executive, using PAT-0045.

Motivation

"Respect travels through every channel, not just the room you're standing in."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

Match each opening line to the relationship it fits: (1) "Hey Hasan, quick question" (2) "Good morning, Ms. Noor, this is Arif" (3) "Dear Dr. Rahman, I hope this finds you well"

A.

peer

B.

supervisor

C.

senior executive

2. Guided Practice

Write three versions of the same short message to a peer, a supervisor, and a senior colleague in your own workplace, using PAT-0045.

3. Recognition

Why might over-CC'ing a senior colleague on every thread "just to be safe" actually undermine the purpose of CC'ing, according to MIS-0073?

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: 1 = peer, 2 = supervisor, 3 = senior executive

2.

Sample. Peer (chat): "Hey Rina, quick question — is the printer on two working?" Supervisor (phone): "Good morning, Mr. Islam, this is Nadia — could I ask you something when you have a moment?" Senior colleague (email): "Dear Dr. Haque, I hope you're well. I wanted to ask about the training schedule for next month…" Check: title + surname for the senior and less familiar people, first name for the peer.

3.

Suggested answer: If every thread includes them regardless of relevance, the CC stops signaling genuine need-to-know and starts reading as covering yourself, which the senior colleague will eventually tune out or find excessive.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together: A Full Workday
lessons.objectives_html:
• Move between different workplace communication skills fluidly within a single simulated workday.
  • Recognize which skill a moment calls for, and switch into it naturally.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

It's an ordinary Tuesday for Arif. By the end of it, he will have given an update, made a request, taken a phone call, sent a chat message, apologized for a small mistake, thanked a colleague, greeted and helped a guest, and addressed his General Manager respectfully — all without stopping to think about which "lesson" each moment belongs to. That's the real test: not using one skill well, but knowing which one a moment calls for.

Key Workplace Lesson

A real workday is not one skill practiced in isolation — it's all of Level 2's skills, arriving in whatever order the day actually brings them, often within minutes of each other. This lesson introduces no new vocabulary or pattern; instead, it asks you to recognize, in the moment, which of the tools you already have is the right one to reach for, and to move between them without a seam.

Listen & Read
9:00 AM. Morning stand-up. Arif gives his update (Module 1).
Ms. Noor: Arif, how's the Chowdhury reservation coming along?
Arif: It's confirmed and ready — I've blocked the room and sent the confirmation email. No outstanding items.
9:10 AM. Right after stand-up, Arif makes a request to Priyanka (Module 2).
Arif: Priyanka, could you cover the desk for about ten minutes around eleven? I need to drop off some paperwork.
Priyanka: Sure, eleven works for me.
10:15 AM. The front desk phone rings (Module 3).
Arif: Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?
Caller: Hi, I need to change my check-out time.
Arif: Of course — let me pull up your reservation.
11:30 AM. A message comes in on the team chat (Module 4).
Hasan (chat): quick q — is the conference room free at 2?
Arif (chat): Yes, it's open from 1–3. All yours.
1:00 PM. Priyanka spots that Arif attached the wrong invoice to a guest email this morning. Arif owns the mistake, then thanks her (Module 5).
Arif: Priyanka, You're right — I attached the wrong invoice to that guest email this morning. That's on me. I've sent the corrected one now, and I'll double-check attachments before sending from now on.
Priyanka: No worries — thanks for fixing it so fast.
Arif: And thank you for flagging it before it went any further — I really appreciate it.
2:30 PM. A guest approaches the desk with a mild complaint (Module 7).
Guest: Hi — my room wasn't cleaned before I checked in this morning.
Arif: Welcome! I understand your concern — your room should have been ready. I appreciate you bringing this to my attention. Let me see what I can do to get that sorted right away.
Guest: Thanks, I appreciate that.
Arif: (A few minutes later) Housekeeping has finished your room. I'm glad we could sort that out. Is there anything else I can help you with? Thanks for stopping by — have a great stay!
4:45 PM. Dr. Rahman, the General Manager, stops by to check on the day (Module 8).
Dr. Rahman: Afternoon, Arif — how's everything going today?
Arif: Good afternoon, Dr. Rahman — smoothly overall. One guest had a room-readiness issue this afternoon, but it's been resolved.
Dr. Rahman: Good to hear. Thanks for staying on top of it.

Common Mistake (MIS-0074)

Mistake: Treating each workplace skill as something that only applies in its own separate "lesson" moment, rather than recognizing which skill a real, mixed situation actually calls for.

❌ (Gives a vague update because a request is on his mind, then makes the request too abruptly because he's still thinking about the update)

✅ (Gives a clear, complete update — then, once it's finished, shifts cleanly into the request, using the right shape for each)

Why it matters: Real workplace moments don't announce which skill they need. The ability to notice the shift — "this is now a request, not an update" — and move cleanly into the right shape is what separates practiced skills from a real, working professional voice.

Common-Mistakes Mini-Scenario

Arif is mid-update to Ms. Noor when Hasan interrupts to ask for help moving luggage. Arif tries to answer both at once, and neither the update nor the request comes out clearly. The fix: finish one exchange, then cleanly start the next — "Let me just finish this with Ms. Noor, then I'm all yours."

Self-Check

  1. Why is switching cleanly between skills, rather than blending them together, part of professional communication?
  2. Look back through Level 2's eight modules — which skill do you personally find hardest to switch into naturally, and why?
  3. Describe your own recent workday as a sequence of communication moments, and name which Level 2 skill each one used.

Motivation

"A real workday is not one skill — it's all of them, in the right order, at the right moment."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

In the common-mistakes mini-scenario, Arif tries to answer an update and a request at the same time. What should he have done instead, according to MIS-0074?

2. Role-Play

Module 8 Assessment: Role-play your own simulated workday, moving through at least five different communication moments from across Level 2 — for example: a work update, a request, a phone call, a chat message, an apology or thanks, a customer interaction, and a hierarchy-appropriate exchange. Switch cleanly between them as the situation changes.

3. Guided Practice

Look back across Level 2's eight modules and list the three skills you personally find hardest to switch into naturally during a busy day. Explain why.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Finish one exchange cleanly before starting the next — e.g. 'Let me just finish this with Ms. Noor, then I'm all yours' — rather than blending both moments together.

2.

Use the Listen & Read workday as the model. Score each communication moment 0–2: 1 point for using the right skill for the moment (update, request, call, chat, apology/thanks, customer, hierarchy), 1 point for a clean switch into it without mixing it with the previous moment. Five moments = 10 points. 8–10: Module 8 complete; 6–7: complete, practice the lowest-scoring moment; 5 or fewer: review the modules behind the weakest moments.

3.

Answers will vary — this is a personal reflection. A useful answer names three specific skills (for example, "declining a request", "following up a second time", "addressing the General Manager") and gives a concrete reason for each, such as a situation where it went wrong.

assessment.title: Level 2 Assessment
assessment.objectives_html:
• Demonstrate the core communication skill from each of Level 2's 8 modules, tested one at a time.
  • Produce short spoken and written responses that combine two modules' language at once, the way real workplace situations rarely stay inside one lesson's boundary.
  • Self-check readiness for the capstone, "A Normal Week," without rehearsing new material.
assessment.body_html:
About this assessment

Every module since Module 1 ended with its own small assessment. This is different: one sitting, three parts, drawing on all eight modules at once — but unlike the capstone that follows it, each item here stands alone. This assessment checks whether a specific skill was learned; the capstone checks whether all of them can work together across a real, messy week. Sit this first, then move on to the capstone, "A Normal Week."

Nothing here should feel unfamiliar. If an item does feel hard, that's useful information — it names exactly which module is worth a quick review before the capstone.

Part A — Reading: choose the best response (items 1–8)

Read each short workplace situation and choose the most appropriate response. There is one item per module, Module 1 through Module 8. (Audio is not available yet, so this part is read, not heard.)

Part B — Speaking (items 9–16)

Respond aloud to each prompt, and record yourself if you can. There is no single correct wording: each response is scored with the criteria below, and a sample answer is given in the key so you can compare. One prompt per module, Module 1 through Module 8.

Part C — Writing (items 17–20)

Write a short response to each of four scenarios. Each scenario combines two modules' language at once, the same way a real situation rarely announces which lesson it belongs to:

  • Daily Updates + Following Up
  • Requests + Apologizing/Thanking
  • Telephone + Digital Messaging
  • Customer Interaction + Workplace Etiquette

Scoring

Part A: 1 point for each correct answer (8 points).

Parts B and C: score each item from 0 to 3 — one point for each criterion it meets. Only criteria that apply to that kind of task are used:

Criterion (1 point)Part B — speakingPart C — writing
TaskDoes exactly what the prompt asks, using the module's structure (for example done/doing/blocked, or decline + alternative).Completes both parts of the two-module task.
LanguageUses the module's phrases and vocabulary accurately.Same, with correct grammar and spelling.
Tone and deliveryRegister fits the listener; clear and easy to understand, without long hesitation or repeated apologies.Register fits the reader and the channel (chat, email, note); polite and appropriately brief.

Maximum: Part A 8 + Part B 24 + Part C 12 = 44 points.

Passing this assessment

"Two tests down, eight modules covered — the only thing left is a normal week."

Pass mark: 31 of 44 (70%), with at least 5 of 8 in Part A. For any item where you scored 0 or 1, review the module named in the item before the capstone.

Nothing in Parts A–C is new. Every scenario echoes a lesson you've already worked through, from the done/doing/blocked update in Module 1 to the hierarchy-aware address in Module 8. If a particular item feels hard, that module is worth a quick review before moving on to the capstone — but there is nothing new to prepare in order to sit this assessment.
assessment.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 1 — Ms. Noor asks, "Where are we on the linen inventory?" Which response best follows the done/doing/blocked structure?

A.

I did some of it earlier, then got busy with something else.

B.

I've finished the ground floor, I'm working on the upper floors now, and it's held up a little on the storeroom key.

C.

It's basically fine, I'll get to it.

2. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 2 — A colleague asks you to finish a task in twenty minutes that realistically needs about an hour. Which response is the best counter-proposal?

A.

Sure, no problem.

B.

Realistically, I can't finish the whole thing in twenty minutes — what's achievable is the first section by then, with the rest done within the hour.

C.

That's impossible, sorry.

3. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 3 — The front desk phone rings. Which is the correct way to answer and open the call?

A.

Hello?

B.

Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?

C.

Front desk, what do you want?

4. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 4 — You have three unrelated things to tell a colleague in chat: a delivery delay, a question about a key, and a shift-swap request. What is the best approach?

A.

Send one long message covering all three topics at once.

B.

Send three separate messages, each with a signal opener like "Heads up — " or "Quick question — ".

C.

Wait until you happen to see the colleague in person instead of messaging.

5. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 5 — You attached the wrong invoice to a guest email, and a colleague spotted it after it was sent. Which response follows the three-part apology structure?

A.

Oops, sorry about that.

B.

That was on me — I attached the wrong invoice. I've sent the corrected one, and I'll double-check attachments before sending from now on.

C.

It's not a big deal, these things happen.

6. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 6 — You have followed up twice already on a maintenance request with no reply, and the guest arrives tomorrow. Which message correctly matches the escalation ladder's firmer, final stage?

A.

Just checking in on this again, no worries if not.

B.

I still haven't heard back on this, and it's becoming time-sensitive — could you confirm by 5 PM today?

C.

Why hasn't this been done yet?

7. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 7 — A guest asks a question you genuinely don't know the answer to. What is the best response?

A.

I don't know.

B.

Let me check on that and get back to you.

C.

That's not really my department.

8. Multiple Choice Assessment

Module 8 — Dr. Rahman, the General Manager, stops by and asks how the day is going. Which response uses correctly hierarchy-aware, respectful address?

A.

It's going fine, thanks.

B.

Good afternoon, Dr. Rahman — smoothly overall, one small issue this morning but it's already resolved.

C.

Hey, all good, nothing to report!

9. Role-Play Assessment

Module 1 — Give a spoken status update on a real or invented task, using the done/doing/blocked structure, in under 30 seconds.

10. Role-Play Assessment

Module 2 — A colleague asks for a favor you genuinely can't do right now. Decline it and offer a real alternative.

11. Role-Play Assessment

Module 3 — Answer an incoming call, identify yourself, and ask how you can help.

12. Role-Play Assessment

Module 4 — You need to tell a colleague something urgent and separately ask a quick, unrelated question. Say both the way you would type them, clearly separated, with the right signal openers.

13. Role-Play Assessment

Module 5 — Apologize aloud for a small mistake you made, using all three parts of the apology structure: acknowledge, own, prevent.

14. Role-Play Assessment

Module 6 — You haven't heard back on a request you sent two days ago. Follow up politely, without sounding pushy.

15. Role-Play Assessment

Module 7 — A customer asks a simple question and then raises a mild complaint. Respond to both, then close the interaction well.

16. Role-Play Assessment

Module 8 — You're running a few minutes late for a call. Give a proactive heads-up, then close out your day by addressing a senior colleague appropriately.

17. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 1 + 6 — You asked the maintenance team about a broken chair in the staff room three days ago and still haven't heard back. At the same time, your supervisor stops by and asks for today's status update on an unrelated task. Write: (1) a first-stage polite follow-up message to maintenance, and (2) a short spoken-style status update to your supervisor using the done/doing/blocked structure.

18. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 2 + 5 — Last week you asked a colleague to swap a shift with you, and the time you originally gave them turned out to be wrong, causing them a scheduling problem. Write a short message that (1) apologizes for the mistaken timing using the three-part apology structure, and (2) makes a corrected request, offering something in return.

19. Short Answer Assessment

Modules 3 + 4 — A guest calls with a request you can't resolve immediately. You tell them you'll check and call them back. Write the chat message you would then send a colleague, asking for their help, marking the urgency honestly so they know how quickly you need a reply.

20. Writing Assessment

Modules 7 + 8 — A guest complains about a late room cleaning just as Dr. Rahman, the General Manager, happens to be walking past the desk. Write (1) what you'd say to the guest, using the listen-acknowledge-offer structure and a proper closing, and (2) the short, hierarchy-aware line you'd then use to briefly update Dr. Rahman on what happened.

Answer Key

1.

Correct: B. The correct option sorts the update into done/doing/blocked (PAT-0025), using present perfect for the finished part and present continuous for the in-progress part, instead of a vague or unsorted account.

2.

Correct: B. The correct option uses "realistically" and "what's achievable is" (PAT-0029), naming an honest, doable scope instead of overpromising or flatly refusing.

3.

Correct: B. The correct option combines the greeting-and-ID formula (PAT-0030) with an offer to help — the standard professional phone opening from Module 3, Lesson 1.

4.

Correct: B. The correct option follows the one-idea-per-message structure (PAT-0033) — splitting unrelated topics so each one is easy to read and answer on its own.

5.

Correct: B. The correct option acknowledges the specific mistake, takes ownership, and names a concrete prevention step (PAT-0035) — the full three-part apology structure.

6.

Correct: B. The correct option uses PAT-0038's firm-but-respectful final stage: it states the fact plainly, names the real urgency, and asks for a specific, actionable answer.

7.

Correct: B. The correct option pairs honest uncertainty with a concrete next step (PAT-0041), rather than leaving a dead end or deflecting the question.

8.

Correct: B. The correct option uses the title-plus-surname convention (PAT-0045) and gives a genuinely substantive update, matching the register a senior colleague warrants.

9.

Sample: "I've finished the arrivals list for tomorrow. I'm working on the group rooming list now. I'm blocked on the final names from the tour company." Task point: done → doing → blocked, in that order, under 30 seconds. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

10.

Sample: "I'm tied up with the 3 o'clock check-ins, so I can't help with the inventory now. What I can do instead is give you an hour tomorrow morning. Would that work?" Task point: a clear decline, a specific alternative, and "Would that work?" Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

11.

Sample: "Good morning, Front Desk, this is Nadia speaking. How can I help you today?" Task point: greeting + department + name + offer to help. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

12.

Sample: "Heads up — the lift on the east side is out of service, so please send guests to the west lifts." … "Quick question — do you know where the spare key cards are kept?" Task point: two separate messages, each with its signal opener. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

13.

Sample: "I'm sorry — I gave the guest the wrong breakfast times this morning, and she missed breakfast. That's on me. Going forward, I'll check the times on the board before I answer." Task point: acknowledge + own + prevent. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

14.

Sample: "Just following up on the request I sent on Monday for the extra key-card printer ribbon — I wanted to flag it in case it got missed." Task point: a softening opener, the original request named, no blame. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

15.

Sample: "Welcome! … Yes, the pool is open until 9 PM — in other words, you can use it after dinner. Does that answer your question? … I understand your concern — your towels should have been replaced. Let me see what I can do right away. … I'm glad we could sort that out. Is there anything else I can help you with? Have a great stay!" Task point: a plain answer with a check, listen-acknowledge-offer, the full closing formula. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

16.

Sample: "Sorry, I'm running about five minutes behind — I'll join the call at 3:05." … "Good evening, Dr. Rahman — the day went smoothly. One guest's late check-out was sorted with housekeeping." Task point: a proactive heads-up with a time, then title + surname and a short, substantive update. Score 0–3 using the Part B criteria.

17.

Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Sample: (1) "Just following up on the broken chair in the staff room — I wanted to flag it in case it got missed." (2) "I've finished the arrivals check. I'm working on the late check-out list. I'm blocked on two room numbers from housekeeping." Task point: the follow-up opens politely ("just following up on" / "wanted to check in on") without sounding impatient, and the status update is correctly sorted into done/doing/blocked with the right tenses — the two skills kept clearly separate rather than blended together.

18.

Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Sample: "Hi Rina, I'm sorry — I gave you the wrong time for Saturday's swap, and it caused you a clash. That's on me; I'll check the roster before I suggest times from now on. Could we swap your Saturday 2–10 PM shift for my Sunday morning, if that suits you? I can take your Wednesday late in return." Task point: the apology names the specific mistake, takes ownership, and states a prevention step before the corrected request appears; the request itself includes a genuine trade-off ("in return" / "I can cover for you"), not just a bare repeated ask.

19.

Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Sample: "Quick question — does the spa have any free slots this afternoon for Room 410? This is time-sensitive: I promised to call the guest back within 15 minutes." Task point: the message states what's needed in one clear idea, opens with an appropriate signal ("Quick question — " / "Heads up — "), and marks urgency honestly using language like "this is time-sensitive" rather than either false urgency or no urgency marker at all, reflecting the promise already made to the caller.

20.

Score 0–3 (Part C criteria). Sample: (1) "I understand your concern — your room should have been cleaned by now. I appreciate you telling me. Let me ask housekeeping to go up straight away. … Is there anything else I can help you with? Have a lovely afternoon." (2) "Good afternoon, Dr. Rahman — a guest in 312 reported a late room clean; housekeeping is on the way up now." Task point: the guest-facing response acknowledges the complaint before offering help and closes the interaction warmly (CF-0008); the line to Dr. Rahman uses title-plus-surname address and gives a brief, substantive summary rather than either over-explaining or being too casual.

capstone.title: A Normal Week
capstone.objectives_html:
• Carry a realistic multi-day workplace stretch, in English, from Monday's standup to Friday's close, without a script.
  • Draw on structured updates, conditional requests and negotiated timing, phone message-taking, chat urgency triage, apology and specific thanks, a graduated follow-up, basic customer interaction, and hierarchy-aware address — switching between them as the week actually demands, not one module at a time.
  • Self-assess a spoken or role-played performance against a real workplace communication rubric, scaled from a single day to a short working week.
capstone.body_html:
About this capstone

Level 1's capstone compressed everything into a single day. Level 2's doesn't, because Level 2's skills don't live inside a single day the way Level 1's did. A follow-up needs a request that was already made and already gone quiet. A graduated escalation needs time to actually pass between messages. Level 2 gave you eight modules' worth of tools that only make sense across a stretch of days — so this capstone gives you a stretch of days.

This is not a new lesson and not a quiz. It's one continuous simulation — a normal working week, told in eight connected steps — built entirely from language you already know. Nothing below is new. The only new thing is doing it all across a week that doesn't pause to let you catch your breath between one skill and the next.

How it's used: read or perform the eight steps in order, then self-assess using the rubric that follows, then do the same eight steps again yourself — as a full role-play, alone or with a partner. The goal isn't to recognize the right answer. It's to produce your own version of each step, in your own words, under the same conditions a real week gives you: no script, and several things happening at once.

The simulation: a normal week at the front desk

It's an ordinary week, several months into the job. One of the front desk's two keycard encoders has been acting up since last Friday, and Arif has already put in a request to Engineering to replace it — a small, unresolved thread that will keep resurfacing all week, the way real unresolved things do.

Step 1 — Monday: the standup update (Module 1)

9:00 AM, Monday. Ms. Noor does her usual round of the desk before the day gets busy. Arif has three things to report, and — by habit now — sorts them into done, doing, and blocked before he opens his mouth.

Listen & Read
Front desk, 9:00 AM Monday. Ms. Noor does her usual round before the day gets busy.
Ms. Fatima Noor: Morning, Arif — how's everything looking to start the week?
Arif: Morning — I've sorted the schedule mix-up from Friday, so that's done. I'm managing check-ins fine with the one working encoder. It's still blocked on Engineering, though — I put in a request for the second encoder last Friday and haven't heard anything back yet.
Ms. Fatima Noor: Alright, keep me posted on that one.

Step 2 — Monday: a layered, conditional request (Module 2)

Mid-morning, Hasan catches Arif between check-ins with a request that comes with its own strings attached — a condition, a specific reason, and a trade-off offered up front. Arif can't say yes to the exact shape of it, so he negotiates the timing instead of just accepting or refusing outright.

Listen & Read
Front desk, mid-morning Monday. Hasan catches Arif between check-ins.
Hasan: Arif, could you cover the desk for an hour on Wednesday afternoon, if you get a chance? I've got a dentist appointment I can't move. I'll take your Friday closing shift in return.
Arif: Wednesday's tight for me — Ms. Noor's got me on the inventory count most of the afternoon. Realistically, I can do the first forty minutes, two to twenty-to-three. Would that work, with someone else covering the last twenty?
Hasan: That actually works better for me anyway — my appointment's earlier than I thought. Forty minutes is plenty. Thanks, I really owe you one.
Arif: No problem — Friday closing's a fair trade.

Step 3 — Tuesday: a phone message that has to be exactly right (Module 3)

Tuesday morning, the desk phone rings. It's the linen supplier, calling about tomorrow's delivery — and Ms. Noor is in a meeting. Arif takes the message the way Module 3 trained him to: get the detail, repeat it back, confirm it's accurate before hanging up.

Listen & Read
Front desk, Tuesday morning. Ms. Noor is in a meeting when the desk phone rings.
Arif: Good morning, Front Desk, this is Arif speaking. How can I help you today?
Golam (caller): Hi, this is Golam from Bengal Linen Supply — I need to speak to Ms. Noor about tomorrow's delivery.
Arif: She's in a meeting right now — would you like me to take a message?
Golam (caller): Yes, please. Tell her the delivery's moving from 9 AM to 1 PM tomorrow because of a truck issue — and I need her to confirm someone will be here to receive it at 1.
Arif: Let me just repeat that back to make sure I've got it — tomorrow's linen delivery moves from 9 AM to 1 PM because of a truck issue, and you need confirmation someone will be here to receive it at 1. Is that right?
Golam (caller): That's exactly right, thanks.
Arif: I'll pass that along to her as soon as she's out of her meeting.

Step 4 — Tuesday: two chat messages, one genuinely urgent (Module 4)

Twenty minutes later, mid-check-in, Arif's phone buzzes twice in quick succession. One message can wait. The other genuinely can't. Telling the difference — and acting on it in the right order — is the whole point of this step.

Listen & Read
Front desk, Tuesday, about twenty minutes later. Arif is mid-check-in when his phone buzzes twice.
Hasan (chat): Quick question — any chance you know where the spare luggage cart went? No rush, just tidying up the storeroom.
Priyanka (chat): Heads up — there's water coming through the ceiling in 214, right above the bathroom. This is time-sensitive, the guest is still inside.
Arif (chat, to Priyanka): On it — calling Engineering now and getting the guest moved. Thanks for flagging it fast.
Arif (chat, to Hasan): Saw your message — dealing with something urgent in 214 right now, I'll check on the cart once this is sorted.

Step 5 — Wednesday: a mistake, an apology, and real thanks (Module 5)

Wednesday, and the aftermath of Tuesday's leak catches up with Arif: he sent housekeeping the wrong room number in the rush, and Priyanka quietly caught it before it became a real problem. Arif owes her two things now, not one — an apology for the mistake, and specific thanks for the save.

Listen & Read
Front desk, Wednesday. Arif catches up with Priyanka about yesterday's leak in 214.
Arif: Priyanka, when I called housekeeping about moving the guest out of 214 yesterday, I told them to prep 216 — but 216 was already reserved for last night. That was on me, I grabbed the first empty room I saw instead of checking the board. Going forward, I'll check the room board before assigning a replacement room.
Priyanka: I caught it when I saw 216 already flagged, so no harm done — moved them to 219 instead.
Arif: Still, I really appreciate you catching that before housekeeping actually prepped the wrong room — that made a real difference. I owe you one.
Priyanka: Anytime, that's what teammates are for.

Step 6 — Wednesday into Thursday: following up, twice, without becoming pushy (Module 6)

The Engineering request from Monday's standup still hasn't moved. Arif follows up once, gently, on Wednesday afternoon — and when Thursday morning brings no reply and a guest arriving that afternoon who needs a fully working desk, he follows up again, a little firmer, without tipping into rude.

Listen & Read
Team chat with Engineering. First follow-up Wednesday afternoon; second, firmer follow-up Thursday morning after no reply.
Arif (message, Wed 3:30 PM): Hi, just following up on the front-desk keycard encoder request from last Friday — wanted to check in when you get a chance.
Arif (message, Thu 9:15 AM): I still haven't heard back on this, and it's becoming time-sensitive — we have a guest arriving this afternoon and only one working encoder. Could you confirm a timeline by midday today?
Engineering (message, Thu 9:40 AM): Sorry for the delay — the replacement encoder will be with you by 11 AM today.
Arif (message): Appreciate you confirming — thanks for sorting this.

Step 7 — Thursday: a question and a small complaint (Module 7)

Thursday afternoon, a guest steps up to the desk with an easy question — and then, almost as an afterthought, mentions something that isn't actually fine. Arif answers the first part in plain language, then shifts cleanly into listening, acknowledging, and offering help for the second.

Listen & Read
Front desk, Thursday afternoon. A guest steps up with an easy question.
Guest: Hi — quick question, what time does the pool close tonight?
Arif: The pool closes at 10 PM tonight, so you've still got plenty of time.
Guest: Great, thanks. Actually, one more thing — the air conditioning in our room hasn't been cooling properly since last night.
Arif: I understand your concern — that shouldn't have happened, especially overnight. Let me see what I can do to get that fixed for you as soon as possible.
Guest: I'd appreciate that, thank you.
Arif: I'll send maintenance up within the hour. Is there anything else I can help you with?
Guest: No, that's everything, thanks.
Arif: I appreciate you bringing that to my attention — have a great evening.

Step 8 — Friday: running late, and closing the week right (Module 8)

Friday afternoon. Arif is a few minutes behind for a scheduled call with the linen supplier, and gets ahead of it before anyone has to ask where he is. Then, at 5:30, Dr. Rahman — the General Manager — stops by the desk on his way out, and Arif closes the whole week with one clean, respectful update.

Listen & Read
Friday. First, a short message before a 2:00 PM call; then 5:30 PM at the desk as Dr. Rahman heads out.
Arif (message to Golam): Hi Golam, I'm running a few minutes behind for our call — I'll be there shortly, around ten past two if that works.
Golam: No problem, talk soon.
Dr. Rahman: Good evening, Arif — how was the week overall?
Arif: Good evening, Dr. Rahman — a fairly full week, but everything's in a good place now. We had a leak in 214 on Tuesday that's fully resolved, and the front desk's second keycard encoder finally arrived yesterday after a couple of follow-ups with Engineering.
Dr. Rahman: Good to hear you stayed on top of it. Have a good weekend, Arif.
Arif: Thank you, you too.

Why this counts as "Level 2 complete"

Look back at what just happened across five days: eight situations, seven different people and teams, five registers (peer, supervisor, external caller, guest, General Manager), one genuine mistake, one thread that took three separate touches to resolve, and not a single moment where Arif had to stop and think about which module he was in. That's the actual target of Level 2 — not just speaking clearly in the moment, but carrying communication across time: giving an update that sets up a later follow-up, taking a message accurately enough that someone else can act on it without calling back, and knowing the difference between a message that can wait and one that can't. Every phrase Arif used above was taught somewhere across Level 2's eight modules; this week was simply the first time they all had to survive contact with each other.

Self-assessment rubric

Use this rubric to score a recording of yourself performing the eight steps (Practice, below), or to score a partner's performance if you're practicing together. It is the same rubric as the Level 1 capstone. Every row applies here, because the capstone is one continuous spoken role-play.

Score area Weight What "good" looks like
Clarity 15% The message is understandable without excessive repetition or hesitation.
Appropriateness 15% Register matches the audience — peer, supervisor, external caller, guest, or General Manager.
Confidence 10% Delivered without excessive hedging or apologizing.
Listening / response accuracy 20% Responds to what was actually said or asked, not a generic memorized line.
Vocabulary 10% Uses workplace vocabulary and expressions accurately in context.
Tone 15% Neither too casual nor too formal for the situation, including across the follow-up ladder's escalating firmness.
Pronunciation 10% Intelligible; stress and intonation roughly match the taught patterns.
Professional behavior 5% Basic courtesy markers present — thanks, an appropriate close, no dropped threads across the week.

How to score it: give each row a mark from 0 to 4 (0 = not shown, 1 = rarely, 2 = sometimes, 3 = mostly, 4 = consistently). Multiply by the row's weight and divide by 4 — for example, 3 for Clarity gives 15 × 3 ÷ 4 ≈ 11 points. Add the rows for a total out of 100. 70 or more: Level 2 complete. Below 70: repeat the steps that use the modules behind your lowest rows, then perform the whole week again.

Score the whole performance, not each step separately. Read or perform the whole eight-step week once, then score each row for the week as a whole. Someone who handles Step 6's second follow-up firmly and respectfully but stumbles on a word in Step 3 is doing better, overall, than one who never makes a mistake but goes silent the moment something doesn't get answered right away — because Step 6 is closer to what a real working week actually demands.

Practice

  1. Full role-play (the actual capstone task): Perform all eight steps in one continuous sequence spanning the week, either with a partner (or several partners) taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded separately and played back in order. Don't read from this page while performing — glance at the setting line for each step, then produce the conversation yourself, in your own words.
  2. Self-score: Immediately afterward, score your own performance against the rubric above. Be honest rather than generous — the rubric exists to show you where to focus next, not to make you feel good.
  3. Written reflection: In 3–4 sentences, describe the one step you found hardest, and why. Was it a language problem (not knowing the right phrase), a timing problem (judging when to escalate or when to wait), or a confidence problem (knowing the phrase but hesitating to use it)? The fix is different for each.
  4. Repeat once: Perform the full eight steps a second time, focusing only on whichever rubric row scored lowest the first time.

Self-check

  1. Which single unresolved thread from Step 1 resurfaces later in the week, and in which step does it finally get closed?
  2. In Step 4, what tells Arif which of the two chat messages needs his attention first?
  3. In Step 6, what changes between Arif's first follow-up and his second — and what stays exactly the same?
  4. Pick any one step above and rewrite Arif's line in your own words, keeping the same meaning and the same register.

You've completed Level 2

"A normal week isn't eight lessons in a row — it's all eight, arriving whenever they want to."

That's the real marker of finishing Level 2: not that every exchange was perfect, but that a full, ordinary, occasionally-messy working week — updates, requests, a phone message, an urgent chat message, a genuine mistake, a follow-up that took three tries, a guest complaint, and a respectful close with the General Manager — happened entirely in English, and it held together across five days, not just one. Level 3 builds on exactly this foundation: the same kind of real working week, with higher stakes, more formal writing, and the first real client-facing and difficult-conversation demands of the job.
capstone.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Role-Play Assessment

Level 2 capstone task. Perform all eight steps of "A Normal Week" in one continuous sequence spanning the week — with a partner (or several partners) taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded and played back in order. Do not read from the page; produce each line yourself from the setting description alone.

2. Short Answer

Look back at Step 6. Name the two things that stay exactly the same between Arif's first follow-up message and his second, and the one thing that changes.

3. Guided Practice

Write your own Step 9 — one more short situation that could realistically happen the following Monday, continuing directly from where the week left off. Say which earlier Level 2 module's language it would use, the same way each step above is labeled.

Answer Key

1.

What to listen/look for: Completes all eight steps in order, adjusting register correctly for each audience (peer, supervisor, external caller, guest, General Manager), sorts Step 1's update correctly into done/doing/blocked, negotiates a realistic counter-timing in Step 2 rather than a flat yes or no, takes an accurate, confirmed message in Step 3, correctly triages the genuinely urgent chat message ahead of the non-urgent one in Step 4, delivers a complete three-part apology alongside specific thanks in Step 5, escalates firmness appropriately (but never into rudeness) across the two follow-ups in Step 6, closes the customer interaction properly in Step 7, and gives a proactive lateness notice plus a hierarchy-appropriate closing update in Step 8. Score it with the self-assessment rubric above.

2.

Suggested answer: What stays the same: the request itself (the keycard encoder) and the polite, non-accusatory tone — Arif never suggests Engineering is at fault. What changes: the second message states plainly that he still hasn't heard back, names the genuine reason it's now time-sensitive (a guest arriving that afternoon), and asks for a specific, actionable answer by a stated time, instead of the first message's softer, open-ended check-in.

3.

Suggested answer: Example: Monday morning, Ms. Noor asks how the week ended and whether the encoder is now fully working. Arif: "All sorted — the new encoder's been running fine since Thursday, no issues over the weekend." (Module 1 — a short, confident status update closing out the previous week's blocked item before the new week's update begins.)

modules.title: Professional Email Writing
modules.purpose: Write complete professional emails — requests, information, follow-ups, reminders, confirmations, apologies, complaint replies and escalations — and manage a whole email thread.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Professional Email
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify the five parts of a professional email: subject line, greeting, opening, body, and closing.
  • Write a subject line that is specific enough to be understood before the email is even opened.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

A guest's air conditioner has been out for two hours in Room 214, and Arif needs the maintenance vendor to know about it right now. He fires off a quick email and moves on to the next guest at the desk. Two hours later, nobody has replied — because nobody could tell, from the subject line or the message itself, that this needed attention today. The problem was never that Arif didn't write the email. It's that he didn't write it as an email.

Key Workplace Lesson

Every professional email has five working parts, and each one does a different job:

  1. Subject line — tells the reader what's inside and how urgent it is, before they open anything.
  2. Greeting — addresses the reader by name, at the right formality level for your relationship.
  3. Opening line — states the purpose in the first sentence, so the reader isn't guessing.
