Rewrite this assumption-led response using PAT-0084, replacing the pitch with two open questions: "We need something for our annual staff retreat." "Perfect, our All-Inclusive Retreat Package covers everything."

3. Role-Play

A client tells you they need "better customer support software." Using PAT-0084, ask open questions to uncover their real priority before suggesting anything.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Open question: What's prompting the timing — is there a specific milestone you're celebrating? Follow-up: what matters most to you here — the schedule, the budget, or the setup? Confirming: so if I understand correctly, flexible space matters more than a large number of breakout rooms — is that right?

2.

Suggested answer: Happy to help with that. What's prompting the retreat this year — is it tied to a specific goal? And what matters most to you here — the activities, the location, or keeping costs down?

3.

What to listen/look for: The learner asks at least one open question and one confirming question before proposing any solution — avoiding MIS-0113's assumption-led pitch.

lessons.title: Presenting a Solution to a Client
lessons.objectives_html:
• Present a solution that explicitly connects back to a need the client named.
  • Reuse a presentation-explanation skill in a one-on-one client context.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif now knows what Meridian Partners actually needs: flexible, easy-to-navigate space for around sixty people, over three days, without a crowded feel. It would be easy to just list the hotel's conference options. It's far more persuasive to show Ms. Cruz, point by point, exactly how each piece answers what she told him.

Key Workplace Lesson

A solution that simply lists features asks the client to do the work of connecting it to their own situation — and clients rarely do that work for you. A solution that explicitly echoes the client's own words does that connecting for them: "Since you mentioned flexible space matters most, here's how this layout solves that." This is the same explaining-and-connecting skill used in a formal presentation, scaled down to a conversational, one-on-one moment — point, evidence, link back to the need, repeat.

Listen & Read
Arif presents a conference-space option to Ms. Cruz, tying it explicitly back to the flexible, easy-to-navigate space she named as her top priority in Lesson 2.
Arif: So, since you mentioned that flexible, easy-to-navigate space matters most to you, I'd like to suggest the Garden Suite for all three days.
Ms. Cruz: Tell me more about that.
Arif: It's a single open floor with movable partitions rather than separate breakout rooms — here's how this solves that crowded feeling you mentioned. We can open the whole space up between sessions, so people move freely instead of shuttling down a corridor.
Ms. Cruz: That does sound closer to what we need. What about seating for sixty comfortably?
Arif: This addresses that directly too — the Garden Suite comfortably seats up to 120, so sixty gives you plenty of breathing room, even with the partitions in place.
Ms. Cruz: That's actually really helpful — it sounds like you were listening closely to what I said earlier.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Based on what you've told me... Connects the solution explicitly to the stated need Professional
This addresses... States plainly how a feature meets a named need Professional
Here's how this solves that. Plain-language link between solution and problem Professional, confident

Vocabulary

  • based on what you've told me (V-0495) — a connector phrase that ties a proposed solution back to what the client explicitly said. "Based on what you've told me, I'd recommend our Garden Suite — it's a single open floor, so there's no need to move between rooms."
  • this addresses (V-0496) — states directly how a specific feature meets a need the client named. "This layout addresses the concern about feeling cramped — the room seats sixty with space to spare."
  • here's how this solves that (V-0497) — a plain, confident phrase linking the solution back to the client's original problem. "You mentioned attendees moving between sessions — here's how this solves that: everything happens on one floor."

Grammar in Context

Structure (PAT-0085 — Solution-to-Need Connector Structure): [Based on what you've told me / Since you mentioned] + [proposed solution] + [explicit link back to the need: this addresses / here's how this solves that]

"Since you mentioned that flexible, easy-to-navigate space matters most, I'd suggest the Garden Suite for all three days — it's one open floor with movable partitions, so there's no need to shuttle people between separate breakout rooms. This directly addresses the crowded feeling you mentioned, since we can open the space up fully between sessions."

Common Mistake (MIS-0114)

Mistake: Presenting a solution as a generic list of features, without ever tying it back to what the client actually said they needed.

❌ "The Garden Suite has 4,000 square feet, movable partitions, built-in AV, and seats up to 120."

✅ "Since you mentioned flexible, easy-to-navigate space matters most, here's how the Garden Suite solves that: it's one open floor with movable partitions, so nobody has to shuttle between rooms."

Why it matters: A list of features asks the client to translate them into relevance on their own. A solution tied explicitly to their own words does that work for them — and shows they were genuinely heard in Lesson 2's needs-discovery conversation.

Professional Tone

The same solution can sound like a generic sales script or a tailored answer depending entirely on whether it's connected back to the client's own words.

  • ❌ Generic/script-like: "Our premium package includes everything you'd need for a great event."
  • ✅ Tailored/professional: "Since flexible space was your top priority, here's how the Garden Suite addresses that directly..."

Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi business custom, presenting many options generously — even beyond what was asked — can be a way of showing hospitality and effort. In English client-facing contexts, presenting fewer options, each explicitly tied to a stated need, usually reads as more attentive and more professional than presenting many options at once, which can come across as not having listened closely enough to narrow things down.

Industry Overlays

  • Corporate B2B client (software vendor): "Based on what you've told me about your team's remote work schedule, here's how this plan solves that — unlimited seats, no per-user fee."
  • IT (managed services client): "You mentioned downtime being your biggest risk — this addresses that directly, with 24/7 monitoring built into every tier."
  • Tourism (travel consultant): "Since you mentioned wanting a relaxed pace over sightseeing every day, here's how this itinerary solves that — only one activity scheduled per morning."

Self-Check

  1. Why is tying a solution to the client's own words more persuasive than listing features?
  2. Complete the connector structure (PAT-0085): "Based on what you've told me, ___. This addresses ___ because ___."
  3. A client told you cost was their top concern. Present one feature of a solution using PAT-0085.

Motivation

"A solution that echoes the client's own words is more persuasive than a better solution that doesn't."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

In "Since you mentioned that flexible, easy-to-navigate space matters most to you, I'd like to suggest the Garden Suite — here's how this solves that crowded feeling you mentioned," identify the three parts of PAT-0085.

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this generic feature list as a solution tied to a stated need, using PAT-0085. The client said cost was their top concern: "Our premium package includes everything you would need for a great event."

3. Role-Play

A client told you that minimizing disruption to their current system is their top priority. Present one feature of a solution using PAT-0085, tying it explicitly back to that need.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Connector: since you mentioned that flexible space matters most. Solution: I'd like to suggest the Garden Suite. Explicit link: here's how this solves that crowded feeling you mentioned.

2.

Suggested answer: Based on what you've told me about cost being your top concern, here's how this package solves that — it bundles the room, catering, and AV into one flat rate, with no per-person add-ons.

3.

What to listen/look for: The solution is explicitly connected to the client's stated need, not presented as a generic feature list — avoiding MIS-0114.

lessons.title: Handling Client Objections
lessons.objectives_html:
• Respond to a client's objection or hesitation without getting defensive.
  • Avoid over-promising to make an objection go away.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Cruz likes the Garden Suite — but she has a concern. "This looks great, but it's a bit more than we budgeted for a three-day event." How Arif responds in the next ten seconds will either keep the relationship on solid ground or put it on the defensive.

A note on scope: this lesson teaches one honest, calm way to respond to a client's objection — acknowledge it, address it directly, and reassure without over-promising. It is an introduction, not the full skill. Negotiating price, handling multiple objections at once, and persuading a hesitant client are covered in depth later in the course, at Level 4.

Key Workplace Lesson

An objection is information, not an attack — it tells you exactly what's standing between the client and "yes." The two most common ways this goes wrong are getting defensive (explaining, justifying, or subtly implying the client is wrong to have the concern) and over-promising (agreeing to anything, including things you can't actually deliver, just to make the discomfort go away). The steady middle path has three moves: acknowledge the concern as fair, address it directly and honestly, and reassure with something specific you can actually stand behind.

Listen & Read
A
Arif responds to Ms. Cruz's budget concern defensively, then over-promises to end the discomfort (❌).
Ms. Cruz: This looks great, but honestly, it's a bit more than we budgeted for a three-day event.
Arif: Well, our pricing is actually very competitive compared to other venues in the area — this is a great deal when you think about it.
Ms. Cruz: I'm not really asking whether it's a good deal — I'm telling you it's over our budget.
Arif: Don't worry, I can just knock 30% off right now, no problem at all.
Ms. Cruz: That's... a big jump from a moment ago. Now I'm not sure what the real price even is.
B
Arif acknowledges the concern, addresses it honestly, and reassures with something he can actually deliver (✅).
Ms. Cruz: This looks great, but honestly, it's a bit more than we budgeted for a three-day event.
Arif: That's a fair concern — the Garden Suite is on the higher end of our range for three days. Let me address that directly.
Ms. Cruz: Please do.
Arif: The rate includes full AV and setup, which most of our other spaces charge separately. Here's what I can say with confidence — if you can confirm by Friday, I can hold this exact rate and waive the setup fee.
Ms. Cruz: That actually helps a lot — let me take that back to my team and see where we land.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
That's a fair concern. Acknowledges the objection as legitimate Professional, diplomatic
Let me address that directly. Signals an honest, non-evasive response Professional
Here's what I can say with confidence. Gives an honest answer without over-promising Professional, assertive

Vocabulary

  • that's a fair concern (V-0498) — acknowledges a client's objection as legitimate before responding to it. "That's a fair concern — the Garden Suite is on the higher end of our range."
  • let me address that directly (V-0499) — signals an honest, non-evasive response to an objection, rather than a deflection. "Let me address that directly rather than talk around it."
  • here's what I can say with confidence (V-0500) — a phrase for giving an honest, specific answer without over-promising what can't be delivered. "Here's what I can say with confidence: we can hold this rate if you confirm by Friday."

Grammar in Context

Structure (PAT-0086 — Objection Acknowledge-Address-Reassure Structure): [Acknowledge: that's a fair concern] + [address directly and honestly] + [confident, honest reassurance without over-promising: here's what I can say with confidence]

"That's a fair concern — the Garden Suite is on the higher end of our range for a three-day booking. Let me address that directly: the rate includes full AV and setup, which most of our other spaces charge separately. Here's what I can say with confidence — if you can confirm by Friday, I can hold this exact rate and waive the setup fee."

Notice what this is not: it isn't a discount offered on the spot to end the discomfort, and it isn't a defense of why the price is fair. It's an honest answer, backed by something Arif can actually deliver.

Common Mistake (MIS-0115)

Mistake: Responding to an objection defensively (explaining or justifying at length) or by over-promising just to make the objection disappear.

❌ Defensive: "Well, actually, our pricing is very competitive compared to other venues in the area, and honestly this is a great deal when you think about it."

❌ Over-promising: "Don't worry, I can knock 30% off right now, no problem at all."

✅ "That's a fair concern. Let me address that directly — the rate includes full AV and setup. Here's what I can say with confidence: if you confirm by Friday, I can hold this rate and waive the setup fee."

Why it matters: Defensiveness makes the client feel dismissed; over-promising creates expectations that may not survive a manager's sign-off, and damages trust the moment they don't.

Professional Tone

Career English Upgrade Ladder — TL-0008: Responding to a client's cost objection

Situation: the client says the Garden Suite is more than they budgeted for.

  • ❌ Dismissive/defensive: "Well, you get what you pay for — it's worth it."
  • Basic: "I understand. Let me see what I can do."
  • Polite: "I hear you — it is on the higher side. Let me look into some options."
  • Professional / diplomatic (taught rung): "That's a fair concern. Let me address that directly — the rate includes full AV and setup. Here's what I can say with confidence: if you confirm by Friday, I can hold this rate and waive the setup fee."
  • ❌ Over-conceding: "No problem at all, I'll just cut the price by 30% right now."

Why Professional/diplomatic is the taught rung: it validates the concern, gives an honest reason behind the price, and offers a specific, deliverable reassurance — without either dismissing the client's budget reality or promising something Arif isn't authorized to guarantee.

Bengali/Hindi note: in Bengali and Hindi business custom, price is very often negotiated openly and immediately, and a quick concession can be read as generosity and goodwill. In many international client-facing contexts, an immediate, unqualified discount can instead read as a sign the original price wasn't honest in the first place. A calm, honest explanation plus one specific, deliverable reassurance usually builds more trust than an instant price cut.

Industry Overlays

  • Retail (client hesitant about cost): "That's a fair concern. Let me address that directly — this model does cost more, but it comes with a two-year warranty the cheaper option doesn't."
  • Banking (client hesitant about a fee): "That's a fair point to raise. Here's what I can say with confidence: this fee is waived entirely if your average balance stays above the threshold."
  • IT (client hesitant about implementation timeline): "Let me address that directly — a faster rollout is possible, but it would mean less testing time. Here's what I can say with confidence: the current timeline gives us a stable launch with no surprises."

Self-Check

  1. Name the three parts of the Objection Acknowledge-Address-Reassure Structure (PAT-0086).
  2. Why is over-promising as risky as being defensive, even though it feels more agreeable in the moment?
  3. A client says your service is more expensive than a competitor's. Respond using PAT-0086.

Motivation

"An objection is information, not an attack."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

In "That's a fair concern — the Garden Suite is on the higher end of our range. Let me address that directly: the rate includes full AV and setup. Here's what I can say with confidence — if you confirm by Friday, I can hold this rate," identify the acknowledge, address, and reassure parts of PAT-0086.

2. Rewriting

Rewrite this defensive response using PAT-0086: "Well, our pricing is actually very competitive — this is a great deal when you think about it."

3. Role-Play

A client says your service is more expensive than a competitor's. Respond using PAT-0086, without being defensive or over-promising a discount you can't confirm.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Acknowledge: that's a fair concern. Address: let me address that directly — the rate includes full AV and setup. Reassure: here's what I can say with confidence — if you confirm by Friday, I can hold this rate.

2.

Suggested answer: That's a fair concern. Let me address that directly — the price reflects everything included in the package. Here's what I can say with confidence: I can walk you through exactly what's covered so you can compare it fairly.

3.

What to listen/look for: The response acknowledges the concern, addresses it honestly, and offers a specific, deliverable reassurance — avoiding MIS-0115's defensiveness or over-promising.

lessons.title: Closing and Following Up with a Client
lessons.objectives_html:
• Close a client conversation with a specific, agreed next step.
  • Combine welcoming, needs discovery, solution presentation, and objection handling into one connected client meeting.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Cruz has seen the space, had her real need heard, and gotten an honest answer to her budget concern. The meeting has gone well — which is exactly when it's easiest to let it drift to a vague, feel-good ending. This lesson is about finishing the job: leaving with a specific next step, and following up in writing before the day is out.

Key Workplace Lesson

A client meeting isn't finished until both people know what happens next — not "we'll be in touch," but a specific action, owner, and date. This closes the loop the same way Level 3's meetings and email modules taught: state the next step aloud, confirm it, and then put it in writing so nothing depends on memory. A written follow-up email that references the client's own stated needs and the discussed solution shows, one more time, that the client was heard — and gives them something concrete to act on or forward internally.

Listen & Read
The full Meridian Partners client meeting, from welcome through close, with Dr. Rahman (General Manager) joining briefly near the end.
Arif: Ms. Cruz, it's a pleasure to finally meet you — thanks so much for making the time to come in today. I hope your journey here was smooth.
Ms. Cruz: It was, thank you. I'm looking forward to this.
Arif: Wonderful. So, what's prompting the timing for this conference — is there a specific milestone you're celebrating?
Ms. Cruz: It's our regional sales kickoff — around sixty attendees, and flexible space matters most to us. We don't want people feeling boxed into small rooms.
Arif: That's really helpful to know. Based on what you've told me, I'd suggest the Garden Suite for all three days — one open floor with movable partitions, so here's how this solves that crowded feeling you mentioned.
Ms. Cruz: That sounds promising. Honestly, though, it's a bit more than we budgeted for.
Arif: That's a fair concern. Let me address that directly — the rate includes full AV and setup, which most other spaces charge separately. Here's what I can say with confidence — if you confirm by Friday, I can hold this rate and waive the setup fee.
Ms. Cruz: That actually helps a lot.
Dr. Rahman: Ms. Cruz, welcome — I wanted to stop by myself. A booking of this size means a great deal to us, and I want you to know the whole team will be looking after Meridian personally.
Ms. Cruz: That means a lot, Dr. Rahman — thank you.
Arif: So, to confirm the next step — I'll put together a proposal for the Garden Suite at today's rate, holding it until Friday, and send it over by tomorrow morning. I'll follow up in writing with everything we've covered.
Ms. Cruz: Perfect, I'll watch for it.
Arif: It's been a pleasure discussing this with you, Ms. Cruz — I'll be in touch by tomorrow.
Ms. Cruz: Thank you, Arif — looking forward to it.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
So, to confirm the next step... Names a specific, agreed action before closing Professional
I'll follow up in writing by... Commits to a written follow-up with a timeframe Professional
It's been a pleasure discussing this with you. Warm, professional closing line Professional

Communication Formula (CF-0014 — Client-Closing-and-Follow-Up Formula)

Structure: [Confirm the agreed next step aloud, with a specific date/owner] + [commit to a written follow-up, naming a timeframe] + [written follow-up email that ties back to the discussed needs and solution] + [warm, professional close]

"So, to confirm the next step — I'll put together a proposal for the Garden Suite at the rate we discussed, holding it until Friday, and send it over by tomorrow morning. I'll follow up in writing with all the details we've covered today. It's been a pleasure discussing this with you, Ms. Cruz — I'll be in touch by tomorrow."

Follow-up email (same day):

Subject: Meridian Partners Conference — Garden Suite Proposal

Dear Ms. Cruz,

Thank you for taking the time to meet today. As discussed, since flexible, easy-to-navigate space was your top priority, I'm recommending the Garden Suite for all three days of the conference — one open floor with movable partitions, comfortably seating your group of sixty.

Regarding the rate: as mentioned, I can hold today's quoted rate and waive the setup fee if you confirm by this Friday.

I've attached the full proposal for your review. Please let me know if you have any questions — I'm happy to jump on a call at any point.

Best regards,
Arif

Common Mistake (MIS-0116)

Mistake: Ending a client meeting on a vague, feel-good note, without a specific next step, date, or written follow-up.

❌ "Great, well, thanks so much for coming in — we'll be in touch!"

✅ "So, to confirm the next step — I'll send the proposal by tomorrow morning, holding the rate until Friday. I'll follow up in writing with everything we've covered. It's been a pleasure discussing this with you."

Why it matters: "We'll be in touch" commits to nothing and gives the client nothing to act on or forward to their own team. A specific next step, confirmed aloud and then in writing, is what actually moves a client relationship forward.

Professional Tone

Closing a client meeting well isn't about extra warmth at the end — it's about precision wrapped in warmth. "We'll be in touch" is friendly but empty; "I'll send the proposal by tomorrow morning, holding the rate until Friday" is precise and still warm. The professional register for a close names a date, an owner, and a concrete action, every time — diplomatic in tone, exact in content.

Full Connected Client Meeting

This lesson's dialogue chains together every skill from Lessons 1–4 into one client meeting, and brings in Dr. Rahman, the General Manager, for the close — a sign of how much weight this three-day corporate booking carries for the hotel. See the dialogue above for the complete script.

Industry Overlays

  • Hotel (this lesson's main scenario): a corporate events client closes with a held rate and a written proposal, with the General Manager joining the meeting for a high-value booking.
  • Corporate B2B: a software client closes a discovery call with a specific date for a follow-up demo and a written recap email.
  • Banking: a business client closes a loan consultation with a specific date for submitting documents and a written summary of next steps.

Self-Check

  1. Name the four parts of the Client-Closing-and-Follow-Up Formula (CF-0014).
  2. Why does "we'll be in touch" fail to close a client meeting properly, even when said warmly?
  3. Write a closing line for a client meeting using CF-0014, including a specific date and owner.

Practice

  1. Recognition: In the dialogue, identify the moment from each of Lessons 1–4 (welcome, needs discovery, solution, objection) as it appears inside this connected meeting.
  2. Guided: Draft your own version of the follow-up email above for a different client need.
  3. Module 6 assessment: perform the full client-meeting role-play (welcome → needs discovery → solution → objection → close), then write a short follow-up email for the same meeting (see the exercises below).

Motivation

"A client meeting isn't finished until both people know what happens next."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Labeling

In the full dialogue, identify which lines come from Lesson 6.1 (welcome), 6.2 (needs discovery), 6.3 (solution), 6.4 (objection handling), and 6.5 (close).

2. Role-Play

Module 6 assessment. Perform a full client-meeting role-play with a partner, covering all five stages in order: welcome and rapport (PAT-0083), needs discovery (PAT-0084), presenting a solution (PAT-0085), handling one objection (PAT-0086), and closing with a specific next step (CF-0014). Then write a short follow-up email for the same meeting, referencing the client's stated need and the agreed next step.

3. Writing

Write the written follow-up email described in CF-0014 for your own role-play in Exercise 2, including a subject line, a reference to the client's stated need, the agreed rate/next step, and a professional close.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: 6.1: it's a pleasure to finally meet you. 6.2: what's prompting the timing. 6.3: based on what you've told me, I'd suggest the Garden Suite. 6.4: that's a fair concern — let me address that directly. 6.5: so, to confirm the next step — I'll send a proposal by tomorrow morning.

2.

Score 0–6: one point for each of the five meeting stages, plus one for a follow-up email that names the client's need and the agreed next step. Pass at 5. What to listen/look for: The role-play moves cleanly through all five stages without skipping any, the objection is handled without defensiveness or over-promising (MIS-0115), the close names a specific next step and date rather than a vague "we'll be in touch" (MIS-0116), and the follow-up email ties back to the client's stated need and the discussed solution.

3.

What to listen/look for: The email includes a specific subject line, ties back to the client's stated need and the presented solution, states the agreed next step with a date, and closes professionally.

modules.title: Professional Grammar in Context
modules.purpose: Correct the grammar that most often breaks in workplace writing — tenses, modals and conditionals, the passive and reported speech, articles and prepositions, relative clauses and comparatives — using real documents.

lessons.title: Tenses and Aspect for Professional Writing
lessons.objectives_html:
• Choose the correct tense/aspect for a status report or email, especially present perfect vs. simple past.
  • Correct a document that mixes tenses inconsistently.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif is finishing his weekly report for Ms. Noor before he sends it. He reads it back once and something feels slightly off, even though every sentence looks grammatically fine on its own. The problem isn't a single wrong word — it's that his tenses keep sliding between "this happened at a finished time in the past" and "this is connected to now." A reader can feel that inconsistency even when they can't name it.

Key Workplace Lesson

Professional writing almost always needs to answer one quiet question for the reader: is this part of a finished past, or is it connected to now? English answers that with two forms, and mixing them up is one of the most common accuracy problems in workplace writing: the past simple and the present perfect.

The past simple (we completed, I sent, the team finished) places an action in a finished time: it happened then, and that time is over — usually with a time expression that says or implies when (yesterday, on Monday, last week, in Q2).

The present perfect (we have completed, I have sent, the team has finished) connects the past to now. It is not only for things that are still going on — it is very often used for actions that are complete:

  • a completed action whose result matters now: "I've sent the invoice" (so it's done — you don't need to chase me);
  • an action at an unstated time up to now: "We've completed three audits this year";
  • a situation or series that continues up to now: "We've completed 60% of the follow-up items so far."

So the key question is not "finished or unfinished?" but "finished time, or connected to now?" The two forms aren't interchangeable, and a careful reader notices when they're swapped.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reads Arif's weekly report draft aloud and points out that the tenses don't match up (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, read this line back to me: "We have finished the audit last Tuesday and we complete 60% of the follow-up items." Does that sound right to you?
Arif: Hmm — it sounds a little off, but I'm not sure why.
Ms. Noor: "Last Tuesday" is a specific, finished time, so that part needs simple past. And the 60% is a result up to now — "so far", the work isn't finished — so that part needs present perfect. Try it again.
B
Arif corrects the sentence, now matching each tense to what it actually describes (✅).
Arif: Okay — "We finished the audit last Tuesday, and we have completed 60% of the follow-up items so far."
Ms. Noor: That's it exactly. Now I know the audit is closed, and the follow-up is still in progress.
Arif: That makes sense — I was just picking whichever tense sounded natural, not thinking about whether it was actually finished or not.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
We completed [task] on [date]. Reports a finished action at a specific past time Professional
We have completed [task] so far. Reports an ongoing or unspecified-time result, still relevant now Professional
As of this morning, we have not yet received... Marks an unfinished situation still open at the time of writing Professional

Vocabulary

No new vocabulary items in this lesson — this lesson applies present perfect and simple past, both already introduced in Level 1 (Lesson 1.2), to full professional writing rather than teaching new terms.

Grammar in Context: Present Perfect vs. Simple Past in Status Writing (GIC-0007)

Structure:

  • Use the past simple for an action at a finished, stated (or clearly understood) time: a date, a day, "last week", "yesterday", "in Q2". Never combine the present perfect with these expressions.
  • Use the present perfect when the action is connected to now: a completed action whose result matters now ("I've sent the invoice"), an action at an unstated time up to now ("We've completed three audits this year"), or a situation that continues up to now (with so far, since, for, yet, already). This is why a report's opening summary — where things stand as of today — often uses it.
  • In American English the past simple is also common with just, already and yet ("I already sent it"); in a formal report, the present perfect is the safer choice.

Formula: [finished, stated time] → past simple. [connected to now: present result / unstated time / up to now] → have/has + past participle.

Worked example — before and after:

❌ Mixed and confusing: "We have finished the audit last Tuesday and we complete 60% of the follow-up items."

✅ Corrected: "We finished the audit last Tuesday, and we have completed 60% of the follow-up items so far."

Notice what changed: "last Tuesday" is a specific, finished time, so it needs simple past (finished, not have finished). "So far" connects the result to now, so it needs present perfect (have completed, not complete or completed).

Common Mistake (MIS-0119)

Mistake: Using the present perfect with a finished-time expression (have finished … last Tuesday), or using the past simple with an expression that runs up to now (since then, so far).

❌ "We have completed the client handover last week, and since then the new team used the system every day."

✅ "We completed the client handover last week, and since then the new team has used the system every day."

Why it matters: A reader uses your tense choice to place events in time: closed and dated, or connected to now. A mismatch makes the timeline harder to follow — and "have completed … last week" is simply ungrammatical in standard English.

Bengali/Hindi support

Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi both have perfect forms (করেছি, किया है), but they combine freely with a finished time: "আমি গতকাল পাঠিয়েছি" and "मैंने कल भेज दिया है" are natural. Translated directly, they give "I have sent it yesterday", which is wrong in English. Before writing a report sentence, ask: is there a finished time in this sentence (yesterday, last week, on Monday)? If yes, use the past simple.

Industry Overlays

  • IT / operations: "The server crashed on Monday" (closed, specific time) vs. "We have not yet identified the root cause" (still open, right now).
  • Banking: "The account was flagged last week" (closed, specific time) vs. "The compliance team has reviewed 70% of flagged accounts" (ongoing, unspecified time, still relevant).

Self-Check

  1. In one sentence, explain the difference in meaning — not just form — between simple past and present perfect.
  2. Correct this sentence: "I have sent the invoice yesterday, but the client didn't confirmed receipt yet."
  3. Write one status-report sentence using simple past and one using present perfect, about a task from your own work.

Motivation

"The right tense tells the reader exactly when something matters, not just that it happened."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Read this sentence: "We have completed the client handover last week, and the new team started using the system." Which verb is in the wrong tense, and why, according to GIC-0007?

2. Rewriting

Correct this sentence using GIC-0007: "I have sent the invoice yesterday, but the client didn't confirmed receipt yet."

3. Guided Practice

Write two sentences about a task from your own work: one describing something finished at a specific past time (simple past), and one describing something still ongoing or unspecified in time (present perfect).

Answer Key

1.

Only "have completed" is wrong: it is paired with "last week", a finished time, so it needs the past simple — "We completed the client handover last week." "The new team started using the system" is correct: starting is a single past event. (If you want to stress that they are still using it, you could add "and has used it every day since", but that is an addition, not a correction.)

2.

"I sent the invoice yesterday, but the client has not confirmed receipt yet." (Also note "didn't confirmed" → after did/didn't the verb is the base form; in American English "the client didn't confirm receipt yet" is also common.)

3.

Sample: "We restocked the minibars on Monday." / "We have restocked 40 of the 60 minibars so far." Check: the past simple sentence has a finished time; the present perfect sentence has no finished time and is connected to now.

lessons.title: Modals and Conditionals for Professional Nuance
lessons.objectives_html:
• Use modals to soften or hedge a written statement appropriately.
  • Use a conditional to describe a hypothetical professional situation clearly.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif is writing the risk section of a project update for Ms. Noor. His first draft says: "This will fail." It's honest, and it's exactly what he's worried about — but written down like that, it reads less like a careful warning and more like an alarm bell. Ms. Noor asks him to say the same thing, just as clearly, without sounding like he's already given up on it.

Key Workplace Lesson

In professional writing, sounding certain and sounding useful aren't always the same thing. "This will fail" claims a certainty you probably don't actually have — and it gives the reader nothing to act on. A hedge — a modal verb like could, might, or may want to — keeps the honesty of the warning while leaving room for exactly what the reader needs: a condition they can still change. And a conditional ("if we don't... / unless we...") does the other half of the job — it names precisely what that condition is.

Used together, a modal and a conditional turn a flat, alarming claim into a specific, actionable one: not just "this is a problem," but "this is a problem if a particular thing does or doesn't happen" — which is exactly the information a manager or client needs to make a decision.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reads Arif's risk note and asks him to soften the blunt, unhedged claim (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, your risk section just says "This will fail." What exactly do you mean by that?
Arif: I mean the rollout is going to fail if we keep the current timeline — I just wrote it quickly.
Ms. Noor: Then say that — the condition matters. Right now it just sounds like a verdict, with nothing anyone can do about it.
B
Arif rewrites the claim as a hedged, conditional statement (✅).
Arif: "This could fail unless we address the staffing gap before the next phase."
Ms. Noor: Much better — now I know exactly what would prevent it. That's something I can actually act on.
Arif: Right — I was so focused on sounding honest that I forgot to make it useful too.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
This could fail unless... Hedges a risk while staying specific Professional
We may want to reconsider the timeline. Softens a recommendation Diplomatic
If we don't [action], [consequence] will likely happen. States a hypothetical clearly Professional

Vocabulary

  • hedge (verb) (V-0519) — to soften a statement so it sounds less absolute, while keeping it clear and useful. "Instead of stating it as a certainty, hedge it with a modal like 'could' or 'might.'"

Grammar in Context: Modal Softeners for Written Hedging (GIC-0008)

Structure: [Subject] + could / might / may want to + [verb] — instead of a flat claim with will or is/are.

Formula: Blunt claim → This will fail. Hedged, professional version → This could fail to succeed unless we address the staffing gap.

Hedging isn't about being vague or avoiding responsibility — it's about matching your language to your actual level of certainty, and leaving the reader a specific condition to act on instead of just a verdict.

Grammar in Context: Conditionals for Professional Hypotheticals (GIC-0009)

Structure: If + [condition, present simple], + [result, will/modal]. Or: Unless + [condition], + [result, will/modal].

Worked example:

"If we don't add a second server, the system will likely fail under peak load."

"Unless we add a second server, the system may struggle under peak load."

Both sentences name the exact same risk — but now the reader knows precisely what would prevent it, which is far more useful than a flat prediction.

Common Mistake (MIS-0120)

Mistake: Writing an unhedged, absolute claim in a risk note or recommendation, instead of a modal-softened statement paired with the specific condition that would change the outcome.

❌ "This will fail."

✅ "This could fail unless we address the staffing gap before the next phase."

Why it matters: An absolute claim without a condition attached gives the reader a verdict, not a decision to make. A hedged statement with a clear "unless" or "if" gives them something they can actually act on.

Professional Tone

A hedge is not the same as being unsure of yourself. "This could fail unless we act" is a confident, precise statement — it's just precise about conditions, not about pretending to know the future with certainty you don't have. In a real workplace, overconfident absolute claims ("this will definitely work," "this will definitely fail") are usually trusted less over time than careful, conditional ones, because they're wrong more often.

Industry Overlays

  • Sales: "The client may want to revisit pricing unless we can confirm the volume discount by Friday."
  • Healthcare administration: "Patient wait times could increase unless we add a second intake desk during peak hours."

Self-Check

  1. Rewrite in your own words: what does hedging a statement actually accomplish for the reader?
  2. Turn this blunt claim into a hedged, conditional one: "The deadline is impossible."
  3. Write one sentence using a modal softener and one using an "unless" conditional, about a real risk in your own work.

Motivation

"A hedge, well placed, is honesty about uncertainty — not weakness."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

In "This could fail unless we address the staffing gap," identify the modal softener (GIC-0008) and the conditional (GIC-0009), and explain what each one is doing.

2. Rewriting

Using GIC-0008 and GIC-0009, rewrite this blunt claim as a hedged, conditional statement: "The deadline is impossible."

3. Guided Practice

Write one sentence about a real risk in your own work, using a modal softener (GIC-0008) and an "if" or "unless" conditional (GIC-0009) together.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: Modal softener: "could fail" — hedges the claim instead of stating it as a certainty. Conditional: "unless we address the staffing gap" — names the specific condition that would change the outcome.

2.

Suggested answer: "The deadline could be difficult to meet unless we get the design assets by Wednesday."

3.

Sample: "We may miss the Friday deadline unless the new linen supplier confirms delivery by Wednesday." Check: a modal (may/might/could) instead of will, and a specific condition with if or unless.

lessons.title: Passive Voice and Reported Speech in Professional Documents
lessons.objectives_html:
• Recognize when passive voice reads more professional than active voice in a report.
  • Use reported speech correctly to summarize what someone said in writing.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif is writing an incident report about a shipment that went out late. His first instinct is to write exactly what happened, in the order he remembers it — including who was responsible. Ms. Noor reads it and points something out: a report's job is to record what happened, not to assign blame sentence by sentence. The same facts can be written in a way that stays focused on the event, not the person.

Key Workplace Lesson

Passive voice — putting the thing affected first, and leaving out or moving the person who acted — isn't weak or evasive writing. In a report, it is often the more professional choice, because it keeps the focus on the event and its impact, especially before responsibility has been established. "Hasan delayed the shipment" names a person, which in an incident report can read as an accusation; "The shipment was delayed" reports the same event without naming anyone.

Notice what the passive does not do: it doesn't change the facts. "The shipment was delayed due to a supplier issue" is not the passive of "Hasan delayed the shipment" — it states a different cause. Only add a cause you have confirmed.

Reported speech solves a different problem: summarizing what someone said, in writing, after the fact. With a past reporting verb (said, told, mentioned), the tense often moves one step back (a "backshift"): "I need it" → "he said he needed it". The backshift is not compulsory: if what was said is still true or still in the future, you can keep the original tense ("he said he needs it by Friday"). But time words and pronouns must always fit the moment you are writing.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reviews Arif's incident-report draft, which reads as blame-focused rather than objective (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, your draft says "Hasan delayed the shipment." Is that actually what we know, or is that what you think happened?
Arif: It's what happened, as far as I know — but I see what you mean, it does sound like I'm pointing a finger.
Ms. Noor: Right — for now, let's report the event and the cause, not the person. We can follow up on responsibility separately if we need to.
B
Arif rewrites the sentence in passive voice, and then summarizes a related phone update using reported speech (✅).
Arif: "The shipment was delayed by two days." I'll add the cause once it's confirmed. And when Dr. Rahman called about it, he said, "I need this resolved by Friday" — so in the report I'll write: "Dr. Rahman said that he needed it resolved by Friday."
Ms. Noor: That's it — objective, accurate, and it still tells the reader exactly what's expected.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
The shipment was delayed due to... Reports an event without assigning blame Objective
It was noted that... / It has been confirmed that... Reports a finding neutrally Formal
Dr. Rahman said (that) he needed the figures by Friday. Summarizes what someone said, in writing Professional

Vocabulary

No new vocabulary items in this lesson — this lesson applies passive voice and reported speech, both introduced earlier in the course (passive voice implicitly through report language; reported speech first touched in Level 2, Lesson 2.4), to full written professional register.

Grammar in Context: Passive Voice for Objective Reporting (GIC-0010)

Structure: [Thing affected] + was/were + [past participle] (+ by + agent, only if the agent genuinely matters).

Worked example:

Active: "Hasan delayed the shipment." → Passive: "The shipment was delayed." (or "…was delayed by Hasan" if the person matters)

The facts stay the same; only the focus changes. If you know the cause, add it as a separate, checkable fact: "The shipment was delayed because the customs paperwork arrived late."

Use passive voice when the event or its result is what the reader needs to know, and naming who did it either isn't relevant yet or isn't the point of the report. Use active voice when the person genuinely matters — for example, when recommending who should fix it.

Grammar in Context: Reported Speech Tense Shifts (GIC-0011)

Structure: [Reporting verb: said / told / mentioned] + (that) + [subject] + [verb — usually backshifted one step].

Worked example:

Direct speech (Monday): Dr. Rahman said, "I need the numbers by Friday."

Reported on Wednesday: "Dr. Rahman said (that) he needed / needs the numbers by Friday." Both are correct: Friday is still ahead, so the present tense is also possible.

Reported the following week: "Dr. Rahman said that he needed the numbers by that Friday." The deadline has passed, so the backshift is needed.

Common backshifts: need → needed, will → would, can → could, is/are → was/were, have/has → had. Time words: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before.

Common Mistake (MIS-0121)

Mistake: Copying the original speaker's time words into a report written later, so they now point to the wrong day.

❌ (Written on Friday, about something Priyanka said on Monday) "Priyanka said she can finish the draft tomorrow."

✅ "Priyanka said (on Monday) that she could finish the draft the next day."

Why it matters: "Tomorrow" in a report written on Friday means Saturday — the reader gets the wrong date. Backshift the tense when the situation is over, and always update time words to fit the moment you are writing. (If you are reporting on the same day, "She said she can finish it tomorrow" is perfectly correct.)

Professional Tone

Passive voice earns a bad reputation because it's sometimes used to dodge responsibility entirely — "mistakes were made" with no follow-up. That's a real risk, not a grammar problem: a good report still names a cause and a next step, even when it uses passive voice for the event itself. "The shipment was delayed due to a supplier issue, and we are contacting the supplier today" is objective and accountable at the same time.

Industry Overlays

  • Retail: "The wrong item was shipped to the customer, and a replacement has been arranged."
  • Banking: "The client mentioned that she had already submitted the documents the previous week."

Self-Check

  1. In your own words, explain when passive voice is the more professional choice in a report.
  2. Rewrite in reported speech: Priyanka said, "I can finish the draft by tomorrow."
  3. Write one sentence describing a workplace event in passive voice, focused on the event, not the person.

Motivation

"Passive voice isn't weak writing — sometimes it's the more honest choice."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Compare "Hasan delayed the shipment" with "The shipment was delayed." Using GIC-0010, explain which one is more appropriate for an objective incident report, and why.

2. Rewriting

Using GIC-0011, rewrite this direct quote as reported speech in a written report: Priyanka said, "I can finish the draft by tomorrow."

3. Guided Practice

Write one sentence describing a real workplace event in passive voice (GIC-0010), and one sentence summarizing something a colleague said to you, in reported speech (GIC-0011).

Answer Key

1.

The passive version ("The shipment was delayed.") is more appropriate for an objective incident report, because it reports the same event without naming a person before responsibility is confirmed. It does not change the facts — if the cause is known, add it as a separate, checkable statement.

2.

"Priyanka said (that) she could finish the draft by the next day." (If you are writing on the same day she said it, "Priyanka said she can finish the draft by tomorrow" is also correct.)

3.

Sample: "Two room keys were reported missing at 6 PM." / "Rupa said that housekeeping would check the lost-property log." Check: the passive keeps the facts of the active sentence; the reported verb and any time words fit the moment of writing.

lessons.title: Articles, Prepositions, and Subject-Verb Agreement in Practice
lessons.objectives_html:
• Correct common article and preposition errors in professional writing.
  • Catch subject-verb agreement errors that undercut credibility.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif's email to a vendor is clear, polite, and gets the point across — but it has a handful of small errors: a missing "the," a wrong preposition, a verb that doesn't quite match its subject. None of them stop the vendor from understanding him. But Ms. Noor points out that a careful reader notices exactly these small things, and they quietly affect how professional the whole email feels, even when the meaning is perfectly clear.

Key Workplace Lesson

Three small grammar areas cause a disproportionate number of the "little" errors that undercut otherwise strong professional writing: articles (a, an, the), prepositions (small connecting words like for, on, at), and subject-verb agreement (making sure the verb matches its true subject). None of these change the meaning of a sentence much on their own — but they're exactly the kind of error a careful, native-English reader notices first, because they're small enough to stand out against otherwise correct writing.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reads Arif's vendor email line by line and flags the small article, preposition, and agreement errors (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, three small things here. "I attached invoice for your review" — which invoice?
Arif: Oh — the one from last week's order. I should say "the invoice."
Ms. Noor: Right. And further down: "I'm responsible of the inventory" — and "The number of complaints have gone up this month."
B
Arif corrects each line, applying the article, preposition, and agreement rules (✅).
Arif: Let me fix all three: "I've attached the invoice for your review." "I'm responsible for the inventory." And "The number of complaints has gone up this month" — because the real subject is "number," not "complaints."
Ms. Noor: Exactly. None of these changed what you meant — but now it reads like it was written by someone paying close attention.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Please find the attached invoice. Correct article use for something specific Professional
I'm responsible for the inventory. Correct fixed preposition Professional
The list of items is missing two entries. Correct agreement with the true subject Professional

Vocabulary

  • subject-verb agreement (V-0520) — the rule that a verb must match its true grammatical subject in number, not the noun that happens to sit closest to it. "Check subject-verb agreement carefully whenever a sentence has a long phrase between the subject and the verb."

Grammar in Context: Articles in Professional Writing (GIC-0012)

Structure: "the" = something specific, already known to the reader. "a/an" = one item from a general group, not yet specified. No article = a general or plural statement.

Worked example:

❌ "I attached invoice for your review."

✅ "I've attached the invoice for your review." (specific — the reader knows which one)

✅ "I need a quote for new office supplies." (general — not yet chosen or specified)

Grammar in Context: Fixed Preposition Pairings (GIC-0013)

Structure: Some pairings are fixed — learn them as one unit: responsible for, depend on, consist of, comply with, apologize (to someone) for (something).

Others change with the meaning, so learn the meaning with the preposition:

  • arrive at a building or point (arrive at the hotel, at the airport, at a decision); arrive in a city or country (arrive in Dhaka, in Delhi). Never "arrive to".
  • agree with a person or an opinion (I agree with Ms. Noor); agree on a decision or point you settle together (we agreed on the launch date); agree to a proposal or request, or + verb (she agreed to the new rate; he agreed to help).

❌ "I'm responsible of the inventory." → ✅ "I'm responsible for the inventory."

❌ "The guests arrived to Dhaka at 6." → ✅ "The guests arrived in Dhaka at 6."

Grammar in Context: Subject-Verb Agreement with Tricky Subjects (GIC-0014)

Structure: The verb must match the true subject of the sentence — not the noun sitting closest to it, which is often a different word entirely in a longer sentence.

Worked example:

❌ "The list of complaints are growing."

✅ "The list of complaints is growing." (the true subject is "list," singular — not "complaints")

With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it: "Neither the manager nor the staff members are available today."

Common Mistake (MIS-0122)

Mistake: Matching the verb to the nearest noun in the sentence instead of the true subject, especially when a longer phrase sits between the subject and its verb.

❌ "The number of complaints have gone up this month."

✅ "The number of complaints has gone up this month."

Contrast: a number of means "several", so it takes a plural verb: "A number of guests have complained." The number of is singular: "The number of complaints has gone up."

Why it matters: This is one of the errors that sounds fine when spoken quickly, but stands out clearly in writing, where the reader has time to check it.

Bengali/Hindi support

Bengali/Hindi note: Bengali and Hindi grammar don't use articles the way English does, so this is often the single most persistent accuracy gap for Bengali- and Hindi-speaking writers — not a small detail, but a genuinely different grammatical habit to build. It's worth naming plainly rather than glossing over: expect this to take real, repeated practice, and expect to still miss a few articles even at an advanced level. That's normal, and it rarely affects whether the reader understands you.

Industry Overlays

  • Hospitality: "The guest is responsible for any damage to the room" (correct preposition); "The front desk team is short-staffed today" (correct agreement — "team" is singular; in British English "the team are" is also possible).
  • IT: "I'll comply with the new security policy starting Monday" (correct preposition).

Self-Check

  1. Correct: "I sent report to a manager yesterday, but she hasn't reviewed it."
  2. Correct: "Neither the client nor their lawyers has responded yet." (Check which subject the verb should agree with.)
  3. Write one sentence using a fixed preposition pairing from this lesson, applied to your own work.

Motivation

"Small errors are the ones a careful reader notices most."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Read: "The number of complaints have gone up this month." Using GIC-0014, identify the true grammatical subject and explain why the verb is wrong.

2. Rewriting

Using GIC-0012 and GIC-0013, correct this sentence: "I sent report to a manager yesterday, but she hasn't reviewed it, and I'm not responsible of the delay."

3. Guided Practice

Write three sentences about your own work: one using "the" correctly for something specific, one using a fixed preposition pairing (GIC-0013), and one with a subject-verb agreement that a careful reader would check twice (GIC-0014).

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: The true subject is "number" (singular), not "complaints" (the nearest noun, but not the subject). The verb should be "has," not "have."

2.

Suggested answer: "I sent the report to the manager yesterday, but she hasn't reviewed it, and I'm not responsible for the delay."

3.

Sample: "The guest in 305 has paid the deposit." / "We agreed on a new check-in time with the tour group." / "Each of the new trainees has completed the fire-safety course." Check: the article fits something specific, the preposition fits the meaning, and the verb agrees with the true subject.

lessons.title: Relative Clauses, Gerunds, and Infinitives for Fluent Writing
lessons.objectives_html:
• Combine two short, choppy sentences into one fluent sentence using a relative clause.
  • Choose correctly between a gerund and an infinitive after a given verb.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Arif's monthly report is accurate, but it reads like a list: short sentence, full stop. Short sentence, full stop. Ms. Noor points out that every fact is correct, but the writing feels choppy — like reading someone's notes instead of a finished report. The fix isn't longer sentences for their own sake. It's connecting ideas that actually belong together.

Key Workplace Lesson

A relative clause — built with who, which, or that — lets you attach extra information about a noun directly onto the sentence that introduces it, instead of starting a brand-new sentence for it. Two short, choppy facts become one smooth one.

Separately, many English verbs are followed by either a gerund (the -ing form, like avoiding) or an infinitive (to + verb, like to avoid) — and which one is correct depends entirely on the specific verb before it, not on logic. This has to be learned verb by verb, the same way you'd learn a fixed preposition pairing.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reads Arif's choppy report draft and points out the short, disconnected sentences (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, listen to this: "We received a complaint. The complaint was about a late delivery. We resolved it the same day." Every fact is right, but it reads like three separate notes.
Arif: I see what you mean — it does sound a bit flat, like a list.
Ms. Noor: Try connecting the ideas that actually belong together, using "which" or "that."
B
Arif combines the choppy sentences into one fluent sentence using a relative clause (✅).
Arif: "We received a complaint about a late delivery, which we resolved the same day."
Ms. Noor: Much better — now the reader sees how those facts connect, instead of having to connect them for themselves.
Arif: I'll go back through the rest of the report and look for other places I can do that.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
...which was resolved the same day. Adds information smoothly with a relative clause Fluent, professional
We decided to extend the deadline. Correct infinitive pattern after "decide" Professional
We should avoid missing the deadline again. Correct gerund pattern after "avoid" Professional

Vocabulary

  • relative clause (V-0521) — a clause that adds information about a noun using who, which, or that, without starting a new sentence. "Combine those two sentences into one using a relative clause."

Grammar in Context: Relative Clauses for Combining Ideas (GIC-0015)

Structure: [Sentence 1, with the noun to describe] + who/which/that + [information from Sentence 2].

Worked example:

❌ Choppy: "We received a complaint. The complaint was about a late delivery."

✅ Combined: "We received a complaint that was about a late delivery." Or, smoother still: "We received a complaint about a late delivery, which we resolved the same day."

Two kinds of relative clause:

  • Defining (no commas) — tells you which person or thing: "The guest who called this morning…", "The complaint that came in on Monday…". Use who (or that) for people and that or which for things; that is more common, especially in American English. When the pronoun is the object, you can leave it out: "the report (that) you sent".
  • Non-defining (with commas) — adds extra information about something already identified: "Mr. Chen, who booked a river-view room, …", "Our new booking system, which went live in May, …". Use who or which — never that.

Which can also refer back to a whole idea: "The delivery was late, which upset the guest."

Grammar in Context: Gerund vs. Infinitive Patterns (GIC-0016)

Structure: [Verb] + gerund (-ing) or [Verb] + infinitive (to + verb) — fixed by the verb itself; memorize each verb's pattern.

Gerund verbs (a few common ones): avoid, consider, suggest, finish, enjoy — "We should avoid missing the deadline again."

Infinitive verbs (a few common ones): decide, plan, agree, offer, want, need — "We decided to extend the deadline."

Common Mistake (MIS-0123)

Mistake: Using the wrong form — gerund instead of infinitive, or infinitive instead of gerund — after a verb with a fixed pattern.

❌ "We decided postponing the meeting." / "We should avoid to miss the deadline."

✅ "We decided to postpone the meeting." / "We should avoid missing the deadline."

Why it matters: There's no shortcut rule for this — it has to be learned verb by verb, the same way vocabulary is learned. Getting it wrong doesn't usually block understanding, but it's a clear, noticeable sign of non-native writing to a careful reader.

Professional Tone

Combining sentences with a relative clause isn't about sounding more complicated — it's about showing the reader how two facts relate to each other, instead of leaving them to work it out. "We received a complaint. It was resolved the same day." makes the reader connect the two ideas themselves. "We received a complaint, which was resolved the same day," does that work for them.

Industry Overlays

  • Education administration: "The parent who called this morning has already been contacted by the office."
  • Tourism: "We should avoid overbooking the tour again, and we agreed to add a confirmation step before every booking."

Self-Check

  1. Combine using a relative clause: "The client sent an email. The email asked for a refund."
  2. Correct: "We suggest to review the contract before signing."
  3. Write one sentence using a relative clause and one using a correct gerund or infinitive pattern, about your own work.

Motivation

"Fluent writing isn't longer sentences — it's better-connected ones."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

Compare "We received a complaint. The complaint was about a late delivery." with "We received a complaint that was about a late delivery." Using GIC-0015, explain what changed and why the second version reads more fluently.

2. Rewriting

Using GIC-0015 and GIC-0016, correct this sentence: "We suggest to review the contract before signing. The client sent an email. The email asked for a refund."

3. Guided Practice

Write one sentence about your own work using a relative clause (GIC-0015) to combine two ideas, and one sentence using a correct gerund or infinitive pattern (GIC-0016).

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: The two short sentences are combined into one using the relative clause "that was about a late delivery," attached directly to "complaint." This shows the reader how the two facts connect instead of leaving them as two separate, disconnected statements.

2.

"We suggest reviewing the contract before signing. The client sent an email that (or which) asked for a refund." (Even shorter: "…an email asking for a refund.")

3.

Sample: "The guest who lost her passport has been given a temporary letter." / "We agreed to send the replacement key by courier." Check: the relative clause has the right pronoun and punctuation; the verb is followed by the correct form (agree + to-infinitive, avoid + -ing).

lessons.title: Comparatives and Formal Sentence Structures
lessons.objectives_html:
• Compare two figures or options grammatically correctly in writing.
  • Combine the module's full grammar toolkit to correct a complete flawed professional document.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Dr. Rahman has asked for a short written summary comparing this quarter's numbers to last quarter's, before tomorrow's meeting. Arif drafts it quickly, in the same quick, spoken style he'd use in a chat message — contractions, short fragments, a comparison that isn't quite grammatical. It's readable. It just doesn't read like something meant for a General Manager. This lesson is also where the whole module comes together: before sending it, Arif corrects one full flawed document using everything Module 7 has covered.

Key Workplace Lesson

Comparing numbers or options is one of the most common things professional writing does — Q3 vs. Q2, this vendor vs. that one, this option vs. the alternative — and it has its own, fixed grammar: comparatives for two things, superlatives for three or more. Alongside that, formal written documents follow a few structural conventions that spoken and chat English don't: no contractions, and no sentence fragments standing in for complete sentences. Neither convention changes the meaning — both are about matching the register of the writing to its audience.

Listen & Read
A
Ms. Noor reads Arif's quick draft for Dr. Rahman, written in a spoken, informal style (❌).
Ms. Noor: Arif, this is for Dr. Rahman, right? "Didn't get the numbers yet. Waiting on finance." That reads like a chat message.
Arif: You're right — I wrote it the way I'd say it out loud, not the way I'd write it for him.
Ms. Noor: And further down — "Q3 was better than Q2" — better how? Give him the actual comparison.
B
Arif rewrites the summary in formal, complete sentences with a correct comparison (✅).
Arif: "We have not yet received the numbers. We are waiting on the finance team. Q3 revenue was higher than in Q2, primarily because of the new regional accounts."
Ms. Noor: That's exactly the tone this needs. Now, before you send it — go back through the whole update one more time and check it against everything we've covered this module.
Arif: Tenses, modals, passive voice, articles, relative clauses, and now comparatives. I'll go through it line by line.

Key Expressions

Expression Function Register
Q3 revenue was higher than in Q2. Compares two figures correctly Professional
This was our highest-revenue quarter this year. Compares three or more, correctly Professional
We have not yet received the figures. Formal, no contraction, complete sentence Formal

Vocabulary

No new vocabulary items in this lesson — it brings together the grammar points of the whole module instead.

Grammar in Context: Comparatives and Superlatives for Data (GIC-0017)

Structure: [Figure/Option A] + comparative adjective (-er / more ___) + than + [Figure/Option B] for two things. The + superlative adjective (-est / most ___) + of/in [group] for three or more.

Worked example:

"Q3 revenue was higher than in Q2." (two figures — comparative)

"This was our highest-revenue quarter this year." (compared against every quarter — superlative)

Grammar in Context: Formal Sentence Structure Conventions (GIC-0018)

Structure: In formal written documents, avoid contractions (write do not, not don't), and avoid sentence fragments — every sentence needs its own clear subject and verb.

Worked example:

❌ "Didn't get the numbers yet. Waiting on finance."

✅ "We have not yet received the numbers. We are waiting on the finance team."

Pattern: Data-Comparison Reporting Structure (PAT-0090)

Structure: [Metric A] was [comparative adjective] than [Metric B], primarily because [reason].

"Q3 revenue was higher than in Q2, primarily because of the new regional accounts." This pattern combines GIC-0017's comparative grammar with a clear, specific reason — turning a bare comparison into a useful one.

Common Mistake (MIS-0124)

Mistake: Writing a formal document in a spoken-register style — contractions and sentence fragments — which reads as unpolished for the document type, even when every fact in it is correct.

❌ "Didn't get the numbers yet. Waiting on finance."

✅ "We have not yet received the numbers. We are waiting on the finance team."

Why it matters: A reader forms an impression of how much care went into a document within the first few lines. Contractions and fragments are exactly the kind of spoken-register habits that signal "written quickly," even in an otherwise accurate report.

Professional Tone

Correct grammar has an unusual property: when it's right, the reader doesn't notice it at all — they just read the meaning. When it's wrong, it's the first thing they notice, sometimes before the meaning itself. That's exactly why this module exists: not to make writing sound more complicated, but to make the grammar invisible, so the reader's full attention goes to the content.

Industry Overlays

  • Banking: "This month's approval rate was higher than last month's, primarily because of the updated documentation checklist."
  • IT: "The new server handled more traffic than the old one, and it recorded our fastest response time this year."

Self-Check

  1. Compare two numbers from your own work using a correct comparative structure.
  2. Rewrite formally, removing the contraction and the fragment: "Can't confirm yet. Checking with the supplier."
  3. In one or two sentences, name the single grammar habit from this entire module (Lessons 7.1–7.5) that you personally need to watch for most in your own writing.

Module 7 Assessment

Correct the following flawed internal update before it is sent to Dr. Rahman. It contains at least one error from each of this module's six grammar areas: tense/aspect, modals/conditionals, passive voice/reported speech, articles/prepositions/agreement, relative clauses/gerunds- infinitives, and comparatives/formal structure.

"We have finished Phase 1 last week, but Phase 2 delay if we don't get sign-off soon. Hasan missed deadline because he didn't received the file on time. He said he needs it two days ago. I'm responsible of tracking the schedule, and the number of open items have gone up. We received a note from client. The note asked for extension. We decided postponing the review, and this month's delay was worse than last month, we're behind on almost everything."

Score 0–6, one point for each area corrected correctly (pass at 5): accurate tense/aspect use, an appropriately hedged conditional statement, correct passive voice and reported speech, correct articles/prepositions/agreement, at least one well-formed relative clause and correct gerund/infinitive choice, and a correct comparative with formal sentence structure (no contractions, no fragments).

Motivation

"Correct grammar is invisible when it's right and unmistakable when it's wrong."
lessons.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Recognition

In "Didn't get the numbers yet. Waiting on finance," identify the contraction and the sentence fragment, and explain why GIC-0018 flags both as informal for a formal document.

2. Rewriting

Module 7 Assessment: Correct the following internal update before it is sent to Dr. Rahman. It contains at least one error from each of this module's six grammar areas (tense/aspect; modals/conditionals; passive voice/reported speech; articles/prepositions/agreement; relative clauses/gerunds-infinitives; comparatives/formal structure). "We have finished Phase 1 last week, but Phase 2 delay if we don't get sign-off soon. Hasan missed deadline because he didn't received the file on time. He said he needs it two days ago. I'm responsible of tracking the schedule, and the number of open items have gone up. We received a note from client. The note asked for extension. We decided postponing the review, and this month's delay was worse than last month, we're behind on almost everything."

3. Guided Practice

Looking back across all six lessons in this module, name the one grammar area you personally find hardest to get right in your own writing, and write two correct sentences using it.

Answer Key

1.

Suggested answer: "Didn't" is a contraction (should be "did not"). Both sentences are fragments missing a clear subject (should be "We have not yet received the numbers. We are waiting on the finance team."). Contractions and fragments read as spoken-register, not formal writing.

2.

Suggested answer: "We finished Phase 1 last week, but Phase 2 could be delayed unless we get sign-off soon. Hasan missed the deadline because he did not receive the file on time. Two days ago, he said that he needed it. I am responsible for tracking the schedule, and the number of open items has gone up. We received a note from the client that asked for an extension. We decided to postpone the review, and this month's delay was worse than last month's — we are behind on almost everything." What to listen/look for: The correction fixes at least one error in each of the six grammar areas: an accurate tense/aspect choice, a hedged modal/conditional in place of the blunt claim, correct passive voice or reported speech with proper backshift, correct article/preposition/agreement, a correctly formed relative clause and correct gerund/infinitive choice, and a correct comparative in a complete, contraction-free sentence — avoiding MIS-0119 through MIS-0124.

3.

Answers will vary. Sample (articles): "I find articles hardest. — I've attached the report you asked for. A guest left a phone at the front desk." Check: one area named, two correct sentences that use it.

modules.title: Pronunciation & Confident Speaking
modules.purpose: Speak clearly and confidently: word and sentence stress, intonation and rhythm, linking sounds, commonly confused sounds, and speaking without filler words. The goal is clear, natural English, not an imitated accent.

lessons.title: Word Stress and Sentence Stress
lessons.objectives_html:
• Identify and produce correct word stress on common professional vocabulary.
  • Stress the right word in a sentence to convey the intended meaning.
lessons.body_html:
Lesson Opening

Ms. Noor overhears Arif reading a reservation note aloud: "The room is comfortABLE," he says, the stress climbing toward the end of the word. She doesn't correct his grammar, or his word choice — both are perfectly correct. She corrects the rhythm: "COM-fort-able," she says, stress landing hard on the very first beat. Same letters, same meaning, same speaker — but only one version reaches a listener's ear as an instantly familiar word. The other, technically understandable, makes the listener stop for a half-second to work it out. In English, where the stress falls is not a small detail. It is often the difference between being understood at once and being understood eventually.

Key Workplace Lesson

English is a stress-timed language. That means two things work together, and both matter for being understood quickly and sounding confident:

  1. Word stress — inside a word of two or more syllables, one syllable is said louder, longer, and usually higher in pitch than the others. Every English word has one correct place for this stress, and native listeners recognize words partly by their stress pattern, not just by their sounds. Move the stress, and even a perfectly pronounced word can become harder to catch.
  2. Sentence stress — inside a sentence, the words that carry the new or important information (usually nouns, main verbs, and key adjectives) are stressed, while small grammar words (a, the, is, to, and) are said quickly and lightly. Which word gets the sentence's main stress can actually change what the sentence means — not just how it sounds.

This is not about sounding like a native speaker or copying any particular accent. It is about being clear, natural, and easily understood — the goal for this entire module, and the one this course asks for everywhere: never a fake accent, always clarity.

Listen & Read
Word stress — correct (✅)
Ms. Noor modeling the correct stress pattern for Arif at the front desk.
Ms. Noor: COM-fort-a-ble. NEC-es-sa-ry. Stress on the first beat, both times.
Word stress — common mistake (❌)
Arif's original version, stress drifting later in the word.
Arif: com-fort-A-ble... nec-es-SA-ry?
Ms. Noor: Close — but try landing on the very first syllable instead. Listen again.
Version 1 — stress on I
Arif explaining a mix-up to Ms. Noor.
Arif: I didn't say she took it.
Meaning: someone else said it, not me.
Version 2 — stress on didn't
Same line, stress moved.
Arif: I DIDN'T say she took it.
Meaning: I never said that at all.
Version 3 — stress on say
Same line, stress moved again.
Arif: I didn't SAY she took it.
Meaning: I didn't say it outright, only implied it.
Version 4 — stress on she
Same line, stress moved again.
Arif: I didn't say SHE took it.
Meaning: I said someone else took it, not her.
Version 5 — stress on took
Same line, stress moved again.
Arif: I didn't say she TOOK it.
Meaning: I said she did something else with it, not "took."

Key Expressions / Model Sentences (marked for stress)

Capital letters mark the stressed syllable.

Word Correct stress Say it like
comfortable first syllable COM-fort-a-ble
necessary first syllable NEC-es-sa-ry
management first syllable MAN-age-ment
available second syllable a-VAIL-a-ble
important second syllable im-POR-tant
develop second syllable de-VEL-op

Some professional words change their stress depending on whether they're a noun or a verb — useful to know, because both spellings look identical:

Word As a noun As a verb
record REC-ord (a written record) re-CORD (to record something)
project PROJ-ect (a work project) pro-JECT (to project figures forward)

Vocabulary

  • word stress (V-0549) — the one syllable in a multi-syllable word that is said louder, longer, and higher in pitch than the rest. "Word stress is what makes 'comfortable' sound instantly familiar or slightly harder to catch."
  • sentence stress (V-0550) — the word or words in a sentence that carry its main meaning, said with more emphasis than the surrounding grammar words. "Sentence stress can change what a sentence actually means, even when every word stays the same."
  • syllable (V-0551) — one beat of sound in a word; "comfortable" has four syllables when said carefully (com-fort-a-ble), and in everyday speech often three (COMF-ta-ble) — the stress stays on the first. "Necessary has four syllables, and the stress belongs on the very first one."

Grammar in Context: Content-Word Stress Pattern (PAT-0098)
