Levels 1 and 2 tested one module's skill at a time, in short, discrete items, because at that stage each skill was still worth isolating. Level 5 doesn't work that way, and testing it as if it did would miss the actual point of the level: a real leader never delegates or gives feedback — they do both in the same morning huddle. A real leader never only chairs a meeting — they chair it, decide it, and then explain the decision to someone who wasn't there. So this assessment is three substantial, combined scenarios, not eight small ones. Each part is scored on four criteria, explained under Scoring below.

Sit this assessment first. It checks that each of the combined skills below is solid on its own terms before the capstone, "The Handover," chains all eight of Level 5's modules into a single continuous week.

Part A — Delegation and feedback, back to back

Setting: It's Monday morning. Arif is running the front-office huddle before Thursday's corporate group arrives, and two things need to happen before the huddle ends.

Rima has helped with VIP welcome folders before (Module 1), but she has never run the full welcome-packet and room-upgrade routine for a corporate group on her own. She needs to leave this huddle owning the welcome packets and room-upgrade list for Thursday — not a checklist to follow, but a task that's genuinely hers. At the same time, Farhan caught a billing discrepancy last week before it reached a guest, and Arif hasn't told him yet, specifically, that this is exactly the kind of judgment call he wants to see more of.

Your task: Play both moments in the same huddle, one immediately after the other.

  1. Delegate the welcome-packet and room-upgrade task to Rima. Calibrate the level of detail to her experience with this specific task (more than you'd give Hasan, who has done it many times) — and hand her real ownership of the outcome, not a checklist to follow.
  2. Turn to Farhan and give him specific, immediate feedback on the billing catch — naming the exact action and why it mattered, not a general "good job."

There is no single correct wording for either part. It is scored with the criteria below, not matched against a model answer.

Part B — Chairing a contested decision

Setting: The corporate group has just departed, straight into a public holiday weekend. Hasan and Rima disagree about how to staff it: Hasan wants the usual senior-heavy roster, arguing it's safer with a smaller, less experienced weekend team; Rima wants a leaner roster, arguing the group is gone, the property will be quiet, and the team has earned the comp time. Both have a real point, and the roster has to be posted today.

Your task:

  1. Chair a short meeting between Hasan and Rima. Open it, invite both to make their case fully, and don't let it drift without a decision.
  2. Make the call yourself, and say openly that it isn't unanimous — don't dress the decision up as something everyone agreed to.
  3. Separately, communicate that decision to Farhan, who wasn't in the room and needs to execute the roster accurately starting tomorrow.

Part C — A career-growth conversation, combined

Setting: This part is about you, not a character — the same way Module 7's own assessment asked you to speak as yourself. Think of a real or realistic professional context of your own.

Your task: In one continuous conversation with a manager (real, imagined, or role-played by a partner), do all of the following in order:

  1. Ask for honest feedback on your recent performance.
  2. Build an evidence-based case for taking on more responsibility — a promotion, a new project, a larger role — using specific, verifiable examples rather than general self-praise.
  3. If the conversation turns to compensation, discuss it without underselling yourself (silently accepting whatever is offered) or overreaching (making an unsupported demand) — anchor it in the value you've actually delivered.

This is the "combined" item: Module 7 taught feedback-seeking, promotion cases, and compensation discussions as related but separate conversations. Here, they happen in one sitting, the way they often genuinely do.

Scoring

Each part is scored on four criteria, 0–3 each (0 = not shown, 1 = partly, 2 = mostly, 3 = fully), so each part is worth 12 points. Watch or read back each part once in full before scoring.

PartCriteria (0–3 each)
A — Delegation and feedback(1) Detail is calibrated to Rima's experience with this task. (2) Real ownership of the outcome is handed over, with the deadline and what done looks like. (3) Feedback to Farhan names the exact action and its impact. (4) Register shifts between the two moments while the voice stays the same.
B — Chairing a contested decision(1) The meeting opens with the outcome needed, and both sides are heard fully. (2) A clear decision is made, with its reasoning, and named as not unanimous. (3) The version given to Farhan matches the decision, with reasoning and next steps, without reopening the debate. (4) Calm, fair, firm tone throughout.
C — Career-growth conversation(1) A genuine, specific request for feedback. (2) A case for more responsibility built on specific, checkable evidence. (3) Compensation discussed without underselling or overreaching, anchored in delivered value. (4) Confident, respectful register with a manager, in your own voice.

Maximum: Part A 12 + Part B 12 + Part C 12 = 36 points.

Passing this assessment

"Three parts, one leadership voice — by the time you sit this, it isn't a test you're cramming for. It's a demonstration of who you already are at work."

Pass mark: 25 of 36 (70%), with at least 6 of 12 in every part. If a part scores below 8, revisit the modules it draws on before the capstone.

Nothing in Parts A-C is new. Every scenario recombines language and formulas Level 5 has already taught — delegation and feedback from Modules 1–2, chairing and deciding from Module 5, and self-advocacy from Module 7. If any one part feels shaky, that module is worth a quick revisit before moving on — but there is nothing new to prepare. Next is "The Handover," where all eight modules run together as one connected week.
assessment.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Role-Play Assessment

Part A — Monday morning huddle before Thursday's corporate group arrives. First, delegate the VIP welcome-packet and room-upgrade task to Rima, who has never run this routine solo before — calibrate your instruction detail to her experience and hand her genuine ownership rather than a step-by-step checklist. Immediately after, turn to Farhan and give him specific, immediate feedback on catching last week's billing discrepancy before it reached the guest — name the exact action and why it mattered, not a general "good job."

2. Role-Play Assessment

Part B — Hasan and Rima disagree about weekend staffing once the corporate group departs into a public holiday: Hasan wants the usual senior-heavy roster for safety, Rima wants a leaner roster to bank comp time. Chair a short meeting: open it, let both make their case fully, then make the call yourself and say openly that it isn't unanimous. Afterward, separately communicate that decision to Farhan, who wasn't in the room and needs to execute the roster accurately.

3. Role-Play Assessment

Part C — Speaking as yourself, not a character, in one continuous conversation with a manager (real, imagined, or role-played by a partner): ask for honest feedback on your recent performance, then build an evidence-based case for taking on more responsibility using specific, verifiable examples rather than general self-praise, and, if compensation comes up, discuss it without underselling yourself or overreaching.

Answer Key

1.

Sample: "Rima, I'd like you to own the welcome packets and the room-upgrade list for Thursday's group. You've done the VIP folders, so you know the standard — this time it's forty guests, and the upgrade list has to match the client's seniority list, which I'll send you. I need a draft by Wednesday noon; done looks like every packet labeled and the list checked against the rooming list. Come to me with anything you're unsure about. … Farhan — quick note while it's fresh: last week you spotted the double charge on Mr. Alam's bill before he checked out. That saved us a complaint and a refund. That's exactly the kind of check I want to see more of." Score 0–3 on each of Part A's four criteria (12 points). What to listen/look for: Delegation is calibrated to Rima's actual experience level and transfers real ownership, not just a list of steps. Feedback to Farhan is specific, names the concrete action and its impact, and is delivered without delay or hedging. Register shifts appropriately between the two moments while still sounding like the same person.

2.

Sample (key moments): "What I need us to walk away with is a posted roster by two o'clock. … I hear both sides of this. Here's the call I'm making: a senior person on every shift, but one fewer person on Sunday and Monday nights. I recognize this isn't unanimous." To Farhan: "We've decided to keep one senior on every shift and drop one person on Sunday and Monday nights. The reasoning is that it covers the risk without overstaffing a quiet weekend. I know it wasn't everyone's first choice; here's what I need from you: post the roster and confirm the night swaps by six." Score 0–3 on each of Part B's four criteria (12 points). What to listen/look for: Opens the meeting clearly, gives both Hasan and Rima a genuine hearing, and reaches an actual decision rather than deferring or dodging it. States the decision and reasoning plainly, including that it wasn't unanimous. The version communicated to Farhan afterward matches what was decided in the room, without editorializing.

3.

Score 0–3 on each of Part C's four criteria (12 points). What to listen/look for: Feedback request is genuine, not rhetorical. The case for more responsibility is built on specific, checkable evidence rather than general self-praise or entitlement. Any compensation discussion is anchored in value actually delivered, avoiding both silent acceptance and an unsupported demand.

capstone.title: The Handover
capstone.objectives_html:
• Carry one connected leadership arc — delegating, giving feedback, coaching, announcing change, chairing a decision, presenting under scrutiny, and having a career-growth conversation — across a single continuous week, without a script.
  • Sustain one authentic, recognizable communication voice through every register the course has taught, from a quiet one-on-one to a senior leadership briefing.
  • Self-assess a full leadership performance against a weighted leadership rubric, and reflect on the entire five-level journey this capstone closes.
capstone.body_html:
About this capstone

On Friday afternoon, Ms. Fatima Noor calls Arif into her office. Starting Monday, she's away for three weeks on a regional Leadership Development Programme — and she wants Arif to cover the parts of her own Department Head role that can't simply wait: chairing the weekly cross-department meeting, presenting the front-office numbers to Dr. Rahman, and being the person the team escalates to when something needs a decision she isn't there to make.

That's the handover this capstone is named for — but it's really two handovers, not one. Ms. Noor is handing part of her role to Arif. To make room for it, Arif has to hand more of his own daily work to his team: delegating further than he ever has, trusting Rima and Hasan with real ownership, and making time to think about who's ready to grow into more themselves. One week, two directions of trust, and every tool this entire course has built, all needed at once.

This is not a new lesson, and it isn't Module 8 Lesson 4's "A Week as a Leader" repeated with new names — that lesson was the rehearsal. This is the performance, and it's longer: eight connected steps instead of six, set against a real reason those eight things all have to happen in the same week, and closing not just Level 5 but the whole five-level Career English course. Nothing below is new material. The only new thing is doing all of it, in sequence, in your own voice, under real pressure — which is, in the end, the entire point of everything this book has taught.

How it's used: read or perform the eight steps in order, then self-assess using the rubric that follows — with the rows adapted to Level 5 — and then perform the same eight steps yourself, as a full role-play, alone or with a partner. The goal isn't to recognize the right answer. It's to produce your own version of each step, in your own words, the way a real week actually demands.

The simulation: the first week of the handover

It's Monday morning. Ms. Noor left for the programme over the weekend. For the next three weeks, part of her job is Arif's — starting now.

Step 1 — Delegate to two team members at different experience levels (Module 1)

Before Arif can take on anything of Ms. Noor's, he needs more off his own desk. He calls Rima and Hasan over separately, in the same morning, and hands each of them something real — calibrated very differently, because they aren't at the same point in their own growth.

Listen & Read
Monday, 8:45 AM, the front desk. Ms. Noor left for the leadership programme over the weekend. Arif speaks to Rima first, then Hasan, a few minutes apart.
Arif: Rima, I need you to take full ownership of VIP-arrival coordination this week — not just Thursday's group, all of it. Here's how I'd break it down: confirm the arrivals list each morning, prep the welcome packets by 2 PM, and flag anything unusual to me before it becomes a problem, not after. Sound manageable?
Rima: I think so — can I check the "flag anything unusual" part with you once, the first time it comes up, just so I know where the line is?
Arif: Absolutely — that's exactly the kind of question I want. After that, trust your judgment.
Arif: Hasan — with me covering more of Ms. Noor's side for the next three weeks, I need someone to own the full front-desk roster, not just draft it for my sign-off. Run it, adjust it, only bring me the ones you genuinely can't resolve yourself.
Hasan: Finally. I've had opinions about that roster for two years.
Arif: I know you have. Use them.

Notice what's different between the two: Rima gets more structure because the VIP-arrival coordination is still new to her solo; Hasan gets almost none, because after this many months running the roster, structure would only get in his way. Same delegation skill, two calibrations — exactly what Module 1 built.

Step 2 — Feedback, then a formal conversation about slipping work (Module 2)

Not every delegation story ends well immediately. Farhan's shift-handover notes for the new booking system have started arriving late, with small details missing each time — out of character for someone who, not long ago, caught a billing error nobody else noticed. Arif mentions it lightly the first time. When it happens again, lightly isn't enough anymore.

Listen & Read
Monday afternoon, a quiet word by the printer. Wednesday morning, a scheduled ten minutes in the back office.
Arif: Farhan — I noticed the handover log ran late again this morning. Everything okay? Just flagging it before it becomes a pattern.
Farhan: Yeah, sorry — it's been a rough couple of mornings. I'll tighten it up.
Arif: Farhan, thanks for making time. Let's talk about the handover logs this week.
Farhan: I know — three late ones, and I still owe you Tuesday's missing detail.
Arif: Right. And I want to say plainly — this isn't like you. A few weeks ago, you caught a billing error nobody else noticed. That's not a coincidence; that's your actual standard. So I want to understand what's changed this week, not just fix the log.
Farhan: Honestly, I've been covering the late checkout rush alone since Priyanka left, and the handover's the thing I rush at the end.
Arif: That's useful to know, and it's on me too — I hadn't connected those. Here's what I want: the handover log filled in as you go, not saved for the end of shift, starting tomorrow. And I'll ask Hasan to build you ten minutes of coverage during the checkout rush this week. Can you commit to your side of that?
Farhan: Yes — and thank you for asking what changed instead of just telling me to fix it.

Step 3 — Coach a colleague through a problem they own (Module 3)

Rima comes to Arif with something that isn't really about the VIP-arrival task at all. A long-staying guest keeps asking her, personally, for late-checkout exceptions beyond policy, and she doesn't know whether to keep granting them or start saying no. In three weeks, she won't always have Arif two steps away to ask. Today's the day that starts to matter.

Listen & Read
Tuesday, late morning, a quiet corner of the lobby.
Rima: Can I ask you about something that isn't really the VIP list? Mr. Chowdhury in 412 has asked me for a late checkout three times this stay — past the 1 PM cutoff, and I keep saying yes because he's a loyal guest, but I don't know if I'm setting a bad precedent.
Arif: What do you think would happen if you said no to a fourth request?
Rima: Honestly? Probably nothing dramatic. He might be a little annoyed, but he'd still come back next quarter — he always does.
Arif: And what's actually worrying you about saying no, then, if it's not really about him?
Rima: I think I'm worried it looks like I'm being difficult, or that I don't understand how VIP guests are supposed to be treated.
Arif: Is there a version of "no" that still treats him like a VIP guest?
Rima: ...Yes, actually — I could offer him a guaranteed late checkout on his next visit if he books it in advance, instead of an open-ended exception every time.
Arif: That sounds like your answer, not mine. Go with it.

Step 4 — Announce a change and address resistance to it (Module 4)

While covering for Ms. Noor, Arif also has to keep her projects moving — including one she'd planned to announce herself. Headquarters wants to see real front-office data from the mobile check-in pilot (the first step in the self-check-in plan Arif presented in Module 6) before the leadership programme ends, which means launching it two weeks earlier than the team had been told to expect. Hasan, mid-delegated roster and all, is the first to push back.

Listen & Read
Wednesday morning, the full front-office team gathered before shift start.
Arif: One change to flag before we start. Mobile check-in is launching two weeks earlier than we'd planned — this Friday, not the original date. Headquarters wants real front-office data before Ms. Noor's programme ends, and this property is the one they're watching.
Hasan: Friday? That's the same week I'm still settling the new roster in. Two big changes landing at once is going to be rough on everyone, not just me.
Arif: That's a fair concern, and I don't want to pretend the timing's ideal — it isn't. Here's the honest reasoning: if the pilot data isn't in Ms. Noor's report, the whole rollout could slip to next quarter, and everyone's been asking for mobile check-in since the double-booking problems started. What would make Friday genuinely workable for you?
Hasan: If we staff the launch weekend properly — not just hope it goes smoothly — I think it's manageable.
Arif: Agreed. Let's settle the launch-weekend staffing this afternoon, with you and Rima both in the room.

Step 5 — Chair a meeting with a contested decision and communicate it afterward (Module 5)

The earlier pilot launch means the first week of mobile check-in overlaps with reduced weekend staffing. Hasan and Rima disagree, again, about how to cover it — and this time it's Arif's decision to make and announce, with Ms. Noor unreachable and the pilot's start date already fixed.

Listen & Read
Wednesday afternoon, the back office. Hasan and Rima, following Step 4's earlier pilot launch. Farhan is not present.
Arif: Quick decision before Friday: how do we staff mobile check-in's launch weekend. Hasan, you first.
Hasan: Senior-heavy roster, full stop. New system, guests who've never used it, and I don't want a trainee alone at the desk when it breaks the first time — because it will.
Rima: I get that, but a fully senior roster this weekend means overtime we didn't budget, and three of us have already banked the comp time from the corporate group. A mixed roster with one senior lead per shift covers the risk without burning everyone out.
Arif: I hear both sides of this — both are real concerns. Here's the call I'm making: for this one weekend, one senior person paired with one newer person on every shift. That's not the fully senior roster Hasan wants, but never a trainee alone either. I recognize this isn't unanimous. Rima, I know it's more cautious than your first choice.
Rima: Understood. I'll still say I think we're overcautious, but I can work with it.
Arif: Noted, and that's fair to say. Let's revisit staffing again after this first weekend's actual data comes in.
Arif: Farhan — for the mobile check-in launch, Friday through Sunday, every shift is one senior person paired with one newer person. The reasoning is that it covers the risk of a brand-new system without the overtime of a fully senior roster. Hasan and Rima didn't fully agree, but that's the call, and it's for this one weekend only. Here's what I need from you: brief the newer staff on who they're paired with — Hasan is posting the roster tonight.
Farhan: Got it — senior-paired shifts, launch weekend only. I'll brief the newer staff today.

Step 6 — Present to senior leadership and hold a hard question under scrutiny (Module 6)

Thursday, the department-head briefing Ms. Noor would normally run. Arif takes her seat for the first time, presenting the front-office numbers and the mobile check-in pilot's launch plan directly to Dr. Rahman — who, true to form, doesn't let anything pass without a real question.

Listen & Read
Thursday, 10 AM, the department-head briefing. Arif is in Ms. Noor's usual seat. Dr. Rahman is present.
Arif: The bottom line is mobile check-in launches Friday, two weeks ahead of the original date, so we'd have real data before Ms. Noor's programme ends. Front-office volume is steady this month, and the launch-weekend roster is covered with a senior-paired staffing model to manage the transition risk.
Dr. Rahman: Two weeks earlier is a meaningful acceleration. What did it cost you to get there, and who absorbed that cost?
Arif: A fair question. It cost the team a roster change with less lead time than I'd have liked — Hasan and Rima disagreed on how to staff the launch weekend, and I made the call to go with the more cautious, senior-paired option rather than the leaner one Rima proposed, specifically to protect against a rough first weekend with a brand-new system. If the data comes back clean, I'd expect us to ease back toward a leaner roster the following week.
Dr. Rahman: And if the data doesn't come back clean?
Arif: Then we hold the senior-paired model longer and I report that honestly in the next briefing — I'd rather bring you an accurate picture two weeks early than a polished one on the original schedule.
Dr. Rahman: That's the right instinct. Keep me posted either way.

Step 7 — A private career-growth conversation with a team member (Module 7)

Everything this week has made one thing obvious to Arif: he can't keep covering two roles alone for three weeks without someone ready to take on more of his own. That evening, he sits down with Rima — not to delegate another task, but to talk, honestly, about where she might be headed next.

Listen & Read
Thursday evening, after the briefing, Arif's small office.
Arif: Rima, I wanted to talk to you about something that isn't a task. This week alone, you've owned VIP-arrival coordination end to end, and you talked yourself through the Chowdhury situation without needing me to solve it for you. That's not "doing well at your job" — that's the actual judgment a Guest Relations Lead role would need.
Rima: I didn't realize that role was something that existed here yet.
Arif: It doesn't formally, yet — which is exactly why I wanted to raise it with you before it's posted anywhere. I'd want to build the case for it using specifics like this week, not just "Rima's ready." Would you want that conversation to go further?
Rima: Yes — and can I ask, if it happens, whether there's a compensation conversation attached to it, not just a new title?
Arif: That's exactly the right question to ask, and yes — I wouldn't bring you a title without the conversation that goes with it. Let's build the actual case together over the next few weeks.

Step 8 — Close by reflecting on leading with an authentic personal voice (Module 8)

That Friday, just before she left for the programme, Ms. Noor had sent Arif one plain question: how are you feeling about all this? Now it's Sunday evening, the launch weekend behind him, and this is where the week — and the whole course — closes: not with a performance of leadership, but with Arif answering honestly, in the same voice he's used since Level 1's first, nervous "good morning."

Listen & Read
Sunday evening, the end of Arif's first week covering for Ms. Noor. She had sent him one plain question by message that Friday, just before she left for the programme; this is his answer, delivered once the launch weekend is behind him.
Ms. Fatima Noor (message, sent Friday): One honest question before I go quiet for three weeks — how are you feeling about all this?
Arif (message, sent Sunday): Honestly? Nervous on Monday, less so by Friday. I delegated more than I ever have, had a hard conversation with Farhan that turned out better than I expected, made a staffing call Rima still disagrees with, and got a real question from Dr. Rahman I didn't dodge. None of it felt like performing "leadership" — it just felt like doing my actual job, at a slightly bigger size than usual. I think that's the point.
Ms. Fatima Noor (message): That is the point. See you in three weeks — and Arif, this is exactly why I picked you.

Why this counts as "Level 5 complete"

Look back at what just happened: eight situations, six named people, four different audiences (a newer colleague, experienced peers, a struggling colleague and a General Manager), one genuinely slipping performance, one real disagreement, one hard question under real scrutiny, and one conversation about somebody else's future instead of Arif's own. Nothing here was easy, and nothing here was scripted — Arif calibrated, corrected, coached, explained, decided, presented, invested in someone else, and reflected, all inside one week, without once stopping to sound like a different person for a different room. That is the actual target of Level 5: not five separate leadership techniques performed well, but one recognizable person using all five, under real pressure, without the seams showing.

Why this counts as "Career English complete"

Pull the lens back further, and this week is also the answer to the question this whole course opened with, back in Level 1: I have a job. What English do I need to survive, communicate, solve problems, work with people, and eventually lead? Every piece of that question has just been answered in one connected story. Arif greeted a stranger at a front gate in Level 1 and, five levels later, briefed a room the General Manager sat in. He once asked a clarifying question because he was afraid to guess wrong; here, he coached someone else through the exact same fear. He once received an instruction he didn't fully understand; here, he delegated one, calibrated carefully, to two different people at once. None of that happened because a new grammar rule was learned this week. It happened because a hundred and eighty-six lessons' worth of ordinary, repeated, recombined English finally became something closer to instinct than study — which was always the actual finish line, not fluency for its own sake, but a working professional life conducted, comfortably, in English.

Self-assessment rubric

It uses the same weighted 0–4 format as the earlier capstones, with rows adapted to Level 5; every row applies, because the week includes delegation, feedback, a contested decision, a briefing and a career conversation.

Score area Weight What "good" looks like
Delegation calibration 15% Instruction detail matches the person's actual experience, and real ownership is transferred — not just a task handed off.
Feedback specificity 15% Feedback names the exact action and its impact, delivered promptly, without vague praise or vague criticism.
Meeting composure 15% Chairs the room fairly, genuinely hears both sides, and still reaches a decision rather than deferring it.
Decision communication 10% States the decision and its reasoning plainly to someone who wasn't in the room, without editorializing or hedging.
Evidence-based framing 15% The career-growth conversation and the leadership briefing both rest on specific, verifiable evidence, not general impressions.
Composure on compensation 10% Neither silently accepts nor overreaches when the conversation touches responsibility, scope, or reward — anchors it in value actually delivered.
Authentic voice 10% The communication style sounds like one consistent person across all eight steps, not a performance of "leadership."
Professional register 10% Tone is calibrated correctly to each audience in turn — a newer colleague, a peer in disagreement, a struggling colleague, and a General Manager.

How to score it: give each row a mark from 0 to 4 (0 = not shown, 1 = rarely, 2 = sometimes, 3 = mostly, 4 = consistently). Multiply by the row's weight and divide by 4 — for example, 3 for Delegation calibration gives 15 × 3 ÷ 4 ≈ 11 points. Add the rows for a total out of 100. 70 or more: Level 5 — and the course — complete. Below 70: repeat the steps that use the modules behind your lowest rows, then perform the whole week again.

Score the whole performance, not each step separately. Someone who fumbles a word in Step 1 but genuinely holds their own under Dr. Rahman's question in Step 6 is doing better, overall, than one who never stumbles but sounds like a different person in every room — because Step 6 is closer to what real leadership actually demands.

Practice

  1. Full role-play (the actual capstone task): Perform all eight steps in one continuous sequence, with a partner taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded separately and played back in order. Don't read from this page while performing — glance at each step's setting, then produce the conversation yourself, in your own words.
  2. Self-score: Immediately afterward, score your own performance against the rubric above. Be honest rather than generous — the rubric exists to show you where to focus next, not to make you feel good about a finished course.
  3. Written reflection: In 4–5 sentences, describe which of the eight steps felt hardest, and why. Was it a language problem (not having the right phrase ready) or a composure problem (having the phrase, but hesitating to use it under real pressure)? Five levels in, the honest answer is very often the second one — and the fix for that is practice, not more vocabulary.
  4. Repeat once: Perform the full eight steps a second time, focusing only on whichever rubric row scored lowest the first time.

Self-check

  1. In Step 1, what specifically changes between how Arif delegates to Rima and how he delegates to Hasan — and why is that difference itself the point, not a flaw in either version?
  2. In Step 2, why does Arif comment lightly the first time and hold a formal conversation only the second time, rather than escalating immediately?
  3. In Step 5, what does Arif do differently when communicating the decision to Farhan afterward, compared to how the decision was actually made in the room with Hasan and Rima?
  4. Look back at Step 8. Why does the capstone end with a private, honest answer to a simple question, rather than a polished closing speech?
  5. Across the whole five-level course, name one specific moment — from any level — that this capstone's Arif could not have handled the way he does here, if that earlier lesson hadn't happened first.

You've completed Career English

"Five levels ago, you rehearsed how to say good morning to a stranger at a front gate. Today, you chaired a room, corrected a slipping performance without flinching, and handed someone else the exact kind of trust you were once given. The book ends here. The career doesn't."

That's the real marker of finishing this course: not that every sentence across five levels was perfect, but that a genuinely difficult professional week — delegation, honest feedback, real coaching, a change nobody asked for, a decision not everyone agreed with, a hard question in front of a General Manager, and a private conversation about somebody else's future — happened entirely in English, in one recognizable voice, and it held together. Arif started this book as a nervous new employee who wasn't sure how to introduce himself. He finishes it covering for the person who once managed him, trusted by name, in his own words, the whole way through. Wherever you are in your own career, that arc is the one this entire book was built to hand you.
capstone.practice_html:
Exercises

1. Role-Play Assessment

Level 5 capstone task, "The Handover." Perform all eight steps in one continuous sequence — with a partner taking every other role, or alone with each part recorded and played back in order. Do not read from the page; produce each line yourself from the setting description alone: (1) delegate to two team members at different experience levels; (2) give ongoing feedback, then hold a formal performance conversation with someone whose work has slipped; (3) coach a colleague through a problem they own, using questions rather than answers; (4) announce a change and address resistance to it; (5) chair a meeting with a contested decision and communicate it afterward; (6) present to senior leadership and hold a hard question under scrutiny; (7) have a private career-growth conversation with a team member; (8) close by reflecting, in your own voice, on what it means to lead.

2. Short Answer

Look back across the whole five-level course, not just this capstone. Describe, in 4–6 sentences, the single biggest difference between how you'd have handled a difficult workplace conversation before starting Level 1 and how you'd handle one now. Be specific about what changed — vocabulary, confidence, structure, or something else.

3. Guided Practice
